A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington D.C.
The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to the New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.
The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across the academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences, to present new research and network with colleagues, may be too risky under a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.
“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students visa to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, who similarly had a staff member of hers detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of conferences have reported smaller attendance at conferences in the U.S. over the past two years, and some have considered the prospect of hosting in other countries.
ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”
Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained, either. Most notably, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.
“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”
Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. While only a third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.
“I think it speaks to how exceptional of a researcher Eva is that she can work on projects that really span multiple disciplines, that require that she go and learn the foundations, not just of AI and machine learning, and not just computational models of the brain, but also understanding how do you run the experiment on the mice. She’s in the lab actually doing the surgery on the mice, gathering the data from the mice, analyzing those data, and running the AI experiments,” said Benjamin Eysenbach, a computer scientist at Princeton and one of Xie’s three advisers.
As an example of the respect she commands among peers, he cited a workshop she convened at last year’s NeurIPS conference, one of the premiere machine learning conferences. Not only did she present research of her own, but she brought together leaders in AI and in neuroscience to see how the two could collaborate.
It was an opportunity both to “introduce these important questions about the brain to folks in AI that might be equipped with new methods, and to help folks working on neuroscience questions define what are the right AI tools,” Eysenbach said.
Krithik Ramesh, a fellow researcher, is among those who has benefitted from her guidance. The two had overlapped at science fair competitions throughout high school, and when he was considering transferring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie had completed her undergraduate degree, he turned to her for counsel. He learned about Xie’s detainment after a friend saw a post on social media. His immediate reaction was disbelief, followed by a sense of unmooring as a fellow researcher.
“We academics exist for the benefit of the public,” he said. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people. That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.”

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.
In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.
Younger women and girls aged 15 to 19 had even less power to say no, compared with older women aged 45 to 49, according to analysis in the report of eight countries with comparable data (Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kazakhstan, Malawi, Mali, Nigeria, Tajikistan and Zambia). The findings align with research showing adolescent girls endure very high rates of intimate partner violence.
“These are really sad figures,” said Jean-Paul Murunga, a lawyer with the global human rights organisation Equality Now. “Especially given that the continent of Africa as a whole has adopted the Maputo protocol, which sets [binding legal standards for] equality between women and men. We still have a lot of work to do to ensure women and girls benefit from these commitments.”
The Maputo protocol, a landmark treaty adopted by the African Union in 2003, guarantees women’s rights and obliges states to protect women from violence. It affirms that marriage must be based on full consent and guarantees women’s right to health.
“The underlying principle is unambiguous: sexual intercourse without free and voluntary consent constitutes sexual violence, including within marriage,” said Murunga. “Marriage does not create perpetual or implied consent. A woman retains the right to decide whether, when and how she engages in sexual activity”.
He said that as a first step rape laws across the continent needed to change. According to Murunga’s 2024 report, rape within marriage is not criminalised in some African countries. Seven countries expressly exempt husbands from prosecution for marital rape, including Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia and South Sudan. Some countries, such as Tanzania and Eritrea, only criminalise marital rape when the couple do not live together.
In countries where child marriage is permitted and marital rape is not criminalised, children are left unprotected. A legal loophole is created for what, outside marriage, would be classed as rape, and young wives have few options when it comes to protecting themselves from sexual violence and exploitation. In Gabon, for example, when a man has married a child he abducted, he can only be prosecuted after the marriage is annulled.
Underpinning these laws is the mistaken belief that marital rape does not exist as a concept because, by marrying, wives are assumed to have permanently consented to sex with their husbands. In many areas, religion plays a key role in affirming these beliefs.
Alimatu Dimonekene, founder of A Girl At A Time, an organisation supporting adolescent girls in Sierra Leone, said a conversation around consent in marriage had yet to begin in Africa. “We’ve not even started the conversation [around marital rape],” she said. “Women will never call it rape; they make excuses for it or even blame themselves.”
She added: “In west Africa, sex is seen as an obligation in marriage. You must do whatever your husband demands.
“Once he has paid your bride price [a traditional marriage custom in which the bride’s family are paid money, livestock or goods by the groom], he owns you and you cannot reject his demands. Whatever he wants, he gets, including in terms of intimacy, finances and raising the children.”

It had been 16 months since Akash Deep last played a Test, much of that time spent recovering from a lower-back stress fracture. While he had made an impact on the opening day of the Wellington Test, dismissing Rachin Ravindra caught behind, it was the delivery that breached Glenn Phillips’ defence and knocked back the top of off stump on Friday that offered a glimpse of what India had been missing.
The dismissal was not merely a product of pace or movement. Akash had cleverly manipulated the crease to create an angle that unsettled Phillips, who had just completed a century and looked set to take New Zealand further out of India’s reach.
“The ball wasn’t moving much. I wasn’t getting any help off the wicket, so I made the batsman play by using angles. I wanted him to play, so I went wide, made him play, and then I bowled one from close to the stumps to play with the batsman’s mind,” Akash explained. “To put the ball from an angle, he came forward to play.”
The execution was as impressive as the idea. Having drawn Phillips forward with deliveries from wider on the crease, Akash changed his angle and attacked the stumps. The right-hander’s defence was breached, and the top of off was knocked back.
For Akash, however, the wicket also marked a personal milestone after a prolonged rehabilitation. Returning to international cricket following a serious back injury is rarely straightforward for a fast bowler, but he credited head coach Gautam Gambhir with helping him through the difficult period.
“It is very difficult to get injured and make a comeback as a fast bowler. It is very challenging, but it made me feel good that our coach, GG sir, used to follow up with me constantly and ask me how my rehab was going, what was going on, and how I had to get stronger,” he said.
Phillips’ dismissal was a reminder that Akash had returned with more than just his fitness. His craft, too, remained intact.

Srinagar- The High Court of J&K and Ladakh on Friday quashed the preventive detention orders of two persons booked under the Public Safety Act (PSA), observing that vague and non-specific allegations violate constitutional safeguards and deprive detainees of their right to make an effective representation against their detention.
A bench of Justice Sanjay Dhar passed separate judgments in the petitions filed by Rashid Bashir Pir and Anayatullah Wani, challenging their detention orders issued by the District Magistrates of Kupwara and Shopian respectively in April and May 2025.
In the case of Pir, the Court quashed the detention order dated May 3, 2025, observing that the grounds of detention contained vague allegations without specifying the details of the alleged subversive activities or the period during which he had allegedly indulged in such activities.
The Court noted that the grounds referred to phrases such as “recent reports received from sister agencies” and alleged involvement in activities inimical to the security of Jammu and Kashmir, without furnishing material particulars.
The court observed that the detainee could not have made an effective representation against his detention in the absence of specific details.
Referring to Article 22(5) of the Constitution, the Court said every ground of detention must be individually specified to ensure transparency and accountability, adding that vague, indefinite or general allegations make it impossible for a detenue to understand the reasons for his detention and effectively challenge the same.
The Court also referred to a Division Bench judgment in Imran Rashid Rather vs UT of J&K, which held that vague and non-specific grounds of detention violate the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution besides depriving detenues of an opportunity to offer a specific rebuttal.
Separately, the Court quashed the detention order dated April 28, 2025, issued by the District Magistrate, Shopian, against Wani.
The Court observed that the grounds of detention did not disclose the particulars of the places or the identities of the subversive elements to whom Wani was allegedly providing logistic support.
It further noted that the period during which the alleged logistic support was provided, as well as details of the alleged anti-national activities, had not been specified.
Holding that the allegations were vague and lacked material particulars, the court said the detainee had been prevented from making an effective representation, resulting in a violation of the constitutional guarantees under Article 22(5).
Allowing both petitions, the Court quashed the respective detention orders and directed the authorities to release them from preventive custody forthwith, provided they were not required in connection with any other case.

(Bloomberg) -- In New York’s neighborhood-level disputes over government projects, even pull-up bars have become a flashpoint.
At Tompkins Square Park in Manhattan, the paint on a set of bars is chipping. But the fitness buffs who work out in the park daily are holding on to them for dear life.
At issue are city proposals to close the outdoor gym for months and replace it with equipment that is more accessible to people with disabilities.
Regulars argue the equipment is sufficiently accessible and that the city could reconstruct it with inferior materials. Some simply dread a monthslong separation from the bars that have become part of their daily lives.
For Theophilus London, the stakes feel particularly personal. About three months ago, when he was struggling and looking to change his life, he found his way to the pull-up bars in Tompkins Square Park.
“I was in a desperate need of a change of lifestyle,” London said on a recent afternoon, between sets at the East Village park. “This park changed my life.”
London, a musician nominated for a Grammy Award with Kanye West in 2016, visits the pull-up bars daily. He is among many park-goers speaking against plans to close the decades-old fitness equipment for renovations.
The park adds to a list of government projects that some New Yorkers have perceived as community interference.
A few blocks southwest, in Nolita, residents protested the construction of an affordable housing project at Elizabeth Street Garden for more than a decade. Across the East River in Brooklyn, plans to build a skate park at Mount Prospect Park concerned neighborhood groups that said the facility would exacerbate the problem of higher temperatures in urban areas.
“The idea that it’s an adult fitness area that needs reconstruction is totally and completely misguided,” said Salo Coslovsky, an urban planning professor at New York University, at a recent local advisory board meeting on the Tompkins Square Park pull-up bars.
Coslovsky questioned the expertise of consultants working on the project. “I don’t know if they actually do pull-ups and push-ups and dips,” he said, adding that thousands who signed an online petition opposing the renovations disagreed with the consultants’ assessment. It now has roughly 3,700 signatures.
The park’s alterations would reconstruct the basketball courts and double the size of the park’s pool. The project received $6.1 million from New York Governor Kathy Hochul through an initiative to improve public swimming facilities, and another $2.8 million from Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to city records.
Department of Parks and Recreation Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said in a statement that she was committed to making parks accessible and that her department has worked to reduce the amount of time the exercise equipment would be closed.
The city is collecting input from residents, including by sending park designers to meetings of the neighborhood advisory board. The meetings have run long to accommodate public comment from people who say shutting down the bars would be a grave mistake.
Jahmal Kirwan is part of a larger group with London that works out at the bars. A lifelong resident of Lower Manhattan, Kirwan said he’s not against improving the park.
About two years ago, he said, the bars and the community around them helped him recover from the “brink of death,” when he was drinking and partying every day. He worries the city could delay the renovations, like other nearby developments, leaving a community without a meeting place for too long as it awaits a finished product.
Kirwan said he’d gone his whole life without attending a local advisory board meeting, until he learned about the looming closure of the pull-up bars. He’s attended over the past few months to voice his concerns.
“It’s like them closing down the rehab,” Kirwan said. In regard to a city proposal to close the bars for about 18 months, he said, “there are going to be people that never get to see the bars, because they might not even survive.”

In Brazil, they rallied online by the millions, sharing videos and spreading memes. In Serbia, they cycled across Europe and ran ultramarathons to make their voices heard.
Both movements burst into international public view last month as they became central during election campaigns to the pushback against authoritarianism. What they also offered, however, was a window into a wider phenomenon playing out across the globe, as youth-led movements reshape political landscapes.
“Gen Z is rising,” said Erica Chenoweth, a political scientist at Harvard Kennedy School. “It is abundantly clear that a significant proportion of gen Z is tired of sitting on the sidelines while their political systems fail them.”
Researchers have documented at least 25 protests around the world in which this age group – roughly those between the ages of 14 and 29 – has played a role.
From Bangladesh to Belgium and Italy to India, it seems gen Z, who account for about a third of the world’s population, have found their voice. “Gen Z may be experiencing a global political awakening,” Chenoweth wrote in a recent essay.
Their reasons for taking to the streets have varied widely, from protesting against corruption and an unequal playing field to calling for more investment in education, affordable housing and action on the climate crisis.
Many of the first protests to make waves were in Asia and Africa. In 2024, students in Dhaka, Bangladesh, made global headlines after they pulled off what was described as the world’s first successful gen Z-led revolution.
The protests began over a quota law but swiftly snowballed into a wider show of discontent against the increasingly autocratic rule of the prime minister, Sheikh Hasina. Two months later, Hasina resigned and fled the country by helicopter after being, as the Associated Press reported, “chased out by young protesters”.
Two years later and 4,000 miles away, students were at the helm of another revolution in Serbia, pushing back against a government that had steadily tightened its grip on the media and stuffed institutions with party loyalists.
Late last month, Serbia’s students’ movement was catapulted from the streets to the halls of power as they ousted Aleksandar Vučić in elections, bringing an end to his party’s 14 years in power.
Students and young people have long been at the forefront of the push for change, the analysts Cait Dallaire and Sebastian Dittgen wrote recently, citing the US civil rights movement and the 2011 Arab spring.
“What is unique about the current movement is the infrastructure of mobilisation: TikTok and X amplify and accelerate grievances; Discord servers and group chats enable decentralised planning; virtual private networks and mirrored content help organisers circumvent internet shutdowns,” they said.
It was this potent combination – young people in the streets and social media – that helped drive Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s comeback to win Brazil’s presidential election last month. After a bruising loss in the first round to the rightwing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, there was dismay in the country’s political left.
That was until students from the Fluminense Federal University mobilised in a pro-Lula march, setting off a wave of similar actions across the country. Soon after, the congressman and Lula ally André Janones, 42, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army” that attracted millions of people looking to help boost pro-Lula content on social media.
On the night of his victory, Lula recognised their power. “I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” he said.
Some politicians have sought to engage gen Z from the start. In the US, Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for New York mayor combined a canny use of social media with a legion of about 50,000 volunteers that had young people at its heart. The New York Times wrote that “volunteering for Mr Mamdani’s campaign became a salve” for young New Yorkers as the campaign became not just about “mobilising, but socialising”.
It was a nod to the global context in which many gen Zers have come of age; one riven by conflicts such as the Israel-Gaza war, the escalating climate crisis and the rise of nationalism, while the rules that have shaped the international order since the second world war are fraying.
In recent weeks, youth-led protests have begun to sweep Europe, from school students in France demanding better conditions in which to work to those in Spain who pitched tents to rally for affordable housing. In Germany, thousands of people took to the streets to protest against the cost of living and call for more investment in education, health and climate action in a movement organised by a group calling itself Gen Z regelt!, or Gen Z will sort this.
Analysts have been swift to point to the link between the protests. “The reasons are different, but they share the same spark: the breakdown of the social contract,” Arancha González, the dean of the Paris School of International Affairs, told the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera. “In Europe, the idea that economies generate wellbeing and social equality has been shattered.”
A similar note of disillusionment threads through India’s Cockroach movement, which began as an online satire and has since swelled into a show of force against the strongman government of Narendra Modi. Fuelled by social media and rooted in democratic ideals, the power of the movement was laid bare this summer after Cockroach-led protests forced the resignation of the country’s education minister.
Equally visible is the pushback by India’s security forces against the movement, detaining thousands, unleashing teargas and beating people with lathis, or wooden clubs. Authorities went to extreme lengths in October to keep them from gathering in central Delhi, barricading roads and shutting down the internet and public transport.
It was a window into another facet that has defined youth-led protests, as research suggests they tend to be met with higher levels of repression, despite the fact that they are no more likely to use violence than others.
In France, lawyers and rights groups say several teenagers have suffered war-like injuries from police weapons. After the 2024 protests in Bangladesh, UN human rights experts said as many as 1,400 people had been killed, mostly by security forces, while thousands more suffered severe, often life-altering injuries.
In a recent analysis, Civicus, a non-profit that monitors global civic freedoms, said: “Because they question the distribution of economic and political power, gen Z-led protests have invariably been met with state violence,” linking the violence meted out to young protesters with their focus on systems and institutions that have long been generally accepted.
In Morocco, more than 2,000 people were charged and many received harsh prison sentences after a 2025 movement known as Gen Z 212 targeted officials over corruption, neglected public services and the lack of opportunities. Weeks later, in Mexico, youth-led protests over corruption and crime led to clashes with police in which dozens of people were arrested.
The outcomes of both of these movements show the varying success of gen Z protests. But at times, the foundations laid in one protest have given rise to others. In the US, much of today’s youth organising was shaped by the pro-Palestine student movement, in which there were thousands of arrests, expulsions and suspensions. Many schools instated anti-protest policies amid a broader rollback of educational freedom on campus.
Students, however, have continued to push for change. Last month hundreds in North Carolina marched in the heat to the polls after their historically Black university was denied a polling site, while thousands across the country have responded to the Cornell 7 case by skipping class, protesting and launching occupations.
As Chenoweth of the Harvard Kennedy School noted, the wave of recent youth-led protests may mark the beginning of a “profound generational transformation in world affairs” – one that could be capable of countering the global trend of democratic backsliding.
Ultimately, however, as Bilal Narjissi, a 17-year-old high school student in a suburb north of Paris recently told the Associated Press, the explosion of youth movements across Europe hints at a wider truth that has long been overlooked across the globe.
“We all agree on one point,” he said. “That young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren’t listened to enough.”

The 'Magic Six': How to strengthen your marriage in midlife
Ever argued with your spouse in the car? NPR's Nina Totenberg can relate.
She and her husband, David Reines, have been married for 26 years, and it's on the road where they're most likely to have a spat. "The car is awful," Totenberg told me, laughing. It comes down partly to the brakes. She taps them "way before" Reines does. And when another driver cuts him off, he sometimes wants to return the favor. Totenberg's advice from the passenger seat: "Don't take the bait."
It's so relatable. And as Reines put it, "You can't not have some conflict after 26 years. I think the secret is how you deal with it." (They began our interview for this episode of Your Turn by giving each other a kiss!)
As we ask "What comes next?" in midlife, who's standing beside us matters a lot. Kids leave home, careers shift, and relationships can change, too. So what does a good partnership look like at this stage?
David and Nina's Four L's
When people ask Reines why their marriage works, he points to four L's:
Love. "You gotta love each other."
Like. Do you actually like each other? For Reines, respect is part of this. He says he has total respect for her work, and she respects his career, too. He is a retired trauma surgeon and now keeps busy as a volunteer at the Library of Congress and serves on boards. Each of them also keeps a strong sense of self. "Although we meld," Reines says. "I still have me, and she still has her."
Lust. Physical intimacy matters. They kiss every day, hold hands, "all the time," and have held off on buying a king-size bed. In hotel beds, they joke, they can't find each other if the bed is too big.
Laugh. He says she has one of the best senses of humor he knows. They laugh together every day.
The Magic Six
I also talked with clinical psychologist Julie Schwartz Gottman who I interviewed for my book, Your Turn. She and her husband, John Gottman, co-founded the Gottman Institute and are two of the best-known names in relationship science, and co-authors of Fight Right: How Successful Couples Turn Conflict Into Connection, where they describe the "Four Horseman" which are four destructive communication patterns that can help predict the breakdown of a relationship.
Gottman points to research that shows many dual-career couples spend little time together and much of the communication can be transactional. Did you call the plumber? Did you walk the dog?
The Gottmans found that couples can improve their relationships by intentionally carving out about six hours a week together, and making changes to small, daily and weekly habits. They call it the Magic Six.
Some of these things may sound obvious, yet oftentimes these are the very things that can fall away when couples are too busy or distracted. And she says it's illuminating when couples actually track progress.
Partings (a few minutes each day). Before you leave in the morning, spend a few minutes communicating about what's happening in your partner's day.
Reunions (about 20 minutes a day). At the end of the workday, share a kiss or physical affection. Then have a 20-minute stress-reducing conversation about your day.
Admiration and appreciation (35 minutes a week). Spend about five minutes a day expressing genuine gratitude or naming a trait you admire in your partner. Or tell a story to remind each other.
Affection (35 minutes a week). That works out to about five minutes a day on physical touch, such as holding hands or cuddling before sleep.
Date night (2 hours a week). Have distraction-free time together to enjoy being together. It doesn't need to be dinner and a show. It can be a low-key hike, a museum visit or any activity you enjoy.
State of the union meeting (1 hour a week). Review what's going well as well as concerns or things that are not working, and then talk things out.
Listen. Don't Fix.
Many partners fall into the trap of trying to "fix" the other person's problems or tell them how to proceed. But the point of the daily conversation is to step away from this mentality.
"Most of us just wanna be seen," Gottman told me. "We wanna be witnessed." Jumping in with advice can cut off the conversation before your partner gets the chance to describe what's bothering them.
Instead, she suggests three simple words: "Tell me more."
It's an invitation, Gottman says. It tells your partner, "I really am interested in what you're saying." It shows them that you care.
Nina Totenberg and David Reines have their own version. Every night at dinner, they sit down and ask, "How'd your day go?" He calls Nina a good listener and she says she enjoys connecting this way and spending time together. They keep each other in check and serve as each other's confidant.
Find Your Rhythm
Gottman also had good news for couples who don't share every hobby. You can pursue different passions as long as you bring them back to the table and stay curious about each other. Some couples want lots of independence, and others want to do everything together. The key is to keep asking: Are you missing me? Do we need more time together, or less?
Totenberg and Reins have found their balance. They agree on watching British murder mysteries together. And when he wants a shoot-'em-up, she heads upstairs for Law & Order. Summer vacations on Cape Cod are friends-only, where they spend days doing what they each enjoy. Winter holidays are for her sisters and family.
As Totenberg put it: "If you find somebody that you really love who loves you back, you should grab that and run for all the world because it's ... an enormous gift."
So, if you'd like: give this a try: Ask your partner one open-ended question. Then say, "Tell me more."

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.

Researchers have identified changes in the metabolic activity of the gut microbiome associated with exceptional longevity in humans, and found that amplifying the same activity in aged mice using engineered bacteria improved metabolic health.
Published in the journal Cell Metabolism, the team's study suggests that specific age-related changes in the gut microbiome may be protective adaptations rather than signs of decline, and could potentially be harnessed to support healthier aging.
Senior author Amir Zarrinpar, chair in circadian biology and medicine, and professor of medicine at the University of California San Diego, said while many studies on aging focus on what goes wrong as one grows old, the findings suggest "some changes in the gut microbiome may actually represent the body's attempt to preserve metabolic health".
"If we can identify those beneficial functions and safely strengthen them, we may eventually be able to develop new ways to promote healthier aging," Zarrinpar said.
The gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microbes living in the digestive tract, is known to change throughout life and plays an important role in metabolism and inflammation, among other aspects of health.
Studies have also found distinctive microbiome features among people who age exceptionally well.
The researchers focused on how gut microbes modify bile acids, substances produced by the liver that help digest fats but also act as signalling molecules in the body.
Studying young and aged mice, they found that aging was associated with an increased microbial activity linked to enzymes called bile salt hydrolases. These enzymes chemically modify bile acids, allowing them to influence pathways involved in metabolism, inflammation and the body's internal clock.
The team also found greater bile acid modification in the mice.
To determine patterns in humans, they reanalysed publicly available data from a human ageing cohort, analysing bile acid measurements from 48 young adults, 107 older adults and 125 centenarians.
The centenarian group showed higher ratios of modified bile acids than both younger groups. An analysis of microbiome data also revealed a greater abundance of a gene associated with bile salt hydrolase activity among centenarians compared with the older adult group.
Further, aged mice -- 82-week-old mice -- were introduced with a strain of bacteria native to the gut engineered to continuously produce bile salt hydrolases.
About 20 weeks after treatment, mice receiving the enzyme-producing bacteria had a significantly improved insulin sensitivity and modestly improved glucose tolerance, compared with mice receiving a non-enzyme-producing bacterium.
By 32 weeks, the treated mice also showed changes consistent with a lower body weight and fat mass and a greater lean mass. Other findings pointed to an increased use of fat for energy, improved mitochondrial function and changes in gene activity related to inflammation and the body's internal clock.

A 10-year-old with a rare inflammatory blood vessel disease underwent surgery at SIMS Hospital, Chennai, to repair a large aneurysm of the aortic arch, the hospital said on Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
The patient was diagnosed with aortoarteritis, also known as Takayasu arteritis, a condition that causes inflammation and narrowing or enlargement of blood vessels. The aneurysm had enlarged significantly, causing breathing difficulty, palpitations, and difficulty lying down. The risk of rupture made urgent surgery necessary. The patient weighed about 18 kg, adding to the technical challenges of the operation. As the aneurysm was located close to the breastbone, opening the chest through the usual approach carried a risk of injuring the enlarged aorta. The surgical team first connected the patient to a heart-lung machine through blood vessels in the groin.
The patient’s body was cooled to 16°C using a technique known as deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. Blood circulation was then temporarily stopped for about 40 minutes, enabling surgeons to remove the affected section of the aorta and replace it with a Dacron graft. Lowering the body temperature reduces metabolic activity and the organs’ oxygen requirements, helping protect them during the period when blood flow is interrupted.
The patient was subsequently rewarmed, restoring his blood circulation. Post-operative assessments showed no damage to the brain, kidneys, intestines, or spinal cord, the hospital said. The patient has resumed normal activities without breathing difficulty but will require continued medication and monitoring to control the underlying inflammation and prevent further aneurysms.
The surgery was performed by a team led by Bashi V. Velayudhan, director and senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, along with Mohammed Idhrees, senior consultant, cardiothoracic surgery, and a team of anaesthesiologists and other specialists.

- GTA 6 player has discovered a glitch that allows players to explore Leonida in first-person.
- The glitch involves changing a controller setting and repeatedly pressing the camera button after closing the in-game phone.
- The first-person perspective offers decent animations, but players must reload their save to return to third-person.
GTA 6 finally launched on November 19, 2026, and if you’re already playing it, you know that the game does not have a dedicated first-person mode like GTA 5. While players can use limited first-person views when using their smartphone or aiming with certain weapons, regular gameplay is restricted to third-person. However, just a day after launch, a player discovered a glitch that allows players to experience GTA 6 from a first-person perspective.
How to Do the First-Person Mode Glitch in GTA 6
YouTuber oneboyler shared a video demonstrating the glitch, which appears to work surprisingly well. Interestingly, the footage shows working first-person weapon animations, despite the feature not being officially available.
The glitch involves changing a GTA 6 controller setting and performing a few actions while sitting inside a vehicle. According to oneboyler’s video, here’s how players can activate first-person mode in GTA 6:
- Open Settings -> Controller and scroll down to change the Touch Pad Button setting from Map (1/2) to Camera (2/2).
- Sit in the driver’s seat of a vehicle.
- Press Up on the D-pad to pull out your in-game phone.
- Put the phone away by pressing Circle on PS5 or B on Xbox, then immediately spam the touchpad or Back button.
- Repeat the last step a few times until the camera switches to first-person.
Once the glitch works, players can exit their vehicle and explore the GTA 6 map in first-person. The video also shows the player using weapons and driving the vehicle, with animations that appear to be already present for even small details in first-person view.
However, the glitch is not entirely perfect, and some animations may look awkward. There is also no simple way to switch back to third-person once the glitch activates. Players must reload their save to restore the normal third-person camera.
For now, Rockstar Games has not confirmed whether a dedicated first-person mode will officially arrive in GTA 6. Still, the discovery suggests that some of the necessary functionality already exists in the game, even if players cannot access it through the regular settings. It will be interesting to see whether Rockstar expands on it in a future update.

England in Australia: T20 cricket the new focus as batters bowl, Adil Rashid eyes recall and 'Sandpapergate' rumbles on
England begin five-match T20 series against beleaguered Australia in Melbourne on Saturday (8.15am UK); Harry Brook's side looking to build-on ODI series win as Adil Rashid eyes recall after being omitted for 50-over matches; Mitchell Marsh does not appear at pre-series press conference
Friday 20 November 2026 11:13, UK
"You could see it going horribly wrong, couldn't you? You could see things imploding."
That was Michael Atherton's take on Australia before the 'Sandpapergate' scandal spectacularly hit the headlines once again following Usman Khawaja's claims in his autobiography.
Three weeks ago, the biggest problems for the Baggy Greens were Test batting woes, including a bang-out-of-form Marnus Labuschagne, and some odd selection decisions.
They pale now, though.
- Pat Cummins under pressure after Cameron Bancroft article
- Reaction to Cameron Bancroft's incredible comments
- Listen to latest episode of Sky Sports Cricket Podcast
That "implosion" Athers predicted on the field has come off it, with David Warner and Cameron Bancroft supporting Khawaja's account that all members of the team were aware of the sandpaper scheme in 2018, and Pat Cummins strenuously denying it.
Australian cricket is at civil war and there is no obvious end in sight.
Questions abound (will Cummins survive as captain? Will Steve Smith, Nathan Lyon and Josh Hazlewood have their say? Does Cricket Australia have any choice but to launch a fresh investigation and not just an open forum?) but answers are in short supply.
England looking to pile more misery on Australia
Runs were also in short supply for Australia in the final two ODIs against England as a side helmed by Mitchell Marsh in the absence of the rested (but surely mentally tired) Cummins were twice bundled out in the low 200s chasing targets of 320-plus.
That meant Harry Brook's tourists were able to bounce back from being pummelled in Perth in the opening fixture - a result which brought back horrible memories of their Ashes thrashing at the venue a year ago - to claim a come-from-behind 2-1 series win.
They will now look to pile the misery on their beleaguered hosts with victory in a five-match T20 international series, starting in Melbourne on Saturday (first ball at 8.15am UK time).
At times in the ODIs, it felt like England were toying with an Australia team whose minds were perhaps understandably elsewhere. Jofra Archer sent out to bat at No 6 in Hobart, for example, and also Brook and Tom Banton being asked to deliver their part-time off-spin.
If Archer's elevation was a one-off - it certainly won't be seen in the T20s with the England quick rested as he prepares for the three-Test assignment in South Africa from December 17 - then the use of Brook and Banton with the ball may be a more regular occurrence, especially in 50-over cricket as Brendon McCullum's side laser in on the 2027 World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.
Head coach McCullum said: "These guys are talented, there is something there.
"We are looking at a World Cup in 12 months' time, and no one knows what the conditions are going to be like. You could end up on a pitch that is exploding and need some options.
"We will keep encouraging them to do that. That World Cup is potentially 13 games in three different countries, fresh pitches, there's not much data on how those pitches will play."
Marsh not expected to attend press conferences during series
Brook and Banton bowled 2.5 overs between them in the ODI series, which is 2.5 overs more than Adil Rashid. The frontline spinner had ample time to pour over the sandpaper storm after being left out for all three games, with Liam Dawson once again favoured.
Rashid will hope to be recalled for the T20s, starting at the weekend on a ground where he helped England beat Pakistan in the 2022 T20 World Cup final. The 38-year-old has played in all 19 of his side's T20Is in 2026, appearing alongside Dawson in 18 of them.
Brook, like Rashid, has fond memories of the MCG. He, too, was part of the T20 World Cup-winning squad four years ago, while he top-scored in a blink-and-you'll-miss-it, two-day Ashes Test there last winter as England claimed their only win of a sobering tour.
Brook was all smiles during his pre-series media duties in Melbourne on Friday, saying he wanted to guide his side to a 4-0 lead over Australia before he departs for the South Africa tour ahead of the series finale in Canberra on December 2.
He also spoke of his excitement that the uncapped James Coles, Henry Crocombe, Eddie Jack and Thomas Rew were able to experience being in an England squad in Australia, albeit without confirming if or when they would make their T20I debuts.
We do not know how Australia skipper Marsh is feeling, though, with the 34-year-old not expected to engage in any media activity with the written press throughout the T20 leg following Bancroft's explosive claims in that detail-filled account in the West Australian.
Marsh was part of the XI for the now infamous Cape Town Test eight years ago.
Cummins, Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc will not feature in the series at all as chat regarding what they did or did not know about the sandpaper use runs rampant.
Cummins and Hazlewood are rested, like they were for the ODIs, while Starc, who also sat out the 50-over encounters, has retired from international 20-over cricket.
Make no mistake, though. The heat is very much on them.
On the field, the heat will be on Marsh and an inexperienced bowling attack - weakened further by injuries to Mahli Beardman (quad) and Xavier Bartlett (knee) - to contain an England side that, despite missing the injured Jacob Bethell and Jos Buttler, is formidable.
Australia will also be out to avoid the top-order collapses of the final two ODIs, a goal that could be made easier by Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker joining Archer in being rested ahead of the red-ball trip to South Africa, which you can watch live on Sky Sports.
What the home side want most, however, is a series win over England and for all this sandpaper chat to stop. The first of those objectives looks tough. The second impossible.

So you’ve been diagnosed with ALS — what now? Maybe you join a clinical trial for a brain implant that could help you do things like move your hand or talk to your loved ones. But can you influence the research as a participant? And what happens to the data collected from your brain when the study ends?
A new report addresses these and other questions, exploring how trials of implanted brain-computer interfaces can better address the interests and concerns of participants, who often join in a last-ditch attempt to improve their communication, mobility, or autonomy.
Published by the BCI Pioneers Coalition last week, the report outlines 13 recommendations for startups, researchers, and regulators on managing post-trial care, informed consent, and neural data privacy.
“These studies can sometimes last years, and it becomes a big part of someone’s life. You want there to be as much agency from the participant as possible,” said Ian Burkhart, who co-founded the coalition, with other participants in early studies of implantable BCI devices, to share patient feedback with developers and researchers. Burkhart said the report emerged out of discussions between him and other study participants, who felt they had very little say in how trials were conducted.
The recommendations arrive as the field moves from a niche, proof-of-concept phase into a humming neurotechnology startup ecosystem with eager investors and multiple clinical trials testing implanted devices’ safety and efficacy. Ethicist and UCLA researcher Anna Wexler believes that scientists need better policies to ensure participants’ rights and autonomy.
“There is no good solution right now. We talk about potentially mandatory insurance policies, escrows, and institutions committing support, but right now we just don’t actually have solutions,” Wexler said during a panel at a recent brain-computer interface industry conference in New York.
STAT spoke with Burkhart about his own experiences as someone with tetraplegia and as a former BCI user shopping around for his next device. He wants to make sure that during his next trial, he has more clarity around the study’s overall expectations, what he can do with the data generated, and what will happen to his care after he is explanted.
You were implanted in 2014 with a device at Ohio State University that helped you move your arm. What happened when the study ended?
When our study was starting to wind down because of some funding issues, the institutional review board said, “Well, we can just have them have the device taken out, and then if it gets funded again, they can just put another one back in.” Like, that’s great when it’s not you that’s going through experimental brain surgery.
To me, it really just minimized my experience down to something more akin to a lab rat versus being a human. The [IRB and the institution] claim to be supportive of the researchers trying to get additional funding and continue the work. And if they really were, they would have seen that it makes more sense to put a little bit more of a pause on it and wait for funding to come through if possible, instead of doing something as disruptive as having surgery.
Can’t patients just say no to this?
Most informed consents right now, they’re more of a one-sided agreement protecting the research team and institution versus protecting what the participants may want. If you don’t agree to something, the alternative is to not participate. And that’s fine when you’re first signing up for a study. It changes once you’ve already been in a study and you’re re-consenting to continue on with the study, especially when there are very limited alternatives for treatment for this patient population.
So it’s your only hope, you’re saying.
Yes. And then, you know, you add in the psychological piece of using these devices to restore function after a disability. To my knowledge, everyone that’s used a device has an acquired disability versus being born with their disability. So they have that capability, and then they have their disability, and that capability is taken away from them, and then these devices help restore some of that function, and then it’s taken away again.
If there’s real technical reasons that the device stops working or we’re not able to use this technology anymore, that’s one thing. But if there’s just a well, it’s easier for us to administratively close the study, and we can start it back up again in the future, that doesn’t seem like a valid reason to take away and have someone psychologically experience a little bit of their injury or their disability again.
How does that compare to other BCI users’ experiences?
They have had similar experiences where they don’t really know what the end of the study is going to look like. And as a participant, you can leave at any time, but also the researchers can kick you out of the study at any time, within their rationale.
It’s a little bit of a challenge there when you are doing something as intimate as going into the lab multiple times a week, multiple hours at a time, and it becomes such a big part of your life. For it to just be abruptly stopped can be really challenging. … You know, Nathan Copeland, he’s passed 11 years [with a device] now.
That’s practically a millenium in this fledgling industry. What should long-term care look like for BCI users?
We’re past the proof of concept phase [for these devices]. Is there any support for people to maintain these devices, not in a way that you know we’re forcing a company or institution to keep up a manufacturing line, but can there be decisions made earlier on that will allow, if you need a new battery, you can get a battery from company A, B, or C? Versus it’s only one company that makes the battery, and if that company’s out of business, then you’re done? What kind of support can be available so that you can potentially slowly wind down the trial and not have it be as abrupt?
I knew when I signed up [for my study] that this wasn’t going to be a forever thing. It was only supposed to be up to a year and a half, but it continued, we were able to reconsent and expand on the study, and it became a much larger part of my life than I envisioned. To then have such an abrupt ending is not something that anyone wants to go through.
I only had access to the device when I’m going to the lab. Now that people are using these devices at home and you know out in the wild, it’s a much more significant change when there is that abrupt end.
The report talks a lot about giving participants more access to their neural data. What are you proposing?
If you give the participant full ownership of that data, there should be a mechanism where the main research team can have first crack at that data, but then after, if the participant agrees, it allows them to open that up and let other researchers who may not have the resources to implant an individual and capture all this data to see what they can learn from that as well.
I feel like I would balk at that if I was a researcher or regulator.
It really just depends on what information it is, how much of a kind of delay that someone may get, and how exactly those experiments are structured. If I could have shared some of the raw data from my study, so someone sitting around in their basement trying to come up with different decoding algorithms, I think that’s beneficial for the field. And you know, if the researchers are actually motivated by what’s beneficial for the field versus getting their credit and publishing another paper and moving on, I think they would be open to that.That’s really the goal out of these types of devices to help individuals with disabilities have more independence, autonomy, agency over their lives.
Are a lot of study participants asking to run raw data through decoding algorithms in their basement?
I’ve certainly met a few. Most of the participants were like, “That’s way over my head.” But I think that there are plenty of people who would like to put their neural data into an AI tool and see what they can learn.
My study has been over for six years now. All that data is hopefully still sitting on a server somewhere. I’m sure there’s something that someone with a fresh set of eyes could make sense of, potentially bringing a little bit of value.
I certainly think it would be interesting to see what I can find out about my own data, being able to go into the research lab but then, on my own time, I can sit at home and run some other experiments that might be different. Get as much juice out of it as we can. Make sure it’s worth the squeeze.

Listed non-banking financial company (NBFC) Mufin Green Finance’s board has approved the acquisition of a 23% stake in insurtech startup BimaPay for a ₹65.8 Cr in an all-cash deal. Mufin Green Finance said that it expects to complete the transaction in the next three to four months, subject to the execution of definitive agreements and relevant regulatory approvals. It is pertinent to note that BimaPay operates under the umbrella of the broader Mufin Group. “.... With an RBI-registered NBFC as a shareholder, we can build products around how lending actually works rather than adapt them later,” said BimaPay cofounder and CEO Hanut Mehta. In a statement, Mufin said that he proposed investment will leverage synergies between the two entities and support the joint development and scaling of premium financing solutions. The transaction will look to combine the listed NBFC’s lending expertise with BimaPay’s tech solutions. “... An ownership stake lets us plan product, data and integration roadmaps over years instead of project cycles, which is what a lender growing at our pace needs,” added Mufin Green Finance managing director Kapil Garg said. The deal is a related-party transaction as Bimapay is a promoter-group subsidiary of Mufin, the listed NBFC said. Founded in 2022 by Mehta, Mohit Gupta and Kapil Garg, BimaPay facilitates financing solutions to enable individuals and businesses to pay insurance premiums in EMIs instead of upfront lump sums. It also works with lending partners and insurers to develop technology-enabled solutions. The startup last raised $2 Mn in an undisclosed funding round led by LC Nueva Investment Partners in 2024. On the financial front BimaPay reported revenue of ₹9.9 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up 203% from ₹3.2 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. According to Mufin Green Finance, the startup also reported a profit before tax (PBT) of ₹1.1 Cr in FY26. BimaPay operates at the intersection of lending tech and insurtech. The two segments are seeing healthy growth on the back of rising smartphone adoption, expanding credit and the rise of AI-driven distribution solutions. According to Inc42 data, the Indian insurtech market is projected to become a $307 Bn opportunity by 2030.

Amazon Prime India head Abhinav Agarwal has left the ecommerce giant after 16 years, ending a stint spanning supply chain, advertising, and its membership business. Announcing his departure in a LinkedIn post yesterday (November 19), Agarwal said his next role would be at the “intersection of commerce, logistics and product”. He did not disclose further details. Agarwal joined Amazon in September 2010 as a network planning manager. He subsequently held roles across supply chain and performance advertising before taking charge of product and engineering for Amazon Prime in India in October 2021. His departure comes amid Amazon’s expansion across ecommerce, entertainment, and quick commerce in India. The company plans to invest $3 Bn in its quick commerce business Amazon Now by 2030, including $1 Bn by the end of 2027. The investment would support the expansion of its dark store network, technology infrastructure, and product assortment to compete with Blinkit, Zepto, and Swiggy Instamart. Meanwhile, Amazon’s streaming platform Prime Video is increasing its focus on intellectual property (IP), franchises, and Indian content that can attract international audiences. Approaching a decade in India, the platform is expanding beyond episodic content into theatrical releases and franchise-led storytelling. About 25% of viewership for its Indian titles comes from outside the country. Prime Video has more than 100 shows in development and production, while over 60% of its original series extend into multiple seasons, underpinning its push to build long-running franchises. Separately, Amazon has announced plans to invest an additional $7 Bn in renewable energy projects in India by 2030, beyond the $4 Bn it has already contracted. It also announced four wind and solar projects across Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, and Rajasthan, with a combined capacity of 934 MW. These projects form part of the existing $4 Bn commitment. The investments will contribute to Amazon’s global goal of reducing the carbon intensity of the electricity powering its operations by 65% by 2030, against a 2019 baseline.

My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
- Published
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.
They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.
"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.
But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.
This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.
Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.
Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.
After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.
"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.
The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.
The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.
After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.
Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.
This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.
After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.
This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.
"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.
Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.
He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.
The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.
"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.
In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.
Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.
"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.
Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.
The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.
However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.
"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.
For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.
He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.
Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.
"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.
They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.
Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.
After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.
"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."
During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.
But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.
Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.
"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".
He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.
But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.
Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.
He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."
He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.
"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.
The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.
Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.
"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs as Iran war fuel costs, losses mount
Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time jobs in Frankfurt and Munich as Iran war fuel costs add to monthly losses of 20 million euros, an internal letter said.
German airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs as its turnaround efforts move slower than hoped, with the energy shock from the Iran war adding to headwinds, according to an internal letter seen by AFP on Friday.
The carrier embarked on a cost-cutting programme in 2024 to stem losses but the measures announced so far are "no longer sufficient", according to the letter sent to staff.
During the first nine months of the year, the airline was losing on average 20 million euros ($22 million) a month, it said.
"The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation," the letter said.
Also read: Polymarket says 'we’ll keep growing' after laying off full-time employees, cutting contractors
Germany's flag carrier now plans to cut 1,000 full-time positions at the Frankfurt and Munich airports, amounting to around 2.5 percent of its roughly 40,000 employees.
Lufthansa, which also operates carriers including Austrian, Swiss and Brussels Airlines, last year announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs across the whole group by 2030, mainly targeting administrative roles.
It was not immediately clear whether the cuts disclosed on Friday were included in this round of layoffs, or in addition. A Lufthansa spokesman declined to give further details.
The Cockpit union, which represents Lufthansa pilots, said the airline was trying to "stir up uncertainty and to put pressure on employees" as the two sides were engaged in negotiations over pay and work conditions.
They accused Lufthansa of announcing the 1,000 job losses without sufficient detail, such as which departments would be impacted and whether the cuts would be part of the previously announced layoffs.
Despite the woes of the flagship airline, the wider group is in good financial health.
It reported a 30-per cent jump in profits for the July-September period, beating forecasts, boosted by demand for premium tickets on long-haul routes.
But surging fuel costs since the start of the US war on Iran are weighing on the group, with its annual fuel bill set to come in two billion euros higher this year than in 2025.

There are buildings which hold memories that run deeper than those of the people walking within them. The Purana Qila is one of them. The walls of the Purana Qila were built by Sher Shah Suri during the 16th century, and as per tradition and substantial archaeological evidence, the ancient city of Indraprastha can be found under it. And now, beginning November 20, the Ministers of culture of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), along with dialogue partners from over 25 countries, have gathered within the walls of the Purana Qila for the first Civilisational Dialogue Forum of the SCO. The idea was proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during his visit to Tianjin in 2025, and is being conducted by the Ministry of Culture along with the Ministry of External Affairs.
If one wants to have a better sense of why India wants to host such a forum, one needs to realise that the term ‘civilisation’ has become a contested territory in international politics. In the two decades since the end of the Cold War, the West had a monopoly over the language of universal principles such as democracy, markets and human rights. While the language was meant to be universally applicable, it implicitly belonged to those who had written the textbooks.
Emerging powers while not rejecting the language, have relativised it. Beijing, for example, moved quickly to institutionalise it. Xi Jinping unveiled the Global Civilization Initiative in 2023. One year later, the UN General Assembly, on a Chinese initiative, designated June 10 as the International Day for Dialogue among Civilizations. In association with the 2023 initiative, China also organised a Ministerial-level meeting of the Global Civilizations Dialogue in July 2025, while the Nishan Forum on World Civilizations launched its 12th edition in September 2026 with the theme ‘Civilization, Order, and Justice’ at the birthplace of Confucius. Even the Internet conference at Wuzhen this month featured a sub-forum dedicated to civilisation. Clearly, China is not just experimenting in this area; it is developing a franchise which signals a much-recycled message — that modernity has many addresses.
India has viewed these developments with the look of a man who has found someone selling his family silver at the fair. After all, India has the better claim of being the centre of civilisation than many of the current claimants vying for the position. The conference in Delhi is India’s attempt to set up its own stall in an organisation that has its secretariat in Beijing. It also fits a pattern of agenda-setting, with the AI Impact Summit earlier this year and the BRICS chairmanship now.
The behaviour of a great power is driven more by what it believes about itself than by what it states as its objective. There are three objectives of India here, and only one is explicitly stated: soft connectivity, which includes Buddhist circuits, Sufi lineages and the trade routes that ran from Taxila to Samarkand much before anyone drew maps.

In an intensive care unit, every second matters. A critically ill patient may be connected to several devices, including patient monitors, ventilators and infusion pumps, while laboratory systems and electronic health records continuously generate additional information. Together, these systems create a large and rapidly-changing picture of the patient’s condition. However, when the information remains fragmented across devices and platforms, clinicians may spend valuable time locating, verifying and reconciling data before they can act.
This makes interoperability a clinical priority in critical care, not simply an information technology requirement. Integration enables systems to exchange data, but true interoperability ensures that the information being exchanged is accurate, interpretable and clinically relevant. This can help care teams coordinate and prioritise interventions more effectively while reducing the need to move between multiple systems to assemble a clinical picture.
