India's religious make-up - what a new Pew study says about Hindus and Muslims
- Published
India will remain overwhelmingly Hindu for decades to come, but its religious composition is projected to shift gradually.
A new study by the Pew Research Center, projecting the world's religious populations to 2070, estimates that Hindus will make up 76% of India's population by then, down from 79% in 2020, while the Muslim share will rise from 15% to 20%.
The shift is rooted largely in differences in age and fertility: Indian Muslims are younger than Hindus and, on average, have more children.
The Pew projections place India at the centre of a wider demographic shift across South Asia.
Pakistan is expected to overtake Indonesia as the country with the world's largest Muslim-majority population, with India moving into second place. Bangladesh, too, is projected to see substantial growth in its Muslim population.
The study projects the religious composition of the world over the next 50-year period, drawing on data from 201 countries and territories, covering virtually the entire global population.
It tracks seven religious groups between 2020 and 2070, assuming recent demographic trends continue. Using census and survey data, it establishes each group's size and age profile in 2020, and factors in differences in fertility and religious switching.
The findings place India at the heart of a changing global religious landscape. The country is expected to have the world's second-largest Muslim population by 2070, after Pakistan, with about 334 million Muslims. Pakistan itself will overtake Indonesia as the country with the largest Muslim population, with an estimated 461 million.
Yet the projections offer little support for the more dramatic narratives sometimes attached to India's changing religious composition.
If current demographic trends continue, the Hindu population in the country is expected to grow by 176 million between 2020 and 2070, the report says. It will continue to account for more than three-quarters of the country's population.
Despite a sharp fall in India's overall fertility, Muslim women still have more children, on average, than Hindu women. Pew attributes the shift primarily to demographic momentum.
Indian Muslims had a median age of 24 in 2020, compared with 29 for Hindus.
Between 2025 and 2030, Pew estimates Muslim women in India will have an average of 2.3 children, against 1.8 among Hindu women.
"We expect religious change in India to be driven almost entirely by long-standing demographic differences between Hindus and Muslims: Muslims are younger and have higher fertility rates," Stephanie Kramer of the Pew Research Center told the BBC.
"The fertility gap has narrowed considerably – from more than one child per woman in 1992 to about half a child in recent years and is likely to keep shrinking," she said.
"But Hindu fertility is already below the replacement level, while Muslim fertility is projected to remain above it for another two decades." (A replacement level is one at which new births are sufficient to maintain a stable population.)
The projections are hardly surprising, says KS James, an Indian demographer at Princeton University.
"The fertility gap between Muslims and Hindus is well established and it means Muslim population growth is likely to remain faster for the next few decades. But fertility is declining across all religious communities and the gap is expected to narrow further," he told the BBC.
"Ultimately, they will converge," he says, adding that the projections do not point to anything dramatically different in India's demographic trajectory.
Demographers push back against claims, often amplified by Hindu right-wing groups, that Muslims will eventually outnumber Hindus. There is no evidence of any significant religious conversion driving population change in India, they say, and the projections do not support such "alarmist scenarios".
The wider South Asian picture is equally revealing, according to the report.
Pakistan's Muslim population is projected to more than double to 461 million by 2070, overtaking Indonesia as the world's largest. India will rank second, with 334 million Muslims, while Bangladesh's Muslim population will rise to 218 million. India and Nepal, meanwhile, will remain the world's only Hindu-majority countries.
There appears to be a global story behind these regional shifts.
By 2035, Muslims are projected to overtake Christians as the world's largest religious group, according to the report. By 2070, their numbers are expected to reach 3.64 billion, up from 2.02 billion in 2020.
Christianity, meanwhile, will have just under three billion followers. Muslims will account for 36% of humanity, compared with 26% today.
But the most dramatic transformation may be taking place thousands of miles west of South Asia, in Africa.
Christianity's centre of gravity is moving steadily away from Europe and the Americas towards sub-Saharan Africa.
The report says that if recent trends continue, more than half of the world's Christians are expected to live there by 2070, compared with 31% in 2020. Pew forecasts that the Democratic Republic of Congo will overtake the United States as the country with the largest Christian population.
The steepest decline is expected to occur in Europe. If current trends continue, by 2070 Europe will be home to 11% of the world's Christian population, down from 22% in 2020, the report says.
The US is projected to lose its Christian majority by 2065, although Christians will remain the country's largest religious group in 2070.
One reason for this changing religious landscape is the growing number of people identifying with no religion.
In UK and France, the "religiously unaffiliated" are projected to become the majority by 2070. South Korea is expected to follow suit.
Yet their share of the world's population is forecast to fall from 24% to 17%, largely because of a decline in China's population.
China accounts for about two-thirds of the world's religiously unaffiliated population. Its expected population decline will more than offset growth in secular populations elsewhere, the report says.
By 2070, there are other unexpected shifts.
The US is projected to become the world's fifth-largest Hindu population, with immigration driving much of its growth.
And Australia's unaffiliated population will overtake Christians as the country's largest group.
Buddhism, meanwhile, faces a demographic squeeze. Its population is expected to fall by more than half in China, Japan and South Korea, reflecting the ageing and shrinking populations of East Asia. Laos and Mongolia are projected to lose their Buddhist majorities.
There are, of course, caveats. These are demographic projections, not predictions of everything that might happen. Pew assumes that recently observed patterns of fertility, migration and religious switching - or conversions - will continue.
"There are many events that could affect religious group populations (including wars, natural disasters, epidemics and changes in economic or social circumstances) that are not analysed here," the report admits.
India's baseline also required projecting the 2020 religious composition from the 2011 census, because the subsequent census had been delayed
Still, the broad direction is unmistakable.
South Asia will remain indispensable to the world's religious story, not just because of India's enormous Hindu population but because of the growing weight of its Muslim populations. Africa will increasingly shape Christianity's future, while Europe and parts of East Asia become more secular.
Clearly, by 2070, the world's religious landscape may look markedly different, shaped less by conversion than by the uneven arithmetic of births, deaths and migration.

Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.
The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.
But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.
The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.
“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.
“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.
“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”
Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.
Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.
“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he said.
Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.
The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.
Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.
Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.
His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders showed Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.
But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor said.
“He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.
Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.
“The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield said. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.
“Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”
The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.
Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.
“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.
Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

Leh, Nov 20: Lieutenant Governor of Ladakh Vinai Kumar Saxena on Friday approved the conferment of honorary ranks to eligible non-gazetted police personnel on the last day of their service upon superannuation, officials said.
The decision, approved last month, aims to recognise the decades of dedicated service rendered by police personnel in the challenging high-altitude and extreme climatic conditions of Ladakh.
Under the approved arrangement, constables and special grade constables will be conferred the honorary rank of head constable, head constables will be granted the honorary rank of assistant sub-inspector (ASI), ASIs will be elevated to sub-inspector (SI), and SIs will be conferred the honorary rank of inspector on their last working day, they added.
The initiative seeks to acknowledge the lifelong contribution of retiring personnel towards maintaining law and order and ensuring public safety across the Union Territory, while instilling a sense of pride and professional dignity among the force, the statement said.
The honorary promotion will be purely ceremonial and will not entitle the personnel to any additional monetary benefits, increase in pay or allowances, pensionary benefits, arrears or other post-retirement financial entitlements, they said.
"The grant of honorary ranks will be subject to prescribed eligibility conditions, including a minimum of two years of service in the substantive rank, satisfactory performance during the preceding five years, absence of major disciplinary punishment and requisite vigilance and integrity clearance," they added.
The decision comes after Saxena had witnessed firsthand the difficult operational conditions faced by Ladakh Police personnel during his visits to different parts of the Union Territory.
Police personnel routinely perform duties at altitudes ranging from 11,000 feet to nearly 20,000 feet, braving low oxygen levels, treacherous mountain passes and extreme sub-zero temperatures, which plunge well below minus 30 degrees Celsius during winters, the officials said.
Saxena had also spearheaded a similar initiative for retiring Delhi Police personnel during his tenure as the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi.
With this decision, Ladakh Police has been brought at par with the policy adopted for the Central Armed Police Forces, Assam Rifles and Delhi Police, the statement added.

REI's 2026 Holiday Sale kicked off November 13 and lasts until November 23 this year. There are plenty of great deals to help you restock your backpacking, hiking, biking, camping, outdoor-loving gear quiver. REI members can use the code HOLIDAY2026 to save an extra 20 percent off one full-price item, and an extra 20 percent off one REI Outlet item. Below are the best deals on all our favorite tents, backpacks, sleeping bags, pads, cookware, outdoor apparel, and more.
There are also sales at Backcountry.com and some of our favorite cottage industry brands like Six Moon Designs, Zenbivy, and more. Not sure what you need? Check out our many outdoor gear guides.
Great Deals on Outdoor Apparel
The 650 Down Jacket is one of the best budget three-season puffer jackets you can buy, more so at this price. At 10.9 ounces, it's reasonably lightweight and has large hand pockets and some very nice internal pockets for stashing a hat or gloves. The kids' version is also on sale in a nice yellow color that's handy for spotting your child in the snow.
The Ghost Whisperer Down Jacket is my top pick for a backpacking puffer jacket. It weighs just 6.7 ounces for a men's medium (7.3 ounces for the men's large I tested), packs down to a tiny little thing (stuffing into its own pocket), and the 1,000-fill-power goose down offers one of the best warmth-to-weight ratios on the market. The men's version is technically on sale right now, but the only size available is small and XXL.
This is my favorite puffer jacket, especially in the shoulder seasons when temps dip a little lower. It features 4.5 ounces of 1,000-fill down (men’s medium), which is half the weight of the overall jacket. The internal TILT lining (short for Thermo Ionic Lining Technology) may or may not do anything; I haven't been able to devise an effective test, but even if it did nothing, the amount of 1,000-fill-power down combined with the scant weight makes this an appealing option for ultralighters. The 7D fabric (which is what keeps the weight low) does need babying, but I haven't had any issues in over a year of use.
This is great deal on a very warm down parka. It's thigh-length, which helps keep drafts up your back to a minimum, and it fits pretty well, though it's definitely boxy (what do you want from a 650-down-fill parka that's designed primarily to keep you warm?). I did find that the main two-way zipper can be fiddly, and does sometimes snag, but it's hardly a deal-breaker, especially at this price.
Deals on Tents
Six Moon Design's Lunar Solo is one of the best single-wall ultralight solo tents you can buy. It's not without its quirks (read the pitching tips), but if you want something more than a tarp, that still weighs just 26 ounces (740 grams), this one is hard to beat. Use the Code YULEHIKE to get the 25 percent off.
Nemo's Hornet tents are some of the lightest freestanding tents around. The 1-person model is my go-to for situations where I might have to pitch on rock or concrete slabs (like staying in towns on a longer bikepacking trip). It's roomy enough for you and all your gear, light enough at 2.25 pounds (without stakes), and packs down remarkably small. It's also held up well in storms, though you will want some extra guy-outs if the wind is really howling (I like Zpacks 1.2-mm dyneema cord for lightweight guylines).
This is the bikepacking version of Big Agnes' popular Copper Spur tent. The only difference, aside from color, is that the pole segments on this model are shorter (to make it easier to store on a bike). The Copper Spur line is very nearly the lightest freestanding tent around (it's just slightly heavier than the Hornet above), and if you happen to use it with trekking poles, you get what I think is the best feature, the covered awning modification for the vestibule. While this is the best deal, the 2-person model is also on sale for 20 percent off.
Sleeping Bad and Sleeping Pad Deals
This is one of my favorite ultralight sleeping bags. There are lighter quilts out there, but when you need the warmth of a mummy bag on those colder nights, this is what I use. It also has the smallest pack size of any bag I've tested in this temperature range. With the included compression sack, this thing is truly tiny. The down fill is PFC-free, 850+ hydrophobic down. The zippers are on the small side, but they slide well and rarely (if ever) snag on the bag. I've slept in this bag down to 20 degrees and never been the least bit cold.
Closed-cell foam pads like the Therm-a-Rest Z-Lite Sol are a must-have. They weigh next to nothing (10 ounces for the small), fold up small enough to lash to the outside of any pack, and double as a chair, extra padding on cold nights, table, you name it. I am too old and too soft to be the sort of ultra-minimalist who gets by with just a Z-Lite, but I still have one around on almost every trip I take.
Nemo's Tensor-insulated sleeping pads have the best R-value-to-weight ratio of anything I've tested. The Tensor All-Season featured here sports an R-value of 5.4 and weighs 18.2 ounces. That alone is impressive, but what I love about the Tensor is that it's thick, comfortable, and most importantly, nearly silent. The lighter Trail model is also on sale at REI. Its R-value is only 2.8, though.
Deals on Camping and Backpacking Gear
I don't usually bring a chair backpacking—I just sit on the ground. But for some reason, I do love a chair when I'm bikepacking, which is where I've used this Nemo the most. It's quite pricey, but it's very light and packs down to a tiny package. The genius part of this chair is that the cover is also a mat that keeps it from sinking into soft ground.
The thing to keep in mind when you shop REI-brand gear is the company's basic proposition: You get 90 percent of the designer item for 70 percent of the price. It's a strategy that works quite well and has generated some really great, affordable gear. This chair is a good example of that. It's not as nice as the Nemo above—it does wobble a bit, side to side, when you move—but it's still comfortable and half the price.
I sincerely hope you never have any need for one of these Sea to Summit bug head nets, but if you do, boy do you. I once did not have one and tried to go backpacking in Michigan’s UP in early May. I lasted about two hours. When I got home, I bought one of these and … still haven't ventured back to that marshy bog of a hike. But I could, and possibly even retain some of my sanity thanks to this thing.
What I said about the chair above goes for this pack as well; it's an excellent value, especially on sale. I was surprised by how comfortable this thing is, especially because, to look at it, the straps are very lightweight and there's almost no padding. It still managed to carry loads up to 10 pounds without straining my shoulders, and the side stash pockets are fabulously large—big enough for a Nalgene bottle or rain jacket. The Flash 22 is made of 70-denier recycled ripstop nylon, which is on the lighter side, but mine has held up well, even coming through some rough canyon hikes in Utah without any more than mud stains.
These two pots are my go-to cooking vessels for larger group meals. I find they're just about perfect for boiling up enough water to rehydrate four servings. I don't take the bowls and silverware into the backcountry, but they're handy for camping.
The Stash is our favorite all-in-one backcountry cook system. The heat diffuser design is what speeds up boil times (Jetboil claims 2.5 minutes, which I was only able to match indoors in still air), but the real appeal here to me is the way this kit all packs down into itself. For weekend trips, this is the simplest system I've tested when it comes to cooking for two.
These dry bags from Sea to Summit have double-stitched, tape-sealed seams that have held up well over the years. I also really like the external lash loops that make it easy to strap to anything with a tie-down anchor.
I like these dry bags for organizing things in my pack. They're not dry bags in the sense that you can submerge them and your gear will be fine, but the 30D silnylon with PCF-free DWR easily sheds a little rain. And they make finding your stuff easy. I put all my cooking gear in a red bag (red for fire), all my water-filtering stuff in a blue bag for, wait for it, water—and so on. I find the 3- and 5-liter bags the most useful, but you can get all the way up to 35L.
I've noticed that, when trying to lighten their load with a smaller, lighter-weight backpack, people then struggle to fit all their gear. The answer for sleeping bags and clothing is this compression stuff sack, which takes my favorite sleeping bag (the Sea to Summit Spark above) and smashes it down to about half the size of the included stuff sack. You can do the same thing to clothing, especially puffer jackets, but also fleece and merino to some extent, to free up more room in your pack.
REI’s Big Haul duffel is a durable, water-resistant, gear-swallowing bag for carrying, well, just about everything. It's one of our favorite ways to schlep your gear when flying. It hits the right balance of robust build materials and pockets without being too heavy to lug around all day. The strap system is cleverly customizable, and you can convert it to a backpack.
Once upon a time, in a galaxy far, far away, I traveled around Southeast Asia with an early version of this Osprey pack, living out of it for almost a year. It stood up well to the abuse of overland travel—more than once, I watched a bus driver tie it to the roof of a bus by cinching it down with a rope, pulling with all his weight right down the middle of my pack, like a cheese cutter. The Farpoint survived, and my gear inside did as well, thanks in part to the thickly padded sides, which provide considerable extra cushioning.

The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?
- Published
The sandpaper scandal, one of the biggest controversies in the history of Test cricket, continues to engulf Australian sport.
Fresh evidence from Cameron Bancroft - the culprit of the ball-tampering in South Africa in 2018 - has heaped pressure on Australia captain Pat Cummins, former coach Darren Lehmann and Cricket Australia.
In a detailed account of more than 4,000 words published in the West Australian newspaper, Bancroft alleges all the Australia players and coaches present in Cape Town eight years ago knew of the plot.
Bancroft's explosive testimony supports claims made by Usman Khawaja, David Warner and Chadd Sayers.
However, Cummins denied Khawaja's version of events in his own extraordinary news conference in Sydney last week. Cummins spoke to the media for 68 minutes in an address broadcast on live television.
Here, BBC Sport collects the most recent accounts of players and coaches involved in the saga that became widely known as sandpapergate.
Usman Khawaja
Batter Khawaja played all four Tests in South Africa and a total of 88 for Australia before retiring from international cricket earlier this year.
Revelations in his autobiography reignited debate around the sandpaper scandal and made headlines across the globe.
"It was all of us," Khawaja said. "Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us.
"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.
"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said, 'Take this as a team'.
"We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team, and so I was always of that stance."
- Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use - Khawaja 
  - Published6 November
David Warner
Warner was Australia's opening batter and vice-captain during the 2018 series. He, along with captain Steve Smith and Bancroft, were the three players punished for the ball-tampering.
The Cricket Australia (CA) investigation in 2018 found Warner developed the plan and that he instructed Bancroft to carry out the cheating.
After serving his ban, Warner returned to play a further 133 times for Australia across formats, including three Ashes series and the 2023 World Cup win. He retired from international cricket in 2024.
In response to Khawaja's book, Warner said: "I thank you for what you've done. It's 100% accurate what you've said. Now everyone knows the truth."
He also accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up, describing the CA investigation as "rushed" and botched".
"As far as l am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," Warner said.
"If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?"
- Warner accuses Cricket Australia of 'cover-up' 
  - Published4 days ago
Pat Cummins
The Cape Town Test was the 13th of Cummins' Test career. A key bowler, he would go on to be named Australia's Test captain in 2021. It is a position he still holds.
Prior to Khawaja's book, Cummins and the other bowlers from Cape Town - Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon - had always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper.
In an extraordinary news conference last week, Cummins called Khawaja's claims that the whole team knew about the plan "100% wrong" and "utter nonsense".
"I said that consistently for the last eight years," Cummins said. "I did not know that was happening.
"He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball-tamper with sandpaper. That's complete and utter nonsense."
Asked if he knew of any plans at any stage to tamper with the ball during the series against South Africa, Cummins said: "No."
Cummins also said he did not remember a meeting where Khawaja had called on the team to take collective responsibility - something his former team-mate claimed.
Cameron Bancroft
Opening batter Bancroft was playing his eighth Test in Cape Town, aged 25. He was the player caught using sandpaper on the field.
He played another two Tests after serving his ban and is still playing for Western Australia. He turns 34 this week.
In 2021, Bancroft said it was "self-explanatory" whether the bowlers knew of the plan, and on Wednesday he backed Khawaja's account, saying Cummins' news conference made him "feel angry, betrayed and alone".
Like Khawaja, Bancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before he was caught - and also said he had conversations with the Australia seamers about whether the ball was "swinging enough".
He said the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper. He also claimed that coach Lehmann and bowling coach David Saker were present in the initial discussions and that Bancroft's role was also discussed in a team meeting before day three.
In an account published by the West Australian on Wednesday, Bancroft wrote: "All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.
"Is it going yet? It's not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball.
"There was even a time I was told to stop out of fear what I was doing was becoming too obvious."
- Bancroft sandpaper claims heap pressure on Cummins 
  - Published9 hours ago
Darren Lehmann
Lehmann was Australia coach at the time of the scandal. He was cleared by the CA investigation and said he had "no prior knowledge" of the plan to ball-tamper.
He resigned after the series and has been Northamptonshire coach since the start of the 2025 English season.
After Khawaja's revelations, Lehmann said: "I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball-tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years."
After Cricket Australia said it would hold an open forum, Lehmann said he has "nothing to hide".
Speaking on radio coverage of the third one-day international against England after Bancroft's account was published, Lehmann said: "I need to sit back, process it and work through each allegation.
"That's what I'll be doing over the next few days.
"I need to have a really good read of it. I need to make sure I'm saying what I want to say."
Steve Smith
Smith, one of the greatest batters of his generation, was Australia's captain at the time of the scandal.
After serving a 12-month ban, he returned for the World Cup and Ashes the following year and has stood in as captain at times since.
He was found to have been aware of the plan to cheat and to mislead the public and match officials.
Smith, who broke down in tears when apologising at a subsequent news conference, as cameras captured the emotional toll of the moment, has not spoken publicly since Khawaja's book was published.
Speaking about the episode in September this year, he said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that in a way.
"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."
Mitchell Marsh
Marsh was bowling when Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town. As an all-rounder, he was not part of the 2021 bowlers' statement.
Marsh was captain during Australia's recent ODI series against England and refused to answer questions on the topic before the series opener.
"I am not here to share mine [story] today," he said.
"I respect Uzzie [Khawaja] has told his story; my focus is on tomorrow. I am not here to go back on South Africa."
Following the conclusion of the series, Marsh did not take part in his post-match news conference, with 26-year-old bowler Jack Edwards taking his place.
Tim Paine
Paine was Australia's wicketkeeper during the South Africa series and was made captain when Smith was banned.
He served in the role until he stood down in 2021 over a historical investigation into sexually explicit text messages sent to a female colleague.
In his autobiography, Paine said the suggestion everyone in the Australia dressing room must have known about the sandpaper use is "rubbish" and claimed he first found out when images appeared on the big screen in Cape Town.
"Everyone out there was shocked when they looked up on the big screen and saw Cameron Bancroft with a piece of sandpaper in his hand," Paine wrote. "I was stunned. We all were.
"My heart sank, I was thinking, 'What the f***?' A sense of dread came over us all."
Bancroft said he discussed whether the ball was reversing with Paine during the second Test.
David Saker
Saker was Australia's bowling coach during the South Africa series.
Bancroft alleged Saker was present for discussions about the use of sandpaper and told the batter he needed to do more to the ball.
Saker was also England bowling coach as recently as last month's tri-series in Pakistan. He was an influential part of England's 2010-11 Ashes win.
In 2021, reflecting on the sandpaper saga, Saker said: "Obviously a lot of things went wrong at that time. There was a lot of people to blame. It could have been me to blame, it could have been someone else. It could have been stopped and it wasn't, which is unfortunate.
"Cameron's a very nice guy. He's just doing it to get something off his chest… He's not going to be the last. You could point your finger at me, you could point your finger at Boof [Lehmann]. Could you point it at other people? Of course you could.
"The disappointing thing is it's never going to go away. Regardless of what's said. We all know that we made a monumental mistake. The gravity wasn't as plain until it all came out."
Mitchell Starc
Starc was an integral part of the vaunted Australia attack in Cape Town and remains so in the present day. He is ranked as the number one bowler in Test cricket by the International Cricket Council.
Left-armer Starc repeatedly denied knowledge of the sandpaper plot, including in the statement released with Cummins, Hazlewood and Lyon in 2021, and in a news conference in the days after Khawaja's claims emerged.
Speaking on 10 November, Starc said: "Obviously, there's differing opinions of eight years ago. We were heavily grilled through the process at the time, and since, and I guess I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed. My recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021.
"I'll stick to what I said five years ago, what I said at the time, eight years ago. Clearly, there's different versions from different people, and I'll leave it where I left it back then."
Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon
Along with Cummins and Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon have remained part of Australia's first-choice bowling unit in the eight years since the sandpaper scandal, forming one of the greatest four-man attacks in Test history.
Seamer Hazlewood and off-spinner Lyon joined Cummins and Starc in releasing a statement in 2021, responding to an interview given by Bancroft to the Guardian newspaper when he said the bowlers' involvement in the sandpaper plot was "self-explanatory".
Neither Hazlewood nor Lyon has spoken publicly since the fresh claims from Khawaja, Warner and Bancroft emerged.
Their statement released with Cummins and Starc in 2021 said: "We pride ourselves on our honesty. So it's been disappointing to see that our integrity has been questioned by some journalists and past players in recent days in regard to the Cape Town Test of 2018.
"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.
"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."
Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland
A swing bowler, Sayers played his only Test for Australia after the sandpaper controversy erupted – the fourth and final match of the series against South Africa in Johannesburg.
Sayers, who retired from first-class cricket in 2021, spoke to Australian radio station SEN in the aftermath of Khawaja's claims, to corroborate the former batter's account.
Sayers claimed to have removed sandpaper from the field in the second Test against South Africa, the match before Bancroft was caught. He also backed up Khawaja's assertion that the entire Australia squad discussed the sandpaper issue after it was revealed in Cape Town.
Speaking on 15 November, Sayers said: "I am comfortable sitting here that I believe everyone in that side knew what was going on and what was being used.
"It was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in the changing rooms.
"After the occurrence in Cape Town, we all sat in the changing rooms after that day's play and, probably for 60 to 90 minutes, we talked about what had happened and I guess where to next."
Spinner Holland, who retired in 2021, was also a back-up bowler on the trip.
He also said there was a meeting held in the fallout from Cape Town about players taking responsibility.
"Once we got back to the hotel we did sit as a group [to discuss] what had happened and who was going to take the blame," Holland told newspaper The Australian.
"To Davey's [Warner's] credit, from what I remember, he did put his hand up and say he would take some of the responsibility, but not all of it.
"To be sitting there and seeing three blokes hung out to dry when you are supposed to be part of a team was a pretty hard watch."
- Australia's Sayers 'took sandpaper from field' 
  - Published3 days ago
Peter Handscomb
Batter Handscomb was Australia's 12th man on the day Bancroft was caught, making frequent trips between the field and the dressing room.
Bancroft's account alleges Handscomb was told by Lehmann, via walkie-talkie, to "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".
Last week, following Khawaja's claims but before Bancroft spoke, Handscomb was asked for his recollections after making a century for Victoria in the Sheffield Shield against Western Australia.
On 11 November, Handscomb said: "I appreciate you have to ask these questions. I've had a nice day today, it's not really something that I want to comment on right now. I'll sort of just let the powers of be do their thing."
Graeme Hick
Former England batter Hick was part of the Australia backroom team on the South Africa tour of 2018.
Hick was made redundant by Cricket Australia as part of a series of cost-cutting measures in 2020.
Speaking to the Sydney Morning Herald last week, Hick said: "I have seen the various statements around the coaches, and I'm very disappointed with the broad nature of them.
"Khawaja puts it simply: 'It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us'. To me, what Khawaja is implying here is absolutely false.

With the Air Quality Index (AQI) crossing 400 at some locations in Delhi, people whose work keeps them outdoors for long hours say they are experiencing breathing difficulties, persistent cough, headaches and burning eyes, often without adequate protection against pollution.
For traffic police personnel, domestic workers, roadside vendors, mechanics and gig workers, staying indoors is rarely an option.
Yogendra Kumar, a traffic inspector posted in outer north Delhi, said pollution-related health risks for traffic personnel persists throughout the year but increases significantly when air quality deteriorates.
“The impact on health is inevitable in the outskirts, as road dust also contributes to pollution alongside emissions. We have no safeguards apart from masks. Prolonged exposure causes breathing problems and a persistent cough,” he said.
Reena Chaudhary, a domestic worker in Palam Colony, said she began experiencing breathing difficulties on the night before Deepavali, with her symptoms worsening on the festival day.
“I leave home around 7 a.m. and return by 9 p.m. I began having headaches and burning eyes the day before Deepavali, particularly while passing through smoke-filled lanes between houses at night. On Deepavali, my condition worsened. I felt dizzy throughout the day, had a persistent cough and just wanted to lie down. But who would work if I did?” she said.
Ms. Chaudhary said she had to walk through smoke on Deepavali night with her dupatta wrapped around her face. Since then, she has been taking her daughter along in case she falls ill and is unable to work.
Ravi, a 21-year-old gig worker who attends college during the day, said he works through the night, picking up rides across the city to support his family.
“Even at night, I can see that the air is dense and heavy. At times, I have to stop near a green area, such as Vande Mataram Marg, just to be able to breathe,” he said.
Mukesh Yadav, an e-rickshaw driver in Palam, said road dust remains a problem throughout the year, apart from smoke from firecrackers and vehicular emissions.
“The area remains dusty even on normal days. Since Deepavali, I have been tying a towel around my face,” he said.
Mr. Yadav works eight to 10 hours a day, making several trips between Palam metro station and Kailashpuri, a one-kilometre stretch that witnesses heavy traffic.
“The only time I am not outdoors is when I am charging my e-rickshaw. I thought my cough was due to the cold, but everyone seems to be coughing, even the passengers. It could be due to pollution,” he said.
‘Pollution higher this year’
An analysis by the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that Delhi’s average PM2.5 concentration in the week preceding Deepavali reached 236 micrograms per cubic metre, the highest in three years. This was 97% higher than the 120 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2025 and 32% above the 179 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in 2024.
The study also found that time-bound restrictions on vehicles had failed to ease traffic congestion, with nitrogen dioxide, a marker of vehicular pollution, accumulating during the evening and remaining elevated until midnight, even after traffic had eased.
“Deepavali pollution is an annual tipping point, but elevated particulate levels before the festival this year show that baseline pollution is higher than in previous years,” said Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director (research and advocacy) at the CSE.
She said cleaner air ahead of winter and measures to contain episodic pollution spikes from farm fires and firecrackers could have prevented such severe pollution during seasonal weather changes.

Srinagar, Nov 20: Allegations of organised malpractice in government recruitment have triggered a fresh political confrontation in Jammu and Kashmir, with Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) leader Iltija Mufti on Friday accusing the recruitment system of being vulnerable to an organised network involving government employees and demanding an independent investigation into the alleged cheating racket unearthed during the Finance Accounts Assistant (FAA) examination.
Questioning the Jammu and Kashmir Services Selection Board’s (JKSSB) description of the incident as an isolated attempt to use unfair means, Iltija said repeated controversies surrounding competitive examinations since 2019 had severely undermined the confidence of educated youth in the government recruitment mechanism.
Addressing a press conference in Srinagar, she alleged that a recruitment mafia was operating in the Union Territory and exploiting thousands of unemployed aspirants who spend years preparing for competitive examinations, only to face allegations of paper leaks, examination irregularities and cancellations.
The controversy follows the November 15 Finance Accounts Assistant examination, conducted by JKSSB for 600 posts in the Finance Department. As many as 1,61,946 candidates were scheduled to appear for the examination across 493 centres in all 20 districts of Jammu and Kashmir.
The examination came under scrutiny after Jammu Police foiled an alleged attempt to facilitate cheating through sophisticated electronic communication devices. Police apprehended suspected facilitators and candidates and seized eight wireless sets, around 22 mobile phones and five vehicles allegedly connected with the operation.
Three FIRs were registered at Police Station Domana, while a Special Investigation Team (SIT) was constituted to investigate the alleged network, identify the facilitators and beneficiaries and establish whether more people were involved.
The investigation has also raised questions about the possible involvement of government employees. Reports have indicated that some officials may have assisted the suspected network by facilitating the movement of examination-related material outside examination centres. Their alleged roles are being examined as part of the investigation.
Rejecting JKSSB’s assertion that the attempt was successfully thwarted and did not compromise the examination, Iltija questioned how the Board could describe the incident as an isolated case while the investigation was still underway.
“How can JKSSB give itself a clean chit so soon? This is not a one-off incident. There is a proper mafia operating in the recruitment system,” she said.
She cited controversies surrounding the recruitment examinations for Police Sub-Inspectors, Jal Shakti, Finance Accounts Assistants and Fire and Emergency Services, arguing that repeated allegations of malpractice had created a credibility crisis for the institution.
Referring particularly to the 2022 Police Sub-Inspector recruitment examination, she alleged that question papers had been sold to candidates for Rs 15 lakh to Rs 20 lakh.
The allegations come against the backdrop of the CBI investigation into the 2022 Police Sub-Inspector recruitment examination, in which the agency filed a chargesheet against 24 accused, alleging that the question paper had been leaked through a network involving intermediaries and officials.
According to the CBI investigation, the leaked papers were allegedly sold to aspirants for amounts ranging between Rs 20 lakh and Rs 30 lakh. The examination, conducted on March 27, 2022, was meant to fill 1,200 posts of Sub-Inspectors in the J&K Police. The investigation exposed the involvement of individuals from different departments and institutions and led to arrests across several states.
Iltija argued that the latest FAA controversy should be viewed against this history rather than treated as an isolated attempt by a few individuals.
She also questioned the use of sophisticated electronic devices, including microchips allegedly inserted in candidates’ ears, despite the Board’s claims of strict frisking, biometric authentication and security arrangements at examination centres.
Questioning the possible modus operandi, she alleged that examination-related information could have been transmitted outside through insiders, including invigilators, before answers were relayed to selected candidates through electronic devices.
She asked authorities to establish how such devices could have escaped detection and whether anyone inside the examination system had facilitated the alleged operation.
Raising concerns over the financial burden on aspirants, Iltija questioned the substantial amounts collected by JKSSB through application fees for various recruitment examinations.
She claimed that the Board had collected approximately Rs 113 crore between 2023 and 2026, with annual collections estimated at around Rs 30 crore.
She questioned the accountability of the institution when candidates were repeatedly required to pay application fees, invest considerable time in preparation and travel to examination centres, only to find recruitment exercises surrounded by allegations of irregularities.
The PDP leader said the financial and emotional cost of repeated recruitment controversies was being borne by unemployed youth and their families.
She also questioned the engagement of Aptech for conducting recruitment examinations, referring to the company’s previous blacklisting and controversies surrounding its selection as an examination service provider.
The engagement of Aptech had itself triggered legal and political objections in 2022-23, with aspirants challenging the decision before the High Court.
The issue, however, requires a distinction: Aptech had been blacklisted for a specified period, which the JKSSB chairman subsequently said had expired in 2022. The controversy also involved questions over the tendering process and the eligibility conditions adopted by the Board.
Taking aim at Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, Iltija questioned his reported remarks that JKSSB was not under his control and challenged the apparent contrast with his earlier review of the institution.
She referred to a high-level meeting chaired by Omar Abdullah on May 22, 2025, to review the functioning of JKSSB.
During the meeting, the Chief Minister had directed the Board to remove procedural bottlenecks, expedite recruitment and ensure a time-bound and transparent selection process.
The meeting was attended by senior government officers, including Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo, Advisor to the Chief Minister Nasir Aslam Wani and JKSSB Chairperson Indu Kanwal Chib.
The Board had also presented a comprehensive account of recruitment activities undertaken since 2019, including posts advertised, examinations underway and selections nearing completion.
Questioning the Chief Minister’s position, Iltija asked how he could review the functioning of the Board and direct officers to improve recruitment when he now appeared to be distancing himself from it amid allegations of irregularities.
“If JKSSB is not under your control, how did you hold a review meeting in May? When you have to take credit, you say you reviewed JKSSB, but when questions are raised over irregularities, you say it is not under your control,” she said.
She questioned what prevented the elected government from ordering an impartial investigation and ensuring accountability at every stage of the recruitment process.
With further recruitment examinations scheduled in the coming days, Iltija called for the suspension of upcoming JKSSB examinations until the investigation into the alleged FAA cheating racket is completed and those responsible are identified.
She argued that allowing examinations to proceed without addressing the concerns raised by the latest controversy could further erode candidates’ confidence in the recruitment mechanism.
The demand comes amid apprehensions among aspirants ahead of the scheduled Jammu and Kashmir Police Sub-Inspector recruitment examination.
She maintained that the government must identify those allegedly operating the network, including any officials who may have facilitated the malpractice, instead of limiting the investigation to those apprehended during the police operation.
Iltija also raised concerns over the continued vacancy in the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission (JKPSC) following the resignation of its chairman, Arun Kumar Choudhary, in August.
She questioned the delay in appointing a new chairman, saying that uncertainty surrounding the institution added to the concerns of aspirants preparing for competitive examinations.
She also raised the issue of the pending rationalisation of reservation and demanded the publication of the report of the government-appointed sub-committee examining the matter.
The PDP leader said candidates had been waiting for clarity on the reservation framework, which she described as an important issue affecting their prospects in government recruitment.
She also expressed solidarity with protesting doctors at Government Medical College (GMC) Anantnag, highlighting concerns over stipends and uncertainty regarding permanent employment among young medical professionals.
Maintaining that unemployment and uncertainty over government jobs had become major concerns for Jammu and Kashmir’s educated youth, she said the government needed to demonstrate its commitment to transparent recruitment through concrete action.
“The dreams and future of the youth of Jammu and Kashmir cannot be held hostage to inefficiency, corruption and lack of honesty,” she said.

The Internet Archive's workers are unionizing
They asked founder Brewster Kahle to voluntarily recognize the union, but will go to an NLRB vote if needed.
Workers at the Internet Archive, home to the Wayback Machine, are unionizing. After signing up to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA), they're asking founder Brewster Kahle to voluntarily recognize the union. As a backup, they've filed for a National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) election. Kahle hasn't responded publicly yet.
Wired reports that over 80 of 124 eligible US workers signed on. None of their asks are radical: better pay, additional benefits that apply to everyone and paths for career development and promotion. Organizing committee member Danielle Leard tied the unionization campaign to the Internet Archive's mission, stating that job security, benefits and livable wages go "hand-in-hand with sustaining the Archive long-term."
There's a recent precedent from another Bay Area nonprofit. Wikimedia Foundation workers joined the CWA in September, but only after the foundation refused to voluntarily recognize the effort and it went to an NLRB vote. Wikimedia workers ultimately voted in favor by a count of 158 to 14.
The Internet Archive has had a rocky few years. In 2023, a judge ruled that it violated copyright law by lending ebooks, and it suffered a major cyberattack the following year that left the Wayback Machine out of commission for weeks. Adding to the troubles, many news outlets began blocking the Archive's crawlers, fearing its archival copies could be used as a workaround for AI scraping. But the news hasn't been all bad: the US Senate designated the Internet Archive as an official US government document depository in 2025.

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.
On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.
Mark Brantley, the premier of Nevis, which has autonomous self-governance in some aspects, said he understood that the “country was given very little choice”, but did not “support the winding down of the program”.
The 42-year-old CBI programme, which St Kitts and Nevis pioneered, allows wealthy foreigners to obtain citizenship and ultimately a passport by investing in infrastructure and other development projects. It has brought billions of dollars into the country and in some years accounted for the largest share of government revenue.
In June, the European Commission wrote to the five Caribbean nations that currently operate CBI programmes: St Kitts and Nevis, Dominica, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and St Lucia. It warned that countries may lose visa-free access to its 29-country Schengen area if they did not phase out CBI.
In Friday’s statement, Drew blamed concerns over the programme on mismanagement by previous administrations, including years of underselling to undercut other countries, a controversial prison project, weak escrow protections and investment sums not being properly paid into the citizenship unit.
He said his government had led major reforms to the Caribbean’s programmes with international partners, including the US treasury, but argued that continuing the programme risked visa-free travel to parts of Europe and access to international banking. That could disrupt services allowing visitors to use overseas cards and families abroad to send money home.
Brantley, however, argued it was unfair for the EU to force St Kitts and Nevis to make a move without offering assistance to navigate the transition to other industries.
“I have not yet seen from the EU any corresponding suggestions of assistance. And we have to realise that these citizenship-by-investment programs, not only in St Kitts and Nevis, but … smaller countries of the Caribbean, have contributed significantly to our gross domestic product and also to ensuring that our people … can get adequate access to water and to education, to healthcare and the like,” he said.
Brantley described the 1 June 2028 deadline the EU gave the country to phase out the lucrative programme as “frankly ludicrous”.
In his statement, Drew said the CBI programme “did a lot of good, but it also created a danger”.
“When one source pays for half or more of everything, you are at its mercy. If it stops, everything stops. That is putting all of your eggs in one basket,” he added.
The prime minister said the government aimed to diversify its economy by strengthening tourism, yachting, and digital and creative industries, among others. He added that the sale of clean, geothermal energy is “at the heart of it” with drilling and exploration already planned.
“I will not pretend that the road is easy. Less CBI money means we must spend wisely and plan carefully. We will. Our plan is to make this change by growing our economy. Raising taxes is not part of that plan,” Drew said.
Antigua and Barbuda has also expressed willingness to end the programme, though it is trying to negotiate a longer transition period. The five Caribbean governments have taken differing positions on the EU demand. According to local media, Grenada has indicated it wants its programme to continue until 2032, while Dominica and St Lucia have responded to Brussels without publicly committing to ending their programmes.
Jermine Abel in Basseterre contributed reporting

The FAA fired several hundred employees in February 2025. However …
DOGE itself did not have the authority to make the firings. In all, 352 probationary employees — meaning those in their first year — were let go; 132 were reinstated the following month. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain critical navigation systems, were among those dismissed.
In mid-November, following a nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration, social media users shared claims that the Department of Government Efficiency, a Trump administration initiative to cut government spending and jobs, laid off hundreds of technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical air navigation systems.
"DOGE laid off 400 technicians in charge of maintaining and upgrading critical FAA navigational systems," one Facebook post (archived) read.
(Facebook user Tom Riley)
Versions of the rumor spread on multiple social media platforms, including X and Facebook. Some posts suggested the alleged layoffs contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. Snopes readers also asked about a possible connection between the layoffs and the disruption.
In short, the FAA fired 352 probationary employees in February 2025, but they were not 400 technicians maintaining critical navigation systems, as the posts claimed. According to the FAA, no airway transportation systems specialists, who maintain such equipment, were among those dismissed. The firings did affect employees in other aviation safety and support roles, and some were later reinstated. There was no evidence that the job cuts directly contributed to the Nov. 13 ground stop. As such, we have rated this claim as mostly false.
We have reached out to the FAA with questions about the firings and whether they affected FAA operations. We will update this article if we receive a response.
FAA fired fewer than 400 employees in February 2025
The job cuts mentioned in social media posts did happen, although the number of employees was slightly lower than social media users claimed. In February 2025, the Trump administration fired 352 probationary FAA employees, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy. Of those, 132 were represented by the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union.
Although social media posts attributed the firings to DOGE, the initiative itself did not have authority to fire FAA employees. The FAA fired the employees as part of Trump administration's broader cuts to the federal workforce.
DOGE was, however, involved in discussions about the cuts. In a May 2025 interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," Duffy acknowledged discussing with Elon Musk — who led the DOGE initiative — which FAA positions should be protected from the cuts.
"We went back and forth, and Elon agreed, the president agreed," Duffy said. He also claimed the agency retained all positions considered critical to aviation safety, saying: "The FAA has 46,000 employees. And if you lost 350, is this affecting our safety mission? There's a lot of things the FAA does. But for us, safety is key. So, no, we've retained all those safety positions."
In response to our questions, the Transportation Department directed us to a Nov. 16 statement on X, which read:
MYTH: DOGE got rid of essential employees that made FAA less safe and effective.
TRUTH: The FAA has around 45,000 employees. Less than 400 were let go via DOGE, and they were all probationary, meaning they had been hired less than a year ago. Zero air traffic controllers or critical safety personnel were let go.
(X account @USDOTRapid)
The department also told us that the dismissals "did not negatively affect the Department in any way."
Who was affected by the FAA firings?
Contrary to social media posts, the dismissed employees were not 400 technicians responsible for maintaining and upgrading critical navigational systems.
According to the FAA's May 2026 workforce plan, no airway transportation systems specialists were terminated as probationary employees. Such employees are specialized technicians responsible for maintaining and repairing "radar, communications, navigational aids, airport lighting, backup power, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment."
The Transportation Department also confirmed this in an email to Snopes, stating, "No ATSS were terminated as probationary employees in February 2025 and the FAA has continued to hire and onboard ATSS since the start of this administration."
However, the firings did affect employees in other positions, including some supporting aviation safety and technical operations. According to the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, 59 of the dismissed employees represented by the union worked in technical operations, 39 in flight standards, 19 in mission support services and 15 in air traffic services.
In an email to Snopes, the union provided the following breakdown of the affected positions and their responsibilities:
Aeronautical information specialists – evaluation, selection and preparation of navigation
maps, routes, chart, procedures and flight paths.
Maintenance mechanics maintain and repair the grounds and buildings where controllers and systems
specialists work. This requires detailed knowledge of specific trades such as carpentry, plumbing, and electrical.
Management & Program Assistants and Aviation Safety Assistants – maintain office records, office supplies, updates, logistics support and maintain data reports.
Environmental Protection Specialists – manage, supervise, or perform administrative or program work relating to environmental protection programs. They ensure compliance with environmental laws and regulations.
The union also clarified that the employees dismissed from the FAA's Technical Operations division worked as maintenance mechanics, environmental protection specialists and management and program assistants. "So no, none of them worked directly on navigation or communications equipment," the union told Snopes — referring to all 132 dismissed employees it represented.
Still, the fact that no airway transportation systems specialists were fired does not mean the other positions were completely unrelated to aviation safety. In March 2025 testimony to Congress, PASS President David Spero warned that the job cuts would increase workloads for employees already working in an understaffed agency, saying, "This action will increase the workload for frontline aviation safety workers and place new responsibilities on a workforce that is already stretched thin."
Another complication is the lack of a consistent definition of safety-critical positions. A September 2026 audit by the Transportation Department's Office of Inspector General found the criteria for classifying such positions varied across FAA offices.
Some employees were later reinstated
On March 17, 2025, the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists announced that the FAA was reinstating all 132 dismissed employees represented by the union, following a federal court ruling. According to the union, the employees were expected to return to work on March 20 and receive back pay.
In an email to Snopes in November, the union said that approximately 40 of those 132 employees were no longer represented by the union. "They could have found other employment before or after the court order, been reassigned to another FAA bargaining unit or taken a detail or promotion at the agency," spokesperson Liz Doherty told us.
Therefore, it remains unclear how many of the dismissed employees were still working for the FAA at the time of the Nov. 13 nationwide ground stop. We also asked the Transportation Department for updated figures on the reinstatements and the employees' current status. We will update this article if we receive a response.
No evidence firings caused the ground stop
As for the nationwide ground stop, there is no evidence that the February 2025 FAA firings contributed to the disruption. As we previously reported, the FAA said the problem involved its older communications network. In a Nov. 15 statement, the agency identified two possible locations connected to the disruption, including a site in Arkansas where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router. As of Nov. 19, the exact cause of the shutdown remained under investigation.
In a statement shared after the incident, the union said its represented technicians "were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop." The union also told us via email that it found no direct connection between the firings and the incident:
PASS sees no direct connection between the February 2025 terminations and Friday's ground stop. All the probationary employees are essential to the aviation ecosystem that keeps the National Airspace System functioning safely and efficiently. However, none would have been involved directly with the router upgrades that appear to have caused the ground stop.
Still, the FAA had broader staffing problems. In its May workforce plan (Page 8), the agency said it did not have enough employees to cover all shifts at 67 facilities. The report also found that airway transportation systems specialists worked an average of 115 hours of overtime in fiscal year 2025.
The union also stressed the need for more technicians, telling us:
PASS fully supports the modernization efforts undertaken by the DOT and FAA. However, the FAA agrees that the airway transportation systems specialist workforce is understaffed and earlier this year released that workforce plan calling for the hiring of 750 more technicians. The workforce needs to be fully staffed, funded and provided the resources need to continue performing their safety critical work.
However, there is no evidence that the February 2025 firings contributed to the November ground stop despite these broader staffing problems.
For further reading, before DOGE stopped operating, we investigated numerous rumors about its activities and impact on federal agencies.

There is an uncanny similarity between Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the virus responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic, and air pollution. During the pandemic, the virus entered our bodies through the air we breathed; harmful particulate matter and toxic gases enter through the same respiratory route. Additionally, both damage multiple organs, including the lungs, heart and brain. Yet, while COVID-19 prompted an unprecedented emergency national response, air pollution continues to be treated largely as a seasonal inconvenience.
The harmful effects of air pollution are well-established. An adult takes approximately 20,000–25,000 breaths daily, meaning that even a relatively miniscule worsening of air quality can have substantial health consequences over time. This alone should make improving the quality of air an urgent public health priority.
