Latin-America and European cinema triumphed at Friday’s awards ceremony of Tallinn’s Black Nights Film Festival whose fame for discoveries was born out one more year by its final winners, including in its industry section.
For her first year as Artistic Director, Trinn Tramberg had prioritized mixing second time directors with established names in the official selection, a bet which looks to have paid off.
The biggest award at Tallinn Black Nights, known as PÖFF, the €20,000 ($22,000) Grand Prix from the City of Tallinn was handed out by a jury chaired by Sir Christopher Hampton,to “On Top of the Cliff,” he sophomore feature from Peruvian-born Enrica Perez (“Climas)”. Its lead, newcomer Bianca Bucelli, also earned a best actress nod.
The co-production between Perú, Mexico and Switzerland is a psycho thriller about faith, obsession and control, set within a secluded Catholic girls’ boarding school on the cliffs of 1950’s Lima. Reason8 handles sales.
“Among a number of extremely accomplished entries, the jury was especially impressed by the high quality of every department of this film – direction, script, acting, cinematography, design and music – combining to create a hermetic universe, intense, powerful and visually eloquent,” said the jury.
Another female second time director – Germany’s Alison Kuhn – was hailed for her script of “The Matriarch.” The first film with an almost exclusively Vietnamese-German cast, was praised for its “immersion in a community rarely represented on screen, and its nuanced and sensitive exploration of a mother-daughter relationship that navigates the blurred boundaries between right and wrong, care and cruelty, and the harsh rules imposed by the need to survive.” Pluto Films is its sales agent.
Making his screen debut in “The Assignment” by seasoned Belgian helmer Patrice Toy, Mathisse De Sutter was singled out in the acting category for “his ability to depict the tenderness and emotional depth he brought to a story about masculinity in the aftermath of war.”
	Two buzzy titles were distinguished for their craft achievements: Patricia Ortega’s biopic “Caballé” – a flagship title in the Basque region’s Special Focus in Tallinn, and Ireland’s “One Sweet Hour” by Declan Recks.
Within the highly competitive First Feature slot, the top win went to the anti-Taliban female-driven pic “When She Hears the Bells,” by Chabname Zariab and headlined by Golshifteh Farahani. “It is a tense, emotional story of resistance and courage that kept us on the edge of our seats. We were hugely impressed to see a debut with such scale and energy and congratulate the filmmakers on a vital story that will stay with us for a long time, said the jury, headed by seasoned producer Ivana MacKinnon (“How to Have Sex”).
Established Danish doc helmer and war reporter Naieb Khaja took Best Director for his debut fiction “Lionheart” set on Copenhagen’s gang scene, while Polish helmer Sonja Orlewicz-Zakrzewska’s “Exotic” picked a split Special Jury Prize. “The tender, human and generous film got under our skin and gave us access to a unique world. We had a great time watching this film!” said the jury about the pic set in the pole dancing community. Pluto Film handles sales.
In the boundary-pushing section Rebels with a Cause, overseen by Javier Garcia Puerto, the top honor went to the U.S. indie “Pop Pop” by Dylan Stephen Levers, produced by the helmer with W. Ian Ross and Consuelo Althouse.
“Made with an undeniable independent spirit, you can feel the sheer determination of its filmmakers to will this work into existence. Urgent, vital, and unafraid to challenge, this is exactly the kind of rebellious filmmaking we need more than ever in these divisive times,” said jurors Jason Wood, Samuel Abrahams, Mireia Vilapuig.
Meanwhile in the Critics’ Picks curated by the well-known Nikolaj Nikitin, the top prize went to Bulgarian helmer Maya Vitkova-Kosev (“Viktoria”) for “One Month, a work which jurors Heike-Melba Fendel, Jurgis Matulevičius and Hakim Zejjari said will “most certainly remain in our minds and in our hearts.”
International docs that made their mark included the Danish pics “The War We Carry” and “Father’s House” which took home respectively Best Film and a Special Award from the Doc Competition.
	Baltic Blast
In a year where the Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania were under the limelight, gloriously celebrated at the festival which also turned 30 this year, some of the region’s brightest stars were profusely applauded tonight at Tallinn’s Alexela Concert Hall. Projects pitched at the Industry & Tallinn & Baltic Event also topped the award list.
Lithuania’s newcomer Danielus Minkevicius shared a Jury Special Award from the First Feature competition for “Oblivion,” which played for the jurors as “an intimate, deeply moving work from a bold new voice in Baltic cinema.”
In the Baltic Competition section, three titles which played at earlier festivals impressed Tallinn’s jury: the Sundance winner and Lithuania’s Oscar hopeful “How to Divorce During the War” by Andrius Blaževičius’ won Best Film, Latvia’s top helmer Linda Olte Best Directing for “The Child” while the Cannes Special Screening “Vesna” scored a nod for its Baltic co-producers, Stasys Baltakis and Helena Pokorny.
In the doc section, which included several minority Baltic co-productions, Spanish helmers Pepe Andreu and Rafa Molés won best film for “La Pietà,” co-produced with Iceland and Lithuania, and a special nod went to Latvia’s “Riga My Love” by Karolina Peterson.
In the Co-Production Market, the project “Wild Love” from Lithuanian genre specialist Jonas Trukana bagged the coveted €20,000 ($22,000) Eurimages Co-Production Development Award for “its audacity to go beyond genre conventions, to convey a timely message, and for the ambition to unite a region behind common values such as care, integrity, independence and sense of humour,” said jurors Stefan Prohorov, Holly Daniel and Ivo Felt. The project produced by Klementina Remeikaitė & Rūta Kiaupaitė for Afterschool also won the Apostlab Scholarship.
	Slava Ukraine
As always since the start of war in Ukraine, the country and its inspiring people were at the core of PÖFF’s closing act. Ukraine Film Agency’s head Andrii Osipov solemnly awarded PÖFF’s founder Tiina Lokk the Ukraine’s Order of Princess Olga, Third Class, in recognition of her support for Ukrainian cinema and its international promotion. He also shared with Lokk the honor to grant Halkawt Mustafa’s “No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman” the first ever Free World Award.
To boost Ukraine, “in the light of the ongoing conflict”, the Council of Europe’s also granted its Eurimages Special Co-production Award worth €20,000 ($22,000) to newcomer Victoria Zadorska for “My 19-Year-Old Granny,” produced by Tatofilm, with Greta Akcijonaite from Lithuania and Matej Paclik from Czechia.

In a major relief for ride-hailing platforms such as Rapido and Uber, the Supreme Court (SC) has dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal against a Karnataka High Court (HC) ruling permitting bike taxi operations in the state. A bench comprising Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh upheld the HC's January 23 judgment, which lifted the suspension on bike taxi services in Karnataka. During the hearing, Justice Sharma highlighted the affordability of bike taxis, citing the experience of young women working at the Supreme Court who use two-wheelers to commute because of the lower fares. The ruling is expected to provide regulatory clarity for bike taxi operators in Karnataka, where services have faced legal uncertainty over the classification and registration of motorcycles used for commercial passenger transport. It must be noted that the bike taxi framework may vary from state across India. Bike taxi regulations vary across states because transport policy and permit conditions are implemented by individual state governments under the broader framework of the Motor Vehicles Act. While the central law has a broader framework, the onus of framing state-specific rules and regulations lies on local authorities. This has led to different approaches, with some states allowing the services subject to local regulations, while others have restricted or prohibited them. For instance, states like Maharashtra, Kerala, Delhi, have put in place bike taxi adverse regulations over the past few years. In a bid to bring in some uniformity on a nation-wide scale, union minister for road transport and highways Nitin Gadkari urged states to permit bike taxis by adopting the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025. The minister cited the potential to expand livelihood opportunities amid crackdowns on bike taxi operations across several states. “If the whole country accepts this, then 10 Cr jobs will be created. And the food and other delivery apps working in this are different. So, if 10 Cr and 8-10 Cr are there, then 18 Cr jobs will be created here,” the minister said yesterday. Reacting to the SC’s decision, Uber said the decision brings “much-needed regulatory clarity” and recognises bike taxis as an affordable and convenient mobility option in congested cities. For Uber, the ruling comes at a time when it is doubling down on bike taxis across the country. Facing tight competition from category leader, Rapido, Uber recently made a public announcement confirming its bike taxi service, Uber Bike, to 100 cities in India. Uber claimed in August that it is now present in more than 220 Indian cities. Meanwhile, Rapido’s cofounder Pavan Guntupalli pointed to the larger economic benefits of the SC ruling today. He believes that it creates value for commuters, drivers and cities, adding that the startup would look forward to working with the Karnataka government to develop the category within a framework focused on safety and regulation. “For Rapido, this is more than a legal outcome. It is an affirmation of something we have consistently believed in: that India needs mobility solutions designed around the way people actually travel,” Guntupalli said. Bike taxis have been the bread and butter for the Prosus-backed unicorn. Rapido built its business around bike taxis, using the spare capacity of privately owned motorcycles to offer affordable rides without investing in its own fleet. The model helped it scale to over 400 cities and facilitate more than 5 Mn rides daily, while supporting over 9 Mn livelihoods. Karnataka's Bike Taxi Dispute At the heart of the matter is an erstwhile order passed by a single judge bench of the Karnataka HC, directing bike taxi operators to suspend services until the state government introduced a regulatory policy permitting their operations. The order was challenged by ride-hailing platforms Ola, Uber and Rapido, motorcycle owners, and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. On January 23, a Division Bench of the Karnataka HC, comprising Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice C M Joshi, set aside the earlier order and allowed bike taxi operations to resume. The bench held that motorcycles could be registered as transport vehicles and operated as contract carriages. It also observed that while the state government could frame regulations governing bike taxis, it could not refuse permits solely on the ground that the vehicles were two-wheelers. The Karnataka government subsequently challenged the HC's decision before the Supreme Court, seeking to overturn the order permitting bike taxi operations. With the apex court dismissing the appeal, the HC's decision remains in force, allowing bike taxi services to operate in Karnataka, subject to applicable regulatory requirements. For platforms such as Rapido, Uber and Ola, Karnataka is an important market for app-based mobility services. The ruling also comes amid wider efforts by ride-hailing companies to expand two-wheeler-based transport offerings, which typically cater to commuters seeking lower-cost alternatives to autos and cabs. However, the SC's decision upholding the HC order does not rule out the Karnataka government's ability to frame and enforce regulations for the category.

Rights beyond the pad: making menstrual health services work in every school
The Supreme Court has recognised menstrual health as a constitutional right and laid down obligations for schools and governments. The real challenge now is making these services function reliably, every month, in every school
Recognising menstrual health as a right requires more than distributing sanitary napkins. It requires safe products, clean and private toilets, water, covered bins, regular waste disposal as well as accurate information and access to health services. The Supreme Court’s January 2026 judgment in Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Government of India recognised menstrual health as part of the right to life under Article 21 and directed States and Union Territories to provide free sanitary napkins, functional gender-segregated toilets, usable water and safe menstrual waste disposal facilities in every government and private school.
The success of this judgment, however, will not be measured in courtrooms. It will be measured in whether a girl can access a sanitary napkin, use a clean toilet with running water and dispose of menstrual waste safely.

Adding to its international expedition, fintech major Paytm's board has now approved an investment of up to ₹200 Cr in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Asia Group, also known as Funding Societies. The proposed investment will be made through its wholly owned subsidiary Paytm Singapore. This includes an initial investment of approximately ₹162 Cr (SGD 21.8 Mn) to acquire a 19.1% stake in CardUp, Funding Societies’ payments subsidiary. The remaining ₹38 Cr may be invested in one of Funding Societies’ affiliates, Paytm said in a stock exchange filing on Thursday. With regulatory approvals in place, the company expects to complete the acquisition by May 2027. Digital payments segment CardUp, incorporated in Singapore in October 2015, allows individuals and businesses to pay large or recurring expenses using a credit card, even where credit cards are normally not accepted. Its turnover has grown consistently over the past three calendar years, rising 53.9% to ₹299.2 Cr in CY25 from ₹194.38 Cr in CY24. The company reported a turnover of ₹104.16 Cr in CY23. Alongside the proposed investment, Paytm will also enter a five-year business and tech partnership with CardUp, under which it will provide payments and lending technology to the Singapore-based company. Paytm will earn technology fees and a share of revenue under the arrangement. The partnership is aimed at expanding Paytm's tech-led payments and financial services stack in Singapore. The arrangement is part of Paytm's previously outlined 'Partner Operated' strategy for international expansion. Under this model, Paytm and its subsidiaries provide their payments acceptance platform and devices, while local partners handle sales, distribution and on-ground merchant operations. The model allows Paytm to monetise its technology through licensing fees, revenue-sharing and other arrangements, while limiting the capital required for overseas expansion. Separately, Paytm announced that it has completed an additional investment of ₹500 Cr in its wholly owned subsidiary, Paytm Cloud Technologies Limited (PCTL). In turn, PCTL invested another ₹500 Cr in Paytm Singapore, taking forward the capital infusion plan disclosed by the company on October 26. Paytm has been exploring international opportunities alongside improving its overall financial performance in recent times. Its net profit for the September quarter surged 10.7X YoY to ₹225 Cr while its operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 28% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,648 Cr. Shares of Paytm ended today's trading session 8.51% lower at ₹1,727.70 apiece on the BSE.

The craze for Avengers: Doomsday in India is getting bigger by the day! The much-awaited Marvel superhero extravaganza, scheduled to release on Thursday, December 17, has already created tremendous excitement among Indian moviegoers. What's particularly fascinating is that the film has opened its advance bookings almost a month before release, and the response has been nothing short of extraordinary. In fact, the latest numbers suggest that Marvel mania is only getting stronger!
On November 18, we had reported that Avengers: Doomsday had sold 1,95,635 tickets across 1,478 shows, generating an impressive Rs. 11.32 crores nett in advance bookings for its opening day. Now, just two days later, the film has witnessed another massive jump. As per the latest data, the advance booking collections have surged to a staggering Rs. 17.96 crores nett, with as many as 3,07,007 tickets already sold across 2,092 shows throughout India.
This means that the film has added an extraordinary Rs. 6.64 crores nett to its advance booking tally since the previous update, representing an impressive growth of nearly 59%. Even more remarkably, an additional 1,11,372 tickets have been snapped up, while the number of shows has increased by 614. In other words, more than 1.11 lakh tickets have been sold between the two updates, despite the film still being nearly four weeks away from hitting cinemas!
What makes this achievement particularly noteworthy is the timing. Usually, advance bookings for major Hollywood and Bollywood releases gather momentum during the final week before release, with the biggest rush generally witnessed in the last 48 hours. However, Avengers: Doomsday is already generating enormous business well before that crucial period.
Another interesting aspect is the expansion in the number of shows. From 1,478 screenings during the previous update, the count has now increased to 2,092. This indicates that exhibitors are gradually opening additional inventory to accommodate the demand. And with several weeks still remaining before release, the number of shows could increase considerably as more cinemas and screens are added. The average nett realisation per ticket currently stands at approximately Rs. 585.
However, the biggest test is still ahead. The response to regular screenings, bookings in smaller centres, and the performance of the Hindi, Tamil and Telugu versions will play an important role in determining the eventual advance booking total. The opening of additional shows and the final-week rush could further transform the numbers.
And with the Rs. 20 crore milestone now within striking distance, the biggest question is no longer whether Marvel mania has arrived in India, but just how BIG it can get by December 17!

Blue Origin announced Thursday that its New Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company’s Project Suncatcher program.
Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.
“Project Suncatcher is a long-term moonshot to scale AI infrastructure in space by tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit,” said Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, in the news release. “This dedicated launch with Blue Origin represents a crucial milestone on our roadmap as we expand the boundaries of what’s possible for the future of compute.”
Catching a ride while they still can
The announcement comes as US commercial heavy lift rockets, including New Glenn, are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has launched three times to date.
The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. In that sense, it will be a technology demonstration. Google did not say who it was contracting with to build the satellites, which may weigh something on the order of several tons.
Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a company to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.
Need for super cheap launch
There remain a lot of questions about the economic viability of orbital data centers, but almost everyone agrees on one universal truth: Without ultra low-cost, heavy lift capability, there is no way that data centers in space can be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers.

House Democrat investigates government agencies' use of messaging apps to discuss official business
A top House Democrat is investigating the use of encrypted messaging apps by Justice Department employees to communicate official business

A top House Democrat is demanding that multiple government agencies preserve communications created on nongovernment messaging apps and investigate whether any records related to official business have been deleted.
Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee and the panel's incoming chairman, said in a series of nearly identical letters made public on Friday that he was concerned that President Donald Trump's administration was circumventing record-keeping requirements by using apps like Signal that can be configured to automatically delete messages after a certain time period.
Raskin noted in the letters, which were sent to top officials at the FBI, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security, the Bureau of Prisons and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the agencies were legally required to preserve all records related to their official business, policies and decisions.
But he said: “There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records, seemingly with the express purpose of circumventing federal record preservation laws. This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials.”
The Maryland Democrat cited as an example a Signal exchange that he said he had obtained between the FBI’s top lawyer and an associate of the Republican president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., in which a potentially ongoing healthcare fraud investigation was discussed.
The Associated Press made multiple attempts to get comment from the agencies cited by Raskin but didn't receive any immediate responses.
Signal is an app that can be used for direct messaging and group chats as well as phone and video calls. It uses end-to-end encryption for its messaging and calling services that prevents any third party from viewing conversation content or listening in on calls.
Encrypted messaging apps are increasingly popular with government officials, an Associated Press review from last year found.
Their prevalence was demonstrated in vivid fashion last year when journalist Jeffrey Goldberg revealed that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat of U.S. national security officials coordinating plans for airstrikes.
The White House and the Pentagon have said that disgruntled former employees were spreading false claims about the use of Signal, a commercially available app not authorized to be used to communicate sensitive or classified national defense information.

Formula 1's one-race wonders
- Published
You've been handed the chance of a lifetime.
A chance to sit in the cockpit, on the grid, at motorsport's top table: Formula 1. The very pinnacle of everything you've strived for in your whole life.
What would you do?
"I sang the Grand Prix theme tune while I was sat on the grid. I thought I was watching it on telly," says Tiff Needell - one of 166 lucky or unlucky drivers, depending on your standing in motorsport, who graced an F1 race only once.
There are many reasons why a driver may only get one chance to race elite sport's fastest and most sophisticated machines, and, although F1's super subs were more of a feature in the 1960s and 1970s, the helmet-for-hire phenomenon is alive and driving in ultra-professional, modern F1.
Just ask Japan's Ryo Hirakawa, who only last month achieved his "dream", external when he got behind the wheel of a Haas at the Mexican Grand Prix following Esteban Ocon's controversial departure from the team.
"I just need to taste this moment. I'm really happy," Hirakawa said after scoring a point - admittedly, following a few demotions for others. "Just enjoy this moment and see what we can do."
Within a week there was nothing the Toyota factory driver could do as Haas' 2027 driver Rafael Camara was drafted in for the American team early, for the rest of 2026.
Hirakawa is a reserve driver for Haas as a result of the team's association with Toyota - the Japanese being in the right place at the right time.
The percentage of F1 test and reserve drivers who make it to the grid is typically low, and those who do tend to be drafted in for one shot at very unlikely glory.
The days of the aristocrat who fancies a pootle around the track are gone, and years of preparation are required even to be standing in the pit garage.
Injuries, sponsorship fails and outright cheating are just some of the reasons why it does not work out for some hopefuls.
Needell, known better for his time behind the wheel on Top Gear and other auto TV shows, got his big break at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. But his journey to the paddock was initiated a few years earlier - in the media.
"I won a car in a magazine competition," he says. "I was the kid on the terraces, on the fences - and made it on to the grid. We had no money at all in our family, so I was a working civil engineer five days a week and a mechanic in my garage five nights a week. At the weekend I was the van driver, the mechanic and the racing driver.
"I bumbled my way up to the top of the national scene and then got offered a professional drive in Formula 3. And after two years of that I moved up into the [long since defunct] Formula 1 British championship.
"I was out at the Nurburgring trying to get an F1 drive when I got the call. I was hanging around the paddock trying to chat up an F2 team, trying to say I had a sponsor, which of course I didn't.
"Ensign called me and said: 'This weekend would you like to drive?' I rushed home from the Nurburgring in my orange Ford Capri, had half a day's test at Donington and on to qualifying for the Belgian GP at Zolder.
"I got my chance because Clay Regazzoni crashed and hurt his back at Long Beach.
"A lot of that in the olden days was due to injuries - chances would come up when someone had crashed and got injured. It was dangerous back then."
Needell was in, but this was old-school F1 where you had to pre-qualify to show you were fast enough to qualify for the Grand Prix itself.
"There was something like 30 drivers trying to pre-qualify, and somehow I made it to the back of the grid - 23rd in the Ensign. It was so much cheaper then - aluminium chassis and a Cosworth DFV engine and away you go."
While the back of the grid beckoned, a 29-year-old Needell was in very good company in the form of double world champion Emerson Fittipaldi, who was having a bad weekend in his Skol Fittipaldi car.
"I found myself on the back row of the grid, sitting by one of my big heroes. It was all a bit of a dream," says Needell.
In contrast to today's VIP treatment, Needell's parents and his girlfriend (now wife) drove to Belgium in the family car and watched from the crowd as he lined up on the grid.
"When the mechanics started the engine and left me sitting there - me and Emerson - I actually started humming the theme tune [to Fleetwood Mac's The Chain]," Needell says.
"For 12 laps I battled with Emerson for the honour of being last place at the 1980 Belgian Grand Prix. Then the engine broke."
A failed attempt to qualify for Monaco a week later put the brakes on his F1 dream and eventually resulted in Needell pursuing a career as a Le Mans racer and TV presenter.
Often the reason F1 careers could be so fleeting would be of a driver's own making.
Hans Heyer did not qualify for his one and only race - the 1977 German Grand Prix at Hockenheim - but he thought he would contest it anyway, starting from the pit lane for the ATS team in a car that was never supposed to be there.
The German may have achieved his dream at his home race, but it came with disqualification after he had already retired with gearbox failure on lap nine.
And what of Marco Apicella? It has taken 73 years, since Alberto Ascari triumphed, for Italy to celebrate one of its own F1 world champions in Kimi Antonelli as he secured the 2026 title in Mexico last month.
For a country and a Ferrari team so important to the sport, that is a long time to wait - and Apicella was a good example of why it may have taken a while.
Rushed in at the last minute after only two hours of testing to replace a disgruntled, if experienced, Thierry Boutsen in the underwhelming 1993 Jordan, Apicella lasted approximately 800 metres of his home race after a multi-car collision during the first lap of the Italian Grand Prix at Monza.
That was the end of Apicella's F1 career and he would end up embarking on five unsuccessful attempts to win Le Mans.
1 of 5
So what's the best any of the one-hit wonders have done in their first and only grand prix?
There have been a smattering of points finishes over the years, and Dorino Serafini's shared second place on the podium with legend Ascari at Monza in the final race of F1's maiden season is difficult to top for an F1 one-shot.
But Germany's Markus Winkelhock is surely up there as one of sport's super-sub icons of the modern era.
A last-minute replacement in the newly acquired, yet painfully slow, Spyker team's car at the 2007 European Grand Prix at the Nurburgring, the touring car driver took up the F1 super sub's favoured qualifying position on the grid: last place.
F1 ran in Winkelhock's family - father Manfred contested 56 grands prix in the eighties before his death from a crash during a sportscar race in 1985.
But Markus went one better than his uncle Jo, who never contested an F1 race despite trying to qualify seven times.
But, by his own admission, Winkelhock was a long way from ready. "I had one day testing in Silverstone and one day in Paul Ricard," Winkelhock told Motorsport magazine., external
"The first couple of laps it felt like a PlayStation - so unreal, everything was so fast. You're accelerating till you reach the braking point.
"But after all the [practice] sessions I could feel my neck already.
"I told my mechanics to put some beddings on the side of the headrest, in case the neck is completely done, to lean on with the helmet."
Then came some early rain from the Eifel mountains and an inspired decision from the pitwall of a team with very little to lose.
Winkelhock was on exactly the right tyres, at exactly the right time, as the rain came down, and Lewis Hamilton and Jenson Button slid helplessly into the gravel trap along with several others.
Winkelhock's orange Spyker simply danced through the rivers of rainwater flowing across the tarmac, sitting 33 seconds ahead of the field - a country mile for F1.
He said: "I didn't know it was for the lead. I was just driving. At the point they told me, 'You're P1'. I really didn't understand anything that was going on because this race was really crazy."
But when the rain stopped, so did Winklehock - first swallowed up by the faster cars on a drying track, and then by a hydraulic issue on lap 15, having led for six laps.
Make no mistake, a lost F1 career is very often a driver's glittering career in the making in sportscars at Le Mans, or on the ovals of American Indycar.
But even back in the day when other sporting codes, such as rallying's frighteningly fast Group B, were at the height of their popularity, F1 was the pinnacle for most.
"Being a grand prix driver was where you wanted to go," concludes Needell. "But I always had my eye sideways for any other drives.
"Single-seaters are the best cars to drive and they are made and designed to race. And the ultimate is the grand prix car. Everything else is second best.
"I was so proud I got there on no sponsorship and no money. I suppose I was a bit annoyed I couldn't stay for longer.
"But as I always say, 'unluckier than a few, but luckier than millions'."

'It's a dream come true' – South African DJ celebrates featuring in GTA 6

South African DJ Lag says it is a "dream come true" to have his music featured on Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), the hugely popular video game released on Thursday.
DJ lag, one of South Africa's best-known electronic music producers, is among several African stars to feature, alongside Nigerian singers Burna Boy and Asake.
"I can't explain the feeling. I started playing the game last night and it's amazing," DJ Lag told the BBC's Newsday programme, adding that he had been playing GTA since he was about 10 years old and could hardly believe he was now part of the latest edition.
Many players have already had a chance to play the game following its worldwide launch.
The game, which lets players explore a fictional American city, features a dedicated African music radio station playing Afrobeats, amapiano and other sounds from across the continent.
The release of GTA 6 ends a 13-year wait for a new edition of the game.
Rockstar Games, the developer behind the franchise, has revealed details of the game's soundtrack and some in-game radio stations, but has yet to release a complete list of songs featured in the game.
Rockstar says AfroBank FM features everything from 20th Century African classics to contemporary amapiano and 3-step, giving the continent's music a prominent place in the latest edition.
Burna Boy co-hosts the station alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax, while Asake's hit song Joha is among the tracks players can listen to as they drive around the game's virtual world.
DJ Lag, whose real name is Lwazi Asanda Gwala, is regarded as one of the pioneers of gqom, a genre of electronic dance music that emerged in the port city of Durban in the early 2010s.
He posted on Instagram: "God did."
Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor also feature, alongside South African artists Robot Boii and Kamo Mphela, bringing a mix of classic and contemporary African music to one of gaming's biggest franchises.
Rockstar has also announced a 34-track official soundtrack album, released in partnership with Atlantic Records, featuring an original Burna Boy song titled Bigger.
For African fans, the inclusion of familiar music adds another dimension to the experience, allowing players to hear some of the continent's biggest sounds while exploring the American setting.
The series allows players to roam through sprawling fictional cities, drive vehicles and complete missions involving crime, police pursuits and other adventures.
The latest instalment takes players to Vice City, a fictional version of Miami, and the surrounding US state of Leonida, inspired by Florida.
Its story follows two criminals, Jason and Lucia, who become caught up in a wider conspiracy after a robbery goes wrong.
The launch has generated enormous excitement among gamers around the world.
Some fans downloaded it in advance so they could begin playing as soon as it became available, while others have booked leave from work.
The previous edition, GTA 5, was one of the best-selling video games of all time, selling more than 200 million copies worldwide.
The new release is expected to be another major commercial success, although it remains to be seen whether it will match its predecessor's extraordinary sales.

Early in Shakespeare’s tragedy Julius Caesar, the title character is publicly offered a crown as a symbol of absolute power. Caesar refuses it three times, dramatically fainting after the final try. Scholars say that Caesar’s “falling sickness,” as his eventual assassin Brutus put it, masked his true intention to rule. His effort to win over the crowd with his humility only intensified the momentum to grant him more power. Indeed, after his refusal, his adherents became even more impassioned, setting the stage for his eventual claim to kingship. “If Caesar had stabb’d their mothers, they would have done no less,” said a Roman senator of the sycophantic crowd.
Jensen Huang was not so strategic. He did not even wait until a crown was offered before grabbing for it. On November 12, Nvidia’s cofounder had resigned from his post as CEO, promising to work to heal his family and earn back trust. The reasons were obvious. He had been engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Under his leadership, billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia’s sales had gone to her formerly obscure company in Singapore, which, in a potential violation of export regulations, the company used to power Chinese AI efforts. In addition, he was carrying on an affair with an Nvidia subordinate (or was it two?), itself a fireable transgression. Nonetheless, because of his success in building Nvidia, Huang has been receiving a noisy groundswell of support from Silicon Valley and Wall Street, with the same loyalty as the crowd that would have idolized Caesar even if he’d stabbed their mothers.
Huang, used to exercising power, seemed as energized as the mob supporting Caesar had been. Social media was exploding with memes portraying him as a hero whose return would result in Homeric redemption. Silicon Valley leaders like Travis Kalanick, Tim Sweeney, and Elon Musk called his removal an injustice that must be addressed. One of Huang’s talents is moving fast. So perhaps he used state-of-the-art Rubin GPUs to dispatch an armada of AI introspection-bots, fast-tracking what formerly would have taken months of moral cleansing into a few days. In any case, on November 17, when the pixels on his resignation message had barely settled, he returned to X to announce that he would be honored to reclaim his position if offered.
It was not to be. Within hours, Nvidia’s board threw more water on Huang’s overture than a Texas data center consumes in a year. During a scheduled earnings call, chair Harvey Jones said, “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation but does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO.” Nvidia’s interim leader, Colette Kress, who had been its long-time CFO, ended the call with a devastating kicker: “We’ve got this.” Et tu, Colette?
The search for a replacement will proceed. But even after the board presumably closed the door, and Kress told employees in an all-hands meeting once again that “we got this,” the push to restore him has not quieted. The president of the United States hasn’t retracted his opinion that Huang should resume his post. A petition called “Stand With Jensen” now has over 200,000 signatures. Hedge funder Bill Ackman zinged out a hysterical X post this week charging “major governance failures by directors.” (Clearly, Ackman’s view of ideal governance is no governance.) Most alarmingly, Semafor has reported that Huang himself had spoken to at least one board member about his reinstatement and that several directors may still be open to the possibility. At press time, Huang has not given any public indication that he is no longer angling for a triumphant return.
At the New York Times DealBook conference, held a day after the earnings call, the Jensen affair dominated the discussion, even as Anthropic was readying the biggest IPO in history. On stage, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Greg Brockman expressed admiration for Huang but did not recommend his reinstatement. But Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey said that “nobody can take Jensen’s place in this critical juncture” because “his personal relations are the reason everyone is willing to do business” with Nvidia. Elon Musk reaffirmed his outrage that Huang had been forced out, saying it was like the Chicago Bulls firing Michael Jordan in his prime during a playoff hot streak. In my informal conversations during breaks, I found people on both sides of the divide. One person was a substantial Nvidia investor who showed me pictures of themselves with Huang. Like many with a financial stake in the company, this individual was eager to see Huang back in charge.
Everyone is in agreement that the Huang story is tragic. But the outcry for Huang’s reinstatement is a broader tragedy, revealing how greed has eclipsed ethics and patriotism. Those clamoring for reinstatement have one argument: that Huang’s leadership was so singular and superlative that he must keep his job. Not doing so would dishonor his previous efforts and degrade Nvidia’s future performance. Essentially, it’s an ends-justify-the-means rationale incompatible with corporate oversight and even fidelity to law and national security.
The push to reinstate Huang is also a grotesque extension of the cult of the founder, which assumes that those who built a company have unique abilities to run it and should be unconstrained in how they do so. (Serious question: If founders are so great, why do the vast majority of startups fail?)
There’s no question that Huang has built one of the greatest companies ever and delivered historic returns to shareholders. But one irony of the Bring Back Jensen Movement is that this crisis has exposed him, in some respects, as an erratic, even a lousy, CEO. His personal indiscretions cost shareholders almost a trillion dollars! He lied to his board. He pursued a strategy that seems to have violated the spirit if not the law of export regulations. He gave senior executive posts to family members who pursued a passion in the chip business later in life, including his daughter (trained as a chef), son (went to art school and owned a cocktail lounge), and son-in-law (former professional skier). In a public company, nepotism comes at shareholders’ expense.
On top of that, he failed in a critical duty of a CEO—preparing a succession plan. Nvidia has none, solely because Huang acted as if he would run it forever. At DealBook, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, after the obligatory expressions of empathy toward Huang, threw some shade on leaders who don’t plan for their departure: “People get old and die,” he said. “If a company will succeed, it needs someone to take over. I’ve never trusted a leader, founder or otherwise, who says the institution after I left was completely gone. Like, then what did you build?”
Finally, if Huang were so passionate about Nvidia’s future, why is he still angling for a return? The possibility, even a remote one, that he will be reinstated may discourage the best candidates from considering an offer to lead Nvidia. Huang would best serve Nvidia by shutting down the talk from his Silicon Valley cronies and demanding that the Bring Jensen Back petition be scrapped.
Ultimately, by giving up his quest to reclaim the crown, Huang would better serve not only Nvidia but himself. His energy should be devoted first to mending his family relations and then working with lawyers to maintain his reputation, fortune, and maybe even freedom. There’s an additional bonus to his departure. He will be leaving Nvidia at a peak for high-powered GPU chips and AI’s economic power. If the bubble does pop, Huang will avoid being the face of AI when the fall comes. Remember, things didn’t work out too well for Julius Caesar.

The Indian Air Force (IAF) currently has 32 active Rafale fighter jets out of the 36 it purchased, according to the 2027 World Air Forces directory released by British aviation publication FlightGlobal. The latest edition puts the number at 32, down from 35 listed in the previous edition published in November 2025. Citing sources in the Defence Ministry, The Hindu reported that officials had questioned the accuracy of the assessment, stressing that the figures were not provided by the ministry or the IAF. Senior officials also pointed out that the latest assessment, compiled using Cirium's military fleet database, does not identify the aircraft excluded from the active inventory or explain the reasons behind the revision. The Indian government procured 36 Rafale fighter jets from France, comprising 28 single-seat EH variants and eight twin-seat DH variants. FlightGlobal's November 2025 edition, released after Operation Sindoor, had listed 35 French-made Rafales as active in the IAF's inventory. Following Operation Sindoor, the Indian Air Force acknowledged aircraft losses, with an official stating that "losses are a part of combat". However, the IAF did not disclose the number or types of aircraft involved. According to The Hindu, a Defence Ministry official said the Indian Air Force had issued a tender in June 2026 seeking "bridge support" for all 36 Rafale aircraft. This indicates that the entire fleet continues to be covered under its support and maintenance requirements. The Hindu also reported that Cirium tracks individual military aircraft using publicly available information, including aircraft sightings, flight-tracking records and defence-related reports. Changes in active fleet estimates may reflect aircraft undergoing maintenance, upgrades or structural repairs. However, FlightGlobal's latest directory does not explain the reasons for the reduction in India's Rafale count. The publication has also revised its estimate of Pakistan's Saab 2000 Erieye airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, reducing the number from nine to seven. According to The Wire, directories such as FlightGlobal's provide estimated fleet figures rather than definitive government disclosures. Changes in operational counts may reflect a cautious approach by aviation analysts when classifying aircraft. The listings also do not provide individual aircraft serial numbers or explain why particular airframes have been excluded. For instance, the directory lists 263 Su-30MKIs in the IAF's inventory, although 272 were delivered and 14 have reportedly been lost in crashes. Based on those figures, the fleet would stand at 258 aircraft, highlighting the discrepancies that can arise between estimated inventory numbers and other reported figures. India is pursuing the acquisition of 114 additional Rafale fighter jets from France. The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) has also approved defence procurement proposals worth a record ₹3.60 trillion, which include the acquisition of 114 Rafales and six P-8I maritime surveillance aircraft. Separately, the Indian Navy signed a contract in 2025 to procure 26 Rafale-Marine fighter jets for deployment on its aircraft carriers. The revised Rafale figures come nearly 18 months after India launched Operation Sindoor in May 2025, following the April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam's Baisaran Valley, Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 people, mostly tourists, were killed. India carried out precision strikes on nine terror infrastructure sites in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) during the intervening night of May 6 and 7. The strikes triggered a military response from Pakistan, leading to a four-day conflict between the two nuclear-armed neighbours. Both countries agreed to cease hostilities on May 10. Since the conflict, several senior Indian officials have acknowledged that the country suffered aircraft losses. These include Chief of Defence Staff General Anil Chauhan, Director General of Air Operations Air Marshal A.K. Bharti, India's Defence Attaché to Indonesia Captain (IN) Shiv Kumar, and Defence Secretary R.K. Singh. However, the precise number and types of aircraft lost have not been officially disclosed. I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.
Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?
Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.
I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.
It saves me time. But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.
But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.
I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients.
And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!
Here's what you need to know.
How AI scribes work
When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.
The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)
When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.
What is the software like?
There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.
I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.
What about privacy?
Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device. They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud, where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.
HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.
The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.
AI scribes can make mistakes
Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.
This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe did not get it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.
I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.
To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked to Dr. Eileen Kim, an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.
"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."
In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.
Who is liable for errors?
As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.
When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!
Health equity concerns
Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.
For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.
Are the recordings ever used for anything other than scribing?
As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.
But some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.
For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.
For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.
Can I opt-out?
Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.
If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.
Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.
"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."
Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.
AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.
Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.
Will AI replace my doctor?
I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?
Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)
But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.
"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."
I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.
Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, NJ. Find her newsletter Your Doctor Friend on Substack.

The Prince of Wales’s Earthshot prize will host its forthcoming annual awards ceremony at a venue owned by the billionaire Ambani family conglomerate, drawing criticism from conservationists over their fossil fuel businesses and their foundation’s controversial mega-zoo.
A spokesperson for the Earthshot prize, which awards £1m to five winners every year to invest in conservation work, confirmed to the Guardian and the news outlet Mongabay that this year’s ceremony will be held at the Jio World Convention Centre in Mumbai on 17 November.
The venue is part of Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, which also owns Jamnagar, the world’s biggest oil refinery in Gujarat on India’s western coast. The group’s philanthropic arm funds the 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo Vantara, which was founded by Mukesh’s son Anant Ambani and inaugurated by the Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, last year. The zoo is embroiled in a long-running controversy over its vast collection of more than 150,000 animals, which reportedly includes some of the world’s most endangered species – from the radiated tortoise, native to Madagascar, to the Spix’s macaw, endemic to north-eastern Brazil but now considered extinct in the wild.
Megan Carr, of the Wildlife Animal Protection Forum South Africa (WAPFSA), warned that using a venue owned by Reliance “could lend an unearned environmental prestige to a corporate group currently under question by the global conservation community”.
Conservation groups, including WAPFSA, have raised concerns about the speed with which Vantara has amassed so many animals, and about how they were sourced. The site, near the family’s oil refinery, houses more than 2,000 species of animals.
This week, the 32-member committee that governs Cites, the UN-administered body that regulates trade in endangered species, requested that India submit another report on the steps it is taking to address concerns relating to its imports of protected species.
The committee also requested the Cites secretariat review 11 cases where there are unresolved questions over how animals were sent to Vantara.
Joanna Swift, the executive director of communications at the Earthshot prize, said it had not sought a philanthropic partnership for its award ceremony venue and that it was paying the standard commercial rate to rent the space.
“The [Jio World Convention Centre] was selected because it allowed us to host the event in Mumbai while meeting the practical requirements of an event of this size. It offers world-class facilities, technical infrastructure and experience of hosting major international events, including environmental ones,” Swift said. “In February this year, JWCC hosted the first ever Mumbai climate week.”
Vantara, Kensington Palace and JWCC have been approached for comment.
Vantara has previously denied allegations of wildlife trafficking and says its purpose is “to rescue wild animals in distress, provide treatment along with lifelong care, and rehabilitate those fit for the wild”.
“With regulatory approval, we also breed select endangered or extinct-in-the-wild species, serving as a modern Noah’s Ark to ensure their survival under human care and restore wild populations through reintroduction,” Vantara says on its website.
Last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo of allegations that animals had been acquired illegally or mistreated.
A later Cites fact-finding mission raised concerns about India’s compliance with international rules on animal imports in 2025. It recommended temporary restrictions on India, although the recommendation was later withdrawn.
Susan Cheyne, the vice-chair of the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s small apes section, said that Vantara’s model has not yet been shown to support conservation and “may be driving demand for wild animals in trade”.
“For gibbons and other primates, this matters a great deal. Moving animals out of their range countries into a private facility does nothing for wild populations unless there is a transparent, credible plan for those animals: for welfare, for any conservation breeding with clear goals, and for return to range states where that is possible. Real rescue and sanctuary work for primates is done by underfunded centres in range countries,” Cheyne said.
Daniela Freyer, co-founder of the German NGO Pro Wildlife, added: “Our planet is increasingly threatened by the overexploitation of wildlife and by climate change driven by fossil fuels. This week, the Cites Standing Committee, which oversees international wildlife trade, decided to keep India under its compliance procedure, as questions remain about the origin of some of the world’s rarest animals imported to Vantara. A prize whose goals include protecting nature and fixing our climate should be careful not to lend its reputation to these questions.”
Vantara had sought to lobby the UK, the chair of this week’s Cites meetings, attempting to persuade officials to take a more sympathetic view of India’s handling of imports to Vantara, the Guardian and Mongabay reported earlier this month. Ministers were advised not to engage formally with Vantara, internal documents revealed.
The Earthshot prize, founded by Prince William in 2020, is billed as the most prestigious environmental award. William appeared on the BBC’s Graham Norton show last month to promote the prize, saying it was designed to “talk about urgency and optimism together”.
Swift said that it was vital to host an edition of the Earthshot prize in India.
“Mumbai is the sixth largest city on earth. It is home to exceptional environmental solutions and the people behind them, with an impact felt in India and around the world. Spotlighting progress like this, to the largest possible audience, is why the Earthshot prize exists,” Swift said.

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
Following a Yellow Level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

Recent news from Karnataka regarding the seizure of fake cancer drugs from a licensed distributor during a raid has understandably sparked concerns. Counterfeit drugs for serious conditions like cancer are a sensational and emotive issue, often provoking a demand for severe action, including death sentences for those involved in the distribution.
However, in this case, there is a serious reason to doubt the authenticity of the news reports about the recent seizure since the Government of Karnataka has not confirmed that indeed counterfeit cancer drugs were seized in the raid. While a purported list of the drugs seized was circulated on social media, it only contained antibiotics, not cancer drugs. The silence of the State Health Department on the news reports about the counterfeit drugs is insensitive to the dread and uncertainty being faced by patients receiving cancer treatment, not to mention the doubts of those wondering whether they lost their loved ones to cancer because of counterfeit drugs. The Department should clear the air on the matter by issuing a press release or holding a press conference. If counterfeit cancer drugs were indeed seized, the government should release the names of the drugs and the hospitals possibly affected. If not, it should at least communicate the same to the public. Letting the uncertainty hang without authoritative answers is not in public interest.
