The ongoing slugfest between the Opposition and the ruling party over alleged electoral malpractices by the Election Commission of India (ECI) is deeply troubling. Elections are the foundation of democratic legitimacy. When citizens doubt the fairness of electoral rolls or institutional impartiality, the damage extends far beyond any single election, weakening trust in the state and deepening political polarisation. India’s strength lies in reconciling diversity with shared citizenship—a strength that must be protected through transparency and an electoral process every eligible Indian can trust.
India’s democracy has never been merely a ritual at the ballot box. It is a living promise that every citizen holds an equal place in the political community. That promise is tested in everyday encounters between citizens and the state: from ration offices to electoral rolls.
The controversy over the ECI’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls brings this test into sharp focus. The ECI states the exercise ensures voter lists remain accurate and free of duplicates, under the principle that no eligible voter be excluded nor any ineligible person included. Clean rolls are essential; no credible democracy can tolerate deceased voters on registers or ineligible persons casting ballots. The issue, therefore, is not whether India should maintain accurate voter lists, but whether the process strengthens public confidence or weakens it.
When procedure becomes anxiety
The SIR exercise, which began in Bihar in 2025 and expanded across other states and Union Territories, has seen contested procedures, shifting timelines, large-scale deletions, and documentation disputes. Reports cite lakhs of notices, “logical discrepancies,” and repeated deadline extensions.
For ordinary Indians, these are questions of belonging, not abstract administration. Voters may be asked to establish links to older rolls or produce documents that poor, migrant, elderly, homeless, or marginalised citizens rarely possess. A name wrongly marked as absent, shifted, or duplicate turns citizenship into a bureaucratic ordeal, shifting the burden of proof onto those least equipped to navigate government offices and digital portals.
The ECI maintains its SIR orders are unanimous and lawful, noting no name can be deleted without prior notice and a speaking order, with appeals to the District Magistrate and Chief Electoral Officer. Formal safeguards matter, yet they do not automatically create trust. Public confidence depends on whether citizens can understand the rules, obtain documents without hardship, and see errors corrected promptly. When shifting deadlines and confusing forms force voters to fight to stay on the rolls, perceived fairness suffers.
Democracy is more than voting
Democracy in India is too often reduced to election day, yet voting is only one moment in a continuous process. Citizens must register without obstruction beforehand and hold governments accountable afterward through courts, legislatures, and a free press.
Democratic backsliding rarely begins by abolishing elections. It begins quietly when legal procedures weaken oversight, political parties deepen social divisions to consolidate vote banks, and public institutions hesitate to challenge power. Media platforms reward outrage over evidence, and citizens increasingly view democratic procedures as weapons between “us” and “them.”
In this environment, the Indian state remains present—more present than ever through digital identification, surveillance, and welfare databases—while its legitimacy weakens. Citizens begin to believe rules are applied selectively, records are unreliable, or institutions serve power rather than the public. This is quiet democratic decay: institutions continue to function, yet trust departs.
The Kaplan warning and the Indian reality
Robert D. Kaplan’s 1994 essay, “The Coming Anarchy,” warned that population pressure, resource scarcity, urbanisation, and sectarian conflict could overwhelm states faster than democratic ideals could save them. He argued elections alone cannot compensate for weak bureaucracy, poor policing, environmental pressure, and social fragmentation.
While Kaplan’s apocalyptic tone appears overstated today, his core insight remains vital for India: democracy requires governability—the state’s practical capacity to deliver security, justice, basic services, and equal citizenship.
India illustrates both sides of this tension. Since 1950, it has sustained universal adult franchise and preserved its constitutional framework through wars, emergencies, and economic crises. Yet India also faces uneven development, environmental stress, urban overcrowding, communal polarisation, unequal access to justice, and pressure on independent institutions. These challenges do not make collapse inevitable, but they create conditions where public trust steadily erodes.
Electoral integrity and inclusion
The SIR controversy matters because it touches the bedrock of democratic citizenship: the right to vote. A clean roll achieved through inclusive verification, clear communication, adequate time, and accessible documentation enhances Indian democracy. Conversely, an opaque, rushed, or burdensome process makes citizens feel their citizenship is conditional. Electoral integrity is not merely the absence of fraudulent votes; it is the presence of fair procedures for every eligible voter. If the state excels at flagging suspected duplicates but falters at restoring wrongly deleted citizens, it shifts the risk of administrative error onto vulnerable Indians.
Rebuilding trust
The remedy lies not in abandoning electoral revision, but in making it visibly fair. Under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, booth-level officers make prior intimations and door-to-door visits before treating an elector as untraceable, while draft rolls are published with a statutory period for claims and objections, backed by appeals to the District Magistrate and Chief Electoral Officer.
These mechanisms must become accessible in practice. Booth-level officers should be equipped to assist vulnerable voters rather than merely hunt discrepancies. Deadlines must reflect the realities of migration, poverty, age, disability, and digital exclusion across India. Notices must use plain local languages, support every deletion with clear reasons, and offer practical routes to restoration.
The ECI states valid grievances received during the claims-and-objections period result in names being restored before the roll is finalised. That commitment must be visible on the ground, not merely stated in press notes. Transparency means explaining decisions publicly, correcting errors promptly, and treating the Indian voter not as a potential offender, but as the source of democratic authority.
The choice before India
If India demonstrates that a clean roll and an inclusive roll are the same objective, it will strengthen its democracy. If it allows citizens to believe administrative purification comes at the cost of political exclusion, it will feed the distrust on which democratic decay thrives.
The coming anarchy, if it arrives in India, will not announce itself through collapsed capitals or empty parliaments. It will arrive quietly: through weakened courts, intimidated journalists, polarised neighbourhoods, depleted resources, unreliable records, and citizens who no longer believe the state belongs to them.
India’s democratic story is not yet Kaplan’s prophecy, but it reminds us democracy must be renewed in ordinary life. It proves itself not merely by removing doubtful entries, but by ensuring the poor, migrant, elderly, disabled, and politically unpopular can secure their place on the rolls without fear.
Anarchy is not written into India’s future. It becomes possible only when societies stop repairing the bonds between citizen and state, between majority and minority, and between power and accountability. The choice before India is not between perfect democracy and inevitable collapse, but between a republic renewed through fairness, trust, and inclusion, and one that slowly hollows out while preserving its outward forms. The coming anarchy will begin wherever Indian citizens are made to feel they must prove, again and again, that they belong.
The writer is a former Indian Army officer. He writes on issues pertaining to Jammu & Kashmir.

Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump, California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway.
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep. Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News.
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health, often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.
But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.
Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.
“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”
At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”
Tu says that Huang has visited his shop three times since 2023, and he always orders the same thing: mango shaved ice with tangyuan (sticky rice balls). The dessert, a blend of tropical fruit and condensed milk, is popular in Taipei’s bustling night markets, especially among first-time visitors to the island.
“When he came in for shaved ice, he would spend half an hour eating a single bowl,” recalled Tu. “Whenever someone came up to take a photo with him, he got right up. He’s not pretentious.”
At a tofu pudding shop near Ningxia Night Market in western Taipei, photos of Huang remain on display alongside those of other prominent technology figures who have visited, including Morris Chang, the founder of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). The store manager, Hsieh, defended the shop’s decision to keep them up.
“I don’t think this changes the fact that he’s a very successful businessman,” Hsieh said of Huang’s affairs with Alice Huang and other women. “Having an affair is a private matter.”
Hsieh, who agreed to be identified only by his surname for privacy reasons, said that Huang had visited the shop four times over the past few years, and on each occasion he seemed friendly and down-to-earth.
In Taiwan, Huang’s culinary indulgences extended well beyond street food. He frequented some of Taipei’s most exclusive restaurants, where he hosted technology executives for what became known in the local press as “Trillion-Dollar Banquets,” a reference to the attendees’ combined net worth of more than 1 trillion New Taiwan dollars.
The dinners often drew crowds of journalists and photographers hoping to catch a glimpse of Huang and his guests. The intense media attention helps explain why so many photographs and videos of Huang with Alice Huang were captured in Taiwan. Restaurant owners, meanwhile, welcomed the publicity, often proudly displaying photographs of themselves with Huang inside their establishments.
But not every food vendor has rallied to Huang’s defense. Some have removed advertisements or photos featuring him, while others have tried to capitalize on the scandal to generate publicity. A night market vendor in Taipei told Taiwanese media that he was considering taking down advertisements associated with Huang out of concern that they could hurt his business.
The Taiwanese tea chain 19 Tea House launched a new drink this week, giving it a name that pokes fun at Huang’s alleged “womanizing” ways. According to the chain, the drink combines osmanthus-infused honey with fresh lemon, offering a blend of fragrant floral notes and sweet-and-tangy citrus flavors.
Support for Huang in Taiwan has also extended far beyond the restaurants he frequented. On Monday evening, Taipei 101, the island’s iconic skyscraper just blocks from one of Huang’s favorite night markets, lit up with messages of support for the former Nvidia CEO, including “Taiwan ♡ Jensen,” “Family ♡ Friendship,” “Thrive Together,” and “Taiwan AI Build Future Together.”
Tech industry figures who supported the initiative told Taiwan’s state-run Central News Agency that the illumination campaign was intended to “help restore Jensen Huang’s reputation,” urging the public not to “kick him when he's down, but instead offer warmth and support during the autumn and winter.”

President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”
Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”
Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.
We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.
So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.
“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.
CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.
The conflict in Ukraine
SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.
During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.
On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.
The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.
Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.
In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.
"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."
But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.
Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.
"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.
The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.
"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."
"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.
When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."
"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."
The journey to the stage
Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.
Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.
Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.
"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.
On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.
"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.
A night to remember
By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.
Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.
They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.
When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.
Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.
As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.
"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."
"We're being seen. We have something to say," he added. "Younger folk, older folk — they can say, okay, we see Black people playing in orchestras. Which is a serious thing."
For Wright, who grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, the ensemble has built a musical bridge she always wished existed.
"When I stepped outside, I was hearing Beyoncé or Brandy," she said. "But when I was practicing in the house, I was practicing Vivaldi." "We come to the edge of the stage, we can meet as many audience members as we can and we talk to them," Wright said. "Some of their children are playing the violin or the viola, and they'll ask us to take a picture or they'll ask us to make a video to inspire their daughter. Because sometimes when their daughter is practicing, they don't get to see the end result. Because practicing can take quite a bit of time. So they want us to show their daughters and send these videos to them to help inspire them."
"My goal is making sure [audience members] leave feeling something awesome or something great," Wright added. "And that's what we're doing. We treat every show as if it's our last."

The High Court of Karnataka has advised the security and police organisations to prioritise the mental health and well-being of personnel entrusted with firearms while asking the authorities to examine existing policies and take appropriate steps to strengthen the mental health and welfare measures for their personnel.
Justice Suraj Govindaraj passed the order while quashing the criminal proceedings against a 37-year-old CISF Sub-Inspector for attempting to kill herself in 2022 by using her service pistol while on duty in Mangaluru. She had attempted to end her life following years of severe mental distress over her inability to conceive a child due to a blocked fallopian tube.
Allowing her petition, the court set aside the lower court’s order and discharged her from the offence under Section 309 of the IPC (attempt to commit suicide). The court ruled that Section 115 of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, creates a mandatory presumption of severe stress, placing the burden on the prosecution to prove otherwise. Since no such evidence was produced, the court held that continuing the trial would be an abuse of the judicial process.
‘Grief and anxiety’
“Personnel serving in these forces are also human beings. They have families, relationships, responsibilities and personal problems. They experience grief, anxiety, financial difficulties, marital discord, illness in the family and other difficulties common to human life. Wearing a uniform or undergoing rigorous training does not make them immune to such problems,” the court said.
Further, the court said that “the expectation that they must remain available for duty at all times and discharge their responsibilities, come rain or shine, irrespective of their personal circumstances or mental condition, requires a change in institutional thinking.”
The concerned organisations must ensure that accessible and confidential counselling, professional mental healthcare and timely treatment are available to personnel at all levels, including those posted in remote and difficult locations, the court said.
Signals of distress
Commanding and supervisory officers, the court emphasised, must be sensitised to recognise signs of distress and facilitate appropriate assistance, and personnel who undergo treatment or experience mental health difficulties must also receive suitable support for rehabilitation and return to duty, based on professional assessment.
“The welfare of personnel and the security of the public are not competing considerations. A force which looks after the mental and physical well-being of its personnel is better equipped to maintain discipline, operational readiness and public safety, the court said.

Flipkart’s Big Billion Days (BBD) sale timing weighed on Walmart International’s sales growth in Q3 FY27, with the segment reporting a 7% YoY increase in net sales to $35.9 Bn. Excluding currency fluctuations, net sales grew 3.3% to $34.7 Bn. Walmart said the shift in BBD’s timing reduced the segment’s sales growth by about 500 basis points, or 5 percentage points, with a corresponding benefit expected in Q4. The shift also weighed on Walmart International’s digital businesses. Ecommerce sales declined 2%, while its advertising business contracted 15%. Walmart expects both businesses to record growth in the second half of FY27 broadly similar to the first half. The effect extended to Walmart’s consolidated results. CFO John David Rainey said the sale’s timing reduced the retailer’s overall Q3 sales growth by about 100 basis points. “As we previewed on last quarter's call, we faced a 100 basis point headwind to top line growth in Q3 due to the timing of Flipkart's Big Billion Days event, or BBD in India, which will be reported in International's fourth quarter results this year,” Rainey said during the earnings call. The change in the sale schedule also influenced inventory levels. Walmart International’s inventory increased 15.6% in reported terms in Q3, partly due to preparations for BBD. Excluding Flipkart, inventory growth was slower than sales growth. Walmart expects BBD’s timing to add about 100 basis points to consolidated sales growth in Q4. PhonePe Charge Skews Comparison While BBD’s timing weighed on sales growth, a one-time PhonePe-related expense in the year-ago quarter boosted Walmart International’s reported operating income growth comparison. The segment’s operating income rose 132.6% to $1.6 Bn in Q3 FY27. The increase largely reflected a lower base following a $722 Mn non-cash compensation charge in Q3 FY26. The charge arose after PhonePe modified certain share-based payment plans ahead of a potential IPO. After adjusting for the charge in the comparison period, operating income grew 14.5% to $1.6 Bn in reported terms, or 7% to $1.5 Bn in constant currency. At the consolidated level, Walmart’s revenue rose 5.2% YoY to $188.8 Bn in Q3 FY27. Net sales increased 5.1% to $186.8 Bn, while operating income grew 16% to $7.8 Bn. Adjusted operating income increased 5.5% in constant currency. Following the Q3 results, Walmart raised its FY27 net sales growth forecast to 4.9%-5.2% in constant currency, from 4%-5%. It also increased its adjusted operating income growth guidance to 8%-8.6% in constant currency, from 7%-8.5%.

As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
- Published
Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.
For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.
Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.
Democrats, who will control Congress come January, have made their position clear. Last Wednesday top Democrat Ted Lieu told Politico the Trump administration had been "1,000%" too deferential to Nvidia, putting national security at risk, while fellow Democrat Zoe Lofgren suggested Congress would now be more likely to restrict sales of AI chips to China.
The BBC has approached the White House for comment.
Beijing's foreign ministry had described the spy claims as a "smear against China".
"The US should stop fabricating so-called espionage narratives to find pretexts for imposing technological blockades," spokesperson Mao Ning said last week.
The ministry also seemed keen to keep the meeting on track, saying the two countries had kept "close communication regarding interactions between the two heads of state".
Another 'spy balloon' incident?
For the last year, Trump and Xi have been seeking to stabilise relations after a damaging tariff war that almost brought trade between the two countries to a standstill.
The Trump administration's decision to permit sales of advanced Nvidia H200 chips to China in late 2025 was seen as evidence that both sides were searching for areas of co-operation, even while competition intensified.
It was a rare move given Washington had spent years trying to limit China's access to the most advanced chips.
Many in the US have long viewed these chips as a national security issue, arguing they could strengthen China's military and surveillance capabilities. Jensen Huang, who rejects that claim, advocated lifting bans on the export of high-performing chips to China. Beijing argues the restrictions are an attempt to contain its rise.
Now that opening may be under threat.
History has taught Beijing and Washington that spy scandals rarely remain confined to the intelligence world.
Analysts in China already see echoes of an incident in 2023 when a suspected surveillance balloon drifted through the skies over the US before an American fighter jet shot it down. Beijing insisted it was a civilian meteorological airship that had strayed off course.
But a planned trip by then US Secretary of State Antony Blinken was cancelled and communication between the two governments deteriorated sharply.
The incident showed how quickly a security dispute could overwhelm diplomatic efforts and push relations into a deep freeze.
"The mere passage of a balloon sent American public opinion and politicians into a state of high alert, as if a "Chinese threat" were looming directly overhead," said the state media outlet, the Global Times this week as it made a direct comparison with the Nvidia scandal.
"No-one on the US side has ever apologised or taken responsibility for the genuine damage this caused to US-China relations," it added.
The state-run outlet also questioned why the Nvidia story had emerged so soon after "the hard-won detente" between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries' leaders in September.
"Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?" it asked.
Trump-Xi summit unlikely to collapse
Both Trump and Xi have significant incentives to keep talking.
China's economy remains under pressure and is increasingly reliant on exports. Xi needs trade to keep flowing and this meeting is a key stepping stone to replacing the current trade truce that is due to expire in January.
Meanwhile Trump has repeatedly touted his close relationship with Xi and argued that maintaining dialogue is essential to managing competition between the two powers.
The US president is in his last two years and faces an uphill struggle to pass domestic legislation after the midterms. To counter this, he could be looking for some foreign policy wins.
He may also hope for Xi's help to end the war in the Middle East.
Neither side will want to be discussing intelligence concerns and technology controls instead of trade, investment and economic co-operation.
The summit is also being carefully choreographed by Beijing to show off its technological prowess in Shenzhen - a deeply symbolic choice of city.
It's home to some of the country's biggest tech companies and has become a showcase for Beijing's ambitions in AI and advanced manufacturing.
Also, given Washington's tighter restrictions on advanced chips, Beijing has options for retaliation.
One of its most powerful tools is its dominance of key rare earth minerals. China processes much of the world's supply for materials that are used in everything from electric vehicles and smartphones to military equipment.
Analysts have long warned that technological restrictions can trigger a cycle of retaliation in which each side reaches for its strongest economic leverage.
That would shift the current trend of US-China relations from engagement back towards mutual suspicion.

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “War,” which had its season finale on Nov. 19 on HBO and HBO Max in the U.S., and drops on Nov. 20 on Sky and NOW in the U.K.
Over eight episodes of “War,” actress Carla Duval (Sienna Miller) and tech bro Morgan Henderson (Dominic West) have been squabbling over the couple’s multibillion-dollar fortune as they prepare to part ways for good. The winners, of course, have been the lawyers.
The series centers around two law firms: the modern and fast-paced Taylor & Byrne, founded by Nicholas Taylor (James McArdle) and Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox), and the stuffy, old-school Cathcarts & Sons, led by St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens) and Beatrice Ubosi (Nina Sosanya).
If there’s bad blood between Duval and Henderson, relations between the lawyers are worse and bloodier still. Which is perhaps why, in a season finale twist, the divorcing couple decide to negotiate their own settlement amicably, and away from their scheming lawyers.
With Season 1 wrapped up, creator and showrunner George Kay sat down with Variety to talk about some of the real-life inspirations for the show, why he decided on that surprising ending and what we can expect from Season 2, which will see Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts return with a new case and new clients.
Carla and Morgan amicably deciding the outcome of their own divorce was unexpected. Did you also consider having them call off the divorce entirely and reuniting?
A little bit. Twenty years ago, I had a company that made a documentary series about divorce, and it was quite grim viewing, unsurprisingly. Especially because it was real people, and there was no charisma going on — [“War” director] Ben Taylor wasn’t directing it, basically, and it wasn’t Sienna and Dominic. So I remember having that at the back of my mind, thinking the thing we don’t want here is to make this grim or bleak or anything. And in fact, one of the phrases that we came up with in the writers’ room was that this divorce would be the world’s most expensive couples’ therapy. Even though you don’t physically stay married, you end up closer together.
You want to leave people feeling: “That was good. I liked hanging out with those people.” They were awful a lot of the time, but everyone’s redeemable. And Carla and Morgan don’t despise each other. They just drifted and drifted and drifted.
Did you consider keeping Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux) as a mole in Season 2 instead of exposing him?
I wanted to end that story in Season 1, because I wanted him to find his home. And so that was always intended as a season-long story, and really wrapped around that is that thing of “Is it possible to be a good lawyer and a good person?” And I firmly think it is.
Well, he was carrying out corporate espionage and sleeping with a client…
We’re not going to extend the espionage thing. But with Johnny, it’s a question of can you ever trust someone who’s done that? Which I think is a relatable thing, whether that’s your relationship or your workplace. If someone’s done something really untrustworthy, can you ever trust them again? So that will linger, and become a big part of Johnny’s story. But the other thing is, we wanted to find a similar character who’s not at the upper echelons of a law firm to really get behind in Season 2. That is Emma Laird, who plays Molly [a junior lawyer at Taylor & Byrne]. We cast Emma, and I remember saying to her, “You’re amazing. Just so you know, please come and do Molly in Season 1, because there’s loads more coming in Season 2.”
Every season, I think it’s worth having someone slightly more junior through which to see the whole thing through a prism of them.
Will we see Carla again at all in Season 2, especially given her relationship with Johnny?
We don’t see her in Season 2. We have guest stars for each season. But we do have a world. So people [in “War”] don’t use X; they use Zephyr. The whole thing keeps kind of bleeding into itself.
The talk show scene, when Carla almost breaks down after seeing a photo of herself and Morgan, was very powerful. What was that like to write?
That was written with a writer called Toby Finlay, who’s brilliant, and we talked about that a lot in the writers’ room. If you can’t arbitrate on a divorce, you’ll go to litigation, and that’s when it will go public, because it’s not protected anymore. And what’s fun about that is when you’ve got a kind of Morgan Henderson and a Carla Duval, and they are very much in the public eye, that scene triggers the going public of the whole thing. So we were always thinking we want this whole thing to blow up in public on chat shows around “The Milliner,” which is Sienna’s film.
We wanted to put the camera behind the chat show host and the guest, because it’s only when you go on stage, you suddenly get the on-stage eye-view of what it’s like to be on a chat show. We’re so familiar with Graham Norton or Fallon or whatever, seeing it from the front. We felt it was such a private thing to see it from the other side, and then you can hear the lights kind of cracking in the heat, you see the light obfuscating the audience and the pressure of that. She’s such a talented actress, Sienna. She can do this thing of having a public smile, but with private worry in the eyes.
Sienna has real-world experience as a public figure, particularly in relation to her private life. Did she have input into her dialogue or storyline?
She was really great in terms of dealing with the script and talking to me about, “I don’t think she’d quite say it like that,” and we would sit there together on set and tweak stuff. But never did we talk about the meta thing of Sienna Miller in the public glare. She was treating it as a proper part.
Was the scene when Carla opens her front door to find a crowd of paparazzi a tribute to “Notting Hill”?
“Notting Hill” plays that much more for laughs with Rhys Ifans in his pants. But actually, I felt that [showed] the press physically bearing down on you.
I really wanted to use it as a way to pressurize Sienna, like that door might physically collapse on her. It was a quicker way into just seeing that the weight of the press attention was right there, so it’s a little nod to “Notting Hill,” just in the sheer kind of [gasp] of opening the door. But it’s not used for laughs.
Was the scene with the leaked CCTV footage a nod to the leaked footage of Beyonce’s sister Solange attacking Jay-Z in a hotel elevator in 2014?
Who was the guy that chased that woman down the corridor? It was awful.
That was Diddy attacking Cassie in a hotel in 2016, which was made public in 2024.
I think it’s more that sort of stuff happens in hotels, and there’s CCTV in hotels. You’re always looking in thrillers to find ways you could kind of revisit. So it wasn’t trying to plug into any one particular incident.
How about the scene where Carla is served divorce papers on the red carpet of her premiere – was that inspired by Olivia Wilde being served at CinemaCon?
I wanted to make it a bit different because — full disclosure — I didn’t want Olivia Wilde to think we were just aping her experience. But also, I thought by distancing ourselves from it, we could make it even worse for Carla by putting it right in her biggest night, her biggest moment. This really is the culmination. She’s on a career comeback at that point. She’s been in some less good movies than “The Milliner,” if you can imagine, and so this was a really special night for her. So using that for dramatic effect felt good.
But the thing that I was really inspired by the Olivia Wilde thing was just how professional and upset she was at the same time. Like we’re talking about Sienna’s ability to [show] the pain it’s caused, and then you see how she’s painting on a smile quickly to get through it. And I really spotted that in Olivia Wilde’s way of dealing with that in that moment, which I thought that just reflected very well on Olivia Wilde. So I was happy to be inspired by that because it’s probably an awful moment in someone’s life, and you’ve got to be choose the right way to kind of be inspired.
Was there any deeper meaning behind the name of Carla’s comeback movie, “The Milliner”?
There were lots of fun names. The script editor came up with a brilliant list of films that are sort of mid-level Euro, kind of awards worthy, like “The Red Violinist of Marseille” and things like that, or you know, “The Harpist of Madrid.” But in the end, it was just “The Milliner.” We had this story that she was undercover in occupied Europe with a hat.
What can we expect from Season 2, which sees Taylor & Byrne and Cathcarts delve into a libel trial?
The thing we look for in the divorce [case] is to analyze the relationships of all the lawyers. And with the libel case, it’s all about reputation. How our reputations are affecting us at work and what our work reputation means to us in life is a really cool thing to have exposed by a libel trial. So it’s about playing those two things off against each other, and bringing in a few new characters and a few new bits of casting to make it believable that what we see as predominantly family lawyers can also have other people in their departments who have libel experience.
Nick Mohammed really comes through in Season 2, which was again part of our pledge to him. And there’s a new hiring at Cathcarts, who starts to — not cause problems, but definitely shakes up the dynamic.
Will Season 2 also have a feel-good ending?
Tonally, it’s adjacent but it’s not exactly the same. And we want to have different aspects. It’s a different album.
There have been a lot of celebrity court cases recently in the U.K., from Russell Brand’s criminal trial to David Walliams’ injunction application over a Guardian expose. Are you paying attention to all of those for inspiration?
I’m actually looking the other way. I’m looking for the thing that affects people and then looking for the legal equivalent. It’s the relationship stories that we’ve seen in movies or in our own lives that we really relate to on an emotional level, and then quickly scouring law to say, “Well, where is that felt?” So it’s less with Walliams or Russell Brand. Like, I’m interested in how the justice system will treat those people, but I’m not using that for inspiration for drama because I don’t know how it feels for anyone involved because I don’t know it. So we’re trying to start with the feeling.
This interview has been edited and condensed.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows police officers beating two Muslim men, Junaid and Asif, with sticks, parading them on the road, and taking them away in Uttar Pradesh in connection with a harassment case. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Uttar Pradesh police beating two Muslim men with sticks and parading them on the road in connection with a harassment case.
Fact: The video shows police officers beating and parading Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush, who were arrested for opening fire outside the house of Sujal Khare in Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, over an old dispute. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, confirmed to Factly that both accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle and the video is unrelated to Uttar Pradesh. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, at around 3:30 am on 07 October 2026, Sahil Bhagoria and Sachin alias Ayush opened fire outside the house of Sujal Khare, a resident of Valmiki Nagar, Ujjain, over an old dispute. They were subsequently paraded from Valmiki Nagar to Desai Nagar, during which police officers beat them with sticks and pipes. A pistol was also seized from them. Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, said police arrested both accused after CCTV footage of the incident surfaced. He further stated that the two men were criminals and had been arrested following a siege.
We then contacted Jitendra Solanki, sub-inspector at Madhav Nagar police station, who told Factly that both the accused are Hindus and that the incident has no communal angle. He dismissed the viral claim, clarifying that the video is from Ujjain, Madhya Pradesh, and not Uttar Pradesh.
To sum up, a video of police beating and parading two men in Madhya Pradesh is falsely shared as a Uttar Pradesh incident with a communal spin.

AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its healthcare assistant’s ability to book appointments, find medicines, and follow up on insurance claims for users in the US. Founder and CEO Anuruddh Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. The startup claims to have helped 10 Mn people understand their health through its AI companion. The development comes after Inc42 exclusively reported in August that the startup was in talks to raise around $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners, with the terms still under discussion. August AI previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding from Accel and Claypond Capital, the family office of Manipal Group chairman Ranjan Pai, in October 2025. Founded in 2022 by IIT-BHU alumnus Mishra, August AI initially built an AI-powered health companion to help users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports. The platform also offers personalised health insights, nutrition guidance, and medication reminders. It is now extending its offering to tasks patients must complete to access care, from finding a doctor covered by their insurance to locating prescribed medicines. According to Mishra, the AI agent calls doctors’ offices, checks availability, and books the earliest available appointment with the user’s approval. It can also call nearby pharmacies to compare medicine availability and prices, review medical bills for potential errors and savings, and follow up with insurers and hospitals on denied claims. The new capabilities are available in beta in the US, with users able to join a waitlist for access. Mishra said August AI spent 24,286 minutes on hold while finding in-network doctor appointments for early users over the past few weeks. This included 366 minutes for a single user. He also claimed the platform helped another user save $1,255 on an insurance claim. The administrative assistant builds on the startup’s existing US healthcare offering. In September, August AI launched August Care, a $39-a-month membership offering telehealth consultations, discounted laboratory tests, prescription services, and insurance guidance. The company says licensed physicians make clinical decisions within the service. August AI’s expansion comes amid increased investor interest in startups using AI to manage healthcare workflows, both for patients and providers. In September, Bengaluru-based Prodoc AI raised a seed round to develop agentic AI solutions for hospital workflows, including patient engagement, appointment conversion and care coordination. Meanwhile, US-based Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in an extension round led by Z47 in October to expand its AI agents for appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills and other administrative tasks.

Job posting seemingly confirms Apple is working on its own AI agent for coding and other tasks
It is hiring a senior engineering manager to build “capable, reliable and safe” agentic tools.
Apple appears to be developing its own in-house AI agent. While we picked up on this development via Mark Gurman at Bloomberg, the news actually comes direct from the company this time. Apple has an open job listing for a senior engineering manager of agentic AI that was posted earlier this week. The description states: "As a senior leader in this org, you will own the technical direction and delivery of our agent platform and the AI capabilities built on it." It includes both general computer use and more technical coding tasks as falling within the future AI agent's purview, with the goal of being "capable, reliable and safe."
Many companies have already launched AI agents for public use this year. That includes heavy hitters in the AI space, such as Dots from OpenAI, Muse from Meta and Gemini Spark from Google. But other businesses not directly working in artificial intelligence are also embracing the agentic path.
Apple, on the other hand, has been a bit more cautious when it comes to agents. It recently warned developers that working with agentic AI "could put users at risk" by unwittingly allowing Full Disk Access. Apple then rolled out new controls earlier this week to give individuals better oversight into what data AI agents can access. Privacy is a frequent buzzword in Apple's recent software launches, so it will be interesting to see how the company walks the line whenever it unveils its own service.

Rams star Nacua suspended for personal conduct violation

Los Angeles Rams wide receiver Puka Nacua has been given a three-game suspension by the NFL for violating the league's personal conduct policy.
In March, the 25-year-old was sued for assault and battery by a woman who says he made an antisemitic statement and bit her on the shoulder on New Year's Eve.
Nacua's attorney has denied any statement was made and described the bite as "horseplay".
That incident came two weeks after Nacua performed an antisemitic gesture during a livestream appearance, for which he later apologised.
The NFL has now concluded its investigation and has suspended Nacua while he is already out with knee and toe injuries.
He was placed on injured reserve (IR) last week, meaning he will miss a minimum of four games. He has been suspended without pay so will forfeit $950,000 (£725,000).
According to ESPN, the NFL told Nacua that "any further violation of the personal conduct policy... will subject him to additional and more substantial discipline, including banishment from the league."
Shortly before Nacua was sued in March he entered a holistic care facility, external to "improve his overall behavior in every aspect of his life" and completed a rehab programme before attending the start of the Rams' off-season programme in April.
Nacua has been one of the NFL's best wide receivers since being a fifth-round draft pick in 2023. He is in the final year of his rookie contract so is set to receive a lucrative new deal after this season.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Manila this week to participate in three important summit meetings. Of these the QUAD Summit has attracted the most attention in the Indian media. Of the other two the India-Asean Summit has got more attention than the East Asia Summit (EAS). However, for India’s interests all three were significant though in different ways. There were also two common denominators in all three and this writer turns to them at the outset.
The first common element, though unmentioned, is the rise of China which is now so advanced that it forms a virtual G2 with the world’s leading power, the United States. The Asean countries live in the shadow of China. Of these Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Vietnam share land boundaries while the seven other Asean states are greatly impacted by it. The Chinese have always sought to exercise influence in the Asean countries but earlier, before, they became the world’s second largest economy and a scientific and technological power, the US was predominant in most of the Asean states. That is not clear cut now. All Asean countries are trying to navigate their diplomatic path carefully and avoid alienating either of the two powers. They wish to hedge their bets not only between the two but also want other powers, especially India, to enhance its involvement in Asean so that they can balance their foreign policies between major powers.
The second element is the Asean desire that its centrality in the region should be acknowledged. The EAS, which includes eight of Asean’s twelve dialogue partners, mentioned this directly in its Joint Declaration. The eight are India, Australia, New Zealand, China, Japan, South Korea, US and Russia. The Declaration declared the EAS member states commitment to “Maintainand supportAsean’s unity and centrality in ASEAN-led mechanisms, reaffirming Asean’s role as the anchor of the EAS framework and in shaping an evolving regional architecture that is open, resilient, transparent, and upholds international law, and support Asean in playing a bigger role in international affairs”. The fact is that a reference to Asean centrality is good to give the group the feeling that it is not allowing any single power to dominate the region or its affairs. It is also helpful to the non-Asean EAS major states that are its members to exercise a degree of self-restraint in extending their influence in the grouping lest their competition brings about great turmoil in a part of the world which has witnessed substantial growth over the past many decades. This self-restraint does not mean that the US and China and even India are not doing their best to enhance their ties comprehensively with Asean states.
India had cordial ties with Asean member countries before the organisation came into existence in 1967. On its part, the group wished to draw India in but it was unwilling to do so. Indian priorities were different during the Cold War and it was indifferent to their desire to intensify relations. Besides then the Asean countries model of development and that of India was vastly apart. The liberalisation of the Indian economy and the end of the Cold War changed Indian priorities. Prime Minister Narasimha Rao coined the term ‘Look East’ to signal India’s transformed outlook towards Asean but the Asean countries, particularly Malaysia under Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, dragged its feet. It was left to Singapore to insist within Asean forums that India was going to emerge as one of the largest economies of the world and that its weight in world affairs was growing though in a benign way. Hence, India’s status should be raised from an initial sectoral dialogue partner to that of a full partner and also be included in EAS when it was established in 2005. Earlier Asean and India agreed to begin an annual summit process in 2002 with the first summit held in Phnom Penh in November that year.
This year’s summit in which Modi, who modified Look East to Act East, led the Indian delegation was the 23rd one. It was also Modi’s 13th. Summing up the direction of this summit Rudrendra Tandon, Secretary East in the Ministry of External Affairs mentioned that Modi told the Asean leaders “... given the geopolitical situation that both India as well as ASEAN member states face, and given India and ASEAN member states’ commonalities, our common values, our common ways of looking at international developments, and our very close people-to-people ties which are rooted in antiquity, India and ASEAN member states must work together to become drivers of stability in Asia”. For this purpose he made some specific suggestions. Tandon noted that these were that Indian and Asean must cooperate in the maritime domain, both should collaborate to combat transnational crime, particularly cyber crime and fraud, cooperate in developing resilient supply chains in the area of critical minerals, that “both India and Asean member states need to move away from being mere consumers of technology to becoming co-creators of technology” and that both needed to upgrade people-to-people contacts and tourism. It may be mentioned that Indians are already travelling in great numbers to some Asean destinations and now India must do more to attract Asean tourists beyond the Buddhist circuit.
In his address to EAS Modi emphasised as Tandon put it “ peace, stability, and predictability in interstate relations”. He also called for “dialogue, mutual respect, and collaboration…”. Modi has stressed this approach since the beginning of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. However, till now Russia and the US who as members of the P5 are responsible for the maintenance of international peace and security have paid scant regard to following the path of peace.

Vote for the first BBC Men's Footballer of the Year
- Published
Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.
Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.
"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.
"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."
The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.
The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).
Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.
Jude Bellingham
Age: 23 Country: England
Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield
Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.
In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.
That meant he joined exalted company as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.
Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.
The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.
Harry Kane
Age: 33 Country: England
Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward
In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.
His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.
Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.
Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.
Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.
Kylian Mbappe
Age: 27 Country: France
Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward
Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.
The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.
Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.
It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.
Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.
He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.
Rodri
Age: 30 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield
Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.
By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.
His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.
Then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.
His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.
Lamine Yamal
Age: 19 Country: Spain
Club: Barcelona Position: Forward
Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.
Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.
For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.
At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.
He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

You can upscale low-resolution photos for free using offline AI tools. Use Upscayl on Mac and Windows, Upscal on iPhone, or Offline AI Image Upscaler on Android. These apps enhance image resolution up to 4x without uploading your photos to the cloud, keeping them private.
If there is one area where AI has truly revolutionized, apart from writing and coding, it is image upscaling. Whether it’s your old photo taken on a Sony Cyber-shot or one that’s completely distorted, you can give it to AI and you can get a clean, high-resolution version without changing its original form.
Not just your old photos, you can also upscale any standard photo taken on modern phones to the highest resolution possible.
However, one downside of using AI to upscale images, especially if you care about privacy, is that your images need to be uploaded to the cloud for any AI provider, processed there, and then sent back to your smartphone.
Although those images won’t be public, some companies use them to train their AI models. This is the reason why many users, even we, think twice before uploading sensitive photos to AI models for upscaling
Fortunately, tools like Upscayl let the AI model run locally on your device and upscale images to the highest possible resolution without your data leaving your device. Although it has specific hardware requirements, most modern PCs and smartphones support it, and it’s faster too.
It also supports batch processing, where you can upscale multiple images at once. The quality is pretty good too. In this guide, I will show you how to set up Upscayl, a local image upscaler on your Mac, Windows, Android, and iPhone.
Table of Contents
How to Upscale Low-Resolution Photos Locally for Free
Please note that the original Upscayl is only available on desktop platforms like Windows, Mac, and Linux; there are also free apps that use similar technology and work well. I will cover everything in this guide together and help you set up a free image upscaler locally on your device. This guide is designed for beginners, so every step is comprehensive and detailed.
You don’t need much setup to upscale images locally. Since everything comes in one package, the process is very straightforward. You can download the upscaler app; it installs the upscaler model locally and includes a beginner-friendly interface, making it even easier for first-time users.
Below are the steps for each device.
How to upscale photos on a Mac with Upscayl
Step 1: Open Safari or any browser, visit upscayl.org in the address bar, and press Return. On the page, click on the Download button at the top right
Step 2: Now, on the download page, you can see download options for various platforms, including macOS. However, do not click on the macOS button. It opens the Mac App Store, where Upscayl is a paid app. The same app is available for free from Upscayl’s own website.
Step 3: Tap on the alternative download option below and select the DMG version of the app
Step 4: Once downloaded, install the app on your Mac
Step 5: Open the app and complete the onboarding steps. They’re straightforward and easy to follow.
Step 6: Now using Upscayl is easy. In the sidebar, under Step 1, tap Select Image, or drag and drop the image into the right pane.
Step 7: Next, once the image is uploaded, under Step 2, choose an AI model. Upscayl Standard is the best choice for most images. You can also select a different model based on your preference.
Step 8: Now set Image Scale to 4x. This setting makes the image width and height four times larger, so a 480 by 320 photo becomes 1920 by 1280 pixels. You can also drag the slider to change it.
Step 9: Next, under Step 3, you can set where Upscayl saves the new upscaled image. To save it in a preferred location, click Set output folder and choose a folder.
Step 10: Finally, under Step 4, click Upscayl. Depending on your settings and your hardware, it can take a couple of seconds to a minute to upscale images.
Step 11: Once it is done, you can compare the changes. Drag the slider in the middle of the picture to compare the original (left) with the upscaled version (right). The upscaled image will be saved in the folder you set in step 9, or next to your original image file on your Mac.
How to upscale photos on Windows with Upscayl
Next, let’s see how you can upscale images on Windows using Upscayl. The process is very similar to the Mac.
Step 1: Open Microsoft Edge or any browser, go to upscayl.org, and click Download in the top-right corner of the header.
Step 2: Now, on the download page, click the Windows button to start downloading (about 250 MB)
Step 3: Once downloaded, click the file to open it and go through the setup process. If Windows prompts you to allow this app from an unknown publisher, click Yes to start installing.
Step 4: Now select the installation folder; I recommend you keep the suggested installation folder and click Install.
Step 5: Finally, once installed, click Finish to complete the installation on your Windows.
Step 6: Now open the app and go through the setup process. It is very straightforward and easy to follow.
Step 7: Using Upscayl is easy; in Step 1, select an image. If you want to upscale multiple images, turn on the toggle that says ” Batch upscale above Step 1
Step 8: Select the image you want to upscale and tap on Open
Step 9: Now select the upscale model. The Upscayl Standard is best for most photos. Tap it and change it based on your preference. You can also increase the image scale to 4x. By default, it is 4x.
Step 10: Now, in step three, select the desired folder where you want to store the upscaled images, or keep the default, which stores the upscaled version right next to the original file, and tap the Upscayl button to upscale your images
How to upscale photos on iPhone with Upscayl
Upscayl.org is not available for mobile phones. However, free apps let you upscale images locally on your device. Some apps also offer an optional paid plan, but most features are free. Here are the two best upscaling apps.
Step 1: Download the Upscal Enhance Video and Image app on iPhone. Use this link.
Step 2: Once the app is installed, open the app and switch over to the image option
Step 3: Now you can select images from Photos or Files. In this case, I’m choosing the image from my files.
Step 4: The app shows your photo’s current resolution and how much you can upgrade it. In my case, my 480 by 320 photo can be upscaled to 1920 by 1280. Next, tap the settings bar just above Start upscaling. It shows the current model, scale, and format. You can tap the settings icon to customize the model, Upscaling methods, and more.
Step 5: Once you’ve made your changes, tap the Start Upscaling button and wait for the image to upscale. Once complete, you will see the completed status; tap Save to Photos to save the upscaled images to your Photos app.
How to upscale photos on Android with Offline AI Image Upscaler
Similar to iPhone, you can download the Offline AI Upscaler app by Bytesweavers to upscale photos locally on your Android
Step 1: Open the Play Store and download the Offline AI Image Upscaler app by Bytesweavers on your Android phone. You can use this link.
Step 2: Now open the app and tap on Choose photo, then select the image you want to upscale
Step 3: The app shows your photo and the resolution it will make. In my case, it’s 1920 by 1280. To edit the model, you can find the model settings below the photo. The default model is set to Photo AI, which is recommended. However, you can also choose a different model based on your needs.
Step 4: Once you’ve customized it, click Enhance Photo, and that’s it. The app will enhance your photo for a few minutes and when it’s done, drag the slider on the photo to compare the original with the enhanced version. Once you’re done, you can save the photo in different formats.
Give Your Old Photos a New Life With AI
This is how to set up an offline image AI upscaler on Windows, Mac, Android, and iPhone. This setup works completely offline, and many of these methods also support batch processing to upscale your images.
However, for local AI image models, Upscayl is currently the best option. However, it is not as good as any online model. Although it reduces pixelation, it adds softness; if the original image is too distorted and has fewer details, it can soften the image. In most cases with decent images, though, the upscaled version works well. But again, it all depends upon the quality of the original image.
Also remember that upscaling an image multiple times doesn’t improve its quality. Only the first output is the highest quality you can get.
