Exposure to extreme heat during pregnancy can lead to severe outcomes, including preterm birth, stillbirth and congenital abnormalities in newborns, prompting experts at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) to highlight maternal health risks and call for targeted adaptation strategies.
The issue comes into focus as countries at COP31 prepare to discuss progress towards the Global Goal on Adaptation, a framework to help nations develop key adaptation measures, including those needed to address the health impacts of climate change.
However, translating growing recognition of climate-related health risks into action remains a challenge, particularly in the absence of adequate financial support.
According to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), only about one per cent of formal climate finance under its financial mechanism is currently directed towards health.
The broader issue of adaptation finance for developing nations is also expected to feature prominently in discussions in the coming days.
Speaking to PTI on the sidelines of COP31, Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at the Wellcome Trust, said the foundation is seeking to highlight the evidence of heat-related impacts on pregnant women through three key areas -- elevating the issues as a risk for women, developing guidelines and preparing health systems.
“We have three key points: recognising that pregnant women are a particularly vulnerable group when it comes to climate-driven extreme heat, developing guidelines to help nurses, midwives and doctors respond to the challenges pregnant women face during heatwaves, and prepare health systems for a new world shaped by climate change, and identify the most vulnerable people so they are protected,” Dangour said.
He said pregnant women were not always recognised as a particularly vulnerable group and stressed that health systems must specifically account for their needs and risks during heatwaves.
“At the moment they are not recognised as such, and they need to be included in clinical guidelines. When it comes to data, we are keen that countries record the impacts of climate change on pregnant women and then work out how their guidelines and processes can protect them,” he said.
“That evidence is important because we can see what works and what doesn’t in different parts of the world, and share that knowledge,” he said.
Former World Health Organisation (WHO) chief scientist Soumya Swaminathan stressed the importance of highlighting the issue at COP31, saying the health impacts of climate change were already being felt and required immediate action.
“It is good that for the last three COPs or so we have had a day focused on health and climate, because everyone is increasingly recognising that the health impacts of climate change are already happening and need immediate action. They are also hitting certain vulnerable groups disproportionately, and pregnant women are one of them,” Swaminathan told PTI.
Citing studies showing that exposure to extreme heat can affect pregnant women's health, pregnancy outcomes and the health of newborns, she said the WHO had recently released a document identifying pregnant women as a high-risk group and recommending measures countries should take to protect them.
She also stressed the need to integrate climate and health data, saying policymakers must urgently begin linking exposure to extreme heat and air pollutants with their effects on human health.
“When heat and air pollution occur together in the same place, the impacts are three times as high as from either risk factor alone. India has many places with both heat and bad air pollution, so we must start looking at these data and correlating exposure to climatic and weather variables, such as heat and pollutants, with health outcomes,” the former WHO chief scientist told PTI.
Swaminathan said there was an urgent need for a research programme to address the issue, adding that sufficient evidence was already available to warrant action. She also called for the government's and states' Maternal and Child Health Programme to factor in heat exposure and take proactive and preventive measures to minimise its impact on pregnant women.
Youssef Nassef, Director of the Adaptation Programme at UN Climate Change, said the first 1,000 days, from conception until a child turns two, were considered the most critical period, as climate-related harm could begin even before birth.
“A lot of what we're talking about in terms of climate impacts generally, but heat in particular, has a severe impact on maternal health, on newborn babies. Unfortunately, in climate finance, about 1 per cent of formal climate finance under the financial mechanism goes to health. There is an incongruence between the needs, the demand and the supply,” he said.
Bhavreen Kandhari, an environmentalist and the co-founder of the ‘Warrior Moms’ movement, underscored that heatwaves have had a significant impact on pregnant women, particularly those living in more vulnerable areas or working in more vulnerable occupations, such as daily-wage workers, construction workers and farmers.
“Daily-wage workers, for instance, have to earn a living. They have to continue working because they simply cannot afford to stop. There is no looking back for them. Vulnerable mothers and other at-risk groups are not thinking about the future, but simply trying to survive this particular season, or, at most, looking ahead to the next one,” she said.

A cyberattack using artificial intelligence targeted the EU in October, official says
An official in Brussels says a cyberattack using software powered by artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October
BRUSSELS -- A cyberattack carried out with artificial intelligence targeted the European Union in October, an official in Brussels said on Thursday, and some of the bloc's digital tools remain offline.
The official did not elaborate on the cyberattack, or say who could have been behind it. It was the first time the 27-member bloc reported a cyberattack using an AI tool.
“AI-assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities," said Thomas Regnier, spokesperson for the European Commission, the executive body of the 27-nation EU.
"Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools," he added. "We have seen many global cyberattacks recently, and of course no one is immune to this.”
Regnier said the EU first detected the incident on Oct. 22 and that authorities launched an investigation while also imposing “preventative measures."
Politico first reported the incidents. The news site said the attack lasted at least 10 days and affected translation and reimbursement tools as well as databases used for salaries and timesheets. Regnier declined to confirm that report.
“We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. So far, however, Regnier said that “we have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting commission staff as a whole.”
The EU agency CERT-EU oversees the digital security of the bloc’s various institutions, which all together employ about 40,000 people just in Brussels.

The Department of Medicine at Assam Medical College and Hospital in eastern Assam’s Dibrugarh has withdrawn an order advising postgraduate trainees (PGTs) of general medicine to defer “personal milestones such as marriage” until they complete their residency tenure.
Prasanta Dihingia, the Head of the Department, withdrew the order hours after issuing it on Wednesday (November 18, 2026). The withdrawal followed a backlash from a doctors’ body.
“With reference to the Order No.MED/2026/5700; Dtd. 18.11.2026, regarding the advisory issued to the PGTs of Dept. of Medicine concerning personal milestones during their residency tenure, it is hereby notified that the Office Order is withdrawn with immediate effect,” the order read.
“Accordingly, the above-mentioned order is cancelled and treated as withdrawn from the date of issuance of this notice. All concerned are hereby informed to take note of the same,” it further read.
Earlier, the Federation of All India Medical Association (FAIMA) condemned the “unreasonable advisory” and demanded its immediate withdrawal.
“What’s next? NOC from the HOD for marriage and family planning? By the same logic, HODs should stay in the hospital 24×7 until retirement. After all, commitment to patient care should apply equally to everyone!” FAIMA posted on X, sharing the controversial order.
The association advised administrators to regulate duty hours, not the resident doctors’ personal lives.
“Residency is a postgraduate course, not a vow of celibacy!” it stated.

Gilead Sciences said on Monday it had signed royalty-free deals with three generic drugmakers to make its experimental Ebola prevention drug available in 127 mainly low- and lower-middle-income countries if it succeeds in trials and wins regulatory approvals.
The deals with Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Eva Pharma and Ferozsons Laboratories cover obeldesivir, and include all African countries reporting cases in the current Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak. Obeldesivir has shown activity against several Ebola-related viruses in preclinical studies but is not approved for any use in any country.
A late-stage trial is testing the drug in people at high risk after exposure. The deals are intended to line up manufacturing and supply before trial results and regulatory filings.
Gilead is also expanding remdesivir licences to cover Ebola-related diseases if trial results are positive and regulators approve the drug. The company has donated more than 38,000 remdesivir vials to the Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and Kenya, including more than 2,000 recently sent to Kenya for investigational treatment and post-exposure prevention.
Remdesivir is not approved to treat or prevent Ebola Bundibugyo disease, and its clinical effectiveness has not been established.

Srinagar, Nov 20: Postgraduate and senior resident doctors at the Government Medical College here began an indefinite strike on Friday, demanding a stipend hike and parity with other states and Union Territories.
The protesting doctors urged the government to address their demands immediately.
"The government must address the long-pending stipend grievances without further delay," All India Medical Students' Association (AIMSA) vice president, Dr Mohit Choudhary, a PG resident at Government Medical College (GMC) Srinagar, said.
AIMSA's key demands include immediate stipend enhancement and parity for postgraduate, senior resident, DNB and MDS doctors across Jammu and Kashmir, besides implementation of maternity leave benefits in accordance with applicable high court directions.
The doctors sought Jammu and Kashmir Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha's personal intervention in the matter.
They also urged the principal of GMC Srinagar to facilitate the formation of a recognised Resident Doctors' Association (RDA) to ensure proper representation of resident doctors.

WASHINGTON — Department of Health and Human Services officials announced Friday that 15 groups around the U.S. will test how well nutrition, exercise, and other lifestyle programs work to improve Medicare patients’ health and save the government money.
The MAHA ELEVATE program aims to generate evidence over the next several years that preventive efforts, such as cooking classes and nutrition coaching for people with chronic conditions, is worthy of Medicare coverage.
The U.S. spends trillions of dollars per year on health care, most of which goes toward treating chronic diseases. However, Medicare does not cover many of the lifestyle interventions that could help people improve their condition or keep them from getting sick in the first place.

Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh): The prelude to the 68th Akhil Bharatiya Kalidas Samaroh began on Friday with a grand 'Mangal Kalash Yatra' featuring 33 cultural groups, followed by installation of the ceremonial kalash at Kalidasa Sanskrit Academy.
Sacred water from the Kshipra was collected at 7 am amid Vedic chants. After visiting Harsiddhi, Bada Ganesh and Mahakaleshwar temples, the procession passed through Ghantaghar Square, Tower Chowk, Shaheed Park, Indira Gandhi Square and Teen Batti Square before reaching the academy.
Rangoli groups, NSS volunteers, Scouts, bands and police band members participated. Folk artists performed 'mayur', horse and umbrella dances, while martial artists demonstrated 'lathi' skills. Social organisations welcomed the procession with flower showers.
'Nandi Paath'
The cultural evening featured 'Kshipra Stuti' by Venunad Ninad Dance Institution, Yakshagana by Karnataka artist Dr Kore Manjunath Hegde and a musical ensemble by Raja Mansingh Tomar Music and Arts University, Gwalior.
Formal inauguration today
Chief Minister Mohan Yadav will inaugurate the Samaroh on Nov 21 at 6 pm. Union culture and tourism minister Gajendra Singh Shekhawat will attend as special guest, while culture minister Dharmendra Lodhi will preside. Padma Shri Usha Barle will present Pandavani singing.
The event is jointly organised by Madhya Pradesh Sanskriti Parishad, Kalidas Sanskrit Academy and Samrat Vikramaditya University.
Three exhibitions to open today
An exhibition featuring 67 line drawings interpreting verses from the 'Purva Megh' section of Kalidasa's Meghaduta will open at Scindia Oriental Research Institute on Nov 21 at 4.30 pm.
Research scholar Tilak Raj Solanki of the School of Fine Arts, Music and Theatre Studies created the illustrations. Committee secretary and university proctor Prof Shailendra Kumar Sharma described the work as a first for the university.
Numismatist Ramchandra Thakur, director of Ashwini Research Institute, Mahidpur, will exhibit ancient coins related to Kalidasa and Avantika. Another exhibition will showcase rare manuscripts on Kalidasa and ancient literature, a first for Ujjain.
All three exhibitions will remain open from 11 am to 6 pm.

Mumbai: The Ghatkopar Police have detained seven Bangladeshi nationals who were allegedly staying illegally in India for the past 10 months. The action was taken by the Anti-Terrorism Cell (ATC) team on Friday (November 20), following a tip-off.
Anti-Terrorism Cell Conducts Operation Near Sant Tukaram Bridge In Ghatkopar West
At around 11.30 am, Police Sub-Inspector Yogesh Patil and his team were patrolling near Disha Hospital, Sant Tukaram Bridge, Jagriti Nagar, Ghatkopar West, based on confidential information. During the operation, they spotted seven men moving around suspiciously.
Upon questioning and verification, the police found Bangladeshi birth certificates, national identity cards and Bangladeshi mobile phone numbers stored in their mobile phones. Further inquiry allegedly revealed that all seven were Bangladeshi nationals who had entered India through illegal routes without obtaining permission from the competent authorities and were residing in the country illegally.
Police Identify Seven Detained Bangladeshi Nationals Aged Between 20 And 37
The police subsequently took them into custody and brought them to the police station. The detained persons have been identified as Mohammad Badrjuzaman Nazrul Islam Modal (35), Sohag Abdul Hannan Rana (30), Monir Kalu Fakir (30), Biplob Mohammad Jahangir Bablu Hossain (20), Nayeem Mizanur Rahman Sheikh (22), Sajid Mohammad Shahajan Hawaldar (37) and Rakib Mohammad Abu Naser Hossain (22).
All seven were currently residing at Garibacha Wada in Dombivli West, Thane district, while their native place is Bangladesh. The Ghatkopar Police are submitting a report to the Foreigners Registration Officer and Deputy Commissioner of Police, Zone-I, Crime Branch, Mumbai, for initiating proceedings to deport the seven Bangladeshi nationals from India.

The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact across the world. Efforts to contain the coronavirus are vital to the health of the world’s population, but they are also exposing children to increased risk of violence – including maltreatment, gender-based violence and sexual exploitation.
As leaders of organisations committed to ending violence against children, we come together in solidarity to share our deep concern, call for action and pledge our support to protect children from violence and reduce the impact of COVID-19 on children in every country and community.
A third of the global population is on COVID-19 lockdown, and school closures have impacted more than 1.5 billion children. Movement restrictions, loss of income, isolation, overcrowding and high levels of stress and anxiety are increasing the likelihood that children experience and observe physical, psychological and sexual abuse at home – particularly those children already living in violent or dysfunctional family situations. And while online communities have become central to maintain many children’s learning, support and play, it is also increasing their exposure to cyberbullying, risky online behavior and sexual exploitation.
The situation is aggravated by children’s lack of access to schoolfriends, teachers, social workers and the safe space and services that schools provide. The most vulnerable children – including refugees, migrants, and children who are internally displaced, deprived of liberty, living without parental care, living on the street and in urban slums, with disabilities, and living in conflict-affected areas – are a particular concern. For many, growing economic vulnerability will increase the threat of child labour, child marriage and child trafficking.
We must act now. Together, we call on governments, the international community and leaders in every sector to urgently respond with a united effort to protect children from the heightened risk of violence, exploitation and abuse as part of the broader response to COVID-19.
Governments have a central role to play. They must ensure that COVID-19 prevention and response plans integrate age appropriate and gender sensitive measures to protect all children from violence, neglect and abuse. Child protection services and workers must be designated as essential and resourced accordingly.
Working with and supporting governments, our collective response must include: maintaining essential health and social welfare services, including mental health and psychosocial support; providing child protection case management and emergency alternative care arrangements; ensuring social protection for the most vulnerable children and households; continuing care and protection for children in institutions; and communicating with and engaging parents, caregivers and children themselves with evidence-based information and advice. National helplines, school counsellors and other child-friendly reporting mechanisms enable children in distress to reach out for help, and must be adapted to the challenges of COVID-19.
Given the heightened risks of online harms, technology companies and telecoms providers must do everything they can to keep children safe online. This includes providing access to cost-free child helplines, age-appropriate services and safe e-education platforms - and using their platforms to share child online safety advice. They must also do more to detect and stop harmful activity against children online, including grooming and the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse images and videos.
As global organisations working to end violence against children, we will continue to advocate for and invest in effective child protection solutions. We will collectively develop and share technical resources and guidance for policymakers, practitioners, parents, caregivers and children themselves. And we will support the courageous health, child protection and humanitarian professionals working around the clock to keep children safe during these unprecedented times.
In recent years, the global community has made significant gains in protecting children from violence. We must not allow those gains to be lost during the current turmoil. We must do all we can to keep children safe now. And we must plan ahead together, so that once the immediate health crisis is over, we can get back on track towards the goal of ending all forms of violence, abuse and neglect of children

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”
The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.
Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:
Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April. What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.

Alberta separatist leaders pursue different paths back into UCP fold
United Conservative Party wants to be united once again, but referendum fallout is making that difficult
Moving on is hard to do.
A month after Albertans voted decisively to reject the prospect of a future vote on independence, many in the governing United Conservative Party are struggling with how to heal the breach blazed by the separatist sentiment that, polling says, was particularly entrenched in their ranks.
- 15 United Conservative constituency presidents won't sign agreement to publicly back Alberta referendum result
- UCP board candidates must sign declaration to abide by Alberta's vote to stay in Canada
The party line is now one of unity. And the party has moved to enforce that, requiring both aspiring board members and leaders of local riding associations to sign a pledge to abide by the results of the referendum, prompting further questions about how unity is actually achieved, and how much disagreement must be embraced, tolerated or stamped out in pursuit of it.
The challenge is personified by the former separatist leaders themselves, several of whom spent months spreading the gospel of an independent Alberta before those dreams were crushed — who now must grapple with their own futures within Alberta’s governing party.
It’s a dilemma that has left Danielle Smith wobbling on a highwire as she tries to keep her party together while the independence movement, never that cohesive to begin with, has begun to turn on itself.
“As a sovereignty-minded individual, I have choices to make,” Chris Scott, founder of a group called Let’s Talk Alberta, told CBC News. He spent months crisscrossing the province in a branded motorhome but, after not getting the result he wanted in October, is now running for a seat on the party’s provincial board.
“Am I going to flog the dead horse for the rest of my life, or am I going to find alignments with those that have disagreed with me?” said Scott.
Chris Scott of the pro-independence group Let's Talk Alberta is seeking a spot on the UCP's provincial board. (Mantai Chow/CBC)
Speaking on stage as part of a board candidate forum in Calgary Wednesday night, Scott told the audience that despite his disappointment, he didn’t see a future in trying to rip the party apart or take down the premier. There are plenty of people on both sides who want to strengthen Alberta sovereignty, he added.
“If we can set our emotions aside and start treating each other as what we’re supposed to be, which is one group instead of enemies, we really only can go up from here,” he said.
Two days after the referendum, Smith released a video in which she drew a line in the sand. Hers was not an independence party, and those few who “remain intent on dividing and turning our party into a vehicle for the independence movement” were invited to go elsewhere, she said.
The first time he watched the video, he was angry, Scott says. He saw it as the party leader telling those who believed in independence to find a different party. But once he set emotion aside, he watched it again and changed his mind. He concluded that Smith only meant that all members were welcome — but shouldn’t try to seek leadership positions and turn the UCP into a separatist party.
His bid for a board seat is a continuation of what he’s been doing all along, he says, in that he will continue to push for a strong and sovereign Alberta. But he plans to do it in a way that puts independence on ice, at least for now.
In his view, that puts him in compliance with Smith’s directive.
When he received the form sent to board candidates, asking them to respect the referendum, he signed it. He suggests that his fellow travellers in the independence movement who can’t move on aren’t able to see past their own anger.
“Any reasonable person would accept and abide by the outcome of the referendum,” he said. “That’s how democracy works.”
But not all of the separatist figureheads share Scott’s convictions.
Mitch Sylvestre maintains that in his neck of the woods, meaning the farmland and oil country around northeastern Alberta, separatism remains a going concern.
The sporting goods store owner, who helped craft the first petition calling for a separatism referendum, argues that the independence-leaning part of the party helped bring Smith to power, and she won’t stay there without them.
Mitch Sylvestre, CEO of the Alberta Prosperity Project, spoke to reporters after the remain side was projected to win in the Alberta referendum. (Kory Siegers/CBC)
Unlike Scott, Sylvestre already has a firm perch in the United Conservative Party, as president of the Bonnyville-Cold Lake riding association. He’s one of the presidents who have refused to sign a pledge to respect the results of the referendum and signed his name to public letters calling on the requirement to be dropped.
He intends to stay with the party and continue what he sees as his ongoing educational campaign, but said he couldn’t answer a question about whether that meant pushing for independence.
But he took a less positive view about the calls for unity expressed at the recent meeting of UCP members.
“We’re not the problem,” he told the CBC News, speaking the morning after the Calgary event.
“I’ve been saying forever that we’re going to work within the UCP, but they’re trying to kick us out,” he added. “The unity has to come from their side.”
It would be impossible for Smith to remove all the separatists from the party, given how many there are, says Duane Bratt, a political scientist at Mount Royal University. In the weeks before the vote, polling suggested that slightly more than half of party voters favoured separation.
Instead Smith has appeared to implement a “don’t ask, don’t tell,” policy, Bratt said, citing a phrase first applied to Smith by political blogger David Climenhaga. There are longstanding rumblings about the convictions of some of her MLAs, but she has turned a blind eye to those who haven’t spoken publicly, he said.
But if the challenge for the party is unity, Bratt said, the general public — who showed up to the polls to firmly reject the idea of independence — is going to want to know that their governing party is not a separatist one.
To do that, Smith will likely have to remove a few high profile separatists, Bratt argues. The party has already kicked out Jeff Rath, another high profile separatist whose membership was recently revoked after publicly clashing with Smith over her leadership.
Jeff Rath, the lawyer for the Stay Free Alberta petitioners, says the premier can't ignore Alberta separation anymore. (Emily Fitzpatrick/CBC)
In an email, the party’s executive director told Rath his “words and actions” made clear that he did not support Smith or the party. Rath told CBC News that the party declined to tell him which of his social media posts triggered the move and that leaving the party hadn’t hampered his efforts to remove Smith from leadership.
He also attended the recent UCP meeting and said the unity talk had fallen on deaf ears.
“The people that she wants to unify with, she’s basically told it’s her way or the highway,” he said.
The question now, Bratt said, is whether Rath’s ouster will be enough to convince Albertans that the separatists are no longer in control over the party.
“The question, ultimately, is how many bodies have to be tossed,” he said.
Removing Rath may not be sufficient, he said, and it would be far harder for Smith to remove someone like Sylvestre, who already has standing with the party.
“That’s a challenge for her,” he said.
But as far as Sylvestre is concerned, the demands by, and on, the premier aren’t his concern.
“We’ve had three different premiers in the last 12 years,” he says, alluding to the political turmoil that saw Jim Prentice, Jason Kenney and Smith all take turns as head of an Alberta conservative party.
“Leaders can come and go.”

New Delhi- The Income Tax Department on Friday said individuals holding foreign bank accounts with an aggregate balance of up to Rs 20 lakh at any time during the previous year will not have to file declaration under the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS), if the funds in such accounts are from disclosed sources.
In a supplementary FAQ on the scheme, the I-T department said the exemption applies to cases where the foreign bank account has not been reported in Schedule FA of the income tax return but the deposits are otherwise accounted for and sourced from disclosed income.
Under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015, assessees with one or more foreign bank accounts and an aggregate balance of up to Rs 20 lakh at any time during the previous year are exempt from Rs 10 lakh penalty for non-disclosure in Schedule FA of the Income Tax Return (ITR). Such accounts are also exempt from prosecution under Sections 49 and 50 of the Act, it said.
However, the I-T department cautioned that the relaxation does not cover foreign bank accounts containing undisclosed income or unaccounted deposits.
“A declaration will be required where the account contains undisclosed income or unaccounted deposits as they are subject to tax and penalty under the BMA,” the FAQ stated.
The FAQ would provide relief to taxpayers holding low-value overseas bank accounts where the source of funds is duly explained, while making it clear that the small-account threshold cannot be used to shield undisclosed foreign income or unaccounted deposits.
The FAST-DS, offering a one-time opportunity to disclose foreign assets and income-hitherto undisclosed, was rolled out on August 15, and will close on December 31. The scheme is aimed at taxpayers such as students, young professionals, technology employees and relocated non-resident Indians who may have failed to disclose eligible foreign assets or income.
Under the scheme, taxpayers will pay 30 per cent tax on the value of the undisclosed foreign asset or income, plus an additional amount equal to the tax, effectively taking the levy to 60 per cent.
The fair market value of assets will be determined as of March 31, 2026.
Issuing the supplementary FAQ to the scheme, the I-T department said exchange rate of Rs 94.6543 per US dollar (the rate as of March 30, 2026) will be the conversion rate for determining the fair market value (FMV) of the a foreign asset.
To a question where a foreign asset was bought partly out of taxed income and partly out of undisclosed income, the I-T department said since the foreign asset has undisclosed income embedded in it, the declaration has to be filed under Category A.
There are two broad categories for filing a declaration under the scheme. Category A includes an undisclosed asset located outside India or undisclosed foreign income which was not offered to tax. The aggregate value of the undisclosed asset in this case should not exceed Rs 1 crore. Here, a total 60 per cent tax will be levied on such undisclosed assets/income.
Category B is for the asset located outside India, which was already offered to tax, but not declared in Schedule FA of the ITR or ITR not filed and the monetary threshold for such assets have been set at Rs 5 crore for filing declarations. A flat fee of Rs 1 lakh would be levied on such declarations.
To a question on who is required to report the account under the Black Money Act, 2015, in case of a jointly held foreign bank account, the I-T department said as each of the joint account holders has an interest in the bank account, they are required to report such interest separately and compliances are required to be met by a taxpayer in an individual capacity.
The I-T department said in the cases where taxpayers with income from various overseas sources have offered only a few streams of income to tax in the ITR, the declaration in FAST-DS will have to be made only for the income or assets that have not been offered to tax in the ITR.
“The declaration may be made only for the asset that was not declared in Schedule FA of the ITR,” it said, adding immunity from prosecution will be available for such income/assets which have been declared under the scheme.
Nangia & Co LLP, Senior Partner, Amit Agarwal, said small bank balances continue to have protection from disclosure. A declaration is unnecessary in the specified case of foreign bank accounts within the Rs 20 lakh aggregate-balance protection, funded from disclosed sources.
“The latest set of FAQs marks an important step in translating the FAST-DS 2026 framework into practical implementation. The clarifications provide much-needed certainty to taxpayers who are required to disclose and should help reduce interpretational ambiguity and encourage greater participation in the Scheme,” Agarwal said.

Do business, not politics: Akhilesh Yadav's message to Meta amid Congress protests
Akhilesh Yadav urged foreign companies to avoid politics as Youth Congress workers protested at Meta offices. The dispute has intensified scrutiny of alleged restrictions on opposition-linked social media accounts.
Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Friday appeared to take a swipe at the controversy surrounding Meta, saying foreign companies operating in India should focus on business rather than politics and should treat everyone equally.
His remarks came amid protests by Youth Congress workers in Mumbai and Hyderabad over the suspension and restriction of social media accounts belonging to Congress leaders.
In a post on X, Yadav said foreign companies should not engage in politics while conducting business in India. He also cautioned the government against putting unwanted pressure on foreign companies and politicising their business operations.
"Foreign companies should conduct their business in our country, not politics. Treating everyone equally is the hallmark of a good and inclusive company. The government should also refrain from putting unwanted pressure on foreign companies and politicising their business," Yadav said.
Yadav's remarks, accompanied by the hashtag #Meta, came as the Congress intensified its protest against the social media company's alleged selective action against opposition leaders.
YOUTH CONGRESS PROTESTS OUTSIDE META OFFICES IN MUMBAI, HYDERABAD
The Mumbai Youth Congress staged a protest outside Meta's office at World One in Bandra-Kurla Complex (BKC), alleging that the suspension of social media accounts belonging to Indian Youth Congress leaders was aimed at suppressing voices critical of the BJP and the RSS.
The demonstration was led by Mumbai Youth Congress president Zeenat Shabrin. Protesters also burnt a poster of Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, who holds the Information and Broadcasting as well as Electronics and Information Technology portfolios.
The protesters raised slogans accusing Meta of favouring the BJP and alleged that the suspension of accounts belonging to Indian Youth Congress national president Uday Bhanu Chib and national in-charge Manish Sharma was an attempt to silence dissent on social media.
"Every citizen has the democratic right to question the government and express their views. Such attempts to take away this right by suspending social media accounts will not be tolerated," Shabrin said.
She said the Youth Congress would continue its agitation against attempts to suppress democratic voices. Mumbai Youth Congress office-bearers, including Pawan Majithia, Amandeep Saini and district- and assembly-level functionaries, also participated in the protest.
In Hyderabad, Indian Youth Congress workers staged a demonstration at Meta's office in Gachibowli, accusing the company of selectively restricting opposition voices and suspending accounts belonging to party leaders.
The protest was led by Telangana Youth Congress president Jakkidi Shiva Charan Reddy, who alleged that Instagram accounts belonging to Chib and Sharma had been arbitrarily suspended or restricted.
The protesters raised slogans against Meta, accusing the platform of favouring the BJP and the RSS while targeting opposition leaders. They demanded the immediate restoration of the restricted accounts, alleging that the action was intended to silence independent and opposition voices.
In a post on X, the Telangana Youth Congress said its workers had entered Meta's Hyderabad office and accused the company of blocking opposition accounts. It gave Meta seven days to lift restrictions on all affected accounts and warned that it would shut down the company's offices across the country if its demand was not met.
The party also said Meta must follow the Constitution of India rather than alleged orders from the BJP and called for an end to what it described as censorship.
Police intervened during the demonstration in Hyderabad and detained Telangana Youth Congress president Jakkidi Shiva Charan Reddy along with several other party workers. They were subsequently taken to a police station.
The protesters warned of nationwide demonstrations if Meta failed to restore the restricted accounts within the seven-day deadline.

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.
The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.
Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.
A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.
Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.
In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.
Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.
Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.
But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.
It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.
Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.
The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.
In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.
Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.
Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.
In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”
Shared envelopes
Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.
Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the WINTER infrared telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s NEOWISE mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar explains. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”
In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.
Decades of data
The researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar says.
To get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.
Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to three-fold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.
Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.
A bomb inside a star
In October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar says, going on to compare the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very quickly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”
The eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar says. He argues that this was the evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.
All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.
The energy budget
To predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao showed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.
During the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.
“Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this new energy source inside it,” Karambelkar says. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very quickly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”
The efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.
Hourglasses
In AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he says. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”
The team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar says. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.
Telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar says.
Jacek Krywko is a freelance science and technology writer who covers space exploration, artificial intelligence research, computer science, and all sorts of engineering wizardry.

The Trump administration has replaced its cybersecurity chief
Sean Cairncross was ousted following several high-profile tech outages.
Sean Cairncross is no longer the US National Cyber Director. The Trump administration has fired him, following several tech outages in the country, according to Reuters. If you'll recall, Microsoft's services recently went down and remained offline for almost a full day, which had affected businesses, hospitals and even governments around the world. The Federal Aviation Administration had also ordered a nationwide ground stop that had disrupted more than 18,000 flights inside, to and from the US.
It's not quite clear why the White House removed Cairncross in relation to those incidents, but the government has been getting flak over its response to cybersecurity threats, including those posed by advanced AI agents and tools. Cairncoss oversaw the administration's cybersecurity strategy, as well as the implementation of related policies across the federal government. According to Axios, however, Trump's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, wanted him out because he "lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job." The president, "fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," Reuters' source said.
In a statement, Cairncross said he was proud of what he had done "to strengthen America's cyber security, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in super intelligence."
Kirsten A. Davies, the Department of Defense's chief information officer, will now serve as the new US National Cyber Director. Davies had held cybersecurity-related posts in the private sector before, including in companies like Hewlett-Packard and Siemens. The administration reportedly believes she has the experience and the credentials needed to be able to excel in the position.

A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its western neighbor.
Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”
Evasive and irregular turns
“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”
When police later questioned D’iu about the incident, the defendant allegedly said he saw a woman get into a car and thought she was “beautiful.” He then told the investigators that he followed her because he “wanted to ask her out on a date.”
Prosecutors didn’t name the company, but both Reuters and Bloomberg, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the case, identified it as Palantir. Ars is unable to confirm that reporting. Palantir representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking confirmation.

Pakistan secured a commanding eight-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second and final Test in Rawalpindi on Friday to clinch its first Test series win of the year.
Sri Lanka, which had avoided an innings defeat on Thursday, was bowled out for 316 on the fourth morning, adding just seven runs to its overnight score of 309-9. Milan Rathnayaka remained unbeaten on 66 off 88 balls, striking 12 boundaries.
Pakistan chased down the modest 90-run target in 13 overs, with Aamer Jamal (34 not out) and Azan Awais (32 not out) guiding the home side to victory. Pakistan lost openers Tayyab Arif (13) and Mohammad Taha (four), but Jamal sealed the win with a boundary off spinner Prabath Jayasuriya.
Mohammad Abbas led Pakistan’s bowling effort with 3-55, while Jamal claimed 3-67 and Razaullah took 2-116.
Pakistan captain Babar Azam was pleased with the team’s performance, particularly given the presence of several newcomers.
“This is a new team with some new players, but they showed some good performances and winning always gives you satisfaction and confidence,” he said.
“We are looking to create a positive environment so everyone has the fighting spirit alive regardless of what the match situation is.”
Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis admitted that his team’s first-innings collapse to 98 had proved costly.
“We have to improve in some areas when it comes to batting and fielding, but we bowled well in patches,” he said.
Pakistan had taken control of the match by dismissing Sri Lanka for 98 before posting 325 in reply. Half-centuries from Rathnayaka, Sonal Dinusha and Mendis helped Sri Lanka avoid an innings defeat, but could not prevent a series loss.
The first Test, also in Rawalpindi, had ended in a draw.
The victory marks Pakistan’s first series win in the current World Test Championship cycle. It had previously drawn series against South Africa and the West Indies, while suffering 2-0 and 3-0 defeats against Bangladesh and England respectively.

- The claim that an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a Russian flag to be hung from the triumphal arch at Atlanta's Millennium Gate Museum to honor an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin is still under investigation.
- The claim circulated after the Russian Embassy in the U.S. posted an image of a Russian flag hanging at the Millennium Gate Museum in Altanta, Georgia. According to the embassy, Rodney Mims Cook Jr., a Trump appointee and the museum's founder, had taken the "initative" to honor the deceased Russian diplomat Alexander Darchiev.
- At the time of this writing, neither organization had confirmed to Snopes that Cook made the decision to hang the Russian flag, or whether he did so in his authority as CFA Chairman or museum founder. Therefore, we leave this claim unrated.
- The New York Times reported on Nov. 18, citing an interview with Cook, that he arranged for the Russian flag to hang from the Millennium Gate Museum triumphal arch in memory of Darchiev. The flag reportedly came down on Nov. 18.
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We have contacted the Millennium Gate Museum to ask whether Cook personally made the decision to hang the Russian flag from the museum's arch in his capacity as the museum's founder and await a reply.
In November 2026, a claim (archived) circulated online that an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump ordered a Russian flag to be hung from the triumphal arch at Atlanta's Millennium Gate Museum to honor an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The claim spread after the Russian Embassy in the U.S. posted (archived) a photo of a U.S. flag hanging on the Millennium Gate Museum in Atlanta, Georgia. The embassy wrote:
🇷🇺 Russian flag has been put on the historical museum of Atlanta @MillenniumGate in memory of the Russian Ambassador to the U.S. Alexander #Darchiev at the initiative of President of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts Rodney Mims Cook-Jr.
Alexander Darchiev was a Russian diplomat (archived) who served as ambassador to the U.S. since March 2025. CNN, citing the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, reported that Darchiev died "suddenly" on Nov. 11 after struggling with a chronic illness.
Following the Russiam Embassy's post, other social media users appeared to criticize the decision to fly the Russian flag in Atlanta. For example, the former Republican Representative for Illinois turned political commentator Adam Kinzinger wrote on Instagram, "Trump's pick to chair the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts" had hung a Russian flag "from an arch in Georgia while Russia is still waging war on Ukraine."
The claim also spread on Reddit and Facebook (archived, archived). Snopes readers searched our site about the claim.
Rodney Mims Cook Jr., who the Russian embassy said took the "initiative" to hang the flag and who other social media posts described as an "ally" of U.S. President Donald Trump, is the chairman of the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, which is a federal design review agency based in Washington, D.C. The CFA approved Trump's White House ballroom project in February and his proposal for a monumental arch in May.
However, Cook is also the founder and president of the Millennium Gate Museum, which hung the Russian flag. Therefore, it was unclear whether Cook took the initiative to fly the Russian flag in his capacity as chairman at the CFA or as founder and president at the Millennium Gate Museum.
CFA Secretary Thomas Luebke wrote via email to Snopes that the commission's jurisdiction was "almost entirely" in D.C. and that he did not know about "the activities of Mr. Cook at the Millennium Gate Museum in Atlanta, an institution for which he serves as President and CEO."
We contacted the Millennium Gate Museum to ask whether Cook made the decision to hang the Russian flag from the museum's arch in his capacity as the museum's founder and await a reply.
Because neither the CFA nor the Millennium Gate Museum had confirmed the Russian Embassy's claim that Cook personally decided to hang the Russian flag from the Millennium Gate in November directly to Snopes, we leave this claim unrated.
The New York Times reported on Nov. 18, citing an interview with Cook, that he arranged for the Russian flag to hang from the Millennium Gate Museum in memory of Darchiev. The flag reportedly came down on Nov. 18.
The Millennium Gate Museum said in a statement on its website that the Russian flag was part of its "long-standing diplomatic custom of marking the death of an accredited ambassador serving in the United States."
It was unclear whether the Millennium Gate Museum had flown a Congolese flag following the death of the serving Congolese Ambassador Serge Mombouli in September 2025, or when the museum had last honored that tradition.
Cook is a 2-time Trump appointee and 'Russophile'
Regardless of which authority Cook used to allegedly hang the Russian flag in Atlanta, it was fair to describe him as a Trump "ally." In an article in the New Yorker in July, Cook reportedly expressed confidence in Trump's design direction, saying that he would "leave us a legacy of such astonishing beauty."
Trump appointed Cook to the CFA in January 2026 after which the commission elected him as chairman. Cook had previously served on the CFA from 2021 to 2022 after being appointed by Trump during his first term.
The New Yorker article described Cook as a friend of Trump and an "unapologetic Russophile." Cook attended the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum, which the New Yorker described as "Putin's Davos," referencing the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum, in June.
It was unclear, owing to differing statements from Cook and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whether Cook attended SPIEF with the blessing of Trump or his administration.
Critique of public flying of Russian flag as US attempts to broker peace deal
According to the Russian Embassy, Darchiev and Cook "met numerous times" and bonded over shared culture and history between their countries.
Regardless of the reported bond between the two men, some social media users criticized the hanging of the Russian flag in Atlanta, which could be perceived as public support for Russia, at a time when the U.S. was once again trying to help broker a peace deal in the nearly five-year war between Russia and Ukraine.
Trump has publicly accused (archived) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of dragging out the war because of "all of the money that Europe is famously giving him, and that Crooked Joe Biden gave him in the past."
Meanwhile, Trump publicly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "friend" when the leaders met at the APEC Summit in China on Nov. 19.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated a number of rumors related to the war in Ukraine.

An old photograph is being circulated on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows Aazad Samaj Party chief Chandra Shekhar Azad wearing an RSS uniform. Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: An old photograph showing Aazad Samaj Party chief Chandra Shekhar Azad wearing an RSS uniform.
Fact: The viral image is AI-generated. There are several visual inconsistencies, including identical faces and extra hands among the people in the image. Further, AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, also indicated that the image was AI-generated. ABVP also denied Azad’s association with the organisation. Hence, the viral claim is FALSE.
A relevant keyword search on the Aazad Samaj Party chief Chandra Shekhar Azad’s alleged association with the RSS found that the controversy began after journalist Swati Chaturvedi claimed during a News 24 discussion that Aazad had been associated with the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP). Aazad denied having any association with the organisation. In response, Chaturvedi shared a 2017 interview with The Quint, in which Aazad reportedly said that he joined the ABVP when he was a young law student. However, the ABVP later denied any association with Aazad in a post on X.
On closely examining the image, we noticed several inconsistencies, including identical faces and extra hands among the people. These anomalies indicate that the image is AI-generated and not authentic.
We also analysed the image using AI detection tools, Hive AI and SynthID, both of which indicated it was AI-generated.
To sum up, this viral Image claiming to show Chandra Shekhar Azad in an RSS uniform is AI-Generated.

Spacetech startup SatSure has raised ₹60 Cr from Central government-backed spacetech VC fund, Antariksh Venture Capital Fund (AVCF). The amount was raised in the first tranche of the startup’s ongoing ₹200 Cr Series B round. As per reports, the round values SatSure at ₹870 Cr. SatSure plans to use the capital to advance the optical payloads built by its subsidiary KaleidEO, scaling its geospatial AI model Dhaarini, and expand international operations. It will also use the funding to execute its multi-satellite constellation mandate under the IN-SPACe-anchored Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership (EO-PPP). The startup is part of the consortium that aims to design India’s first fully indigenous commercial Earth observation satellite system, led by Pixxel. SatSure has now raised ₹427 Cr in institutional funding to date, excluding government grants, from investors like Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures, Omidyar Network India, and Kotak Mahindra Bank. Its ongoing Series B round is expected to comprise ₹165 Cr in primary equity, ₹25 Cr in venture debt and ₹10 Cr in secondary transactions, with full closure scheduled on a rolling basis through December 2026. Founded in 2017 by Prateep Basu, Rashmit Singh Sukhmani and Abhishek Raju, Bengaluru-based SatSure operates across the Earth observation value chain. SatSure develops geospatial foundation models and offers enterprise data analytics for banks, insurers, critical infrastructure companies, and governments. Its investors HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank are also its customers. The startup claims its product line, which is part of the RBI’s Unified Lending Interface, enables public-sector banks to underwrite farm loans in minutes. Dhaarini, its Large Earth Observation Model, was also previously awarded a ₹24.6 Cr grant under IN-SPACe’s Technology Adoption Fund (TAF) Scheme. Meanwhile, SatSure’s Series B lead investor, ₹1,600 Cr Antariksh Venture Capital Fund (AVCF), is a state-backed fund anchored by India’s space sector regulator and promoter IN-SPACe. In March 2025, IN-SPACe selected SIDBI Venture Capital to manage the fund, which aims to promote homegrown spacetech startups and boost private investment in the sector. This is the AVCF’s first investment in the downstream data and AI layer of India’s commercial space economy. It also backed satellite maker Dhruva Space earlier this year. “Leading SatSure’s Series B round reflects AVCF’s thesis of backing full-stack enterprises that pair indigenous orbital infrastructure with downstream decision intelligence.
