Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.
The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)
Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.
Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, it also caused a rift within the family.
Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years
Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.
For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.
Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians
India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.
In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press
Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.
In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …
The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.
Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.
In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’
Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.

European troops from 11 countries drill in Poland for a potential postwar Ukraine mission
Thousands of European troops are taking part in a major military exercise in southeastern Poland
NOWA DEBA, Poland -- Thousands of European troops are taking part in an unprecedented military exercise in southeastern Poland to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.
Led by France and the U.K., the multinational force is a non-NATO military initiative of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a wider political group of 37 nations supporting Ukraine.
The two-week exercise that began on Nov. 9 is for the first time checking this coalition's ability to deploy in Ukraine once the war ends. It is aimed both at testing deployment plans and sending a message to Russia and the Trump administration that European countries are stepping up militarily.
The exercise took place as leaders from Ukraine and nearly 40 other delegations met in Berlin to underline their support for Kyiv and explore Ukraine’s postwar security arrangements. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.
U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine. Kushner and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure European leaders about U.S. President Donald Trump’s discussions on ending the nearly 5-year-old war at his historic trilateral talks with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, according to Kushner.
Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance’s Article 5, in which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them.
After the meeting on Thursday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the military exercise in Poland “shows that the Coalition of the Willing is ready to contribute with the United States of America to securing a peace.”
Around 2,800 personnel from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Spain, Sweden and the U.K. are taking part in the two-week exercise, with Poland providing the logistical backup and Turkey participating from Istanbul.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that 1,100 troops from France were deployed, and that “we have terrestrial, air but also maritime operations, a dozen countries that are active in this coalition.”
The exercise in Poland follows 12 months of planning by the Multinational Force-Ukraine, or MNF-U, said U.K. brigadier Campbell Close, who serves as deputy commander for operations of the French Army's 1st division. That division is in charge of the land part of the “Koalicja” exercise in Poland.
“This is a deployment exercise,” Close said on Monday at the Nowa Deba military training ground in southeastern Poland. “We have rehearsed the entry into theater, the arrival of thousands of troops and now move on to Nowa Deba training area where we are conducting integration training with eight allies.”
“I should stress we are a defensive force,” Close said.
He also praised Poland for a “no mean feat” in terms of handling the logistics of moving thousands of vehicles, people and their equipment in a short period of time.
If deployed once a ceasefire is in place, the force would help regenerate and strengthen Ukraine’s armed forces, provide the reassurance needed to open the country’s skies and help clear mines in the Black Sea, Lt. Gen. Tom Bateman, commander of MNF-U, said earlier in November. It would not have peacekeeping or peace-monitoring functions.
Coalition troops arrived in Poland by sea, air and land, the Polish government said in a statement, before traveling by rail and road to Nowa Deba, where they have been training together since.
They rehearsed transporting personnel and equipment across Poland, carried out joint command-and-control exercises, and flew fighter jets and an aerial refueling tanker in preparation for helping Ukraine reopen its airspace. They operated surveillance drones, drilled responses to drone attacks and trained in trench warfare in wooded areas.
The initial idea of the Coalition of the Willing group of nations was to provide Ukraine with security guarantees similar to NATO’s Article 5. In the absence of a NATO commitment to fulfill this function, France and the U.K. decided to go ahead with plans for a separate European proposal of countries willing to come to Ukraine’s aid if necessary.
Last year, Putin said that any foreign troops inside Ukraine would be considered “legitimate targets.”
The multinational force may have a purely defensive function, but it would still need to be a “combat force for their own force protection,” said Ed Arnold, a Senior Associate Fellow at the RUSI military think tank in London.

The earliest example of the footage appeared on a Dearborn news agency’s social media account on June 28, 2026, months before the midterm elections. The video shows Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura.
On Nov. 3, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history as the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, resulting in numerous claims focusing on his religious identity. Footage spread online claiming to show Muslims in Dearborn, Michigan, demanding the implementation of Shariah, or Islamic law, in the United States.
The footage appeared on Facebook and X with captions calling it "an invasion" by Muslims. One post stated: "Thousands of Shia Muslims marched in Dearborn demanding Sharia in Michigan and rejecting American law. Now that they have a Muslim senator, they will become more emboldened than ever."
The footage in question was not taken after the Nov. 3 elections. A local Dearborn news agency shared it on Instagram on June 28 with a caption saying that it showed Shiite Muslims observing the holy day of Ashura, which has nothing to do with implementing Shariah. As such, we rate this claim miscaptioned.
Details indicated that the footage was not shot in November, including the facts that all the people marching are wearing T-shirts and the leaves on the trees are green. In November, Dearborn is cold and leaves have changed color and fallen.
Using Google's reverse image search tool, we found what appeared to be the original source of the footage. On June 28, the Instagram and TikTok account for local news organization dearborn.org, which focuses on immigrant Arab and Muslim news, posted the same footage in a reel (archived) with the caption, "From the Annual Ashura march in Dearborn."
A local newspaper, the Detroit Free Press, also covered the same march, posting photographs of the same men in black shirts, green vests and black-and-red vests.
As we have previously reported, Ashura is a holy day for Shiite Muslims. The reel shows a group of men participating in a religious ritual during Muharram, the first month of the Muslim calendar. The month is an important mourning period for Shiite Muslims in particular as it marks the anniversary of the seventh-century Battle of Karbala (in present-day Iraq) and the martyrdom of the Prophet Muhammad's grandson Imam Hussein.
It is common practice for Shiite Muslims to observe the period by wearing black, crying and beating their chests, particularly on Ashura, the 10th day of Muharram.
Similar footage of another procession went viral after Zohran Mamdani, who is a Shiite Muslim, became the Democratic nominee for New York City mayor in 2025. The footage spread with miscaptioned text claiming that the procession was taking place in New York City because of Mamdani, when it was actually from Azerbaijan.
For more reporting on El-Sayed, we have previously covered the claim that he would force Michigan students to learn Arabic numerals (they already do), the true claim that he called Michigan "the capital of Arab America" and a false rumor that he said it was acceptable for young girls to see male genitals in their locker rooms because "they are going to see them on the internet anyway."

China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
- Published
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

Whatever happened to the diamond that went missing in F1 crash?
- Published
Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?
If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.
A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.
Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?
Someone, somewhere, knows something.
The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.
Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport.
"My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport.
"It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."
His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.
They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie.
"I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says.
"One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."
Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.
The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.
Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.
What happened next, though, was not part of the script.
While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.
The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.
Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.
Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.
Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.
In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.
Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.
It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back.
"I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.
He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage.
"I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says.
"That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."
By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.
But there were plenty of theories.
Theory: it was not a real diamond
Sidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond.
"I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says.
"Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk.
"There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."
Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth.
"David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell.
"Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car.
"I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."
Theory: someone pocketed it
"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell.
"I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit].
"Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer.
"It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."
There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.
Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up.
"What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find.
"Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car.
"There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones.
"Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."
Theory: Klien crashed on purpose
Sidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.
And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose.
"For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.
Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to.
"Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell.
"He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond.
"No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."
While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond.
His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers.
"When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there.
"It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."
In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue.
"No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell.
"I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."
Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."
Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1.
"You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.
Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
- Published
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
Ukraine, the balancing act
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
China's growing nuclear arsenal
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.
The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.
Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Will everyone stick to the script?
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
Xi's problems at home
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.
A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.
Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.
At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

Indonesian daycare principal jailed for five years over child abuse case
- Published
The former principal of a daycare centre in Indonesia has been sentenced to five years in jail over the abuse and neglect of children in the unlicensed facility.
In April, a raid of the Little Aresha centre in the city of Yogyakarta exposed the culture of abuse within its walls – where toddlers were found with their hands and feet tied with rags.
The case sparked nationwide outrage and prompted further scrutiny of childcare centres across Indonesia, many of which authorities say are not properly licensed.
Little Aresha's principal, Anita Palupi Indahsari, was charged along with 11 staff members and the head of the foundation running the centre.
On Thursday, Yogyakarta judge Sunaryanto ruled that Anita had "allowed violence against children to be carried out continuously" and was "legally and convincingly guilty", according to AFP news agency.
The judge also ordered Anita to pay 510 million rupiah ($27,900; £21,300) in fines, failing which, her property will be seized and auctioned.
But some of the victims' families found the verdict - half of the ten-year jail term that prosecutors were initially arguing for - incommensurate with the traumatic impact their children had suffered.
Tri Susilawati, a parent present at Thursday's hearing, urged prosecutors to file an appeal, arguing that it was not adequate for "what they have done to our children".
Prosecutors have sought a 10-year prison sentence and a 900m rupiah fine for Diyah Kusumastuti, the chairperson of the Little Aresha Foundation, who is yet to be sentenced.
The 11 caregivers employed by the centre were each handed jail terms ranging between two to three years – lower than the five-year terms prosecutors had sought.
The victims' families had protested against the earlier verdicts, with some saying the sentences were "far from what [they] had hoped for".
"It is very unfair," said Imedia Dwi Anjani, a victim's father.
The April raid at Little Aresha came after a former employee lodged a police report claiming that children had suffered inhumane treatment at the centre.
Police estimate that 53 out of the 103 children at the centre were mistreated. They also found as many as 20 children crammed into tiny rooms measuring about 3m (10ft) by 3m.
Yogyakarta's police chief Eva Guna Pandia said at the time that staff had tied some of the children up so they would not disturb others, AFP reported.
The centre was closed shortly after the raid.

Quick Answer
Ente Photos is a privacy-focused Google Photos alternative offering 10GB of free storage, end-to-end encryption, open-source code, selective album backups, cross-platform access, easy photo imports, collaborative sharing, and on-device AI features like face recognition and Magic Search.
When we think about a dedicated photo app, we instantly remember Google Photos or the default gallery on our phone. We do not have many trustworthy options. That’s when I came across Ente. Ente is a dedicated photo app available as a standalone app to install on Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, and Linux operating systems.
Is Ente the real challenger to the Google Photos app? Can we replace the gallery on our phones with Ente? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
Features That Make Ente a Worthy Photo App
Ente has some exciting features that really make it stand out from the few others available. Here’s what makes it worthy.
Generous Free (Forever) Storage Plan
Ente offers a 10GB free storage plan for your photos and videos. Ente claims the plan is free forever. 10GB of free cloud storage dedicated to photos and video backup seems a good deal. That too without any ads.
Google offers 15GB of free storage space for each Google account. There is no dedicated storage space for the Google Photos app. As Google’s free storage is tied to all Google products as a whole, Ente’s 10GB looks big.
If you exhaust the generous free space on Ente, you can upgrade to a paid plan that offers storage starting from 50GB to 2TB for a monthly or annual subscription.
End-to-End Encrypted Backups
The photos and videos you back up on Ente are end-to-end encrypted by default. Ente claims they never use our data to train their models or spy on us.
The photos we back up via Google Photos are not end-to-end encrypted. Google may use our data to train their AI models, serve us customized ads, etc. You can prevent Google from using your data to show you personalized ads, but they can read your data. That’s where Ente succeeds.
The backup is end-to-end encrypted with keys before it leaves our device. The encryption keys are derived from our password using advanced key derivation functions. That means only the password you set can decrypt the data.
As the source code of Ente is publicly audited, the trust factor improves. When I tried to sign up on Ente, it provided me with a recovery key or the master key that I can use in case I lose my password.
The encryption process involves only us, the users, and they can never access the data. Even in the unfortunate event of a data breach, our data can remain safe as it is end-to-end encrypted.
Fully Open-Source Platform
Ente’s entire codebase for photos and its other apps is available for public audit on GitHub with more than 29k stars. The stars do not necessarily mean the project is good, but they give some form of trust.
The internet rewards the sensation. If someone had found a mismatch between Ente’s tall claims and the code, they surely would have flagged it and made an issue out of it.
Backup of User-Selected Albums
When you give permissions for Google Photos on our device, it backs up all the available albums, photos, and videos. We cannot select or ignore certain albums.
Ente, on the other hand, gives users the option to select which albums to back up. The albums that we choose not to back up are ignored by Ente as well. I loved this feature personally, as a lot of unnecessary data gets uploaded and wastes storage space. We can also customize the albums for backup anytime.
Easy Accessibility on All Platforms
Ente Photo has an app for every major operating system. We can install its app on Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. If we do not want to install the app, we can use it on the web through Ente.com.
Import Data From Google and Apple
Just download the Google Takeout that only has Google Photos data, import it into the Ente desktop app, and you are all set. It’s that simple to import data from Google Photos.
If you are an Apple user, just install the Ente app on your mobile device. Ente will read the data directly from your iCloud library and import it.
If you have iCloud shared albums, select the photos you want to import into the Ente app, and then save them to your device library for Ente to read them automatically.
Better Sharing and Collaboration Features
Ente Photo app provides us with three ways to share albums with others. You can share with a person on Ente, create a public link and share it with non-Ente users, or create a collaborative link to let non-Ente users add photos without an Ente account.
This does not put pressure on non-users to create an Ente account before collaborating with Ente albums, unlike the Google Photos app.
On-Device Machine Learning Features
There are a few machine learning-based features, like Magic Search, where you can search for photos with descriptions of how you remember them, Face Recognition, Memory Lane, Map and Location, and Jump to Date. These are all the latest advances in AI features.
To protect and maintain your privacy, all the machine learning happens on your device itself and is never sent to Ente’s servers. The machine learning feature is not enabled by default. You have to enable it manually and choose to disable it whenever you need to do so.
Is Ente Photos safe to use?
Yes, the Ente Photos app is safe to use to back up your photos and videos. It provides end-to-end encryption based on your password, and only your password can decrypt the data. Once you forget your password and also lose the recovery key they provided, you may never get to access the backup. The entire codebase of the Ente Photos app is available for public audit on GitHub.
How do I transfer photos from Google Photos to Ente?
You can transfer photos from Google Photos to the Ente Photos app in two ways. You can either download Google Photos data from Google Takeout, or download the entire library from the Google Photos app and drop it into the Ente Photos desktop app. It will read the data and import it to back it up safely.

On Nov. 18, Democrats nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, pushing him closer to leading the Democratic majority and becoming the first Black lawmaker to hold the position.
Amid the closed-door vote — which he won with an overwhelming 251-11 majority — people claimed Jeffries once said during a speech at an American Israel Public Affairs Committee event that Jerusalem is the "sixth borough" of New York City. AIPAC is a pro-Israel lobby group.
For example, one X user wrote (archived): "Hakeem Jeffries says in a past speech at AIPAC that Jerusalem is the 'sixth borough' of New York City and says he visits there 'to catch up with my constituents.'"
Jeffries has reportedly received upward of $1.74 million from AIPAC over the years. Recent polls show that voters, particularly younger constituents, increasingly oppose U.S. support for Israel amid its war on Gaza, which the U.N. has declared a genocide.
Clips purportedly showing Jeffries producing the quote in question spread on TikTok, Bluesky and Reddit, together amassing millions of views.
The footage is authentic, meaning not the product of an artificial intelligence tool or digital fakery. Jeffries did say the comment about Jerusalem being a borough of New York City while speaking at an AIPAC conference in March 2020. Therefore, the quote has been correctly attributed to him.
As of this writing, AIPAC's official YouTube account still publicly lists the video, from which the clips above originate (archived). While being interviewed, Jeffries said (at minute 2:30):
Someone said to me, they said, "Hakeem, you're going to Israel a fifth time?" I said listen, I'm from New York City. And back home, back home in New York City, we consider Jerusalem to be the sixth borough. And so I'm just trying to catch up with my constituents.
It is unclear whether his comments were meant to be taken seriously. The interviewer and members of the audience can be heard laughing in response to his remark.
Snopes contacted Jeffries' office seeking comment. We will update this article if we receive a response.
By June 2023, Jeffries told the American Jewish Committee that he had been to Israel six times, more than any other country he had visited. As early as July 2014, he told a crowd in New York: "Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever."
Although a petition calling for House Democrats to choose a different speaker gained more than 1.2 million signatures, Jeffries ran unopposed.

A record share of Japanese people views ties with China and Russia negatively, a government survey showed, underscoring the diplomatic challenges facing Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Some 93% of respondents described Japan-China relations as poor or somewhat poor, the highest since the government began posing the question in 1986, according to preliminary results of a Cabinet Office survey released Friday. The figures aren’t fully comparable as the survey methodology changed in 2020. A record 93.7% also viewed ties with Russia negatively.
The findings come at the end of a week of high-profile diplomacy in Asia, where Takaichi came face to face with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen. Her relations with both have been strained. A yearlong standoff with China persists, and ties with Russia worsened after Moscow arrested a Japanese journalist in October and seized assets of Japan Tobacco this month.
Tokyo’s relationship with Beijing has deteriorated since Takaichi told parliament last November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could threaten Japan’s survival, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its right to collective self-defense. Beijing demanded she retract the remarks. China also imposed export restrictions and launched personal attacks against the Japanese leader.
At this week’s summit in Shenzhen, Takaichi exchanged handshakes and smiles with Xi, though the two held no formal talks. Her reception in China was otherwise distant, with a cool welcome at the airport and a place in the back row of the leaders’ family photo.
Takaichi also spoke with Putin for 30 minutes and raised Russia’s seizure of Japanese assets and the arrest of the Japanese journalist, but Russia has yet to acknowledge that the meeting took place. Moscow’s takeover of Japan Tobacco’s Russian operations is expected to push the company into a net loss for the year ending December, the company said Thursday.
The souring view of China and Russia contrast markedly with Japanese sentiment toward South Korea. Some 62% of respondents expressed affinity toward the country, up from 35% in 2020. South Korea is an important partner in addressing global challenges, a Foreign Ministry official who oversaw the survey said, adding that bilateral ties have become increasingly vital amid a difficult regional security environment.
The survey targeted 3,000 adults nationwide from Sept. 17 to Oct. 25. Preliminary results were based on responses received by Oct. 16, with final findings due next year.

Xi projects China’s global influence after hosting Trump and Putin at APEC
China’s President Xi Jinping has emerged from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with a diplomatic win, reinforcing his global standing despite limited substantive progress
BANGKOK -- Results matter in the international arena, but so do optics. This week’s high-level meetings in China gave President Xi Jinping a win, reinforcing his image as a central player in global diplomacy.
As host of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on Wednesday and Thursday, Xi welcomed the leaders of 21 nations representing some of the world’s largest economies that account for about 60% of global economic activity. He also convened the first formal gathering of the three biggest nuclear powers: the United States, Russia and China.
“History tells us that when major powers live in harmony, the world is at peace, and when they engage in confrontation the world is thrown into turmoil,” Xi said on Thursday before the start of closed-door discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“Our three countries should set an example by working together to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability and make greater contributions to human progress,” he added.
The summit in China's capital city was seen as emblematic of the nation's superpower status. The trilateral meeting on Thursday produced no major breakthroughs, but the image of the three leaders seated at an enormous round table with Xi at the center and Trump to his left and Putin to his right will become part of diplomatic history.
“For most, the image was a suggestion that the world increasingly revolves around Beijing’s power and preferences,” Rush Doshi, director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in an article for the council. “And for U.S. allies in particular, it was unsettling because it suggested that Washington will prioritize engagement with the other great powers over that with its own partners.”
“Xi’s clearest diplomatic gain in Shenzhen was bringing Trump and Putin to the same table,” said Yaqi Li, a Chinese foreign policy researcher at the ISEAS — Yusof Ishak Institute.
China positioned itself as a force for global stability and a go-to talking point in recent years. Xi started the meeting with Trump and Putin with a reminder of how the three countries fought together in World War II.
“History is the best textbook,” Xi said, presenting the talks as a way to push for peace for humanity. “We must remember history, learn from it and work together to shape the future.”
The meeting resulted in a joint declaration that was light on commitments and did not tackle major issues in a substantive way.
“They're using this opportunity … to highlight that China is a great power, and they're in a different status relative to other countries,” said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
Xi and Trump held their third meeting this year, highlighting the personal rapport they have built that both men said was important to the bilateral relationship between their nations. China's government highlighted the “constructive strategic stability” of the relationship while Xi commended the U.S. president for his role.
“The efforts you have made are there for all to see and will go down in history,” Xi told Trump.
There were no announcements about existing trade issues between the countries such as U.S. complaints that China has not fulfilled its commitment to buy from U.S. farmers and export more rare earth materials. Nor were there announcements about the Board of Trade and the expected framework to allow trade in nonsensitive goods worth $30 billion on each side.
It was unclear if officials taking part in a diplomatic channel to discuss artificial intelligence issues met in Shenzhen, said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
However, “AI seems to be the one area where some progress has been made, with China affirming its concerns about safety and security and welcoming bilateral work,” Cutler said.
Whether the personal rapport between Xi and Trump can persist will be tested soon, according to Craig Singleton, senior fellow and senior director of the China Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
“Xi treated Trump with respect in Shenzhen. He will test his resolve in Miami next month, when the bill for Beijing’s trade commitments comes due,” Singleton said in an email.

Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.
Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.
Loading...
In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.
While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.
"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."
Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.
But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.
"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."
The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.
On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.
Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.
"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"
But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.
The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."
"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."
To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.
"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.
But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.
The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.
NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

Quick Answer
LastWave, Musify, Convx, Spotube, and SimpMusic are free open-source clients for YouTube Music and Spotify. They unlock premium perks without subscription fees or ad tracking, offering background playback, offline downloads, time-synced lyrics, lossless audio, and customized interfaces without locked controls.
Subscription prices are going through the roof. And when you stack multiple subscriptions together, it can put a big hole in your pocket. For listening to music, we usually depend on Spotify and YouTube Music. They are the default music streaming sources for millions across the globe. Though there are alternatives from which you can hear high-quality audio, they just can’t match the ease of popular apps. But you are bombarded with ads, and several features are locked behind a paywall unless you pay.
Thankfully, you don’t have to search the internet for free options. Developers around the world have built free apps that give you many of those perks. Below are five of the best, what each does well, and what to watch out for before installing.
Table of Contents
Why are open-source music apps worth a look?
To be clear, most of these apps are clients. This means that they don’t store any music themselves. They plug into a service like YouTube Music and show it in a cleaner, ad-free interface with extra features on top, which you’d usually get after paying for a premium subscription. For me, Spotify has been the go-to music streaming app, but slowly the app has become quite greedy.
After a few times, the next and previous song buttons get locked, and it asks you to pay to unlock them. I mean, what is wrong with companies today? Thankfully, I have now ditched Spotify and have picked one of the below open-source music options.
That has three practical effects:
- No ads and no subscription fees. Everything below is free.
- Most of these apps have no ad trackers or tracking SDKs.
- New features are constantly added, and some of them aren’t even available in paid apps.
The catch is that these apps rely on unofficial methods to fetch music, so they can break when YouTube or Spotify changes something. Treat them as great free alternatives, but not as rock-solid replacements. Let us take a look at the free alternatives.
Best free open-source music apps
LastWave
If you care about how your music sounds, LastWave is the one to install first. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. Most of us would care about the free music that we get with LastWave, but you will soon appreciate the quality of music that it offers. And since it is a YouTube Music client, you are getting access to almost every song that is available on YouTube.
The headline feature is lossless FLAC audio, up to 24-bit/192 kHz. When you press play, the song starts playing right away on the fastest available stream, and while you listen, the app fetches the lossless version in the background and switches over once it’s ready. On compatible phones and headphones, LastWave also plays the Dolby Atmos version of a song automatically. For those who own a USB DAC or a pair of IEMs, there’s a bit-perfect mode that sends raw, unprocessed audio straight to your device.
The app is packed with features that normally sit behind a subscription. The lyrics are synced word-by-word and pulled from sources like Apple Music, Musixmatch, and LRCLIB. There’s a 10-band equalizer with presets for thousands of headphone models, and smart playlists that build mixes from your listening history. Plus, you have the option to import playlists from Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube Music in seconds, and even sync your Spotify liked songs.
Musify
Not everyone wants a hundred settings and toggles. Some people just want to listen to their favorite music without having to deal with ads and a hundred pop-ups about purchasing the subscription between two songs. Musify is for people who just want to open an app, search for a song, and press play. It’s a lightweight Android app built around Material You, which means its colors automatically match your phone’s theme and wallpaper.
Using it is fairly easy. You search for songs, albums, artists, or playlists and start streaming over Wi-Fi or mobile data. If you want to save data or listen on a flight, you can download tracks and play them offline. It lets you create your own playlists, rename and reorder them, or import existing ones from online sources. The player shows lyrics so you can follow along. You can also control the quality of the audio.
There are no annoying banner ads, no audio ads, no sign-up, and no tracking inside the app, and the interface is translated into dozens of languages by the community. I found this to be a great choice for older phones, or for a parent or sibling who finds complicated apps annoying.
Convx
While most open source music apps work well, there are only a few that also feel nice to use. Convx comes in the second category. If you like iOS’s “Liquid Glass” design, then you would love Convx. It brings iPhone’s Liquid Glass design to Android, with frosted, see-through menus, floating controls, and album-inspired colors that change with whatever you are playing.
Under the pretty surface, Convx is a complete music player. You can browse and stream music, save songs for offline listening, build queues and playlists, set a sleep timer, change playback speed, and tweak the sound to your taste with an equalizer. What makes it stand out among the heavy hitters is its DJ-style playback. You also get automix, crossfade, and smooth transitions between one song and the next. Lyrics are synced word by word and come from several providers, plus it gets animated artwork.
Convx can play local files and even songs stored on a home server or NAS through SMB and WebDAV. You can choose the option to import your Spotify playlists, show what you’re playing on Discord, scrobble to Last.fm, recognize songs playing around you, and use Listen Together to sync playback with friends.
Spotube
Spotube is the veteran here, with over 46,000 stars on GitHub, and it works differently from the rest. Instead of being locked to one service like Spotify or YouTube, it runs on plugins. You choose your own music sources, metadata, and playlists through plugins made by the community, or if you’re good with it, you can write one yourself.
The biggest advantage is that it works everywhere. Spotube runs natively on Android, Windows, macOS, and Linux. This means you can use the same app on your phone and your laptop. It’s small, fast, and light on data. You can import and sync playlists from popular music services or manage them locally. It gives time-synced lyrics from public lyric databases no matter which source you use. Offline downloads are supported, with proper metadata and ID.
Privacy is one of the biggest highlights of Spotube. It collects no telemetry and no user data. Installing it is also easy, because you can download it through winget, Scoop, Chocolatey, Homebrew, Flatpak, and F-Droid.
SimpMusic
SimpMusic is that one app that does everything. It’s a free YouTube Music client for Android and desktop that borrows many of Spotify’s best ideas. You can play music from YouTube Music or regular YouTube without ads, and it gets you background playback. You can browse the home feed, charts, podcasts and moods, search everything on YouTube, cache songs for offline playback and use Android Auto.
SimpMusic Wrapped gives you a year-in-music recap just like Spotify’s. Then there is monthly recap playlists and listening charts that stay on your device. There are three Now Playing styles, including one that looks like Apple Music, and the lyrics are synced in 12 languages. You can even share lyrics as an image.
You can switch to 1080p video with subtitles, skip sponsor segments with SponsorBlock, see dislike counts with Return YouTube Dislike, and use a 10-band equalizer with AutoEq headphone profiles.
Which one should you pick?
If you care most about sound quality, I would suggest LastWave. If you want something simple, pick Musify. If design matters to you, try Convx. If you want plugins and an app that runs on every device you own, choose Spotube. If you want the most features in one place, install SimpMusic. The best part is that all five are free and can be installed side by side, so you can try a few and keep your favorite. You will get access to unlimited songs from the best sources in good quality. Let us know which one you chose, and comment below if you have a different app that you use for listening to music.

MAHA PAC spends on itself
MAHA PAC leaders blamed the election losses of the movement’s preferred candidates on the powerful forces supporting their rivals.
The problem is the MAHA PAC didn’t spend much of its own fund to push back against those forces, Daniel Payne, Isabella Cueto, and Chelsea Cirruzzo report. Instead, filings show it spent big on its allies, boosters, and an affiliated nonprofit.
Those investments often came at the expense of spending on political races, including for MAHA candidates in competitive districts.

Sanders’ Medicare for All plan
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is feeling optimistic about the first stage of his plan to vastly expand health coverage in the U.S. He predicted in a Wednesday press conference that Democrats will pass legislation lowering the Medicare eligibility age while President Trump is still in office, and that Trump might not veto it.
In the first year of his plan, Congress would lower the Medicare eligibility age to 55; add dental, vision and hearing benefits; and guarantee free Medicaid coverage to children until age 19.
And he pushed back on the assumption that Trump would veto such a bill.
“I am not absolutely certain that Trump would not sign it,” he said.
The health committee does not have jurisdiction over Medicare, but Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), who is expected to lead the committee that does have jurisdiction, said he is on board with Sanders’ plan. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) also supports the “Medicare for More” and “Medikids” proposals, an indication that the party is quickly moving toward common ground on a health care agenda that averts divisions between its liberal and moderate wings.
Sanders also gave insights into the health care investigations he might undertake, including of health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the insurance and pharma industries.
“Taking a hard look at the way the insurance industry runs, how they distort health care. Taking a hard look at the pharmaceutical industry as to why we pay by far the highest prices in the world for prescription drugs. Those are areas that need investigation,” he said.
Why was Overton pulled? Who will run the FDA?
Those are two of the seven burning questions Margaret Manto outlines for the FDA’s future after Heidi Overton’s nomination to lead the agency was pulled.
One of the biggest mysteries is why the White House pulled her. Mysteries beget rumors, especially on Capitol Hill, and the biggest rumor is that President Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller was behind it. Overton was supposedly not MAHA enough for Miller.
The agency’s current acting commissioner, Kyle Diamantas, has reportedly declined to take the role permanently and wants out at the end of the year.
Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), who lost his reelection bid, is rumored to be in the running. But it doesn’t look like he could get confirmed before Democrats take control of the Senate.
Read more about who MAHA may rally around and what the turmoil means for an agency that regulates 20% of the U.S. economy.
Rep. Carter wants the job
But does the White House want the Georgia Republican as FDA commissioner?
Buddy Carter is free. The pharmacist and advocate for reforming drug middlemen gave up his House seat to run for Senate. He came in third in the primary.
And he wants the job. Carter said he told the White House he’s interested — the White House did not come to him.
“I think they’ve got other plans,” Carter told STAT.
Republicans surprised by withdrawal of Overton’s nomination
Republicans said they were caught off guard by the Trump administration’s withdrawal of Overton on Tuesday night.
“Before I went to bed, I thought we were voting on Overton,” committee member Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) told reporters as she exited the hearing room where senators had planned to vote on Overton.
“So I haven’t given much thought to what the White House may do next, and maybe the White House hasn’t either,” she said.
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), chair of the health committee with jurisdiction over the nomination, said Overton had sufficient support to win confirmation. He also said the White House told the press before telling him.
Murkowski was among the holdouts, but she declined to say Wednesday morning whether she had planned to vote for Overton.
“You are asking a theoretical question that doesn’t have a reasonable response to it,” she told reporters.
Cassidy blocks Trump’s NSF nominee
Cassidy also cancelled the Wednesday vote on Jim O’Neill, whom Trump nominated to lead the National Science Foundation, Daniel and Margaret report.
O’Neill has held high-ranking posts at HHS and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He would have led the NSF for six years if confirmed. But Cassidy said O’Neill didn’t have the support to advance.
