On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
'Brainstorming process'
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
'Endless betrayal'
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Environmental exposures during pregnancy and childhood, including tobacco smoke, indoor air pollution and dietary quality, may be associated with health outcomes such as BMI and behaviour, with many of these links persisting into adolescence, a new study has found.
Researchers, led by those at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (ISGlobal), identified six prenatal and 42 childhood exposures associated with multiple outcomes and health families simultaneously.
The study, published in Science Advances, provides an atlas of associations between early-life environmental exposures and health, highlighting factors that may be relevant for prevention and policy action.
"Our approach allowed us to jointly analyse associations between the early-life exposome and multiple health outcomes instead of studying each one separately," first author Augusto Anguita-Ruiz, ISGlobal and University of Barcelona researcher, said.
The researchers used an outcome-wide exposome approach to study associations of exposures with health across four domains -- cardiometabolic, mental health, respiratory, and allergic problems.
The exposome refers to the totality of environmental exposures a person experiences throughout life, including factors such as diet, tobacco smoke and air pollution.
The exposures examined included diet, physical activity, sleep and other individual behaviours, as well as tobacco smoke, indoor and outdoor air pollution, chemical pollutants, metals and characteristics of the built environment.
The authors "identified a set of 'master regulator' exposures, such as maternal smoking, indoor air pollution, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and dietary and urban factors, that influenced multiple health domains, with effects persisting into adolescence."
Senior co-author Valérie Siroux, researcher at the French National Institute for Health and Medical Research (Inserm), said: "Although no exposure was associated with all four domains, around one in three of the selected exposures was linked to more than one, suggesting that certain exposures can have broad and multisystemic effects on health."
Maternal smoking during pregnancy was associated with higher BMI and more externalising behaviours, such as aggression and impulsivity, in children during both early childhood and adolescence, as well as more ADHD symptoms during adolescence.
Higher maternal meat intake during pregnancy was also associated with several mental health outcomes and asthma in children, as well as wheezing and dermatitis during childhood.
Associations between environmental exposures and health parameters observed in early childhood were found to persist in adolescence.
The observation suggests that early environmental conditions may leave relatively durable health signatures, the researchers said.

As a congressman, Duffy voted for bills that allocated or continued FAA funding in 2011, 2013 and 2018. Duffy’s representative told PolitiFact in 2025 that the reason for his opposition to the 2019 bill was that he felt it did not provide enough funds.
In mid-November, a nationwide ground stop halted flights across the United States. In response, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called on Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for the Federal Aviation Authority. However, many blamed Duffy for allegedly opposing a bill that would give funding to the FAA in 2019, when he was a congressman.
A clip went viral in which CNBC asked Duffy about his purported voting record.
Duffy did vote against the 2019 bill that would have given the FAA more funding, and as a result we've rated the claim true. However, that is not the entire story. Duffy also voted in support of three previous bills that increased FAA funding.
Snopes reached out to the Department of Transportation. A spokesperson directed us to the 2025 PolitiFact story that highlighted three previous instances when Duffy supported funds for the FAA. A spokesperson for Duffy told PolitiFact that the 2019 bill only represented a small funding increase.
A CNBC anchor asked Duffy about his opposition to the 2019 funding, "When you were a congressman, in 2019 you actually voted against support for the Transportation, Housing, and Urban Development Agencies Appropriation Act, and that would've given more funding to the FAA. Do you regret that vote?"
In response, Duffy said:
I've seen those articles. All the FAA reauthorizations that funded the FAA, I voted for all of those. That vote was not a funding ― a proposal for the FAA. I was on the record voting for all the FAA funding. But the question is what is this Congress going to do?
Duffy referred to three previous instances in which he supported bills that gave additional funding to the FAA. In 2011, Duffy voted in support of the "FAA Modernization and Reform Act," which approved $63.4 billion to the FAA over the next four years.
In 2014, he voted in favor of the "Federal Aviation Administration Continuing Appropriations Resolution," which passed the House but not the Senate.
In 2018, he voted for the "FAA Reauthorization Act," which approved $96.7 billion in funding for federal aviation programs over five years.
In 2019, Duffy voted against the "Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act," which would have given $17.7 billion in total budgetary resources to the FAA. The House Appropriations Committee noted the funding amount was "$310 million below the fiscal year 2018 enacted level and $1.6 billion above the request."
At the time, Duffy did not give a reason for his "No" vote. When we asked the Department of Transportation to clarify over email, a spokesperson referenced his 2025 comments to PolitiFact, in which his office said the bill represented only a small funding increase.
Republicans opposed the 2019 bill for a range of reasons, including that U.S. President Donald Trump would have vetoed it. The bill—which bundled funding for various agencies and put up for a vote during a government shutdown—was passed by a Democratic-controlled House but stalled in the Senate.
On Nov. 14, Democrats questioned Duffy's call for additional funding for the FAA. Members of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure noted:
Congress approved $12.5 billion for the Department of Transportation to make necessary safety upgrades to our air traffic control system. Fifteen months later, the administration's obligated $4.3 billion but only spent $1 billion, leaving $8 billion unobligated and $11 billion unspent. Explain to Congress, again, why they need more money?
Duffy said this was not true. In a CNN interview, he said:
I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there's no money for that. There's no money for towers. Our towers are old.
The spokesperson for the Department of Transportation emphasized to Snopes over email that in 2025, Democrats opposed the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, in which Republicans allocated $12.5 billion for air traffic control. The act passed with almost exclusively Republican votes. In September, Duffy had asked for $30 billion to upgrade the FAA systems. After the November ground stop, he upped the request to $50 billion.
In sum, Duffy has supported FAA funding in the past, but did vote against the 2019 bill.
For further reading, Snopes has reported on Duffy's other statements regarding the FAA as well as the unfounded claim that Duffy's son-in-law has ties to an artificial intelligence air traffic management tool.

The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed the Karnataka government's appeal challenging a Karnataka High Court judgment that allowed bike taxi services to operate across the State, providing relief to aggregators Ola, Uber and Rapido.
A bench comprising Justices Satish Chandra Sharma and N Kotiswar Singh passed the order, leaving the High Court's decision permitting bike taxi operations undisturbed.
The dispute originates from a January 23, 2026 judgment delivered by a division bench of the Karnataka High Court, comprising then Chief Justice Vibhu Bakhru and Justice CM Joshi. The bench had overturned an earlier order directing bike taxi operators to suspend their services until the State government formulated a regulatory policy.
The High Court had allowed appeals filed by aggregators Ola, Uber and Rapido, motorcycle owners and the Bike Taxi Welfare Association. It ruled that motorcycles could be registered as transport vehicles and operated as contract carriages, subject to regulatory requirements prescribed by the State.
Challenging the High Court's decision, the Karnataka government approached the Supreme Court, citing concerns over passenger safety, insurance coverage and the lack of adequate safeguards for users of bike taxi services.
The government had contested the continuation of bike taxi operations in the absence of a regulatory framework addressing these concerns.
Several auto and taxi driver associations had also challenged the High Court's decision. They argued that permitting bike taxi services without imposing equivalent regulatory obligations would adversely affect conventional transport operators.
With the Supreme Court dismissing the appeals, the Karnataka High Court's January 23 judgment allowing bike taxi services to operate across the State remains in force.

Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) lets you uninstall multiple Windows apps at once for free. Select unwanted apps, remove them in batches, and clean up leftover files to reclaim storage. It also supports quiet uninstallation, but review your selections carefully before deleting anything.
An easy way to free up storage on your Windows PC is to remove unnecessary apps — ones you no longer need. You identify the apps and delete them one by one. It’s pretty straightforward as long as you’re dealing with a couple of apps. If the number is higher, the method starts to feel tedious.
This is where a one-click uninstaller comes in handy, allowing you to delete multiple apps at once. Bulk Crap Uninstaller (BCU) is one such app. Here’s how it works and how to use it to bulk uninstall Windows apps on your PC.
What Is Bulk Crap Uninstaller, and What Makes It Better Than Other Tools?
Bulk Crap Uninstaller (also called BCUninstaller or BCU) is a bulk uninstaller that makes uninstalling multiple apps on your Windows PC at once incredibly easy. It can scan your computer comprehensively and find everything from Windows Store apps (pre-installed by Microsoft) and third-party apps to Steam games, portable apps, and Chocolatey packages. You can then select what you want to remove. This adds them to a queue, and the app handles uninstallation for you.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller stands out from other bulk uninstallers, including some paid alternatives, in a few ways. First, it can find broken or un-uninstallable programs and force uninstall them. Second, it can scan your file system and find leftover or orphaned items (files, folders, registry keys) left behind by apps you deleted manually. That way, you can safely and easily delete them and reclaim storage space. And third, it offers a “quiet uninstallation” mode that eliminates the need to click through dialog boxes and instead uninstalls the selected apps silently in the background.
How To Use Bulk Crap Uninstaller to Bulk Uninstall Windows Apps on Your PC
Bulk Crap Uninstaller is free to download and use. Go to the Bulk Crap Uninstaller website, and you’ll see multiple ways to download the app there. You can choose any method; the easiest is to download the installer from SourceForge. Next, run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions to complete it. Once installed, the app will require configuration. Configure it per your preference; you can change the settings later if you don’t like them. I recommend enabling the Select using checkboxes and Show items in groups options.
Once configured, Bulk Crap Uninstaller will scan your computer and populate a list of all installed programs, including hidden apps, Windows Store apps, Steam games, portable apps, orphaned shortcuts, and leftover registry keys. You’ll see additional details, such as size, version, publisher name, installation date, and certificate, next to each listing. You can use filters and sort options to filter out and sort items in a specific order.
Go through the list and tick the checkbox next to the apps you want to uninstall. The status bar at the bottom will show how many items you’ve selected and how much space deleting them will free up. Finally, click the Uninstall button at the top. The app will open a dialog box showing your selection. Hit Continue while checking (and changing, if required) the settings, and click Begin Uninstallation.
You’ll see a prompt asking if you’d like to create a Restore Point. Select accordingly, and the app will uninstall the selected apps. While it deletes apps, you’ll see the uninstallation status in a dialog box. At any point, if you want to cancel the uninstallation, click the Cancel button.
Once Bulk Crap Uninstaller finishes uninstalling the selected apps, it will ask if you want to delete the leftovers too. Review the listed files carefully, uncheck the ones you don’t want to delete, and click the Delete selected button to get rid of them. Be sure to back up your registry if you’ll be deleting leftover registry keys.
When you uninstall apps this way, you’ll need to click through multiple dialog box menus to complete the uninstallation. You can save yourself this hassle by clicking the Quiet Uninstall button instead of Uninstall after selecting apps for deletion. Bulk Crap Uninstaller will try — wherever possible — to uninstall apps silently. You won’t see visual confirmation in this mode.
Other Bulk Crap Uninstaller Features You Should Know About
For most people, the standard uninstallation process we checked out above is enough to get the job done. However, Bulk Crap Uninstaller has a few advanced features that can help you get the most out of the app.
For example, Bulk Crap Uninstaller offers a CLI version called BCU-console. It’s a great option for those who want to clean up their PC without dealing with multiple windows. Similarly, it lets you run an uninstallation script with your selected apps to automate deletion. This can be useful for cleaning up new PCs, too. Just feed the app a list of all the pre-installed apps from Windows, and it will remove them. You can go through Bulk Crap Uninstaller’s documentation to learn more about using scripts.
Bulk Crap Uninstaller can also run portably. So, you can put it on a USB flash drive and run it directly. This is handy when you want to uninstall apps on a PC running very low on storage space or one that isn’t connected to the internet and can’t download the Bulk Crap Uninstaller app.
Last but not least, Bulk Crap Uninstaller is highly configurable. As such, you can configure its behavior per your preference. Click the gear icon in the top toolbar to access the app’s settings. Here, you can change things like where to look for apps, which items to show/omit, and how the list appears. You can also configure the default behavior of quiet uninstallation and how many concurrent uninstalls the app can perform, among other things.
What I’m Not a Fan Of
I’ve used Bulk Crap Uninstaller on my PC for a while, and although it does its job well, there are a few aspects that I’m not a fan of and wish were better. The biggest one is that the app’s interface can seem intimidating, especially to first-time users. In other words, it looks more like a developer tool than a regular consumer app. It’s best to spend some time exploring different menus and options the app offers before jumping straight into uninstalling apps.
Then, there’s the risk of over-cleaning. Because Bulk Crap Uninstaller can scan deep system components, too, it’s important to double-check the selection — and not blindly trust the populated list — before uninstallation. You can configure the settings to minimize the risk. Another thing I’ve noticed is that the quiet uninstallation mode sometimes doesn’t work: some apps don’t obey it and keep popping up dialog boxes that require confirmation before uninstallation. Although rare, some users have complained about aggressive registry scanning, wherein Bulk Crap Uninstaller highlights shared keys (those used by other apps too) for removal. You can avoid this by reviewing the registry keys highlighted for deletion.
These aren’t drawbacks of Bulk Crap Uninstaller, though; they’re just a trade-off for its advanced capabilities. For this reason, it’s important to configure the app before you start using it and be completely sure about the actions you perform using it. You should also create a Restore Point when dealing with apps with broken uninstallers or stubborn leftovers. This way, if the cleanup goes wrong and renders your PC unusable, you can roll back to the last working state and undo the action.

Indian national, Nikhil Gupta, was sentenced to 235 months (nearly 19 years and seven months) in prison by a US federal court on Friday for his role in a murder-for-hire plot targeting Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. US District Judge Victor Marrero announced the sentence in the Southern District of New York. Pannun, who holds American and Canadian citizenship, was present in court when the verdict was pronounced.
Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The plot involved attempts to hire a hitman to kill Pannun on American soil.
The sentence of 235 months is at the lower end of the US Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months. Last week, the US government had sought a 293-month prison term, arguing that Gupta's actions warranted a severe punishment.
In a 20-page submission to the court, US Attorney James McDonald described Gupta's conduct as "as brutal as it was brazen".
"He was a crucial participant in a foreign plot to execute a US citizen on US soil. 
The Court should impose a sentence that reflects the magnitude of the crime and sends a message that the violent silencing of voices in this country will not be tolerated," McDonald said.
The US government alleged that Gupta and his co-conspirators, including at least one Indian government employee, plotted to kill an American citizen because of the "victim's political ideology".
"It is a crime of the utmost seriousness and demands an equally serious penalty…. the Government submits that a sentence at the top of the United States Sentencing Guidelines range of 235 to 293 months’ incarceration is necessary to serve the legitimate purposes of sentencing," the submission said.
What Gupta's lawyers argued
Gupta's lawyers had sought a substantially reduced sentence of 144 months, followed by three years of supervised release. They backed the Probation Department's recommendation for a downward variance from the sentencing guidelines.
His defence argued that Gupta had no previous criminal record and was suffering from untreated alcohol dependence at the time of the offence. They also said that a lengthy prison term would carry significant consequences for the 55-year-old.
"Gupta does not minimise" the seriousness of his actions, his lawyers told the court. They acknowledged that he had agreed to arrange a murder but argued that the punishment should be proportionate.
"He agreed to arrange the murder of another person, and that conduct warrants a term of imprisonment. But the sentence this Court imposes should be sufficient, and not greater than necessary, to serve the purposes of sentencing as to this defendant," his lawyers said.
Gupta expressed regret in letter to court
In a letter submitted to the court, Gupta said he wished he could "turn back time to 2023 and undo my mistakes".
He added that when he looked back at his actions, "I don’t even recognise the man I had become."
Gupta said he had become distant from his family in early 2023 and started drinking heavily almost every night. He also expressed regret over the suffering caused to his family and others.
"I deeply regretted the suffering I caused them and the people around me," he wrote.
He also told the court that he was "so thankful that my actions did not result in the loss of human life or injury", adding that such an outcome "would have been the greatest regret of my life."
How the murder plot unfolded
According to the indictment, other public court documents and statements made in court, Gupta worked with associates in India and elsewhere in 2023 to plan Pannun's assassination in the US.
The alleged plot involved co-defendant Vikash Yadav, whom US prosecutors identified as an Indian government employee.
At Yadav's direction, Gupta contacted a person he believed was a criminal associate to arrange a hitman to kill Pannun in New York City. However, the person was actually a confidential source working with the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA).
Yadav subsequently agreed, through arrangements brokered by Gupta, to pay the undercover source $100,000 to carry out the killing.
On or around June 9, 2023, Gupta and Yadav arranged for an associate to deliver $15,000 in cash to the undercover source as an advance payment for the planned murder.

Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., on Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.
His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.
Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.
Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.

The Delhi High Court (HC) on Thursday sought responses from the Enforcement Directorate (ED), Bureau of Immigration, and Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) after Tina Ambani, wife of Reliance Group chairman Anil Ambani and a former Bollywood actor, filed a petition seeking disclosure of any existing look-out circular (LOC) against her. According to LiveLaw, Justice Mini Pushkarna issued notice to the government agencies, with the ED and SFIO responding that they would file responses. Ambani has approached the court as she plans to travel to Thailand, the UAE, Oman and Bhutan to meet friends and family from December 10. Her counsel told the court that there were no pending summonses from either the ED or the SFIO. However, she wanted the agencies to clarify whether any LOC had been issued against her before she undertakes the planned travel. Appearing for Ambani, advocate Arshdeep Singh Khurana said, "Two agencies had summoned me, the SFIO and ED. There are no pending summons now, and they have not called me. I wish to travel from December 10 to visit my family. This is a disclosure petition seeking that if there is an LOC, they may tell me, and if there is no LOC, then it may come on record," Bar and Bench reported. In her petition, Ambani expressed apprehension that the SFIO may have sought an LOC against her as part of its investigation into Reliance Group companies, or that the ED may have issued one in connection with its money-laundering probe under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). She stated that the SFIO had issued her a summons on July 20, 2026, under Section 217 of the Companies Act, 2013. The ED, meanwhile, had issued two summonses to her in February under Section 50 of the PMLA. Ambani told the court that she had responded to the ED's summonses through written communications dated February 16 and 20. She also replied to the SFIO's summons through her lawyers on July 29. Subsequently, in a letter dated October 5, she offered to appear before the agency in person on October 29 or 30. However, according to her petition, the SFIO neither scheduled her appearance nor issued another summons. She further stated that she had written to the Bureau of Immigration on August 28, seeking confirmation of whether an LOC had been issued against her. A copy of the representation was also sent to the SFIO, but she allegedly received no response from the authorities. Ambani argued that being kept unaware of the existence of an LOC, if one had been issued, would prevent her from challenging the restriction. Her petition states, "The continued subsistence of an LOC against a person who is not even permitted to know of it, and the refusal to disclose even its existence, renders illusory the remedy available in law against an LOC, offends the principles of natural justice, and violates the Petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution of India.” The investigations concern loans exceeding ₹40,000 crore obtained by companies belonging to the Anil Dhirubhai Ambani Group from a consortium of public and private sector banks. Investigators suspect that a substantial portion of the borrowed funds was diverted through complex financial transactions, dealings with related entities and inter-corporate transfers, instead of being used for the purposes for which the loans were sanctioned. As part of its money-laundering investigation, the ED summoned Tina Ambani twice in February for questioning. The agency is understood to be examining a suspected financial trail linked to the purchase of a luxury condominium in Manhattan, New York. Separately, the SFIO also summoned her earlier this year in connection with its investigation into the affairs of Reliance Group companies. The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets through Friday, with the S&P 500 down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% by mid-afternoon.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 4% by afternoon trading as shares in major tech companies continued to fall.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell off continued.
Nvidia shares had plunged by more than 11% by the afternoon, while Musk's firms SpaceX and Tesla had both fallen by more than 6%.
Meta was down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 3.5%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

Around one in five pregnant and lactating women in Assam’s Barak Valley and adjoining districts of Tripura suffer from suboptimal levels of ‘Thiamine’ (vitamin B1), according to a study by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN), Hyderabad, highlighting a continuing public health concern in the region.
The study, ‘Re-Emergence of Thiamine Deficiency Among Pregnant and Lactating Women in Northeast India’, published in the Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences, examined the prevalence of thiamine deficiency and its link to dietary practices in areas where beriberi cases have previously been reported, said a press release on Monday.
Researchers conducted the community-based study during 2023-24 among 1,083 women from 120 villages in Assam’s Barak Valley and neighbouring parts of Tripura. Thiamine status was assessed using biochemical and functional indicators to determine the extent of deficiency.
The findings showed that about 20% of participants had inadequate thiamine levels. Based on blood thiamine measurements, 4.9% were deficient, and 15.2% had marginal levels. A separate functional assessment produced similar results, with 8.5% showing severe deficiency and 12.1% marginal deficiency. Pregnant women were found to be more vulnerable than lactating mothers.
Thiamine is an essential micronutrient that supports energy metabolism and healthy nervous system function. Deficiency can lead to serious health complications, making adequate intake particularly important during pregnancy and breastfeeding.
According to Mahesh Kumar Mummadi, NIN scientist and lead author of the study, dietary assessments revealed that most women consumed rice-based diets with limited diversity. Practices such as consuming stored rice, repeatedly washing rice before cooking, chewing betel nut and drinking salted tea were associated with a higher risk of deficiency.
NIN director Bharati Kulkarni said the findings underscore the need to look beyond routinely monitored nutrients in maternal health programmes. She called for greater dietary diversity, regular nutritional surveillance and targeted supplementation in high-risk regions. Researchers also noted that since the study focused on areas with previously reported beriberi clusters, the findings may not be representative of all pregnant and lactating women across India.

Nigeria moves to end jail terms for attempted suicide
- Published
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide, proposing medical support instead of prosecution for those who survive.
The proposal seeks to shift Nigeria's approach from criminal punishment to treatment and rehabilitation.
It follows years of calls for reform from mental health professionals. A separate bill seeking to decriminalise attempted suicide has already passed its second reading in the Senate.
Under Nigeria's law, attempted suicide is a criminal offence with those convicted facing up to one year's imprisonment, a fine or both.
The Senate bill also seeks to replace criminal penalties for attempted suicide with medical treatment, rehabilitation and support.
It was sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, who has argued that prosecuting people who survive suicide attempts could discourage those experiencing suicidal thoughts from seeking help.
He also warned that families might conceal such incidents for fear of prosecution and social stigma.
He stressed that the bill is not aimed at legalising or encouraging suicide attempts but rather protecting the survivors.
Tinubu's proposal has been welcomed by Senate President Godswill Akpabio, who had previously suggested that people who survived suicide attempts should be sent to prison.
"We are saying that suicide is a crime for now. Therefore, if you attempt it, we will send you to prison," Akpabio had said.
However, after receiving the Tinubu's proposal, he sought to clarify his earlier remarks, saying they did not apply to people experiencing mental health conditions.
He added that punishing people whose actions were influenced by mental health conditions would be insensitive.
Tinubu's letter follows sustained calls from mental health professionals for the law to be changed.
At a parliamentary public hearing in May 2024, the then president of the Association of Psychiatrists of Nigeria, Professor Taiwo Obindo, urged lawmakers to remove criminal penalties for attempted suicide.
"Why do we, as a nation, then punish individuals who are ill and need medical attention rather than prosecution?" he asked.
Drawing on his experience as a psychiatrist, Obindo said most people who die by suicide have a history of mental illness.
Akpabio has referred the president's amendment bill to the relevant senate committee for further consideration.
Nigeria is among several African countries where attempted suicide remains a criminal offence.
Ghana decriminalised attempted suicide in 2023, while Kenya's High Court ruled in January 2025 that the law criminalising it was unconstitutional.

French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.
The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.
Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.
The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.
She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".
French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.
The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.
The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be delayed until after the 2027 state elections, with the government concerned about a potential backlash from merchants and trade associations. Citing industry sources, Financial Express reported that the government, RBI, and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) are yet to agree on an implementation date, despite much of the regulatory and operational groundwork being complete. Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa, and Manipur are due to go to polls in the first half of next year. A senior industry official cited by the publication described a deferment until after the Uttar Pradesh polls as a worst-case scenario. Discussions remain focused on finding a suitable rollout window. While minor modifications are possible after implementation, the official ruled out substantial changes to the framework. MDR is a fee charged to merchants for processing payments. Under the proposed framework, eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract a 0.4% charge, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Transactions of up to ₹2,000, person-to-person transfers, and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt. The rollout was initially scheduled for October 15 but was deferred until after Diwali, with NPCI citing the festive season. The payments body said it would notify a revised implementation date separately. Meanwhile, NPCI has notified the UPI Vyapaar Saksham scheme, which will use a portion of MDR collections to support QR code and soundbox deployment among small merchants. The scheme will run for three years from the implementation of UPI MDR. Shares of fintech companies Paytm, Pine Labs, and MobiKwik fell sharply in morning trade following the report of a possible further delay in MDR rollout. At 11:05 AM IST, the stocks were trading around 9%, 5%, and 7% lower, respectively. During the session, Paytm parent One 97 Communications fell as much as 9.1% to ₹1,715, while Pine Labs declined 5.5% to ₹159.90. MobiKwik parent One MobiKwik Systems dropped as much as 8.7% to ₹206.80.

It is rare for a prominent Indian VC firm to go through a churn at the top without people on the ground in Bengaluru and Delhi talking about what might be happening. And so it is with Fireside Ventures. “A single partner leaving is pretty much routine. Two top level exits in a matter of weeks with even the resumes of junior staff floating around in rival firms surely means something more,” an investor associated with a consumer tech VC firm told Inc42, referring to the recent sequence of events at Fireside Ventures. But there could be more at stake here than just the two exits, even if that is where the focus currently lies. Earlier this month, when Fireside Ventures announced that cofounder and partner Vinay Singh would step down to explore “the frontiers of agentic commerce”, the move was widely seen as a personal one. Singh was said to be leaving to pursue what he believed was the next big shift in consumption. His exit, however, could not be viewed in isolation when, just 10 days later, as Inc42 had exclusively reported, Prayag Mohanty, a principal at the firm who had led several of Fireside’s early-stage bets, also moved out. Two senior exits in under two weeks would be a talking point at any VC firm. The two departures and the succession question have created a buzz in VC circles about the future of Fireside, one of India’s largest consumer focused VC firms with ₹5,300 Cr in AUM Fireside does run a deliberately lean investment team, but multiple people Inc42 spoke with said the two exits after closing a ₹2,265 Cr fund less than a year ago, in December 2025, cannot be considered a coincidence and that the “real story” lies at the very top. Kanwaljit Singh, the founder and managing partner who has been the face of Fireside since he set it up in 2017, has expressed his intent to move away from the firm’s day-to-day operations. He may take on a mentor or chairman role, though the exact contours have not been decided yet, sources said. “Kanwaljit has told some of the founders in Fireside’s portfolio that Fund IV could be the last fund he is associated with. This is truly a big move for the entire VC firm, and handing over the baton to the top executives has been in the works for a while now,” people aware of these discussions told us. That has opened up the most consequential question a founder-led fund can face: Who comes next? According to the people Inc42 spoke with, the answer has not been settled. The process of finding the next leader has triggered differences within the firm, with at least two senior executives, Kannan Sitaram and Dipanjan Basu, who were elevated to the positions of cofounders, being seen as successors. Fireside currently lists Kanwaljit Singh, Sitaram, Basu and Adarsh Menon as partners. Besides these, the firm has five principals who, along with the partners, make up the deal-flow bench. The succession plan under way at the VC firm paints cofounder and partner Vinay Singh’s departure in a different light. If the firm is indeed looking for someone to take over the reins, it would have made sense to pass the torch to Vinay Singh, who cofounded the firm. Fireside Ventures did not respond to Inc42’s queries by the time of publishing this report. Two Exits, One Pattern Viewed individually, the two departures do not appear to be directly linked to the succession process currently under way at Fireside. Vinay Singh, an IIM Bangalore alumnus who worked at Hindustan Unilever and BankBazaar and founded car servicing platform Stepni before Fireside Ventures, had said publicly that AI was reshaping commerce “faster than most of us expected”. In particular, he had a strong view on agentic commerce, and remained a leading voice from Fireside championing the agentic commerce wave in India’s consumer tech story. That conviction is being seen as a trigger for his departure. But his move is a little surprising as he could still have pursued his agentic commerce vision without exiting Fireside, especially when the newer bets in consumer tech are increasingly concentrated towards AI now. Mohanty, meanwhile, is understood to be preparing to launch his own consumer fund, according to people familiar with his plans. This would be a natural next step in his journey as an investor. Mohanty has invested in early stage startups since 2013, first as a Principal at IvyCap Ventures and, since January 2020, at Fireside. He drove several of the firm’s seed stage bets over the past year, including a ₹8 Cr round in Gurugram-based men’s personal care brand Unbound, a ₹20 Cr round in Noida-based Oroos Confectionery and another ₹8 Cr seed round in kids wellness startup Wellopia. But the people Inc42 spoke with say the timing of these exits tells a “bigger story”. “Any VC firm where plans of succession are being talked about does experience a churn, especially when the lifecycle of a new fund easily spans 7-10 years. That is the normal course. If Kanwal passes the baton to younger folks, disagreements over who should lead the deployment can be part of the process. And this is where the churn is expected,” an operator-turned-senior partner at a Mumbai-based VC firm said. The churn, in fact, may not end with just the two departures. Some other members of the investment team are also exploring opportunities outside Fireside, two separate sources divulged to us, Singh has always maintained that the firm deliberately keeps its investing team small and builds out a “centre of excellence” around it, spanning go-to-market, marketing, corporate development, ESG, finance and HR. “In a firm of that size, losing a cofounder and one of five principals in the same month is not a marginal change. It is a fifth of the deal-facing bench, especially when they have been your faces for some key deals,” an investment banker who has worked in one of the Big Four consultancy firms said on condition of anonymity. The Kanwaljit Singh Factor To understand why Kanwaljit Singh’s potential step back is causing ripples, it is important to understand how central he has been to Fireside Ventures. The Fireside founder came to the venture capital world from retail and FMCG. He spent 13 years at Hindustan Unilever, from 1987 to 2000, across sales, marketing and product innovation. He then spent three years as general manager (marketing) at Intel for India and the SAARC region, and was a director at The Carlyle Group’s India technology practice from 2001 to 2005. His first brush with the VC world was in 2005, when he cofounded Helion Venture Partners. There, he spent a decade leading consumer and consumer tech investments for the firm which had an AUM of about $600 Mn. In 2017, when most Indian VCs were still chasing internet marketplaces, he set up Fireside Ventures to do something not many else had thought of: back new-age D2C consumer brands at the earliest stage. And the bets paid off spectacularly. Fireside Ventures was an early backer of boAt and Mamaearth, at a time when the D2C as a category barely existed in India. Mamaearth’s parent Honasa Consumer went public in 2023 and boAt’s parent Imagine Marketing has filed for a ₹1,500 Cr IPO. The VC firm’s portfolio now spans 65+ brands, including The Sleep Company, Pilgrim, Traya, Yoga Bar, The Good Bug, Slurrp Farm and Inito. Fireside says it was the first institutional investor in over 74% of its portfolio companies. Across the platform, Fireside says its portfolio generates more than $1.6 Bn in revenue and is worth over $7 Bn. Naturally, for those on the other side of the table — whether limited partners (LPs) or founders — it was hard to separate Fireside from Kanwaljit Singh. “Fireside is Kanwal and Kanwal is Fireside. You have to give it to him for spotting such winners and for the fund’s LP and investor relationships. He had an eye for consumer deals when D2C was in its infancy in India,” a senior partner at a rival VC firm acknowledged. The returns also back this. Fireside's Fund I ranked first among 11 Category I AIFs of the 2018 vintage in CRISIL's AIF benchmarks, based on INR IRR and DPI, as of September 2024. And underpinning all of it is the money Singh has raised. According to people familiar with the VC, every one of Fireside’s four funds was raised largely on the strength of Kanwaljit Singh’s personal relationships and track record. The shift in Fund IV, from a largely domestic LP base to sovereign wealth funds and global institutions, is important to note. “Institutional LPs tend to underwrite people as much as track records, and they scrutinise key-person risk closely,” one senior investor quoted above added. Fireside has also been unusually disciplined about fund size. In July 2026, Kanwaljit Singh reportedly said that Fireside Ventures could have raised “2x” its fourth fund but chose not to, arguing that a bigger fund would break the approach that generates returns. He also described his role as having evolved into “a more classic CEO role”, driving vision, strategy and culture. Partners, he said, run sectors and investment stages. “Today, it is all about legacy,” he said, adding that the aim was to “build a lot of bench strength to keep the legacy going”. In that light, a transition may have been in the works for a while. The question is whether the rest of Fireside was ready for it, and whether everyone agrees on who should lead. People Inc42 spoke with described Fireside Ventures as, in effect, “Kanwaljit’s brand”. He holds most of the decision-making power and his legacy relationships with LPs and the biggest founders in Fireside’s portfolio. So, whoever takes over from Singh will have to convince these LPs and founders that all that the Fireside playbook is about the system and the experience that comes with investing over the course of a decade, and not just about one person. “The biggest answer needs to be given to the LPs and institutional investors when the transition of this sort takes place. Unlike the leadership transition in any startup or corporate where the issues will be solved between board and management, the investors involved here can question the deployment lifecycle of the fund among many other issues,” the Bengaluru-based senior investor quoted above added. It’s not yet clear whether Singhs’s plans have been formally communicated to Fireside’s LPs as of now, company sources told Inc42. The Carry Question When senior partners leave Indian VC firms, the conversation usually turns to carry – the share of a fund’s profits that goes to its managers. As Inc42 reported earlier this year and in the past, carry is the main breaking point among partners in large firms, particularly when there is a gap in the vintage of the partners. Those on the founding side usually come with years of experience and decades of relationships, but new partners and new principals tend to carry forward the baton when a new generation of investment opportunities emerge. Naturally, fund managers want a larger share of the upside they helped create, and also want the track record attribution that comes with it. However, at Fireside, it is not yet clear whether carry is a factor. But according to some investors and partners at other firms Inc42 spoke with, it could turn into a crucial issue now that a succession plan appears to be under way. In a founder-led fund, the founder often holds a large share of the carry, reflecting the role in raising the money. When that founder steps back, carry for the current and future funds has to be redistributed. That makes the succession question an economic and commercial one as much as one about leadership and relationships. Kanwaljit Singh has said publicly that compensation at Fireside Ventures is “shared across the team” rather than concentrated on whoever backed the biggest winner. He also once revealed that multiple people work on each portfolio company under a ‘One Fireside’ approach, so that no single person is the sole point of contact. Whether that philosophy survives a change in guard will be a key question. Notably, the debate around partner payouts is playing out globally too. Earlier this month, Sequoia Capital said in a memo that it had made several internal changes that have the effect of “flattening the partnership”. The firm is now owned and operated by seven general partners under the stewardship of Alfred Lin and Pat Grady, and said it wants “every partner to flourish”. Sequoia’s restructuring has nothing to do with Fireside, but one senior corporate governance advisor told us that it “shows the direction in which LPs and younger partners are pushing away from founder-centred economics and towards a more evenly shared model”. The succession plan has one other important question: whether Singh's move would invoke the key-person clause in Fireside's LP agreements. Notably, most institutional VC funds carry such a clause, also called the ‘key person’ clause. It names individuals whose continued involvement is critical for LPs, and it is part of the fiduciary responsibility of the firm’s partners. If one of the key persons leaves, or substantially reduces their time commitment, a ‘key person event’ clause may be triggered. Typically, the fund’s investment period is then suspended until limited partners agree on a replacement. One of the investors that Inc42 spoke with for this story said a founder moving to a chairman or mentor role is the kind of change that could test such provisions. LPs would then look at how much of the committed corpus will be deployed, and whether the firm has enough senior executives left to keep investing, especially after two senior exits. There is no indication yet that any such clause will be triggered at Fireside Ventures, or that a change has been communicated to its LPs. The terms of Fireside’s LP agreements are not public, but investors in other firms typically have a fair idea of what these agreements contain. Fireside’s Fund IV, meanwhile, is early in its deployment cycle. It plans to back 30-35 brands from it, with initial cheques of $1 Mn to $12 Mn, and Kanwaljiti Singh has said he prefers to deploy each fund in roughly three years. The firm has stayed active this year, leading ₹30 Cr rounds in maternal care brand Promom and D2C grocery startup Anmasa. The Spin-Out Season The churn at Fireside Ventures coincides with a wave of senior partners leaving established VC firms to set up new ones. Ashish Agrawal, Ishaan Mittal and Tejeshwi Sharma left Peak XV Partners to set up Mettle Capital, targeting $350-400 Mn. Shailesh Lakhani, Harshjit Sethi and Mayank Porwal, also former Peak XV partners, launched Ambition Capital which is looking to raise $250 Mn for its maiden fund. These exits came down to a mix of carry, autonomy and the question of who writes the firm’s next chapter. Fireside’s situation is obviously different, but the core challenges are more or less the same. According to people Inc42 spoke with, several of the newly floated funds are actively looking to hire experienced principals and partners from established firms. This also attracts some principals and lower level investment team members at other funds. “A consumer team with a proven early stage track record, at a firm in leadership flux, is an obvious target,” said an industry insider. But starting a new fund and running it successfully are two different things. Any new funds that come up from this churn will also need experienced hands to crack LP relationships. “The churn right now is real, but to say that these newly floated funds founded by ex-partners and principals can shake the foundation of storied firms by poaching top dealmakers will be an exaggeration,” a founding partner of a consumer tech VC firm told us. For Fireside Venture’s portfolio and its founders, the practical concern remains that of continuity. Many of them were backed by Kanwaljit Singh personally, or by the likes of Vinay Singh and Mohanty who have both left. The firm will have to reassign board seats and portfolio responsibilities as when all changes are final. “The challenge here is to navigate the established relationships some of these partners will have with the portfolio founders and if these shoes are too big to fill for any newcomer,” an executive at a senior corporate advisory firm said. Nothing about Fireside’s transition is final yet. Founder Kanwaljit Singh has not publicly announced any change in his role and his firm continues to invest actively out of its latest fund. Only those close to him are aware of his intentions. The signals, however, are hard to miss, especially after the departure of Vinay Singh and Mohanty, and word of churn inside the firm. Fireside Ventures now faces the test every founder-led fund eventually comes across. Can it convert its founder’s reputation into an institution? In the past, Kanwaljit Singh has said the firm should outlast any individual. The next few months will reveal whether that vision comes true.

Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola
- Published
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.
Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.
The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.
Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.
"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.
"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.
"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."
Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.
"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.
"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."
Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.
"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.
"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."
Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.
But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.
"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.
"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.
"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
- Published
This judgement that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people is historic. Myanmar now carries the stain of being the first state to have been found to have violated the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Rohingyas are getting justice that is long overdue. At least 10,000 were killed when their communities were attacked by Myanmar's security forces and local militias in 2017.
In the huge camps in Bangladesh where more than one million Rohingya refugees have been living since they fled the terrible events of 2017, crowds gathered around screens to watch the President of the ICJ, Judge Yuji Iwasawa, deliver the court's verdict.
He recalled some of the evidence heard by the court since the Gambia brought the case to the court in 2019, with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It described acts of mass murder, rape, torture and the destruction of villages, sometimes with Rohingya residents burnt to death inside their homes.
- Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules 
  - Published4 hours ago
The decision by a majority of nine votes to six at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will also have a significant impact on the other genocide cases currently being heard by the court by reasserting and clarifying the standard of evidence needed to prove genocidal intent.
They include South Africa's case that Israel committed genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza in its response to the Hamas attacks of 7 October 2023. Israel has repeatedly and vehemently denied the allegation.
The court's landmark decision also reinforces those who believe in the rules that were made to regulate the way that power is wielded after World War Two. The 1948 Genocide Convention was a vital part of the structure that was built around the United Nations to stop a repeat of the unfettered brutality, war and genocide in the years before the defeat of the Nazis.
The rules and conventions established after 1945 have been under unprecedented pressure in the era of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. On the day of their summit in China, the ICJ issued a reminder that international law still exists and perhaps can show that the use of force against civilians has consequences.
Lawyers will study the way in which the Gambia proved the crucial point that the state of Myanmar intended to commit genocide.
Proving intent is the biggest challenge in a genocide case at the ICJ. Showing that atrocities occurred is not in itself enough.
The key phrase from the Genocide Convention, adopted by the United Nations after the Nazi Holocaust of European Jewry, defines the crime as "acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national ethnical, racial or religious group".
The people who framed the Convention in the years after World War Two, led by Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish survivor of the Holocaust, deliberately set a high bar of proof.
That is why it has taken so long for the ICJ to deliver a ruling that genocide has been committed.
In an ideal world for lawyers and investigators, they would assemble evidence from government documents and military orders. In practice, that is hard if not impossible to get.
Governments harbouring genocidal intent do not publicise their objectives. Instead, the Court has inferred evidence of genocidal intent from the actions taken by Myanmar's security forces and local militias against the Rohingya people.
According to Janina Dill, Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government of the University of Oxford, "Genocidal intent can be inferred from a pattern of conduct… It does not mean the commission of atrocities had to follow only one goal, genocide. If that were the case, demonstrating that atrocities also followed other goals (like counterinsurgency, punishment or displacement) would negate genocidal intent.
"The court was incredibly clear that these are plausible goals, but it ruled that the totality of the evidence cannot be explained without genocide being one objective."
In other words, even if a state has been attacked, and if it orders its forces on to the offensive claiming self-defence, the sum of its actions could add up to genocide.
The justices made clear that each case needed to be treated on its merits. But because the court's decisions affect the way the law is interpreted, the Myanmar case does have an impact on the other genocide cases that are being heard by the ICJ. The most prominent is the one brought by South Africa against Israel over the killing and destruction it has inflicted on Palestinians in Gaza.
The British barrister, Philippe Sands KC, part of the Gambia's legal team, was in the chamber of the ICJ in The Hague to hear the verdict. Sands told the BBC's World at One programme that when they were arguing the case against Myanmar at the ICJ in January this year, Gaza was "the elephant in the room. Everybody knew that the court's approach in this case would have implications in the next one".
The approach taken by the ICJ justices in the judgement on Myanmar, he told the BBC, clarifies the standard of evidence they require to prove genocide.
"If the Gambia had lost, South Africa's case would, in effect, be over.
"But the Gambia now having succeeded, the door remains open for South Africa. That doesn't mean that South Africa will win. It doesn't mean that the International Court of Justice will find there was a genocide in Gaza. It means that the evidentiary standard has been defined very clearly, and it will be now for the parties in that next case and in other cases to meet those standards."
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.
The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.
That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.
The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes… we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".
It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attaché in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.
Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.
Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.
But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".
Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.
He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.
She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.
But whatever the threats coming from the Trump Administration, it is clear that delivering justice to the Rohingya people will refocus attention on Israel's conduct in Gaza, South Africa's case at the ICJ and on the continuing plight of Palestinians in the ruins of Gaza, where more than 1,400 have been killed by Israel since the ceasefire just over a year ago.
It would be wrong, lawyers say, to view the Myanmar case as a dress rehearsal for the case against Israel.
"It risks distracting from the Rohingya, who should appropriately be our focus," according to Janina Dill, from Oxford University.
"Litigation on their plight is not a test case for a conflict that the world has chosen to pay more attention to."

Maintaining physical and mental capacities is key to ensuring that older persons remain functionally independent. With age-related conditions such as visual and hearing impairment, memory and mobility issues often remaining undetected or unaddressed in the elderly, the National Centre of Ageing (NCA), Guindy has started to focus on providing integrated care to help older persons maintain functional ability. This is in line with the World Health Organisation’s (WHO) integrated care for older people approach (ICOPE).
According to the WHO, numerous physiological changes occur, and the risks of experiencing a decline in physical and mental capacities (intrinsic capacity) and having more than one condition (disease) increase when people age. This could manifest as cognitive decline, limited mobility, hearing loss, malnutrition, vision impairment, depressive symptoms, urinary incontinence and falls. ICOPE is WHO’s approach to provide a continuum of integrated care that helps to reorient health and social services towards more person-centred and coordinated care. It supports optimising intrinsic capacity and functional ability in older age, it said.

The Karyavattom campus of Kerala University (KU) has emerged as a hotspot of dengue in the city, where over 50 cases have been reported since November 9. Health department suspects that this is a gross underestimation, as the transmission is likely to have begun weeks before
Intermittent spells of rain, followed by hot and humid weather, have led to the spike in dengue cases in Thiruvananthapuram, even when the general dengue case trend has been on a slow decline since July across the State.
In the last 10 days, Thiruvananthapuram district has reported 200 probable cases of dengue and 97 confirmed cases.
On Monday, following a meeting called by the Health department, which was joined by the Vice Chancellor, some KU syndicate members as well as public health experts of the School of Public Health under Kerala University of Health Sciences, it was decided to shut the Karyavattom campus and the hostel buildings for three days so that intense vector control measures can be taken up and a break in disease transmission can be achieved.
“District health officials and vector control teams had visited the campus and hostel and we found that solid waste management was a huge issue in the campus. Plastic disposable containers used for food delivery which are disposed of carelessly are emerging as a major contributor to vector breeding in urban areas.. Rain water stagnation in these containers which are strewn around is a major hazard. Indoor plants in hostel rooms, broken manholes and blocked drains leading to rainwater stagnation have all led to intense mosquito breeding inside the vast campus,” a senior Health official said.
The Health department has also decided to serve notice to the KU Registrar under the Kerala Public Health Act, for allowing the campus to be a breeding ground for mosquitoes and posing a public health issue
Teams from the Pangappara health centre have been at work on the campus since November 10 but the district vector control team and the Corporation health staff will be joining them now. Fogging will be done to kill adult mosquitoes and indoor space spraying inside the hostel room, which will be accompanied by a source reduction campaign, officials said.
The district health administration has identified several pockets of dengue within the city itself, where an abundance of breeding sources and intense vector breeding has been spotted
Health officials point out that several large government properties with vast, ill-maintained grounds are also turning out to be hotspots for dengue in the city.
“The Cliff House compound and the sprawling official bungalows around it are all major breeding grounds for mosquitoes. In the Cliff House, seven police personnel there on guard duty were down with dengue, following which a district health team had visited the location. In some of the bungalows where renovation works are going on, building materials and discarded parts of equipment are all thrown about carelessly, leading to rain water stagnation and mosquito breeding,” a health official said.
Health officials said that without public participation, source reduction and mosquito control cannot be taken up successfully.
Kollam district too has reported a significant number of dengue cases over the last 10 days.
In November so far, the State has recorded 739 confirmed cases and 2,056 probable cases of dengue and three probable dengue deaths.
