Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

People with diabetes could be at a 53% higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, compared to those living without the metabolic disorder, a review of studies has found.
Researchers, led by those from Australia's Curtin University, conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies. They found that if 1,000 people living with type 2 diabetes were followed for a year, an estimaated average of 4.7 would develop Alzheimer's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder in which memory and thought processes steadily decline with age.
Cognitive risk prevention should be integrated into diabetes care, they said.
"Individuals with T2D (type 2 diabetes) experienced approximately five AD (Alzheimer's disease) cases per 1,000 person-years and a 53 per cent higher risk of AD, supporting the rationale for integrating cognitive risk prevention into diabetes care," the authors wrote in the study published in the journal Alzheimer's Research and Therapy.
Study author Emmanuel Adewuyi, an investigator fellow at Curtin University's school of population health, said the review was important as it quantifies the relative risk and incidence of Alzheimer's in people living with type 2 diabetes.
"While many earlier reviews combined different types of diabetes or dementia, this review focused specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease and estimated how often new cases occurred," Adewuyi said.
"Relative risk tells us how two groups compare, while incidence tells us how often new cases occur: putting those numbers together gives us a clearer picture of the burden of Alzheimer's disease among people living with type 2 diabetes," the author said.
Databases including MEDLINE, CINAHL and Embase were searched from for publications since inception until April 2026. Forty studies, involving 27,102,559 data points, and looking at the incidence of Alzheimer's disease among people with diabetes or link between the two disorders were analysed.

The government rolled out its first indigenous vaccine against the H5N1 strain of bird flu. Bird flu has been a major problem for the sector over the last 20 years, with hundreds of outbreaks and huge losses to farmers. Developed by the ICAR-National Institute of High Security Animal Diseases (Nihsad) in Bhopal, the vaccine will be priced at ₹1-2 per dose. Agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said it is designed to help contain outbreaks and to improve disease prevention in the sector as a whole. The country has had over 500 cases of avian flu since 2006, resulting in the death or culling of millions of birds. It's still a concern as it can also infect mammals and, rarely, humans. The government anticipates that the low-cost vaccine will improve access for small-scale farmers and enhance the country's preparedness for future avian flu outbreaks. The first outbreak was in Navapur, Maharashtra, in 2006, resulting in the deaths of around 10 lakh chickens. To contain the infection, lakhs of additional birds had to be culled and buried. Subsequently, around 9 lakh chickens died in 2021, while another 2 lakh died this year, Chouhan said. The affordable vaccine is expected to make preventive vaccination accessible to small poultry farmers, helping protect poultry stocks and livelihoods. According to the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (Apeda), India ranks second globally in egg production with 149.11 billion eggs in 2024–25, and poultry exports reached 2.46 million tonnes valued at $317.79 million in FY2025–26. At the event in Bhopal, Chouhan also announced the establishment of a state-of-the-art animal disease research laboratory in the city at an estimated cost of ₹300 crore, strengthening India's research and diagnostic infrastructure. Highlighting the economic burden of animal diseases, the minister said livestock and poultry are important sources of supplementary income for rural households. He cited annual losses of ₹22,000 crore from foot-and-mouth disease, ₹20,000 crore from lumpy skin disease, ₹9,212 crore from brucellosis and ₹4,683 crore from peste des petits ruminants. Together, these diseases account for an estimated annual economic burden of around ₹56,000 crore. The government has administered 147.16 crore free vaccine doses against foot-and-mouth disease under the National Animal Disease Control Programme, while scientists have also developed indigenous vaccines against lumpy skin disease, classical swine fever and African swine fever. The latest H5N1 vaccine adds to Nihsad’s portfolio of indigenous animal vaccines and is expected to strengthen India's preparedness against highly pathogenic avian influenza. Vijay C. Srinagar- Srinagar’s air quality readings differed sharply on Friday, with a real-time pollution tracking platform placing the city’s Air Quality Index (AQI) at 354, in the severe category, while official data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) recorded it at 59, categorised as satisfactory.
According to AQI.in, Srinagar recorded an AQI of 354 at around 2:51 pm, placing it in the severe category and ahead of several Indian cities reporting elevated pollution levels.
The platform’s rankings placed Hisar in Haryana second with an AQI of 328, followed by Ludhiana at 309 and Amritsar at 302. Delhi, which frequently records high pollution levels during winter, stood ninth with an AQI of 277, while Gurugram recorded 240.
However, data from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) presented a contrasting picture, placing Srinagar’s AQI at 59, categorised as satisfactory.
The wide disparity between the readings reported by the two platforms highlights the variations in air quality measurements and underscores the need to distinguish between third-party real-time estimates and official monitoring data.
AQI.in’s dashboard also showed elevated concentrations of particulate matter, with PM2.5 recorded at 191 micrograms per cubic metre and PM10 at 248 micrograms per cubic metre.
PM2.5 particles are particularly concerning because their small size allows them to penetrate deep into the respiratory system and potentially enter the bloodstream, increasing the risk of respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses.
The reported deterioration in air quality comes as Kashmir enters the winter season, when low temperatures, weaker winds and atmospheric conditions can contribute to the accumulation of pollutants.
Srinagar’s geographical setting, surrounded by mountains, can also restrict air circulation under certain weather conditions. Temperature inversion, a phenomenon in which warmer air above prevents cooler air near the ground from rising, can further trap pollutants close to the surface.
The CPCB’s revised action plan for Srinagar identifies vehicular emissions as a major contributor to the city’s pollution burden. Road dust, construction activities, traffic congestion, biomass and municipal waste burning, diesel generators and fuel combustion are among the other sources of pollution.
Winter heating also contributes to the pollution load as households increasingly depend on fuel-based heating arrangements during the colder months.
According to historical readings displayed by AQI.in, Srinagar’s AQI was recorded at 29 on November 13 before rising sharply to 402 on November 19. It stood at 354 on Friday.
The India Meteorological Department has forecast largely dry weather in Kashmir between November 19 and 28. The absence of rainfall or snowfall during this period could mean fewer opportunities for precipitation to wash pollutants out of the atmosphere.
The CPCB monitors air quality at eight locations in the Srinagar region, while PM2.5 monitoring is undertaken at five locations.
The contrasting readings notwithstanding, the reported spike in particulate pollution highlights the importance of sustained monitoring and emission-control measures as winter sets in across the Valley. (inputs from KNO)

GTA 6 made $3.79 billion in its first day, but Rockstar's workers still lack job security
The historic launch is happening while Rockstar workers vote on union recognition.
Unsurprisingly, a lot of people have bought Grand Theft Auto 6. Rockstar Games announced Friday that, based on company estimates, the open-world crime game made $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales and sold 32.5 million copies in pre-release. That last total is notably above the 20 million pre-orders some analysts expected Rockstar to sell ahead of the game's launch.
"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of Grand Theft Auto VI," Sam Houser, Rockstar's president and founder, said in a statement. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you."
GTA 6 has easily lapped the previous entry in the series, Grand Theft Auto 5, which made over $800 million worldwide from about 11 million units in its first day of sales in 2013. GTA 6 is more expensive, starting at $80 rather than GTA V's $60, but clearly demand has built up in the 13 years it took Rockstar to get the series' latest entry ready for launch.
After years of industry-wide layoffs, it's not clear if the game's early success will actually translate into security for Rockstar Games' workers. According to a Guardian op-ed from a Rockstar North developer, the studio's staff are worried that layoffs could happen even though the game is making money hand over fist. Rockstar workers are voting on whether they'll recognize their branch of the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain between November 12 and November 26. "We go where the team goes," Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar's head of publishing, told Bloomberg in October. "So if they want a union, they will have a union."
At the same time, Rockstar has been accused of union busting. The studio laid off a group of more than 30 developers in October 2025, most of whom were trying to organize its workers. Rockstar says it terminated its former employees because they were sharing confidential information, and their case has played out in an employment tribunal in the lead-up to GTA 6's release. The result of the union vote or the tribunal could shape the studio's future just as much as its latest game being a smash hit.

At an Italian hedgehog hospital, tiny patients face the strain of a warming climate
Italy's only hedgehog rescue center is overwhelmed with underweight hoglets due to climate change
NOVELLO, Italy -- When an underweight hoglet arrives at Italy’s only hedgehog rescue center, it is placed in an incubator, given fluids and oxygen if needed, and assigned a name — a small gesture of hope that it will survive.
Prolonged drought and unusually high summer temperatures linked to climate change have made the La Ninna rescue center in northern Italy's Piedmont region busier than ever. The center cared for 450 animals two years ago and more than 700 last year, with a similar number expected this year.
“We’re in the middle of autumn, and we are literally being inundated with tiny hedgehogs weighing 100 to 200 grams (3.5 to 7 ounces)," said veterinarian Massimo Vacchetta, who founded the center 14 years ago after recognizing the animals' increasing vulnerability. “They were born late in the season because of global warming and cannot survive outside.”
A hedgehog needs to weigh at least 700 grams (1.5 pounds) to hibernate successfully, Vacchetta said.
A decade ago, late-season second litters typically arrived by early September. Now, some are born as late as November, leaving the hoglets too little time to get to a healthy hibernation weight before winter.
The center, funded mostly through donations, has eight full-time staff along with a host of volunteers. It is equipped like an emergency clinic, with incubators, ultrasound equipment and oxygen tanks.
Staff members name the animals to distinguish them and as “a form of hope,” said Elisa Mangione, who wore a hedgehog-print medical top.
“It is precisely that name that gives them existence; they are here for a purpose, and with the goal of returning to their natural habitat,” Mangione said.
By mid-November, the center was caring for some 300 hedgehogs and Vacchetta was expecting another 100 to 200 before winter. About two-thirds were hoglets. The rest were adults that were either ill or severely malnourished due to a shortage of insects and other invertebrates, whose populations have been affected by drought and high temperatures.
The food shortage has forced the nocturnal animals to forage even during the day, Vacchetta said.
“All those arriving now will stay until spring because, obviously, the conditions outside don’t allow them to survive," Vacchetta said.
Most are found locally, but thanks to word of mouth and social media, reports of hedgehogs in distress arrive from all over Italy. In such cases, the center offers practical advice or suggests taking the animal to the nearest wildlife conservation centre.
To better understand what puts the animals under stress, the carcasses of those that do not survive are sent to the University of Turin for examination.
“We are seeing an increase in infectious agents, biological agents, primarily bacteria and various parasites,” said Maria Teresa Capucchio, associate professor at the University of Turin's veterinary sciences department.
Warming temperatures mean hedgehogs are still wandering the countryside as winter begins instead of hibernating, and they start emerging as early as February, before the insects they feed on are available, she said.
Illness, food shortages and increasing exposure to human activity — including agricultural chemicals, netting and traffic — are all contributing to declining hedgehog numbers, she said.
While hedgehogs are at risk of extinction in England, this is not yet the case in Italy, Capucchio said.
Vacchetta and his team are working to give as many as possible a chance of survival.
“We are on the front lines of the battle to defend animals, which are facing a major crisis due to climate change,” Vacchetta said. “People do not realize the gravity of the situation because these are silent deaths. Animals fall ill and die far from our sight.”

Supporters of Mamata All India Trinamool Congress (AITC) were allegedly attacked on Friday (November 20, 2026) by supporters of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) outside a police station while party leader Abhishek Banerjee was being questioned by Kolkata Police at the Girish Park police station.
Videos of the scuffle and the assault on women supporters of the Trinamool were shared on social media and by the Mamata AITC. In the videos, groups of women alleged to be BJP supporters were seen chasing another group of women. Supporters of the Trinamool had gathered outside the police station in support of Abhishek Banerjee. The BJP leaders denied allegations of the assault but claimed that Trinamool supporters were trying to incite tensions by gathering outside the police station.
“@BJP4Bengal workers gathered outside Girish Park Police Station today, seemingly intent on harassing, heckling and assaulting our workers, did not even spare ordinary citizens and parents who had come to pick up their children from school,” the party shared on social media. The Mamata AITC leader raised questions on the role of politics.
The police complaint against the Diamond Harbour MP was filed in connection with remarks reportedly made by him on 29 October, in which he criticised sections of the police administration, alleging that officers were acting under political pressure. Mr. Banerjee took to social media to share videos of BJP leaders, including Suvendu Adhikari, alleging threats to the police when they were in the Opposition.
After the BJP came to power, several FIRs were registered against Abhishek Banerjee. He has been summoned to appear before the police on numerous occasions. Later in the day, the Trinamool leader filed a Zero FIR at Girish Park Police Station, highlighting how Suvendu Adhikari, Dilip Ghosh, and other BJP leaders threatened the Kolkata Police and the West Bengal Police on multiple occasions.
“The expertise and urgency shown by Girish Park PS in connection with Abhishek Banerjee’s matter—we hope the same expertise and urgency will be shown by them in connection with this Zero FIR, and that they will investigate the matter,” Arka Nag, an advocate representing Trinamool Congress leader, said.

Donald Trump and Anthony Albanese have heralded plans for new joint Quad military exercises designed to push back on China’s expansionist ambitions, with the US president promising the grouping with India and Japan will guarantee “peace through strength”.
Albanese met Trump, India’s Nahrendra Modi and Japan’s Sanae Takaichi in Manila late on Tuesday in talks about enhanced cooperation on AI, critical minerals, infrastructure and maritime security.
“These nations represent some of the most important partnerships in the entire world,” the US president said.
“They’re among the most successful nations in the world, and in certain ways among the most powerful nations of the world. Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific.”
Trump said: “As we continue to protect peace through strength, we are also working together to advance super intelligence, SI, the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the industrial revolution.”
The Australian prime minister praised Trump and said a new Quad business forum to be held in 2027 would build economic growth across the region.
Leaders in the group – established as China seeks to build its military might and exert influence across the region – say they will cooperate to maintain peace and stability with Beijing.
“When we work together for our common view in the Indo-Pacific of peace, security, stability, and prosperity, then the world will be a safer and more secure place, and the Quad has a critical role in achieving that,” Albanese told the summit.
The plan for new military exercises involving maritime patrol aircraft is likely to prompt strong criticism from China.
Albanese said Australia would deploy its P8-A Poseidon and P3-C Orion maritime patrol aircraft as part of the operation in early 2027.
Asked what he would tell Chinese leader Xi Jinping later this week about the plan, Albanese said military exercises were common.
“We want peace and security in the region. That’s the objective here. It’s not about any one country. It’s about our own sovereignty, but also about peace and security in the region,” he said
The Quad leaders want the group to present a multilateral coalition of resistance against Beijing, seeking to undermine its dominance, including in the South and East China seas.
Takaichi said the Quad would help shape the future of the region.
“We would like to realise a free and open Indo Pacific by strengthening resilience of countries in the region and promote their freedom to decide for themselves across a wide range of areas including maritime security, economic security, energy and critical and emerging technologies.”
Before the meeting, as the four leaders posed for a group photo, Trump praised Modi and Takaichi as “tough”, before gesturing to Albanese and saying: “We’re OK too.” Albanese laughed at the remark.
The first meeting of the Quad leaders since 2024 came as Albanese and Trump both prepare for setpiece engagement with China’s president later this week. Albanese will visit Xi in Shenzhen on Friday, a day after three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump said he wanted talks with the North Korean leader, Kim Jong-un, but conceded he was not the host of the China summit and it was up to Xi to issue an invitation. The US president said he could have a one-on-one meeting with Putin “if it’s available”.
Quad military exercises would build on progress from the recently completed Malabar joint exercise near Japan, where sailors completed anti-submarine and anti-surface warfare drills.
Trump also talked up the Aukus nuclear deal with Australia. “We make the greatest submarines anywhere in the world, and we’re working with Australia and others on that,” he said.
Trump said the US was poised to catch up to China on rare earth production within 10 months, backed up by speedy progress from Australia, Japan and India.
He was accompanied by cabinet members Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Howard Lutnick and Jamieson Greer, as well as his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
Privately, officials believed the meeting alone showed the group was progressing. Australian officials welcomed the engagement of Trump in regional affairs as he enters the final two years of his presidency.
Trump took credit for reinvigorating the grouping, and said he placed a premium on relations with Albanese, Modi and Takaichi.
“When they have difficulty, when they want to tell me something, my phone is always open, and the Oval Office is always open to you, and you know that,” he said.
Albanese said before the meeting he would push Trump on ending the war in Iran, a conflict which has produced an unprecedented global energy shock and badly distorted conditions in the Australian economy.
It was Albanese’s first meeting with Takaichi since a weeks-long saga about comments he made on a podcast about her gift of melons presented to him during a visit to Australia in July.
Earlier, Albanese took part in the East Asia Summit where he called for regional partners to work together to boost AI protections. Trump, who calls the technology “superintelligence”, said it represented “the greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution”.

Cummins retains Cricket Australia support as captain
- Published
Pat Cummins will retain backing from Cricket Australia (CA) to remain as Test captain despite ongoing and explosive allegations about the sandpaper controversy.
A detailed testimony from Cameron Bancroft supported previous claims made by Usman Khawaja that the entire Australia team – including Cummins – knew of the plan to tamper with the ball during a Test match against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.
Cummins has always denied involvement in or knowledge of the cheating plot, and reiterated his stance in a 68-minute address to the media last week.
CA has regularly spoken of its support for Cummins, and the fast bowler will be allowed to continue in the captaincy role he has held since 2021. A statement could be issued over the weekend.
Cummins, 33, is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December. A squad for the series opener against the Black Caps has not yet been named.
With the support of CA, a decision on Cummins' future as captain would now appear to rest with the player, who has shown no indication he will resign.
The row over the sandpaper saga, one of the biggest controversies in Test history, has engulfed Australian sport since Khawaja's claims first emerged two weeks ago.
In 2018, Bancroft, then-captain Steve Smith and his vice-captain David Warner were punished for Bancroft's act of rubbing sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa at Newlands.
Khawaja, who retired from international cricket earlier this year, wrote in his autobiography that the entire Australian team knew and should have taken responsibility.
The former batter's account was supported by his childhood friend Warner, along with Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland, both back-up bowlers on the tour.
In response, Cummins called a news conference where he promised to answer all questions about his part in the controversy, in the hope of "never having to speak about it again".
He called Khawaja's assertions "100% wrong" and "nonsense".
However, Cummins' address to the media motivated Bancroft to publish his own account of more than 4,000 words in the West Australian newspaper.
"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.
"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."
Bancroft alleged he had conversations with all of the bowlers about how much the ball was swinging, and that the entire group of players and coaches celebrated when the ball-tampering yielded success.
Batter Bancroft also implicated Darren Lehmann, who was then the Australia head coach, and David Saker, the bowling coach.
Lehmann, now the coach of county side Northamptonshire, is due to commentate for the BBC and Australian radio station ABC on the first T20 between Australia and England in Melbourne on Saturday.
Saker was part of the England coaching staff for the one-day tri-series in Pakistan in October.
The 60-year-old has been employed by England on an ad hoc consultancy basis, an arrangement that has now ended.
England have firmed up new coaching teams under Test head coach Stephen Fleming and his white-ball counterpart Brendon McCullum.

Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.
The report on "endocrine-disrupting chemicals" (EDCs) released by the United Nations Environment Programme and World Health Organization "conservatively" estimates the health and environmental costs of EDC exposure at over $1 trillion annually.
"The scientific evidence is clear: EDCs are a global and growing threat to human and environmental health," warns the report written by international scientists, calling current regulations "uneven and insufficient."
EDCs are chemicals that interfere with, mimic, or block the hormones that regulate the development and behaviour of our organs.
They are in everything from toys and makeup, to building materials and clothing.
The report released late Tuesday is the first such comprehensive look at EDC impacts in 14 years, and finds increasingly clear links between them and a range of diseases.
"The evidence is so strong that it's irrefutable at this point," said Laura Vandenberg, report co-author and professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
The report examined thousands of studies on chemicals like bisphenols, phthalates and parabens.
Evidence of links between these chemicals and disease is strongest for certain neurological conditions and reproductive problems including sperm decline.
But there is also growing confidence that EDCs are linked to diseases like type 2 diabetes and asthma that have spiked globally.
"Because these changes are occurring rapidly, they are unlikely to be explained primarily by genetic change," the report says.
Sufficiently worrisome
Scientists looked at associations between EDC exposure and health conditions, as well as the mechanisms by which exposure could cause harm.
The findings vary, with "strong evidence" of developmental and neurobehavioral effects, but "emerging" links between EDCs and cardiovascular disease.
However, the overall risk is strong because EDCs are so ubiquitous and likely to impact health at tiny levels, Vandenberg said.
Among those most at risk are workers in the chemicals and recycling industries, particularly in countries with weak regulations.
A 2024 study by the International Pollutants Elimination Network NGO fitted participants with silicone wristbands that absorbed chemicals.
Lab tests of the wristbands found that plastic waste and recycling workers in Thailand and Kenya were exposed to over 20 hazardous chemicals, while even control subjects working in offices were exposed to at least 11.
There are around 1,000 identified EDCs, but experts say many chemicals have simply not been tested properly and their impacts remain unknown.
They are also concerned about "synergistic" impacts -- the way exposure to multiple chemicals may amplify health effects.
The "proverbial million-dollar question" is what level of EDC exposure triggers any given health impact, said Frederic Leusch, professor of environmental toxicology at Australia's Griffith University, who was not involved in the report.
But even absent an answer, Leusch believes "the hazard is sufficiently worrisome that we need to take action to reduce our, and our environment's, exposure."
It scares politicians
Many countries have regulated certain EDCs, often targeting bisphenol A, particularly in children's products.
But regulators have struggled to determine which chemicals should be regulated, and what an appropriate exposure level might be.
"It scares politicians, to some extent, because it's such a complicated area," said retired professor of environmental chemistry Ake Bergman, who worked on the previous editions of the EDC report in 2002 and 2012.
Like other experts, he warned there is no known safe exposure level for most EDCs.
"We have some that are really acting at extremely low concentrations."
In a statement, the International Council of Chemical Associations industry group called for "science-based" approaches to regulation that protect health and the environment "while enabling society to benefit from the products, technologies, and innovations that are essential to modern life and sustainable development."
Many EDCs are in plastics, and experts say oil firms are increasing plastic production as demand for fossil fuel energy falls.
"We need to stop the expansion of plastic production,... reduce exposures to EDCs, and ban the worst actors," said Tracey Woodruff, report co-author and professor at Stanford University.
"While more science is always needed, we don't need more science to act."

ICJ verdict noted; India consistently supported speedy return of Rohingya people: MEA
New Delhi, A day after the UN's top court ruled that Myanmar "committed genocide" against the Rohingya group in 2017, India on Friday said it has "taken note of the verdict" and asserted that New Delhi "consistently supported" the safe, speedy and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya people from Rakhine state.
At his bi-weekly media briefing, Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal was asked to comment on the historic judgment by the International Court of Justice .
"On the ICJ verdict… we have taken note of the verdict. India has consistently supported safe, speedy, and sustainable return of the displaced Rohingya people from the Rakhine State," Jaiswal said.

The Telangana Standards Authority for Food and Essential Drugs (TG SAFE) has issued show-cause notices to 90 medical shops across Hyderabad for violations involving the sale of habit-forming drugs and antibiotics without following prescribed regulations.
The notices were issued following a special enforcement drive conducted by the drugs wing of TG SAFE, along with its enforcement wing and excise enforcement personnel, on Thursday (November 19). The department said it would initiate further action, including suspension or cancellation of drug licences, against the establishments found violating the rules.
The inspections were carried out at medical shops in areas including Koti, Abids, Basheerbagh, Nampally, Khairatabad, Panjagutta, Ameerpet, SR Nagar, Sanathnagar, Erragadda, Yousufguda, Madhura Nagar, Jubilee Hills and Banjara Hills.
Officials detected violations such as selling prescription medicines without valid prescriptions issued by registered medical practitioners, failure to maintain prescription and Schedule H1 drug registers, and dispensing medicines in the absence of registered pharmacists. Medical shops were also found selling drugs without issuing bills and failing to maintain or produce sales and purchase records.
The enforcement drive focused on the illegal sale and diversion of habit-forming drugs, including Tramadol, Alprazolam, Nitrazepam, Codeine-containing cough syrups, Tapentadol, Pregabalin and Zolpidem. Officials also checked the indiscriminate sale of antibiotics. Decoy operations and test purchases were conducted to verify whether such medicines were being sold without prescriptions.

Oscar-winning documentarian Laura Poitras is acutely aware of the importance of the weight of words when describing issues of great sensitivity. Her work has dealt with Edward Snowden’s NSA whistleblowing, the Sackler family’s role in the opioid crisis, and Iraq under U.S. occupation, among other burning sociopolitical issues of the 21st century. With “They’re Here,” the lauded director turns her lens on the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Co-directed with Rachel Lauren Muller, “They’re Here” combines footage captured by the filmmakers with material provided by activists on the ground in Minneapolis during violent ICE raids in the aftermath of the killing of Alex Pretti and Renée Good. In the short film, images of a victim barricading himself in the trunk of a car to get to work give way to a volunteer resistance organization tracking ICE raids through a citizen-fed counter-surveillance software system. In the film, words like “war zone” are used to describe what it felt like to be in Minneapolis in January of this year.
Speaking with Variety out of IDFA, Poitras says language has been “really important in all of my work.” “We have to reject the euphemisms of the government to describe things. This was a paramilitary occupation of an American city that created an effective war zone.”
“My co-director, Rachel Lauren Mueller, lives in the neighborhood that we filmed, so she can talk about the fact that there are helicopters hovering, tanks and people being executed in broad daylight,” she adds. “We need to use the word execution, use the word abduction, kidnapping, occupation, paramilitary force. Because those are the actual English words that describe what’s happening. When you use words like deportation, you’re capitulating to the government’s narrative, which I don’t think we should ever do.”
Poitras was also interested in the idea of citizens using their phones and available technology at hand to counter-surveil ICE, which she believes to be a “very effective form of resistance.” “State powers need to know that they’re being watched, that they can’t do this violence in secrecy with total impunity. There will be accountability. There has to be accountability.” Citizens, the filmmaker says, know “that this is a paramilitary occupation of the United States happening with absolutely no accountability,” and their footage is a way to “have a record that can be used both as a deterrent and as evidence and to tell the truth.”
“As a political statement, it’s important to say that the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house,” she adds. “There’s only so much we can do. But there is something that’s powerful about documenting and counter-surveilling what the state is doing and making sure that they know that they’re also being watched and make them nervous about that.”
“They’re Here” is permeated by a sustained sense of dread, borrowing from genre to amplify both the loud, anxiety-inducing frenzy of the raids and the dystopian images of lined-up people slowly marched into freight planes from the same airport where thousands of Americans jet off to holidays. The visual language was inspired by films like Alfonso Cuarón’s “Children of Men” and RaMell Ross’ “Nickel Boys.”
“We very much wanted to use the tools of cinema to capture the sense of horror that was unfolding and to create that uncanny distance of a reality that is unfolding as we speak,” she says. “We’re seeing so much violence, and we don’t want to repeat it. How can we denormalize it and put the audience in a perspective of both fear and terror, but also a critical distance where you understand how profoundly abnormal what’s happening in the United States is right now?”
When asked if witnessing the citizen-led efforts in Minneapolis fed a sense of hope, Poitras says she doesn’t know if “hope is the right word given the state of the world,” but that she believes resistance “does have an impact.”
Addressing the Democrats’ recent success in the U.S. midterm elections, she note, “These victories of the progressive movement in the U.S. didn’t happen overnight because of some charismatic people. Yes, of course, there are great candidates, but it was years and decades of work laying the foundation without visible results and with many defeats. When you see these successes, you realize, ok, this is a moment. There are tipping points and tables are turned and nobody can surrender our democracies.”
On top of presenting “They’re Here” at IDFA and being on the festival jury, Poitras hosted an awards screening and Q&A for Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’s doc-phenomenon “You Can See Everything” while on the ground at the Dutch festival.
“It’s totally, 100% a documentary,” she says, quickly rebuffing any idea that the majorly successful film could be anything but. “It’s dealing with ethical questions of documentary and lifting the fourth wall. Plus, it’s fantastic drama. There’s this chess match, this psychological thriller between Nathan Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans that is just fascinating.”
The director pointedly says she wants to “reject any ideas that documentary filmmakers are going to reject this film because everybody loves to talk about the film.” “Everybody is so excited about both what it is doing in terms of the genre and pushing boundaries, and also it’s a fantastic success. There is also love for both of these filmmakers.”
“What’s so beautiful to watch is that it’s not a film that’s going to give you answers,” she continues. “It will provoke endless questions instead, and that is such a fantastic story device. I also think it makes us all think about everything we look at anytime we see reality on camera. And what is reality?”
Poitras believes the film is going to be “taught in every film school because of how much it teaches us about documentary filmmaking.” She is also “thrilled” for Oppenheim and Fielder’s success and the film’s gigantic box office, which looks en route to surpassing $100 million globally before the end of the month. “We consider them part of our community, not other. To have this success is just great.”
“I think it’s a lock for a Best Picture nomination, and it deserves it,” she concludes.

Karan Johar and Kareena Kapoor Khan revisited memories from Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham (2001) aka K3G at a special Airbnb preview event in Mumbai, marking 25 years of the popular family drama. The filmmaker and actress attended an exclusive preview of a recreated Raichand House at Juhu Gold Studio, where members of the press were given a first look at the immersive experience inspired by the film.
Karan Johar reveals shooting famous Poo scenes of Kareena Kapoor Khan from K3G was therapeutic; recalls how Shah Rukh Khan ‘teased’ him for doing the scenes himself
Titled ‘At Home with the Raichands’, the installation recreates elements from the lives of Rohan and Pooja, popularly known as Poo. The space includes a recreation of Poo’s iconic room and wardrobe, bringing together details associated with the film’s much-remembered characters.
During an interactive conversation at the event, Kareena spoke about how she approached playing Poo, a character that has remained a recognisable part of Hindi cinema’s pop culture. She credited Johar’s direction for shaping the character’s distinctive personality and style. Kareena said, “No, I just followed the director. I've always said I'm a director's actor and that's why I'm amazing in all the amazing director movies and the ones I'm not amazing in, and you know I can be a director, so you know I followed him in every step of the way and I think he was just perfect. He was fab.”
Johar, meanwhile, recalled how much he enjoyed directing the portions featuring Poo. He revealed that he would often enact the character’s lines during rehearsals, to the extent that Shah Rukh Khan once jokingly questioned whether he was rehearsing the scenes himself instead of letting Kareena perform them.
View this post on Instagram
Recalling the incident, Johar said, “There came a time in a rehearsal and Shah Rukh (Khan) came up to me and said, ‘Abhi tu isko karne dega ya tu baar baar khud rehearsal karta jaayega?’, because I was so enjoying the character. Let me tell you my most joyous moments on the K3G set were the days that we were shooting with the character Poo. It used to be my detox, relaxation, therapy, because the film was of course large and of course had so much opulence and high volatile emotion.”
He further described the experience of shooting Poo’s scenes as a welcome break from the film’s emotional intensity, adding, “That character was just my holiday, really. It was like my spring break. I loved every bit of it.”
Kareena also spoke about how she drew from Johar’s expressions and mannerisms while performing the role. She said, “It was like just the way, I just imitated the way, like I've never spoken like that before, so I'm just imitating what Karan would like, you know, show us. No, that says about me, but yeah.” Johar responded, “Oh, you did it so well.”
The Airbnb experience will open to fans as part of the platform’s 25th-anniversary campaign, ‘At Home with the Raichands’. The free, two-hour interactive experience will run from December 1 to December 6, 2026. Booking requests will open on November 23 at 12 noon IST, with 180 guests set to get the opportunity to visit the recreated Raichand House. Meanwhile, Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham aka K3G will also be completing 25 years this year, on December 14.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.
At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.
“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.
He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.
“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.
“We want them to build it here.”
With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.
The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.
China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.
In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”
He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”
Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.
“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.
“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”
He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.
“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.
Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”
And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

Every year in Delhi, the arrival of the winter months also signals the beginning of what residents widely call “pollution season”. A thick toxic smog shrouds the city, home to 30 million people who have no choice but to breathe the poisonous air as they go about their daily lives, often while suffering from wheezy coughs, nausea and itchy eyes. While successive state governments have brought in measures intended to improve air quality, the situation has remained the same for more than a decade. Delhi is widely regarded as the world’s most polluted city. Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Pollution season usually begins around the same time as Diwali, the Hindu festival of light. Amidst the plummeting air quality, people still gather in the markets for festival shopping and at festivities outside. Diwali is also known to cause a surge in the pollution levels, due to the tens of millions of cars that hit the roads and the use of firecrackers for the celebration. In previous years, firecrackers were banned, but this year the state government has allowed “green” firecrackers”. However environmentalists argue that these are still highly polluting.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The causes of Delhi’s apocalyptic pollution are multi-faceted. In recent years, one of the biggest causes has been vehicle emissions, from the almost 10m cars, rickshaws, motorcycles and trucks on the city’s roads. It is also the season where farmers in the neighbouring states of Haryana and Punjab often burn their fields to ready them for the next crop. These fires are illegal but still occur. Factory emissions, dust from construction and rubbish burning also contribute to the toxic air quality levels.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
So far, the air quality index (AQI) has already soared above 650, more than 30 times the limit the World Health Organization (WHO) deems to be safe. Air pollution is linked to numerous serious diseases, particularly respiratory, and hospitals have already reported a surge in patients suffering from breathing difficulties.The pollution season is expected to last until January, when the weather warms up.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
Millions of Delhi’s residents are poor families or migrant workers, who have no choice but to go out to work in the toxic air, often suffering long term impacts on their health. Doctors and campaigners have described the pollution as a “health emergency”. According to a study last year, at least 15% of deaths in the capital are linked to air pollution. Pollution now kills more people in Delhi than obesity of diabetes.Photograph: Yanni Rawat/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock
As in previous years, the state government has introduced various restrictions to try and bring air quality levels under control. Coal and firewood have been banned as fuel. Construction has also been halted and so have older diesel and petrol cars. Offices have been instructed to get people to work from home to limit traffic on the roads. Trucks can often be seen spraying water on the roads. However, it is widely acknowledged that, so far, these restrictions have had little impact on the pollution levels. Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
The pollution has been a problem for so long in Delhi that it has become normalised and people carry on with their daily lives in the toxic smog.Residents rarely wear masks outside and the parks will still be full of families and children and people exercising outside.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
While rich and middle class families will buy air purifiers for their homes, they are unaffordable for most poorer families who often live in makeshift tents or informal homes. As a result, breathing clean air during pollution season has become a luxury privilege in Delhi.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
The pollution is not restricted to Delhi alone. All across north India, in states such as Punjab and Haryana, the air is also toxic due to coal-powered plants, vehicles and farm fires. Cities such as Amritsar in Punjab, on the border with Pakistan, also suffer from extremely dangerous air quality levels during the winter months. Photograph: Narinder Nanu/AFP/Getty Images
Campaigners say more money needs to be invested into proper public transport and better vehicle emission regulation in Delhi to tackle the root causes of pollution. Every year, the number of cars on Delhi’s roads keeps rising, releasing more harmful pollutants, and yet few the percentage of electric vehicles remains very low.Photograph: Bhawika Chhabra/Reuters
Delhi has an extensive bus and metro network, but it is not sufficient to cope with the huge daily demand and still has poor connectivity in many areas. Most people still rely on polluting rickshaws, cars and motorcycles to get them to the bus stops or metro stations. Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
Delhi’s topography – a city built in a bowl-like valley, which has little breeze or rain in the winter months – means most of the emissions get trapped over the city as the cold weather hits and cloak the city in brown smog. Some call it Delhi’s “death shroud”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images
In past years, the state and national government has been accused of manipulating the data to disguise how bad pollution levels are in the capital. Last year, it was found that water was being sprayed around the air quality monitors, allegedly to bring down the readings. Campaigners and opposition politicians have alleged that a lot of data from the air quality measuring stations has gone “missing”.
Environmental campaigners have argued that much more extreme measures are needed to bring pollution under control, similar to how Beijing successfully cleaned up its air in recent years. However, others have argued this would have an economic cost that India, as a developing country, can not afford.Photograph: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Getty Images
One of the plans being prepared by the government this year is to experiment with “cloud-seeding”, to create rain which would clear the skies. But many residents and campaigners say that until the root causes are tackled, these plans are nothing more than a “gimmick”.Photograph: Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge.
India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities.
So when, last week, Travel + Leisure named India its destination of the year for 2027, I found myself considering what it means that the country holds such multitudes. The magazine’s recognition will undoubtedly add to its growing appeal as a travel destination. But expectations built around India can differ from the experience of being there, particularly for women.
My own experiences of travelling in India largely surround my work as a journalist, often visiting places that would never make it into a travel guide. I remember the towering chinar tree outside the home of a woman in Kashmir whose son had been killed in an encounter with the security forces; the rolling hills of Odisha, where we travelled to meet a guerrilla fighter; the tiny hut in Chhattisgarh where, after a 13-hour journey, our team found a meal of rice and lentils. These scenes have stayed in my mind, for their landscapes as much as for the stories and circumstances.
Ultimately, such experiences were far more illuminating than those from a conventional travel itinerary, and taught me to navigate uncertainty and embrace discomfort. For this week’s newsletter, I spoke to three women about the journeys in India that stayed with them and what travelling here has meant to them.
‘The only sounds you hear are of nature’
One of the most memorable journeys for travel writer Shivya Nath was a trek through the Tirthan Valley in Himachal Pradesh, with a crew of local women.
Trekking has always been a male-dominated industry and Nath, author of the book Rootless and Restless, was struck by the personal journeys of the women leading the expedition. (She travelled with an organisation which trains women to become guides, overcoming social and family restrictions.) “For some of the women, spending even two nights away from home required negotiating with their families,” she told me.
The route wound through dense forests in the Great Himalayan national park, across ancient bridges, over gushing, undammed rivers, accompanied by the soundtrack of birdsong. “The only sounds you hear are of nature,” she recalled. Along the way, they stopped to forage lingri, a seasonal wild fern used in regional cooking, which they later prepared at a riverside camp they set up for the night.
The following morning, the group hiked to a waterfall, standing together on a large rock in the middle of the cascading water. Being with “just a group of women who love being in the outdoors, was a really powerful feeling for me”, she said.
For Afsha Sethi, a corporate leadership professional from Bengaluru who has travelled extensively in India, one of her most cherished travel experiences is an unlikely one. As part of an extracurricular project when she was in high school, students were paired with a local community through an NGO. She spent a week shadowing a farming family growing rice and areca nut in Karkolli, in northern Karnataka.
Walks through lush forests with waterfalls were a daily routine. “We would come back with leeches on our legs, and then put salt to get rid of them,” she recalled.
The trip also brought her into contact with something she had not encountered before. When her roommate told the host family about getting her period, their sleeping arrangements were shifted to the courtyard. “It turned out to be a great experience, because the weather was very nice and [we were] looking at the stars and just chatting late into the night,” she said. It reminded her that travelling through India can mean encountering different social conventions.
‘The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it’
The travel boom in India is led by domestic travellers. The country recorded almost 2.95bn domestic tourist visits in 2024, a jump of 17.5% from the previous year, according to recent government data. Overall, India ranks 31st in the World Economic Forum’s Travel and Tourism Development Index 2026, up eight spots since 2024.
Women accounted for 43% of foreign arrivals, an interesting counterpoint to India’s reputation as a challenging destination for female travellers.
But the boom raises questions about what happens to the places being discovered. “Social media has definitely accelerated the over-tourism problem,” says Nath. “I think one of the most basic things travellers can do is to avoid geotagging locations.” She suggests choosing community-owned tourism initiatives that allow local people to benefit directly from visitors.
Nayanika Gaffino, a mother and recreational athlete who has also clocked up the miles around the country, has seen this happen first-hand in Goa, where she lives. “The moment somebody puts up something on Instagram, everyone throngs to it … even though it doesn’t have the capacity to handle so many people,” she says, adding there are beaches her family now avoids because of this.
Travelling with girls, Gaffino also has to consider practicalities such as hygiene and access to clean public toilets and safety. As such, she gravitates towards boutique properties that are accustomed to hosting families with children.
Nath acknowledges that solo travel can require extra vigilance. On solo trips, she prefers family-run homestays or guesthouses where someone is aware that she is on her own and can watch out for her. At the same time, she adds, India can be an intensely hospitable place where people generously invite you for tea or a meal.
Discovering a place, she says, should also include finding ways to preserve the very qualities that led you to it in the first place. The journeys the women described involved seeing a side of India that differed from their own expectations. This is what makes al-Qazwini’s understanding of wonder relevant for me. To approach something with wonder is not to be impressed by just beauty or uniqueness but to have a curiosity about what it might show us – its possibilities and its limitations.

Congress described this as an attempt to stifle voices of criticism, while the foreign ministry said that visa-related decisions are “sovereign functions” but did not share further details.
Lawsuit | The US state department has served summons in a civil lawsuit brought by Khalistani separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannu against national security adviser Ajit Doval and former research and analysis wing, Samant Goel, according to the Hindu. The foreign ministry described the lawsuit as “frivolous”.
Culture | A 50-year-old Navaratri festival at Wesleyan University, in Connecticut, has made it an unlikely home for Carnatic music and dance traditions. Although such festivals take place at cities around the world, few institutions have become as significant a platform for Indian music and dance.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Shaunak Sen, director of the Academy Award-nominated All That Breathes, recommends: “If you find yourself in the oft-trodden window of wanting to watch something for an hour after dinner, but feel drowned in the mediocre flotsam of the big streamers, I have a suggestion watch the strangely inventive short films of the artist-bureaucrat SNS Sastry from the 1960s and 70s [on YouTube]. Unlike the regular pedantic state films of the time, Sastry somehow created avant garde, surreal, even funny films, funded by the Films Division of India. I Am 20, which interviewed young adults born in the year of India’s independence, is an inquiry into a certain national zeitgeist. Between the candour of the participants and the sharpness of their complaints, one can scarcely believe this was made under the aegis of the government.”

Firecrackers were responsible for most of Delhi’s fine particulate matter of PM 2.5 – about 71% – in the hours after Diwali celebrations, according to a first-of-its-kind assessment by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. Vibe check
AI anxiety is everywhere. Pranav Bhasin’s comedy We Were Here has brought that to screens in a short film that is making an impression internationally. Bhasin’s mockumentary is about three retired men in a small Indian town who, persuaded that artificial intelligence is taking over human jobs, fight back by impersonating household appliances. One becomes a dish antenna, another a vehicle’s reverse camera and a third a microwave. The situation becomes more complicated when one of their children takes a job at an AI company. “Do you want artificial intelligence?” “No, I have real one,” goes one caustic exchange.
The New Yorker released the film on YouTube and it’s eligible for Oscars consideration after winning at the Palm Springs International ShortFest.

Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
- Published
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.
Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.
The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.
Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.
This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.
The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".
This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.
Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.
At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.
A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.
Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.
Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.
In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".
He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".
Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".
"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.
He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.
Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.
The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu, has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.
The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.
His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.
"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.
He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.
The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.
The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.
Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.
They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.
