- The Ugandan general who lobs grenades on Twitter 
  - Published30 October 2022
Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.
He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.
Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.
His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.
Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.
The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.
Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.
He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.
"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."
But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.
"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.
He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.
The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.
Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.
"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.
He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.
Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".
Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.
On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.
"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.
He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.
The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.
It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.
Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.
Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.
Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.
He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.
Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.
Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.
Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.
"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.
At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.
He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year, extending his rule into a fifth decade.
Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.
He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.
But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.
At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.
Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.
There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.
Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.
Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.
He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.
"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.
The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.
The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.
The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.
Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.
Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba.
The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.
For now, Museveni remains in power.
But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.

V8 engines returning to Formula 1 in 2030 as FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem describes move to 'reconnect with DNA' of the sport
Multiple Formula 1 drivers had backed for V8 engines to return to the sport; FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has confirmed V8 engines will return from 2030 after a 17-year absence; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Friday 20 November 2026 20:24, UK
Formula 1 will return to V8 engines from 2030 in a move FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has described as "an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA" of the sport.
Earlier this week, Ben Sulayem teased the possibility of V8 engines ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, live on Sky Sports F1, with the sound of a screaming F1 car with a caption: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."
On Friday, the FIA announced a technical framework had been unanimously agreed between the FIA, Formula One Management (FOM), the teams and Formula 1 power unit manufacturers to move to a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 power unit.

The agreement means the more popular V8s will make a comeback in 2030, 17 years after the sport abandoned them in favour of "road relevant" engines, a decision already backed by several drivers.
The current power unit, which is around 53 per cent electrically powered, has been criticised by some drivers this year as it has led to an unusual style of driving and racing at some tracks, with the drivers sometimes unable to push flat out in a traditional manner.
"This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1," said Ben Sulayem.
"From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.
"The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition."
Verstappen: F1 going in the right direction
Max Verstappen has been one of the most vocal critics of the new 2026 power units and warned the long straights in Las Vegas this weekend will be "painful" to drive on as the cars will effectively slow down before the braking zone.
Verstappen feels the FIA have listened to the drivers and realised the 2026 regulations are "not what you want" and, if he was in charge, would get rid of the turbo aspect completely and effectively have a fully normally aspirated engine.
"In some tracks then you're not allowed to race because it will be too loud because if it's up to me I would take the turbo off," he explained.
"I would get rid, maybe you can use it as a push to pass, but not too much of the battery side. But then on some tracks, you're not allowed to race, so fuel consumption goes up a lot without a turbo, so you need a bigger tank if you don't want to do refuelling in the races, so I understand that you want to have a turbo.
"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that not something realistic. This [news] is good. This is for sure in the right direction."
Lewis Hamilton, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are the only drivers who drove in the previous V8 era which ended in 2013.
Most of the grid have driven V8-powered F1 cars in demonstration of show runs at fan events and Mercedes driver George Russell says it's important for a hybrid element to remain so the cars can have over 1,000 brake horsepower.
"When I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps," said Russell.
"It's about just that high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era. The purists will say take away all electrical power, but I think when you look at how a lot of these cars have evolved in recent years, and the power output from some of these electrical motors these days, Formula 1 is going to continue to be the fastest race cars on the planet, you need to have it, that's just the reality.
"You need to have some sort of hybrid, because the power you get, you can't really produce that just solely on internal combustion."

I return to my room as my mother-in-law leaves for her office in the building adjacent to our home. I am about to start my bath when I hear a series of explosions, as of firecrackers, but different. I freeze. Someone comes pounding frantically on my bathroom door. It is Ongmu, the children’s nanny, crying hysterically. I fling open the door, my heart thumping. She is gesticulating wildly, speechlessly, towards the garden.
I run along the path leading to Akbar Road. I see the white Ambassador car slowly moving towards the same path. I hesitate. I stop, heart in my mouth. Dread, panic, fear. I feel suffocated. I can’t breathe. I am about to collapse. No, no, I can’t. I have to walk to the car. I see her being carried into it. I understand; I scream.
I’m in the car now, crouching on the floor, facing her … Blood – blood on her sari, blood on her chest. Her large eyes are wide open; her face wears a surprised expression. She doesn’t move. I attempt to speak to her, to call out, “Mummy, Mummy”, but no word comes out. I try again; she doesn’t reply.
Her aides are in the front of the car, screaming. Heavy, slow traffic, the car barely moves, it has no siren. One red light, then another. Then the hospital. The gate isn’t opening. Chaos. We are stopped; someone looks through the window in a questioning attitude. They let us in.
We reach the emergency department, teeming with people. We are stopped again, not allowed in, we have to wait for our turn. Someone calls out to the driver, signals him to move forward. They identify us; she is placed on a trolley. We are led somewhere – an operation theatre? They ask me to follow. I’m taken to a room nearby. No, no, I want to stay by her, I insist. I want to know. I have to see. They don’t reply; they are immersed in their emergency procedures.
I feel confused, lost … I don’t recognise anyone there. I’m shivering under my dressing gown. I feel scared, my mind is racing. Where is Rajiv? I try to remember. I can’t, I can’t. The children, yes, they’re in school; they must be brought home. Oh God, no, no. Let them be safe, let Rajiv be safe … Whom do I tell, whom do I speak to? I sense someone in the room. I don’t know who it is. I try to speak, to put some words together; nothing comes out. “There’s blood all over her clothes,” someone says. Some clothes are brought in for me. I am helped into them in a nearby closet.
Hours go by, agonising hours. More people come in and crowd around. I signal a question to the doctor; he shakes his head. I understand, yes, I understand. I break into sobs, uncontrollably. Someone tries to calm me. I feel numb, cold.
At two in the afternoon of 31 October 1984, Indira Gandhi was declared dead. I was driven home to collect some clothes for her body to be changed into. On the way, a group of men tried to stop our car, banging on its windows. They were angry, shouting something I couldn’t understand.
At home, the children, Rahul and Priyanka, rushed to my arms in tears. When they had been abruptly picked up from school by black-uniformed commandos, they sensed a catastrophe. Once home, they saw some of the staff sobbing. They asked question after question. “Where’s Mama?” “Why have we been brought home?” “Where’s Papa?” “What’s happened?” “Where’s Dadi?” “You aren’t telling us the truth!” My friends Nina and Sterre had been with them, trying to calm them down, not knowing what to say to them. I wanted to sit with them and hug them, to break the news to them gently, but I was unable to – I had to go back; Rajiv was coming to the hospital.
Rajiv had been in West Bengal at a political rally when his cavalcade was stopped by a police patrol. He was told there was a message from Delhi to say he should rush back – a serious accident had taken place. He was driven to the helipad, from where he flew to Calcutta and then to Delhi. He’d heard on a BBC bulletin that Mrs Gandhi was wounded and in a grave condition. Nobody told him directly that his mother was no more, but he understood.
He landed at 3.30pm and was driven straight to the hospital. He walked in with other people, and I remember longing to be left alone with him for a moment at least. We held each other, and as he spoke to me, it sunk in that he was saying something I didn’t want to hear. “I have been asked … They want me to be sworn in as prime minister.”
I felt as if a knife had been plunged right into my heart. I felt a pounding in my chest, a rage welling up deep inside me. I was about to explode. I attempted to hold it in. “You have been asked to? How dare they ask? How dare they? Who are they? Why you, why does it have to be you? Why did you allow them to ask you? No, it cannot be; this time it’s not going to be!” Seized by utter pain and anguish, soaked in perspiration, I felt like throwing up. I wanted to scream, to ask for help. “Someone please help me put an end to this.”
I burst out crying, pleading, begging him with folded hands, “No, no, you can’t think of it. You have to stop them, you must refuse, you must say no – for the children’s sake, for yourself. You can’t do this to us. They will kill you; they will kill you, too!” I cried out. He replied, “They will kill me anyway.”
We brought my mother-in-law home. The dining room had been emptied out, and we laid her body down on the floor, her feet pointing south as Hindu custom decrees. The same evening at around 6.30pm, Rajiv was sworn in as prime minister of India. I was too broken to even register what was happening around me. His mother lay there, her body pierced with more than 30 bullet holes. I knew, I knew it then in my heart: Rajiv’s path would lead to the same end.

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.
Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.
He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.
Federal prosecutors said south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.
Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.
Sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.
Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.
The election of a new president is scheduled for next year.
Prosecutors said the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.
The plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.
CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.
By June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.
Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

Dry weather is expected to prevail across Jammu and Kashmir until November 30, with temperatures likely to dip further in the coming days, even as night temperatures improved marginally across most parts of the region.
Srinagar recorded a minimum temperature of 0.2 degrees Celsius on Friday, moving above the freezing point after several days. The temperature was up from minus 0.2 degrees Celsius recorded the previous night.
A weather department official said that tourist resort Pahalgam in south Kashmir recorded a minimum temperature of minus 2.2 degrees Celsius, up from minus 2.8 degrees Celsius a day earlier, while Gulmarg recorded minus 0.4 degrees Celsius against minus 1.0 degrees Celsius.
Kupwara in north Kashmir registered a minimum of minus 1.1 degrees Celsius compared to minus 1.3 degrees Celsius the previous night.
Qazigund recorded minus 0.8 degrees Celsius, unchanged from the previous night, while Kokernag registered 0.7 degrees Celsius against 1.0 degrees Celsius a day earlier.
In the Jammu division, Jammu city recorded a minimum temperature of 11.7 degrees Celsius against 10.8 degrees Celsius the previous night. Katra recorded 11.0 degrees Celsius, Banihal 9.4 degrees Celsius, Batote 7.2 degrees Celsius and Bhaderwah 3.2 degrees Celsius.
Despite the marginal rise in temperatures, signs of the prevailing cold remained visible in parts of south Kashmir, where icicles were seen covering vegetation in the Kokernag area of Anantnag district.
The marginal improvement in night temperatures comes amid the onset of winter across the Valley, with several higher-altitude areas continuing to record sub-zero temperatures.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.
The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations
To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.
The findings are striking. They included:
Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received
Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials
Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”
“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”
Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g. OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
The Wild West in the age of AI
The most concerning of the findings was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:
Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.
Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.
Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.
As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging, and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:
The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.
This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.
The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.
Moore said that the most effective means for preventing leakage is to host models using on-premises servers. That option is expensive, though. For those who can’t afford a self-hosted system, the next best option, Moore said, is to receive service directly from a first-tier provider that provides “one contract and a privacy policy to read.” Moore said that even then, there’s no guarantee no data will leak, but that the measure minimizes the chances. AI users should also avoid accepting default provider or reseller pools and instead pick upstream providers themselves.
The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.
Dan Goodin is Senior Security Editor at Ars Technica, where he oversees coverage of malware, computer espionage, botnets, hardware hacking, encryption, and passwords. Canada·THE FIFTH ESTATE
A Montrealer died in Istanbul. Authorities blame food poisoning but what we found suggests something else
Illegal use of pesticide in Turkey linked to deaths of other tourists and residents
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino, a healthy 24-year-old Montrealer, died suddenly in Istanbul on June 17, 2025.
A Turkish autopsy report concluded the cause of death was food poisoning.
But for her family, that doesn't add up.
A joint investigation into Deveaux-Cattino's death by Enquête and the fifth estate revealed a different poison at work and 12 similar deaths.
The recent medical school graduate had decided to celebrate by taking a trip with a few of her closest friends.
"She'd never been to Turkey," said her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. "She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country."
The group hit the tourist trail and its highlights, including the requisite balloon ride in Cappadocia.
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino had never been to Turkey before her trip in 2025, says her sister, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino. ‘She thought it was a super beautiful, vibrant country.’ (Radio-Caanda)
With only two days to go, Bérengère and one of her friends headed for Istanbul, a city she'd longed to visit.
- Watch the full documentary, "The Invisble Killer," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.
They checked into Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel and went straight out to explore. They soaked up the sights and street food, then settled down for a proper meal, a chicken casserole followed by Turkish tea and baklava.
The next morning, they woke violently ill.
Laurie recalls the final days
The details of those final days come from Laurie, the woman who travelled to Istanbul with Bérengère. What happened on that trip left her traumatized and we've agreed to protect her identity and not use her real name.
She said that within minutes of waking, Bérengère was throwing up.
"Then I started feeling unwell," Laurie said, "and suddenly we were taking turns running to the bathroom to vomit until we realized that whatever it was, it wasn't just going to pass."
They called the front desk and an ambulance took them to hospital.
‘My sister is younger than me,’ said Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino, right. ‘I’d never imagined a life without her.’ (Submitted by Deveaux-Cattino family)
'Things aren't going well'
That same day, across the ocean in Montreal, Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino saw her screen light up: Laurie was FaceTiming her.
"I thought: 'This isn't normal. Something's off. This is going to be bad news,'" said Deveaux-Cattino. "She says 'Élo, we're in the hospital in Istanbul, and things aren't going well. I've been told to contact the family.'"
Deveaux-Cattino and her father, Henri Cattino, scrambled to find flights to Istanbul. While waiting for their connection in Paris, Deveaux-Cattino called the embassy.
"I said: 'Please, can you tell me if my sister has died?'" said Deveaux-Cattino. ”And she said: 'I'm very sorry, Éléonore, but your sister is dead.'"
Three days into their trip to Istanbul in November 2025, the Böcek family from Hamburg fell ill. Five days later, all four family members were dead, poisoned by phosphine gas. (@ismailsaymaz/X)
The Böcek family
The Deveaux-Cattinos repatriated Bérengère's body and asked the Quebec coroner's office to examine it. They buried their daughter and sister without confirmation of the cause of death.
As they waited for answers from Turkey, the family speculated about what else could explain Bérengère's death: Organ trafficking? Alcohol poisoning? Medical malpractice?
Then, in November, as we were investigating, a diplomatic source texted with a tip that pointed to an entirely different explanation.
"A family of four has just died in Istanbul. Watch this report."
The Böceks, a Turkish-German family from Hamburg, were visiting Istanbul. Their hotel was blocks from where Bérengère and Laurie stayed. All four fell ill and died within days of each other.
Investigators initially suspected food poisoning there, too. But within days, authorities concluded that another poison had been at work: aluminum phosphide, a highly toxic agricultural pesticide used to kill rodents and insects.
The 'bomb'
Exterminators call aluminum phosphide "the bomb." It is used in pellet form. Once the pellets are exposed to air, they release phosphine gas. Exterminators say that when placed in a sealed room, the gas kills every living, breathing thing within 72 hours. In Turkey, it's illegal to use in urban areas.
But, like all big cities, Istanbul has a bedbug problem.
Exterminator Birkan Cihan said he can barely keep up with calls from desperate home and hotel owners. Some ask whether he treats bedbugs with "gas." He doesn't.
"We tell them their neighbours could die from it, and that they could, too. But they say: 'We have no choice, it's the only thing that works,'" Cihan said
The phosphine gas these pellets emit is so potent and volatile that it can spread through a building, even if the area being treated is sealed.
In the case of the Böcek family, fumigation in the neighbouring room was determined to be what killed all four of them.
Investigations by Enquête and the fifth estate have found similar cases. In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand.
In 2012, two sisters from Quebec, Audrey and Noémi Bélanger, died of phosphine poisoning in Thailand. (Submitted by Bélanger family)
'That doesn't make any sense'
Just before Christmas 2025, the Deveaux-Cattinos received the autopsy report from Turkey. It concluded that food poisoning caused Bérengère's death. Unconvinced, they handed the report to the Quebec coroner's office.
"The coroner here ran some tests, and she couldn't confirm that food poisoning was the cause of death because, usually, there are signs of intestinal irritation," Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino said. "There were none in my sister's case."
We showed the Turkish autopsy report to another Quebec pathologist. Although not authorized to speak publicly, he also questioned the autopsy's conclusions.
"Two young, healthy women who end up in the hospital with food poisoning — OK, I'll buy that. But to die of it so quickly, without any signs of bloody diarrhea or other complications, that doesn't make any sense."
Turkish freelance journalist Ayse Adanali covered the story of the death of the Böcek family in Istanbul in 2025. (Radio-Canada)
Women and children
In Turkey, we started working with Ayse Adanali, a freelance Turkish journalist who'd covered the Böcek story.
Together, we documented nearly 30 cases of phosphine poisoning, including a dozen deaths, since 2023 in Turkey.
Some were tourists, like the two Dutch teenagers found dead by their father in their Istanbul hotel room in August 2025. But most of the victims were Turkish, like Karan Yazıcı, a three-year-old boy poisoned in Istanbul in April 2025 following a fumigation in the neighbouring apartment.
The majority of the victims are women and children. Members of the same family were often poisoned together. While some survived, others died. In most cases, food poisoning was initially blamed for making them sick.
'This is not food poisoning'
Şebnem Korur Fincancı is a human rights activist, professor emeritus and leading forensic pathologist in Turkey.
She's studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas.
Turkish forensic pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı has studied aluminum phosphide and knows how difficult it is to identify victims poisoned by phosphine gas. (Radio-Canada)
She'd never heard about Bérengère; her death had not been covered by Turkish media.
"This is not food poisoning," she said after reading the Turkish autopsy report.
"I don't think that this is food poisoning because there is no story of diarrhea, only throwing up."
She added that the timing of Bérengère's decline suggests food poisoning couldn't be the culprit.
"Rather, it is the pesticide poisoning."
Fincancı sees one undeniable detail in this report, a finding common to all victims of phosphine gas poisoning she's examined: something called metabolic acidosis, which increases the levels of acidity in the body.
"There is the metabolic acidosis, which also indicates the pesticide intoxication," she said. 'It is one of the main findings of these kinds of cases."
She believes there could be more cases of phosphine poisoning than currently reported.
"With all these misdiagnoses, we have to consider the situation."
Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and her friend, Laurie, stayed at the Seven Days Hotel in Istanbul. (Radio-Canada)
150 bites
We scoured hundreds of Google and Tripadvisor reviews for the Seven Days Hotel to see if they'd had a bedbug problem around the time of Bérengère and Laurie's stay.
One stood out: A tourist claiming he'd been bitten 150 times during his stay in June 2025.
We tracked him down. He confirmed he stayed in Room 107, the room next door to where the two women stayed 10 days later.
The windows in those two rooms open onto each other.
That left one critical question: Had Room 107 been treated after his stay? And, if so, with what?
We contacted hotel manager Bahattin Demir. He remembered Bérengère and Laurie and had gone to the hospital after they'd been admitted.
We told him about the tourist in Room 107 and asked him whether extermination work in that room could have killed Bérengère.
"I don't think so, because if it was that product, I'm sure that, you know, everybody would have this problem," he said.
Inside Room 108 at the Seven Days Hotel where Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino and Laurie stayed. (Radio-Canada)
He said exterminators spray the rooms in the hotel monthly. He offered to contact them and find out what product they use, but then wrote back, referring us to them for more details.
The extermination company is called Wolves.
A contact called them for us. We're protecting her identity because undercover work can lead to jail time in Turkey.
Posing as an Air BnB owner in Istanbul's Fatih district, she claimed to be struggling with bedbugs.
The employee was cautious on the phone.
He didn't name the product specifically, but his detailed description is similar to how aluminum phosphide is used.
"For 72 hours, nobody goes in, the doors are locked and nothing living enters."
- Deaths of Quebec women in Thailand may have been caused by pesticide
- Phosphine pesticide used to kill bedbugs causes Fort McMurray baby's death
We called Wolves for an interview. The employee who answered the phone was not authorized to speak, but denied using aluminum phosphide.
Neither the hospital that treated Bérengère nor the Forensic Medical Centre where her autopsy was performed replied to our inquiries.
The tourism police similarly declined our interview request.
Going over notes Laurie had shared, we noticed she and Bérengère had left the window open the first night. But the next evening, to avoid being woken by the call to prayer, they closed it and turned on the air conditioning. And that was the night they got sick.
We asked pathologist Şebnem Korur Fincancı whether phosphine gas residue could build up in air conditioners.
"Of course," she said.
'Those who are gone'
The Böceks' case went to trial in June 2026. The defendants were charged with criminal negligence causing the deaths of this family of four. The ruling came down within days. The owners of the extermination company were found guilty and sentenced to 18 years in prison. The hotel owner and employees received 12 to 13 years.
While awaiting the verdict, the paternal grandfather, Yilmaz Böcek, commented that even the stiffest penalty could never bring back his children and grandchildren.
"Those who are gone never come back."
Éléonore Deveaux-Cattino wants Bérengère to be remembered.
"My sister is younger than me. I'd never imagined a life without her. We used to be two against the world … now I'm all alone," she said.
"But I'm stubborn. And since she can no longer speak, I'll speak for her. I'll never let her go."
In the summer of 2026, the government of Canada added a new entry to its travel advisory for Turkey, alerting travellers to "cases of poisoning linked to the use of chemical pesticides in tourist accommodations in Istanbul."
After this story first aired on Oct. 15, 2026, Turkish consular officials contacted us, confirming the investigation into Bérengère Deveaux-Cattino's death in Istanbul remains open.

Mountains of scientific evidence support both the negative and positive effects of our eating habits on our health. Research shows that a healthy diet can help those suffering from chronic health conditions like Type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure.
This is where “food is medicine” comes in. Food is medicine, also known as “food as medicine” and “food prescriptions,” is a movement dedicated to providing healthy food – fruits, vegetables and sometimes healthy proteins – based on a clinician’s prescription in order to prevent, manage or treat specific clinical conditions.
Prescribing food to patients is intended to convey that food is just as important as medication for health and wellness.
As researchers whose work focuses on food access and health in rural communities, we have firsthand experience running food is medicine programs in our local area in northern Mississippi. This experience has shown us the benefits and limitations of these programs in our community.
Fighting food insecurity
Food is medicine programs can be delivered through curated food boxes, grocery vouchers and medically tailored meals. Most programs are collaborations between nonprofit organizations, health clinics and healthcare providers. The goal of food is medicine is to improve patient health, especially for those with chronic conditions, while reducing healthcare costs.
Increasingly, food is medicine programs have become lifelines for people with food insecurity. In 2024, more than 47 million Americans, including 7.3 million children, lived in food-insecure households – meaning they were at some point uncertain of having, or did not have, enough food for everyone in the household.
Internationally, the number of people experiencing hunger rises to roughly 673 million. Rural populations are more likely to be food insecure due to the loss of local grocery stores and distance from urban centers. Unlike a food bank, food is medicine programs provide only healthy foods, which are often curated by a dietitian, to optimize patient health.
Forward momentum
Though food is medicine isn’t formally connected to the Make American Healthy Again movement, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. has brought new energy and attention to the concept. In January 2026, the second Trump administration launched a campaign encouraging Americans to “Eat Real Food.”
But the food is medicine movement actually began more than 60 years ago. One of the early providers who prescribed food as medicine was civil rights activist and multiple Nobel Peace Prize winner Dr. Jack Geiger. In the 1960s, he co-founded community health centers in South Boston and the Mississippi Delta.
When government officials chastised him for prescribing food to patients in the Delta, Geiger responded, “The last time I looked at my textbooks, the most specific therapy for malnutrition was food.”
Since then, thousands of community organizations like Community Servings and Project Open Hand have provided healthy food to vulnerable community members.
In 2023, the president of the American Heart Association convened an advisory group of researchers and physicians to review current food is medicine research and suggest next steps for work in this area. This advisory has suggested that these programs could help prevent or manage chronic conditions, saving the U.S. healthcare system an estimated US$4.3 trillion annually.
Food is medicine has also started to gain international momentum. In 2025, the Rockefeller Foundation supported a meeting of international scholars, policy experts and practitioners that established the Food Is Medicine Global Alliance. This organization plans to help integrate, sustainably finance and routinely deliver food is medicine programs worldwide by 2030. So far, it has released several reports highlighting the current food is medicine environment and made resources available to providers looking to start their own programs.
Food is medicine in our local community
Food is medicine programs can use food from local farms or grocery stores, and the means of getting the food to patients varies. The four projects we have run to date have been relatively small and local.
One was a food box pickup program that supplemented fruits and vegetables for 55 households whose members demonstrated food insecurity. We followed the participants for two years and found statistically significant reductions in weight, waist circumference and triglyceride levels in the primary adult participants.
For two of our other programs, including one that is ongoing, we partnered with local farmers. One was a pilot test of a food box delivery program for housebound people. Both the recipients of the food and the farmers reported high satisfaction with the program’s delivery and felt the program strengthened community connections while also supporting local agricultural livelihoods.
What other researchers have found
One recent large-scale literature review identified 14 trials of food is medicine interventions and found that these approaches often positively influenced diet quality and food security.
Another review of food is medicine programs for people with diabetes found significant increases in fruit and vegetable intake and reductions in blood sugar levels. This data supports our own previous findings.
However, the effect of food is medicine programs on long-term health outcomes has been inconsistent, in part because many trials have been too small or not rigorous enough to determine causation. In some cases, the “dose” – that is, the amount of food provided – is limited by grant funding. Our food box pickup project supplemented only four to five meals each week, which may have been insufficient to significantly improve all health outcomes.
Moreover, it will be important for researchers to consider the logistics of making these programs work in various local food environments. Global factors like changing weather patterns and, more recently, delays in fuel and supplies from the Strait of Hormuz have increased prices of staple food products like cereals and vegetable oil and led to shortages of cooking oil in some countries.
Food is medicine can be appealing because it makes intuitive sense. But going forward, larger, high-quality studies are needed to adequately track clinical outcomes from the various types of food is medicine programming. If studies show food is medicine is beneficial, it could lead to a shift in how healthcare practitioners approach diet for patients with chronic illness. Access to healthy food would be considered as essential as medications for patients with chronic illness.
Meagen Rosenthal, University of Mississippi and Natalie Minton, University of Mississippi

The World Health Organisation warned on Friday (November 13, 2026) of surging respiratory illnesses in Gaza, with worse expected after heavy rains flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians.
“The numbers already show the pressure. Acute respiratory infections are 33,000 cases higher than at the same time last year,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told reporters in Geneva from Jerusalem.
Poor living conditions and severe overcrowding are driving up infections as Gaza’s population is squeezed into an ever-smaller area, WHO said. The crunch has worsened as the Israeli military expands its control by advancing the “Yellow Line” — a demarcation established under October’s U.S.-brokered ceasefire.
“That means people are living in more crowded conditions, where of course the spread between humans of a virus is much more prone to spread,” Ms. Van De Weerdt explained.
The Israeli military told Reuters the Yellow Line aims to protect Israeli civilians and army troops from threats and that adjustments to its location follow the ceasefire agreement and international law, and are not intended to harm the civilian population.
“The IDF categorically rejects the claim that it operates to deliberately reduce the area available to the civilian population in the Gaza Strip.”
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said that more than 93,000 tents and over 8,600 trucks carrying tarpaulin sheets, blankets and winter clothing have entered Gaza since the Board of Peace, UN agencies and NGOs launched the winterisation plan. Equipment intended for the reconstruction of Gaza will be permitted to enter only after Hamas has been fully disarmed, it added.
Last week COGAT said that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions before the heavy rain, in coordination with international organisations.
Respiratory infections currently make up 11% of all consultations, with the WHO expecting cold weather, flooding, overcrowded shelters and poor ventilation to push these numbers higher.
“It is shocking that just a few days of rain really showed us what the coming months will bring. And winter has not even fully set in. The worst really is yet to come,” Ms. Van De Weerdt said.
Nearly a million displaced people in Gaza live in flood-exposed areas, and 400,000 of them are in locations that are considered at extremely high risk, according to the WHO.
The agency said flooding heightened the risk of contaminated water, while standing water gave mosquitoes and pests more places to breed. Dampness encouraged mould and bacteria that are major drivers of respiratory infections, especially in young children, it said.
While the majority of medicines are getting into Gaza, the WHO faces difficulty getting laboratory supplies, which it says are vital for diagnosing patients before they can be treated.
“To prevent outbreaks, we really call to let laboratory equipment enter Gaza today, so that we can avoid a public health disaster on top of a disaster.“
COGAT said Israel has facilitated the entry of all medicines requested by international aid organisations and has not rejected any requests received, adding that X-ray machines, oxygen generators, batteries, generators, and other equipment have entered Gaza.

Disseqt AI, which builds AI agents for AI governance and testing, has raised $8 Mn (about ₹75 Cr) in a funding round led by Gresham House Ventures. Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners, and Enterprise Ireland also participated in the round, along with angel investors like cricketer Rahul Dravid and senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce, and Meta. The startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its global enterprise customer base and scale operations across the UK and international markets. “Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. This gap often stops ambitious AI projects from going live, and it is what we built Disseqt to close … This funding lets us bring that standard to more enterprises around the world,” said CEO and cofounder Apoorva Kumar. Founded in late 2025 by Kumar, Manish Atri, and Cyril Treacy, Disseqt operates an independent governance and testing layer for enterprise AI agents. Essentially, it ensures that AI systems are behaving as intended and meet regulatory requirements. The platform enables compliance, security, and IT teams to test agentic workflows for vulnerabilities and data-leak risks prior to deployment. It can enforce real-time policy guardrails in production, block non-compliant outputs, and maintain audit trails independent of underlying model providers. While its commercial operations and headquarters are in Ireland, Disseqt’s engineering and AI teams are based in Bengaluru. It has customer-facing operations across the UK, Ireland and India, according to its website. Atri, its COO, is also India-based. Both Kumar and Atri are graduates of IIIT Allahabad. Besides, it has also partnered with major Indian IT companies like Infosys, Cognizant, HCLTech, Mphasis, and Tata Technologies as ‘Global System Integrators’ to deploy its platforms for their enterprise clients. This adds to the uptick in investor interest in AI startups. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding more than tripled YoY to $438 Mn in the September quarter. The surging investor interest in AI comes even as the overall funding landscape remains relatively subdued, with the cumulative funding raised by Indian startups increasing by just 5% YoY.

Ujjain (Madhya Pradesh): The traditional donkey fair at Kartik Mela on Badnagar Road began with the worship of donkeys and an offering of 'gulab jamuns' on Friday.
The unique celebration attracted visitors as livestock owners also organised a symbolic wedding between a male and female donkey, accompanied by chants praising the animals.
Regional corporator Chhotelal Mandloi attended as chief guest. Traders from across Madhya Pradesh arrived to buy and sell donkeys.
Manoj Babulal Prajapat and Prajapat community youth president Radheshyam Bilonia said donkey prices ranged from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000 this year.
Despite declining use in modern times, donkeys continue transporting goods in rural areas.
Animals named Salman, Shah Rukh, Aishwarya, Jacqueline, Shabnam and Shabana became attractions for visitors.
Prajapat said the community had organised the fair for years ahead of 'Kartik Purnima', preserving its traditional significance.

Japan, India agree to enhance military and defense industry cooperation
Japan and India have agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills
TOKYO -- TOKYO (AP) — Japan and India agreed to enhance their military and arms industry cooperation, including allowing Japanese troops to conduct live-fire missile training at Indian firing ranges in future joint drills, as their defense and foreign ministers met Thursday in Tokyo.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi joined their Indian counterparts, Rajnath Singh and S. Jaishankar, at the “two-plus-two" meeting in Tokyo.
The two Asian powers have been rapidly deepening security, defense and economic ties in recent years amid growing tension and uncertainty in the region. India and Japan also are part of the Quad grouping with the United States and Australia that aims to counter China’s influence.
“Through our cooperation, we hope to serve as the anchor for the Indo-Pacific region,” Motegi told a joint news conference after the talks.
This defense industrial cooperation will proceed under the framework of “design with Japan, make in India,” Singh said.
As an island nation with limited space to safely conduct missile tests and training, Japan needs defense partners that can provide facilities for its military to practice live-fire drills essential to improving missile capability. Japan struck a similar arrangement with Australia this year.
Japan has been fortifying defenses in its southwestern region to deter China's growing military activity and started deploying long-range missiles this year, including Type-12 surface-to-ship missiles mobilized in Kumamoto on the southern main island.
Japan has also significantly relaxed its postwar pacifist principles in recent years and lifted a ban on lethal weapons exports as part of its security, defense and economic growth strategies.
On Thursday, the four ministers agreed to promote cooperation in defense equipment and technology and to accelerate negotiations toward achieving the transfer of Japanese naval radio antenna UNICORN to India.
They reaffirmed deepening cooperation in a range of areas including air and maritime security, information sharing, search and rescue operations, naval shipbuilding and artificial intelligence, according to a ministers' joint statement after the talks.

YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.
Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

A few of the largest pharmaceutical companies have told a Congressional committee that they do not plan to start new clinical trial sites in the Xinjiang region of China or at hospitals affiliated with the Chinese military.
The disclosure was made by the House Select Committee on China, which last June opened investigations into five companies — Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer, and Bristol Myers Squibb — over concerns about intellectual property exposure, military entanglements, and ethical standards at trial sites in sensitive regions of the country.
All five companies indicated they would not initiate new clinical studies at sites linked to the People’s Liberation Army, which is the military wing of the Chinese Communist Party. In letters sent to the drugmakers, the House committee noted rising concern over the possibility of security risks.

Quick Answer
The Dreame X60 Ultra Complete offers powerful suction, heated-water mopping, a slimmer design, and smarter obstacle handling. At ₹1,34,999, it delivers an impressive cleaning experience with greater convenience, though the value of its premium features depends on your home’s needs.
When I reviewed the X40 Ultra, it was the first robot where I didn’t have to plan a backup round of cleaning. Months later, the L40 Ultra AE beat it on suction and mopping for Rs 20,000 less. The X60 Ultra Complete has to answer a question both reviews left open: what does a Dreame flagship do that the cheaper model does not?
On paper, quite a lot. It also costs more than twice what the L40 Ultra AE did, so the real question is whether the additions change daily cleaning in an Indian home or mostly change the spec sheet.
Table of Contents
Design and Build: Slimmer Robot, Smarter Moves
At first glance, the X60 Pro Complete looks like any other premium Dreame device. You get the familiar circular body, a large docking station, and a design that is more functional than flashy. But there’s one important difference. At just 7.95 cm tall, the X60 is noticeably slimmer than the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE. And that’s thanks to the retractable navigation sensor that pops up when needed and slides back into the body when the robot needs to squeeze under low furniture.
This might sound gimmicky at first (remember OnePlus 7T Pro?), but it has a practical value. In 2026, most robot vacuums already do a decent job of cleaning open floors. The real challenge is getting under sofas, beds, and cabinets without getting stuck. The X60 needs just over 8 cm of clearance to enter these spaces with its sensor retracted.
The price of that slim body is a 235 ml onboard bin, which is significantly smaller than what we saw on the L40 Ultra (395 ml) and X40 Ultra (350 ml). That means the robot keeps returning to the dock to empty the bin more often than expected in heavy sessions, especially if you have a pet at home. Not a big deal, but the trips do add time.
The slimmer body isn’t the only trick up the X60’s sleeve. Dreame has also upgraded its obstacle-climbing system, allowing the robot to lift itself over raised thresholds and door tracks that might stop a regular robot vacuum. This is particularly useful in Indian homes, where bathrooms, balconies, and even some rooms have raised entrances.
Genuinely, this is a big step-up (pun intended) in the evolution of robot vacuums. But you should ask yourself this question: are the obstacles in your home tall enough to trouble a decent mid-range robot vacuum and require a top-of-the-line robot? So while the X60’s climbing ability is impressive on paper (single thresholds up to 4.5 cm and double-layer steps up to 8.8 cm), how much value it adds depends on the layout of your home. If your existing robot already moves between rooms without getting stuck, this upgrade alone won’t justify spending significantly more. In fact, your home’s layout, flooring, and the presence of pets matter far more than the specifications alone. We’ve covered these and other factors in our robot vacuum cleaner buying guide.
The dock is significantly shorter and wider than the L40 Ultra I tested last, and its gold-accented finish looks more at home in a living room than the matte black L40. The trade-off is the capacity: 4.2 liters of clean water and 3 liters of dirty water, down from 4.5 and 4 liters on the L40. The 3.2-liter dust bag is unchanged.
As I pointed out in my earlier Dreame reviews, the company continues to ship its robot vacuums with a bulky 16A plug, and the X60 Ultra Complete is no exception. Most Indian homes don’t have a 16A socket conveniently located where you’d want to place the docking station, making an adapter or a dedicated socket an unnecessary hassle for such an expensive product.
Cleaning Performance: Does the Extra Power Make a Difference?
Dreame has made a big deal of the X60 Ultra Complete’s suction power of 35,000 Pa, and understandably so. But having reviewed the X40 Ultra (12,000 Pa) and L40 Ultra AE (19,000 Pa), I’ve reached a point where raw suction figures don’t excite me as much as they once did. Both those robots were already capable of keeping my floors clean without much intervention. So with the X60, I was less interested in how much more powerful it was and more curious about whether that extra power translated into noticeably cleaner floors.
On tile and stone floors, the X60 Ultra Complete does an excellent job of picking up everyday dust, crumbs, and pet hair. The extending side brush also does a great job of cleaning along walls and around furniture legs, areas where robot vacuums often leave some dirt behind. Hair handling is noticeably better than on the X40 Ultra, which struggled with long human hair and clumps of dog fur.
Obstacle avoidance is something Dreame has mastered, and it’s no different on the X60. In my month-long testing, it easily avoided the usual suspects like cables, socks, and small toys. But that was the case with the cheaper L40 and X40 vacuums, too. While it handled thick carpets well, light fabric rugs were pulled towards its inlet a couple of times.
Two newer touches stand out on the X60 Ultra. The robot maps the house during its first clean, so there is no separate mapping run. Also, its proactive-light dirt detection spots hair and light liquids and adjusts cleaning. Image processing happens on the device, per Dreame, and the app shows when the camera is active.
Mopping Performance: Where the X60 Makes a Stronger Case
When I interviewed Manu Sharma, the head of Dreame India, he made an interesting observation: for Indians, a house isn’t truly clean until the mopping is done. And that’s where the X60 Ultra Complete brings some meaningful upgrades. Unlike the X40 Ultra and L40 Ultra AE, which used hot water only to wash the mop pads at the dock, the X60 actually mops the floor with water heated to 40°C. The pads spin at up to 230 RPM, apply 15 N of downward pressure, and extend towards walls and furniture legs to clean areas that regular circular mops often miss.
For everyday mopping, the results are quite impressive. Footprints, light spills, and the grime that builds up on floors throughout the day are handled well. Even some dried stains can be removed, although older, stubborn stains may need a second pass or a targeted zone clean. This is one area where the X60 makes a stronger case for its premium pricing, especially if you mop your floors daily rather than occasionally.
There is one catch, though. The X60 tends to leave floors noticeably damp after mopping. Not enough to make them dangerously slippery, but enough for water marks to show up on wooden-finish tiles. Thankfully, you can adjust the water level in the Dreame app, and I’d recommend starting with a lower setting before increasing it if needed. For homes with carpets, the mop pads can lift up to 21.5 mm to avoid wetting them. You can also have the robot leave the pads at the dock when vacuuming carpets, which is the safer option for thicker rugs.
Multifunction Dock: Almost Hands-Free, But Not Quite
A big part of what you’re paying for with the X60 Ultra Complete is its multifunction docking station. Once the robot finishes cleaning, the dock takes over. It empties the dustbin, refills the robot’s water tank, washes the mop pads, and dries them with hot air. This also makes the smaller onboard dustbin less of a concern, as the robot can return to the dock and empty itself whenever needed. It’s the sort of convenience that makes you forget how much work goes into keeping a robot vacuum clean.
But don’t mistake this for a completely hands-free system. During my testing, I had to refill the clean-water tank and empty the dirty-water tank roughly every other day. Your experience will vary depending on the size of your home, how often you mop, and the water settings you use. You’ll also need to replace the dust bag occasionally and clean the dock’s washboard and other parts. Then there are the recurring costs of dust bags, filters, brushes, and cleaning solution. Dreame includes a decent number of spare accessories in the Complete package, which is nice, but you’ll eventually need to buy replacements. For my usage of roughly 800 sqft home, that’s like replenishing every 6 months or so.
The dock itself is fairly large and needs a permanent spot in your home. Make sure there’s enough room to remove the water tanks comfortably, and preferably place it somewhere you won’t have to carry a tank full of dirty water across the house. These might sound like nitpicking, but when you’re spending this much on a robot vacuum, even small inconveniences are worth pointing out.
App and Battery Life: Plenty of Features, Room for Improvement
I’ve said this in my earlier Dreame reviews, and I’ll say it again. The Dreamehome app can do almost anything you want, but finding the right setting can sometimes be a task in itself. The X60 Ultra Complete is no different. You can clean individual rooms, set up no-mop zones, save up to four maps, and control the robot using Alexa, Siri, Google Home, or Dreame’s own “OK Dreame” voice commands. There’s plenty to play around with, but the app could really do with a simpler interface. Stain Recognition is still in beta, while Matter support is something Dreame has promised through a future software update.
There are some new pet-specific features, too. The X60 can recognize pet bowls, give extra attention to areas where pets spend time, and even locate your pet using its camera. You can also use the camera for live video and two-way communication. There’s an Apple Watch app for starting cleaning sessions and checking their status, along with phone widgets for quick access to cleaning routines.
As for battery life, the X60 packs a 6,400 mAh battery, the same capacity as the X40 Ultra and larger than the L40 Ultra AE’s 5,200 mAh unit. However, a bigger battery doesn’t necessarily translate into longer cleaning sessions, especially with all the extra features running. The good news is that charging is much faster than on the L40 Ultra AE. In my testing, charging times ranged from around 90 minutes to just over two hours, compared to roughly three and a half hours for the L40. Battery life itself isn’t particularly impressive for a flagship, especially in larger homes, but the robot can return to its dock, recharge, and resume cleaning from where it stopped. So, unless you’re in a hurry to get the entire house cleaned in one go, this shouldn’t be much of a concern.
Dreame X60 Ultra Complete Verdict: Worth the Price?
At Rs 1,34,999, the Dreame X60 Ultra Complete is not an easy robot vacuum to recommend, especially when the L40 Ultra AE costs less than half as much and already does an excellent job of keeping floors clean. But after spending time with the X60, I can see where the extra money goes. The slimmer design helps it reach places other robots struggle with, the improved obstacle-climbing system is useful for homes with raised thresholds, and the heated-water mopping is a meaningful upgrade over the X40 and L40. Add reliable vacuuming, better hair handling, excellent edge cleaning, and a multifunction dock that takes care of most of the dirty work, and you have a very capable cleaning system.
That doesn’t mean it’s without flaws. Despite the improvements, I still noticed some hair around the rollers. Mopping can leave floors wetter than I’d like, and stubborn stains may need another pass. The smaller 235 ml dustbin means more trips to the dock during heavy cleaning sessions, while battery life is good enough rather than exceptional. The Dreamehome app remains powerful but unnecessarily complicated, and the dock still needs regular attention. And yes, Dreame continues to ship a 16A plug, something I’ve complained about in my previous reviews. These aren’t deal-breakers individually, but they are harder to ignore at this price.
The X60 also faces some serious competition. In India, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X11 OmniCyclone, and Narwal Flow 2 offer their own take on premium robot cleaning. In the US, the Roborock Saros 20, Ecovacs DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone, and eufy Omni S2 are worth considering against the X60 Max Ultra Complete. I haven’t personally tested these competing models, so I can’t tell you whether they clean better or worse than the Dreame. But based on their features, they’re certainly worth comparing before spending this kind of money.
And that brings me back to the question I raised at the beginning of this review. Does the X60 Ultra Complete do enough to justify its substantial premium over the L40 Ultra AE? For most homes, probably not. The L40 already handles everyday vacuuming and mopping well enough that the X60’s extra suction and smarter features won’t necessarily translate into noticeably cleaner floors. But if you have low furniture, tricky thresholds, pets that shed a lot, and want the most advanced cleaning system Dreame currently offers, the X60 makes a stronger case. You’re paying less for a dramatic improvement in cleaning and more for the ability to clean difficult areas with less intervention.
If you’re unsure which of these premium features you actually need, try our interactive robot vacuum buying checklist. It lets you choose features based on your home and cleaning needs, so you can decide where it’s worth spending more and where you can save.
The X60 Ultra Complete is an excellent robot vacuum, but it’s also a reminder that the best robot vacuum isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It’s the one that cleans your home well enough that you stop thinking about cleaning. And Dreame had already come remarkably close to achieving that with its cheaper models.

- Slim design gets under low furniture
- Impressive obstacle climbing and avoidance
- Heated-water mopping with excellent edge coverage
- Improved handling of pet hair and long hair
- Multifunction dock reduces manual cleaning effort
- Super premium pricing
- Small onboard dustbin means more dock visits
- Mopping can leave floors noticeably damp
- Dreamehome app remains overly complicated
- Bulky 16A plug remains an inconvenience
