In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down, and waiting for their rides home to arrive. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.
Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and cancelled the alert, which notified not only other school officials on the chain, but also the Baltimore County Police Department, that no response was needed.
The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.
According to a lawsuit filed by the current and former students, Taki Allen, Yui-Osa Ogbeide, Devon Thompson Jr., and Keith Winfield III, due to “both technological and human errors,” school officials called police to the scene anyway, and the cops responded with force.
At least six patrol cars arrived with lights flashing, and some cops emerged with guns drawn. The teens froze and cooperated, confused and scared for their lives, their lawsuit said.
“No one told the students what they were suspected of,” the lawsuit said. “Officers separated the students, ordered them to their knees on the concrete, handcuffed them, and searched their persons and property.”
Only after the cops failed to find a gun did students learn that it was the school’s AI gun detection system, Omnilert, that triggered the police response. Allegedly, one of the responding officers muttered, “stupid AI cameras” and “fucking Omnilerts,” while another told the students that “AI is not the best.” Finally releasing the students, one officer seemed to acknowledge that they had put the teens in danger.
“Hey, thanks for not running away, that would have been a real problem,” the officer allegedly said. Walking away, another joked that the boys should remember to “be careful with your chip bags.”
Teens traumatized
The cops did not just target the suspected gunman but apparently told the other teens that they were guilty “by association” when they asked why they were searched.
Suing to stop any other teens from facing allegedly life-or-death situations due to officials’ blind trust of AI, the teens have asked for an injunction barring BCPS from using Omnilert until they can effectively establish protocols to prevent police responses to false alerts.
The lawsuit alleged that students’ constitutional rights were violated, as students were unlawfully searched and detained.
Damon Hewitt, president and executive director of the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law—a nonpartisan nonprofit that’s representing the teens in the suit—said that “overreliance on artificial intelligence technology mixed with inept communication and coordination among key officials is a toxic mix.”
The complaint noted that BCPS was among the earliest adopters of Omnilert, and officials have touted it as “the largest deployment of AI visual gun detection” as a means to supposedly protect students. Instead, they alleged that Omnilert is marketing a defective product as triggering “near-zero false positives” without effectively requiring the adequate human review that claim depends on.
“We need a reckoning on how AI is being used, especially concerning public safety and kids,” Hewitt said. “We are fighting to deliver justice in this case, but it also holds lessons for educators and police officials across the country who should think twice before putting our children’s fate in the hands of AI.”
All the teens feel less safe on campus and less trusting of police following the incident. They also suffered from physical pain—including ”deep red marks” on their wrists from handcuffs—as well as “acute and lasting emotional distress, fear, anxiety,” and “humiliation.” Further, the teens report that rumors follow them around, falsely claiming that there was a gun and damaging their reputations.
Car pick-up will never be the same. The student falsely flagged as the gunman, Taki Allen, “no longer feels safe waiting for rides or spending time outside the school after hours” and “frequently pays for rides home from private car services to avoid waiting for rides from friends or family.” Keith Winfield’s house was very close to the school, but his mother, Frieda Winfield, said his anxiety was so bad that he would call her “multiple times after football practice ended to confirm that she was on her way to pick him up.”
Frieda Winfield called for change following her son Keith’s chilling interaction.
“The police told my son this could have been a real problem,” Frieda Winfield said. “No child in Baltimore County should face this kind of danger while waiting outside his own school for a ride home from his mother.”
What went wrong?
The teens’ lawsuit targets Omnilert and responding Baltimore County Police Department officers. It also challenges Baltimore County Public Schools and individual school officials who allegedly failed to establish proper protocols to prevent a police response to a cancelled alert.
Later investigating, the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) for Education concluded that Omnilert’s system had no “bias.” But OIG acknowledged that the “delegation of authority” process that Kenwood High School set up didn’t stop its principal, Kate Smith, from noticing the alert, failing to see it was cancelled, and texting a school resource officer to deploy police 15 minutes later—all while acknowledging in that text that the object in the alert was “maybe not” a gun. Smith apparently was never trained on the Omnilert system, OIG’s report indicated.
The OIG agreed with teens that things should change. Immediately after the incident, an internal Omnilert training link was shared with BCPS staff, and OIG recommended that schools conduct bi-annual trainings moving forward.
They also recommended that the BCPS Department of School Safety “review its protocol” and reduce the number of individuals who receive campus gun alerts. That could help ensure “internal notification controls are followed” and police “are fully informed of a verified threat,” the OIG said.
Without changes, the OIG acknowledged that “the loss of alert notification controls could place not only BCPS staff and students at risk but could also place responding law enforcement in a potentially tragic situation.”
Another change offered a technical solution that may have prevented the tragic event. The OIG recommended that school officials switch to using the Omnilert app. Since Smith opened the alert in a text message window on her phone, they suggested that she could easily have overlooked the cancellation text message if her first instinct were to enlarge the image or review the camera footage.
These recommendations aren’t enough for current and former students suing, one of which remains an active student who claims the principal never apologized and instead made light of the incidents using cry-laughing emojis in texts with other school officials. Teens alleged that Smith should have known that more than “99 percent of OGD Alerts in Baltimore County Public Schools were false positives that required no police response,” as the OIG’s report said, and she should have prioritized students’ safety and verified the threat before calling in police.
“BCPS’s failures amounted to deliberate indifference to the constitutional rights of its students,” their lawsuit alleged.
The teens asked a court for an injunction barring the use of Omnilert until BCPS staff and police are adequately trained. In their complaint, they alleged that none of the officers on the scene had reviewed the camera footage before responding, and none of the officers informed of the alert cancellation intervened.
BCPS silent; Omnilert defends tech
BCPS declined to comment on the lawsuit, pointing Ars to a statement issued to parents following the incident. That statement did not directly apologize to students but did say the school would provide “ongoing counseling and emotional support” to them while promising to take steps to prevent future incidents.
Blake Mitchell, Omnilert’s vice president of marketing, told Ars that Omnilert is reviewing the complaint.
“What these four students went through on October 20, 2025 should not have happened, and we are truly sorry for the fear they and their families experienced,” Mitchell said. “We understand why they want answers.”
Mitchell said that Omnilert is “built to send anything that could be a firearm to trained people for review, because missing a real gun is the worst possible outcome.” He also reiterated that the OIG investigation found no bias in Omnilert’s system and seemed to agree that it was the school’s authority delegation that failed the students, not necessarily the technology.
“In this case, the school’s designated safety staff reviewed the alert and cancelled it within about two minutes, and everyone who received it was notified,” Mitchell said. “That is exactly why human review matters, and why a cancelled alert must stay cancelled.”
Len Kamdang of the Lawyers’ Committee representing the teens told The New York Times that teens want BCPS and Omnilert to acknowledge that “what happened to them was unacceptable.”
“This case is ultimately about how human beings allowed AI to substitute for their judgment,” Kamdang said.
As a mother, Frieda Winfield told a local news outlet that she was shocked by the incident, despite deliberately teaching her son to be cautious around police. The boys’ caution “saved their lives in my opinion,” she said.
“I was angry. I was fearful,” Frieda Winfield said. “The biggest part was fear, because they’re young men. Young Black men, and they were at school, and they didn’t understand why what was happening, happened to them.”
Kamdang told NYT that “for anyone with children, that is a scary, scary situation. For a Black student, especially a young Black man in America, that is a life-or-death situation.”
As AI tools are increasingly positioned as public safety solutions, the Lawyers Committee is pushing for police reform when cops or officials appear to be blindly trusting AI, their press release said. They noted that “this injustice also raises a broader concern regarding the use and reliability of AI-powered technology in public safety where accuracy is essential in life-and-death situations.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Salah scores twice as Egypt and Nigeria win Afcon 2027 qualifiers

Tolu Arokodare was the hero as Nigeria boosted their hopes of reaching the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) with a 3-1 home win over tournament co-hosts Tanzania.
With the East Africans already assured of a spot at the finals, the Super Eagles are battling for the one qualification spot available in Group L and have little margin for error after losing 3-0 in Guinea-Bissau in September.
Alhassan Yusuf kept his composure to slot Nigeria into a second-minute lead in Uyo from Ademola Lookman's pass, but the visitors equalised through Alphonce Msanga just after the half-hour mark.
Arokodare climbed off the bench at half-time and cleverly flicked home Wilfred Ndidi's low ball to restore the lead for the West Africans in the 52nd minute.
And the Ajax striker, who is on a season-long loan from Wolves, gave the Super Eagles breathing space eight minutes later when he controlled Moses Usor's cross from the left and smashed in from 12 yards out.
With three games played in the group, Eric Chelle's side are now one point behind leaders Guinea-Bissau, who drew 1-1 with Madagascar on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Mohamed Salah scored twice late on against Malawi as Egypt cruised to a 5-0 victory in Ali Maher's first match in charge.
Achraf Hakimi netted two stunning goals and Yassine Bounou saved a penalty to help Morocco continue their unbeaten start with a 5-1 win over Niger.
Meanwhile, Tunisia are in danger of missing out on the finals for the first time since 1992 after suffering a 2-0 defeat at home against Libya, and Kenya scored a last-minute equaliser to end South Africa's perfect start.
The third round of qualifying culminates with three games on Saturday, while the fourth round of fixtures are split across Monday and Tuesday.
Salah and Hakimi shine
Egypt reached the semi-finals of Afcon 2025 and the last 16 of this year's Fifa World Cup under Hossam Hassan but parted company with the 60-year-old earlier this month.
The Pharaohs had taken four points from their opening two games in Group B, with Salah substituted after an hour in their 0-0 draw with Angola before missing the win in South Sudan.
The former Liverpool forward returned as captain against Malawi, and Egypt cruised into a 3-0 lead at the break through goals from Nasser Maher, Omar Marmoush and Mohamed Hany.
Salah got on the scoresheet when he stooped to head in a cross from the left and rounded off proceedings by dinking in a penalty after Hamza Abdelkarim was tripped in the box.
Victory in Maher's first game at the helm puts Egypt three points clear of Angola, who take on South Sudan on Saturday.
In Group A, Morocco had also looked like they would ease to three points against Niger in Casablanca after Yassir Zabiri's early effort and a brilliant long-range strike from right-back Hakimi put them 2-0 up after 27 minutes.
But Mohamed Abdourahmane headed in to halve the deficit and Niger had a chance to level from the spot on the stroke of half-time after a handball by Noussair Mazraoui.
However, Atlas Lions goalkeeper Bounou moved to his left to keep out Youssouf Oumarou's penalty, and Hakimi made it 3-1 in first-half stoppage time with a dipping free-kick from distance.
Youssef En-Nesyri steered in the fourth in the 77th minute from a Hakimi pass and Ayoub Oufkir completed the scoring from close range in the final minute.
Earlier in Group A on Friday Gabon beat Lesotho to move on to six points thanks to two second-half goals from Denis Bouanga.
The LA FC forward smashed the right-hand upright with a penalty but broke the deadlock with a header a minute later and then scored from 12 yards when the Panthers were awarded a second spot kick.
Tunisia downed as McCarthy frustrates Bafana
Tunisia have appeared at a record 17 consecutive Afcons but are winless and bottom of Group H - another section with just one qualifying place on offer - after defeat by their North African neighbours Libya.
The Carthage Eagles could complain about refereeing decisions going against them in Sfax, with Ali Maaloul penalised for a shirt pull on Muad Eisay just before half-time and Ali Youssef converting the resulting spot-kick.
Tunisia had a goal ruled out following a marginal offside call in the second half and three minutes later a low shot from Hamdou El Houni made it 2-0 to the Mediterranean Knights.

The White House has appointed a new national cyber director after Sean Cairncross stepped down from the role in the wake of widespread outages that disrupted air travel, banking and other critical services.
Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, was named as the top cyber security official for the administration, according to posts to social media from various members of Donald Trump’s cabinet.
"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Ms Davies wrote in a post on X.
"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come… But only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
Her new role will see her oversee cyber security policy and strategy across the federal government. The appointment will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth congratulated Ms Davies on X, writing: "She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cyber security landscape."
President Trump faced widespread criticism as Americans contended with a cascade of outages that halted travel, severed work networks, restricted access to banks, and disrupted classified communications.
Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to the public or concealing details about the true origin of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control, and the National Security Agency have all been affected.
On Tuesday, Mr Rubio sought to reassure Americans, saying there is "zero" information suggesting the technical failures are linked or caused by a malign actor.
The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, during which he downplayed the incidents, declaring that "things like that happen."

Magnus Carlsen suggested Champions League-style seedings for draws.

The pilot event of Total Chess in Budapest has led to plenty of conversation about the format, the points system and the rules for players forfeiting games.
Almost every player out of the 24-player field has had their say about what they like and don’t at an event that is being held to test the rules for a full-fledged Total Chess tour the next year with three events that culminate into a world championship title.
Kjell Madland, the man behind Total Chess, believes that not “too many things will change” for the tour next season. But he has said that the organisers will hear feedback from a host of stakeholders, most importantly the players, before deciding on the final form that the next year’s four tournaments will take.
He did indicate that the organisers will tweak rules to prevent a situation where players forfeit games, something that world No.1 Magnus Carlsen did against Bibisara Assaubayeva (in fast classic games) and Vladislav Artemiev (in rapid games) before Richard Rapport and Abhimanyu Mishra followed suit as well.
“We didn’t expect that this (forfeits) would be a big discussion. But at the same time, it’s very good that it happened in the pilot event, and not in the first event of the World Championship tour next year, because it’s not possible to change something when you have started the tour. You need to have the same rules all the time throughout the tour. So now we have the possibility to discuss this in the working group,” Madland told The Indian Express.
“We are very happy about how the tournament has been so far. When it comes to rules and regulations and some adjustments, of course we need to look at that. We have asked players and others about what they think and I feel that there are just small things that need to be done,” Madland added.
Madland pointed out that at an event like the one that ended on Friday with 24 players competing, there was likely to be an avalanche of feedback from everyone involved.
Their job over the next few months before the start of next year’s tour would be to sort out the feedback.
“We want to see if there are things that many people feel. Because when you talk to people, it’s different things. Some have suggestions about the points system, some about adjustments in the group stage. We can change things if many people are saying something. But I don’t think there are very many things we need to change,” Madland added.
Some players have spoken about being exhausted by playing in the format, especially two fast classic games a day in the group stage and then playing seven games across fast classic, rapid and blitz in the knockout stages.
“We wanted it to be like this because when you want to find the best chess player overall, they need to fight. They need to have a very tough competition. If you are chasing a big title, then players should, of course, be tired. It’s the same when they are playing 14 games in the classical World Championship, where they play a game for maybe six or seven hours a day as well and are very, very tired,” he added.

Body of Melbourne Cup horse found dumped in Sydney skip
- Published
The body of a top Australian racehorse has been found dumped in a skip bin, hours after its trainer revealed the horse had died from colic.
In a video shared online, only two weeks after So You Are raced in the Melbourne Cup, the deceased racehorse appeared to be lying in a large metal bin surrounded by other household rubbish in Sydney.
Trainer Bjorn Baker - who shared news of the horse's death from colic on Monday - has said he was "deeply distressed" by the video, and called for a "full explanation".
Racing NSW, the state's industry regulator, said a preliminary investigation had found the horse was later properly buried, but called the way its body was handled "completely unacceptable".
"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said in an statement shared online.
"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death."
So You Are had a successful run during spring, winning four times at respected races including the Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.
The five-year-old recently finished eight in the Melbourne Cup, which was won by Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles III.
The racehorse had received urgent treatment after a severe bout of colic, but was "unfortunately unable to be saved" and was euthanised under anaesthesia, Racing NSW said.
"So You Are was then transported for burial, and was being held temporarily, awaiting burial, when these images were recorded," it said.
Burial at a licensed landfill is typically recommended for animals that die from euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process, according to the racing body.
"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner," it added.
In a statement, REC Equine Specialists - the hospital where the horse died - said a contractor had been hired to dispose of the So You Are's body.
"We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that."
"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally."
The company added that it had stopped using the contractor, and was reviewing its processes to make sure they known exactly how horses are handled after leaving their hospital.
"No owner should have to go through what So You Are's connections have experienced this week. We will make sure it does not happen again."
Jowett's video appeared to be filmed at a public rubbish drop-off and land facility called Lucas Heights, in Sutherland Shire, south of Sydney.
The waste management company that runs the landfill site said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported.

At 16 years old, Henrijs Dandzbergs is too young to vote. Or drink. Or smoke. Or drive unsupervised. But he’s not too young to win half a million dollars for his AI-guided-missile startup.
In September, Dandzbergs, who was born in Latvia, was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort. The startup accelerator counts companies like Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash, and Reddit among its alumni; Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its vaunted history.
His startup, Polemos Industries, is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, can be fired from portable launchers, and can resist jamming attempts. “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” Dandzbergs tells WIRED. “A lot of people that have found success in engineering early on have had a passion for blowing stuff up.”
In conversation, Dandzbergs is poised and articulate. He talks about “attacking hard problems,” breaking things down to “first principles,” and how the Ukraine conflict has forever altered the theater of war—a personal fixation, given his country's proximity to Russia. He projects an unassailable confidence in his own abilities.
“He’s a pretty exceptional person,” says Harj Taggar, a YC partner assigned to mentor Dandzbergs. “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.”
Dandzbergs has resolved to apply these unusual talents to figuring out how to optimize targeted killing. His startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.”
As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long; his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia, and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves.
Early in his schooling, which mostly took place online, Dandzbergs demonstrated a clear talent for science and math. His room started to look like a lab, littered with schematics, robotics, Raspberry Pis, and 3D-printed components.
When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia. His parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk–linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering. His lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone.
Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine. In Latvia, Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border. With the sovereignty of Eastern European nations under threat, new defense startups began to pop up across the region. Dandzbergs wanted in.
“A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare—that’s my drive,” he says.
To stretch his technical skills, Dandzbergs started to take part in hackathons, where software and hardware engineers compete to develop the most sophisticated prototype from scratch.
In April of this year, he flew to London to take part in a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers. The prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco, and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US.
Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts, much like how a software engineer might use AI to generate code. Though his teammates are both a few years older, Dandzbergs pushed for them to include even more intricate features in the prototype. “It was amazing,” says Tihenko. “The imagination of Henrijs in the hardware space is just crazy.”
Seeing that they stood no chance of beating Dandzbergs’ group and other front-runners, teams started to drop out of the competition, according to Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges. “What they built was incredibly impressive,” he says. “No one had ever seen that before.”
When the organizers crowned Dandzbergs’ team victorious, somebody handed him the mic. “I’m 16 years old,” he said.
The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC. They won a place in the summer program, but Dandzbergs wavered over whether he should drop out of high school. The trio also sparred over whether the startup should focus on applying the technology to the defense sector, Dandzbergs’ primary area of interest. Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership. “It was hard,” says Tihenko. “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.”
By the summer, Danzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own. He had spotted a gap in the market, he claimed, for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine. His products, he added, would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems.
YC initially tried to steer him away. Dandzbergs was promising a lot of everything, all at once. It wasn’t clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was the right thing for him to do. “There’s a paternal element to it,” says Taggar. “You don’t want to be screwing up people's lives—and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.”
Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies—from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos—aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles. The more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes.
“You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” says Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “There are trade-offs.”
But Dandzbergs wasn’t going to be dissuaded, and YC figured that somebody else would probably invest in his idea. The incubator invited him to join its fall program. “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” says Taggar. “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”
So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design. By the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile.
If he does ultimately succeed, though, Dandzbergs will need to confront an assortment of hairy ethical quandaries. Who should have access to these new missiles? What if a technical error were to result in friendly fire? Can he make peace with his technology being used to end somebody’s life?
Dandzbergs claims that he has come to terms with these issues. He says he takes solace in the belief that his motivations are pure: to protect the US and its European allies.
By his logic, autonomous weapons are an inevitable part of the future, so he might as well be the one who builds them. “I choose not to shy away from the emergence of modern conflict as a global issue. I simply don’t have a lot of respect for people that do,” he says. “I want to be part of it. I want to move with the future of warfare.”
But others who have found themselves in a similar position say it’s difficult to know in advance how somebody will deal with the knowledge that their invention has killed people.
McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director, launched a drone startup in his early twenties. Initially, he had meant for the drones to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too. He left around the same time.
“I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” he says. “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”
Polemos Industries announced itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video. Set to the ticking of a clock, it featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens.
The video climbed to the top of the trending page on X. In the responses, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company. “Coming for him,” Dandzbergs responded.
Dandzbergs recognizes that people are likely to dismiss him for his age. But he considers youth one of his biggest advantages. “Please don’t say I’m sacrificing my childhood,” he says. “This is the childhood I dreamed of.”

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecuties individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians”.
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically.”
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of the Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater US willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

How Premier League's big six keep getting richer
- Published
Ten games into the Premier League season, the top five places are dominated by big six clubs.
Only second-placed Brighton, a club with a model which must be the envy of many of their rivals, have muscled their way in.
In pure financial terms, it should come as no surprise.
The six biggest clubs - Manchester United, Liverpool, Manchester City, Arsenal, Tottenham and Chelsea - now generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the division's other teams.
And the gap is growing. Every season.
BBC Sport breaks down how the finances of the big six have exploded, examines new trends and the impact on the transfer market, and asks how much it really matters.
Big six get richer and the gap grows
Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.
In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.
Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.
This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.
Let's look at how the gap has grown.
We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.
This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.
In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.
So what has driven this huge escalation?
In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.
Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs.
"The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said.
"You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."
Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.
It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.
For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.
But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.
Champions League widens the gulf
It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.
This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football.
But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.
When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.
This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.
At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.
The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.
Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.
The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.
Stamford Bridge - Chelsea's big problem
Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.
In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.
Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and City.
Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.
Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.
Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.
Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed.
"Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017.
"As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."
Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m.
"Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs.
"Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."
Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.
But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.
How new rules allow big six to spend even more
You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).
PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.
That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).
There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive.
"This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six.
"SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."
So what does this mean?
The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.
This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market.
"Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said.
"It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."
Most of the big six - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.
Surely this will inflate the transfer market?
If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.
Look at this summer.
Premier League clubs spent £3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the £3.53bn set in 2025-26.
The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year.
"Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said.
"Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under £100m."
Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.
And you can see why it is concerned.
In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.
Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than £40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.
Does this financial disparity really matter?
So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.
And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.
Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.
They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.
Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.
But it is a precarious business for these other clubs.
"The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said.
"The big six can afford to make signings which are £60m and £70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."
And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.
The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.
Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending £945m on players in the past five years.
The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.
But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.
And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

Srinagar- Postgraduate (PG) and senior resident doctors at Government Medical College (GMC) Srinagar have launched a peaceful protest demanding an enhancement in their stipends and parity with their counterparts in other states and Union Territories.
The protesting doctors said their stipend-related grievances had remained unresolved for a long time and urged the Jammu and Kashmir administration to intervene and address their demands.
The All India Medical Students Association (AIMSA) extended support to the protesting doctors, with its Vice President Dr Mohit Choudhary, a PG resident at GMC Srinagar, urging the government to take immediate steps to resolve the issue.
AIMSA Chief Advisors Dr Mayeen Afsan Ahmed and Dr Sushant Dhabade also sought the personal intervention of Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha to ensure an early resolution of the demands.
Dr Ahmed also urged the college principal to facilitate the formation of a recognised Resident Doctors’ Association (RDA), saying it would provide an institutional platform for addressing the concerns and ensuring proper representation of resident doctors.
AIMSA Chief Advisor Dr Iftikhar Hussain expressed solidarity with the protesting doctors and called for timely administrative intervention to resolve their grievances.
The association’s General Secretary, Dr Mohammad Tasadduk Kawser, stressed the need for a functional Students’ Union or Class Union to ensure effective representation of students.
Earlier, AIMSA President Dr Mohammad Momin Khan reiterated the association’s commitment to safeguarding the rights and interests of medical students and resident doctors. He expressed hope that the Lieutenant Governor would personally intervene in the matter and ensure an early resolution.
The key demands include an immediate enhancement of stipends and parity for PG, Senior Resident, Diplomate of National Board (DNB) and Master of Dental Surgery (MDS) doctors across Jammu and Kashmir.
The doctors have also sought the implementation of maternity leave benefits in accordance with applicable High Court directions.
The association said it expected the administration to address the long-pending issues through an early decision. (KNS)

Fact Check
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by ATN Bangla, a Bangladeshi media outlet.

The Aadhaar Enabled Payment System (AePS) processed 100.87 million financial transactions in October 2026, up 6.7% from 94.50 million seen in September, according to the National Payments Corporation of India’s (NPCI) monthly figures for cash withdrawals, BHIM Aadhaar Pay and funds transfers. The NPCI data also revealed that cash withdrawals made up 98.2% of these payments.
Key observations from the NPCI data
Increase over September: According to the data provided by NPCI, AePS averaged 3.25 million financial transactions a day in October, compared with 3.09 million seen in the previous month. A year ago, the average daily financial transactions in October was 3.50 million. This points to a drop of 7.69% in October 2026 compared to a year ago.
Payment types:
- Cash withdrawals in October 2026 rose 7.0% to 99.09 million from 92.64 million in September. However, it remained well below 108.43 million seen in October last year, shows NPCI data. Their transaction value rose 7.7% to Rs 24,383.47 crore in October from Rs 22,642.99 crore seen in September 2026. However, it should be noted that this is the value of cash withdrawals, not all AePS payments.
- BHIM Aadhaar Pay fell 4.3% to 1.78 million in October 2026 from 1.86 million seen in previous month
- Funds transfers were reported as zero at a precision of 0.01 million in both months. Smaller volumes could round to zero. However, NPCI has not explained a measurement break in its funds-transfer volume series from 2022.
NPCI derives these three-monthly payment series from daily data and says they may differ slightly from headline totals. Its broader “total approved” count amounts to 528.05 million in October, up 3.8% from 508.58 million observed in September. However, it is not just the number of payments, it also includes authentication events. NPCI supplies no balance-enquiry figure in these series and does not define on-us authentication.
Aadhaar authentication
As per the Unique Identification Authority of India’s (UIDAI) Authentication Dashboard, 2.44 billion biometric, demographic and one-time password (OTP) authentications was recorded in October 2026, up 0.5% from 2.43 billion seen in September. The sum was 24.1% above October 2025’s 1.97 billion. However, the dashboard does not label the unit of its underlying counts, which are assumed to represent transactions. These channel sums differ from UIDAI headline totals published through the Press Information Bureau (PIB).
Authentication channels: UIDAI’s dashboard breaks October down as follows:
- Biometric authentication rose to 1.61 billion from 1.55 billion in September.
- Demographic authentication fell to 305.08 million from 309.10 million.
- OTP authentication fell to 524.13 million from 569.56 million.
Face authentication: According to UIDAI data, 304.81 million face authentications were seen in October 2026, up 2.1% from 298.54 million observed in September, up 19.8% from 254.53 million a year earlier. That was 12.5% of the dashboard’s October channel sum, compared with 12.3% in September; the share divides face authentications by the same dashboard’s biometric, demographic and OTP total.
Aadhaar e-KYC: As per the UIDAI’s e-KYC dashboard, 746.20 million electronic know-your-customer (e-KYC) transactions were recorded across its biometric and OTP channels in October. This means in October the e-KYC transactions went down 1.5% from 757.32 million seen in September. However, when it is compared to the same period last year, it goes 93.2% from 386.18 million seen in October 2025. AePS payments and e-KYC count different services; these figures are not a combined transaction total.

A new report commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine urged the scientific community to respond more aggressively to claims of errors or manipulated data in published research, saying that papers containing findings that can no longer be trusted should be more swiftly corrected or retracted.
The report encouraged journals to complete editorial review of potentially problematic studies within 12 weeks, or within six months in more complex cases. The authors also stressed that study authors need to hold onto original data, adding that being unable to produce these records when concerns about a finding’s authenticity are raised could lead to a retraction. And the expert panel wrote that it is no longer “prudent” for researchers to argue against retraction of their work by asserting that flawed findings in one part of a study don’t impact the paper’s overall conclusions. That’s because issues with any part of a study can cast doubt on other findings.
The authors called on universities and other research institutions to respond more quickly and completely to research integrity inquiries, in part by making findings from internal inquiries available to journals, funding organizations, and the broader public. And the National Academies report suggested that funding organizations tie grant awards to researchers and institutions agreeing to abide by strict standards for the conduct of research and addressing errors.
“While the committee’s recommendations might appear aspirational, we are certain that the funding agencies, the public officials who legislate financial and regulatory support for science, researchers, and, most importantly, the public must be assured that the record of scientific knowledge is intact and reliable,” wrote University of California, Berkeley, cell biologist Randy Schekman, chair of the committee that produced the report.
An advanced copy of the report was sent to media outlets and embargoed until 11 a.m. Eastern Time on Thursday. But Jennifer Walsh, a National Academies spokesperson, told STAT in an email that “the report is being paused pending further review of some of the citations.” She did not provide a new release time and, as of Thursday evening, the report has not been published on the nonprofit’s website. Reporting by Science alleges that 10 of the report’s references contain apparently fabricated first names for co-authors, suggesting that a large language model may have written the references. The National Academies delayed publication after Science flagged the apparent issues.
The 157-page National Academies report comes at a time when concerns about the reliability of the scientific record have drawn increasing public attention, contributing to distrust in scientific institutions. High-profile investigations at leading research centers such as Stanford University and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have in recent years shined an uncomfortable spotlight on how studies published in top journals can contain doctored data. Meanwhile, the number of scientific articles published each year has risen from 1.3 million in 1995 to 6.7 million in 2025, increasing the number of studies that potentially require corrective action.
Retractions have become more common in recent years, with the report noting that more than 5,000 studies were retracted worldwide in 2025. But the report alleges that this rate is lower than expected given current estimates of the proportion of problematic articles, with fewer than 0.22% of studies from any given year retracted. Data from Retraction Watch indicate that, on average, retractions happen nearly 2.4 years after a study is published.
Correcting the record more often and more quickly, the authors wrote, won’t just require clearer policies from funding organizations, journals, and universities. It will take a cultural shift in science toward viewing correction and retraction as essential tools in maintaining the reliability of the record, not as a professional failure. They encouraged stakeholders to think of the consequences of not taking corrective action on studies, from policymaking and public health decisions made based on faulty data to researchers wasting time and taxpayer dollars when they attempt to follow up on a flawed finding.
“Serious consequences for the scientific enterprise and for society in general result either from failing to correct the scientific record or from failing to do so in a timely way,” the panel wrote. “These consequences make changing the process essential.”
While many corrections and retractions result from honest errors, the Trump administration has cited cases of alleged research misconduct as justification for its focus on “gold standard” science. In the new report, experts noted that these incidents can weaken public trust in science.
“It is critical that the scientific ecosystem continues to prioritize maintaining the integrity of the scientific record so that it remains trusted and trustworthy,” the authors wrote. “Even if these cases are rare, just one such incident erodes the public’s trust.”
That recognition spurred the National Academies, a 163-year-old nonprofit created by Congress to advise the nation on issues of science and technology, to assemble a team of university, journal, and academic leaders to explore what should be done. They included Holden Thorp, editor-in-chief of the Science family of journals; Schekman, a Nobel Prize-winning researcher and former editor-in-chief of the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences; and Mark Barnes, a lawyer with the firm Ropes & Gray and former associate provost for research at Harvard University. The group was tasked with identifying current practices and suggesting new standards for stakeholders.
The authors lay out what they frame as an “ideal timeline” for addressing concerns with published studies. That includes four weeks for an editor to determine whether a concern is potentially credible, meaning that it is specific, makes sense, and merits a closer look. The committee then allots another four weeks for contacting authors and determining whether their response adequately resolves a concern before initiating a full review. They note that an initial notice, such as an editorial expression of concern, should be added to a study within 12 weeks.
It’s a well-intentioned timeline, said Lisa Rasmussen, a bioethicist at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte. But Rasmussen, who is also editor-in-chief of the journal Accountability in Research, said that editors like herself are already stretched thin with work that is often poorly compensated. She noted that, in the past five years, the number of studies submitted to her own journal has increased almost tenfold. Rasmussen and a co-editor-in-chief often message each other with drowning emojis to sum up how they are doing.
“I think under the best of circumstances, it’s very reasonable. That’s certainly the kind of time frame that I try to abide by,” she said. “I think it’s just going to be increasingly difficult for people to handle the volume of concerns [and] queries that they’re receiving in the time frame.”
Rasmussen noted that much of the rise in submissions took place after large language models powered by artificial intelligence, such as ChatGPT, became readily available. The report touches on the impact of AI on research integrity, noting that these tools have simultaneously allowed researchers to manipulate or fake data while giving journals and universities new tools to spot suspect results. But to Rasmussen, the report’s discussion on AI was surprisingly brief given the technology’s disruptive potential.
“AI is being used to review. AI is being used to critique. AI is being used to fabricate data. So it’s like jet fuel for all of the stuff they talk about in the report,” she said. “But it’s almost as though the report was written pre-ChatGPT.”

Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.
The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.
As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.
But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.
This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.
Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.
“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”
She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.
Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.
The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.
Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.
Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.
At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.
The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.
“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.
This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.
During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.
Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.
But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.
A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.
In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.
If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.
Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.
But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.
One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.
NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.
The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.
Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.
"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.
She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.
"It felt unbelievable"
After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.
"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."
Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change. At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.
The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.
"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.
This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.
"I felt like I was losing my mind"
In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.
"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."
She found that work through Helen Keller Intl, a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.
"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."
One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.
Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.
"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.
In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.
Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.
Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.
"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction"
Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.
"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."
Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.
"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."
Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.
"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."
Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.
"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."
"Everything has been wiped out"
Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.
Colder temperatures are threatening those who still live in temporary shelters or flimsy tents. "Winter in these areas is very harsh," says Joshi. "Exposure to cold, overcrowded living, poor ventilation in the tent, damp bedding and inadequate clothing can also increase health risk."
Responders are winterizing tents and getting families into safer shelters, says Joshi, in addition to providing food and medical care.
In the longer term, there's the question of rebuilding what was leveled.
"We still haven't really seen [plans] on where to rebuild, how many homes are needed, how do we fix the water systems, how do you rebuild the schools?" says Pandey Rana of Helen Keller. "Like everything has been wiped out."
Preliminary estimates put the cost of rebuilding at roughly $5 billion, a steep figure for the small nation. The U.N. Climate Fund, aimed at helping countries harmed by climate change, approved $20 million for recovery. Domestic and international donors have contributed over $100 million in additional funds, but it's still far short of what's needed.
For now, aid organizations are focused on the immediate needs of survivors. Tamang says the daily work helps keep her going amid so much loss.
"What else can I do," she says. "Life goes on, and we have to accept what nature has brought upon us."

A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a six-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been sacked following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition -- which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch.
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on February 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity", the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was sacked and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui, a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies.
