The U.N.'s top court rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
International Court of Justice issues ruling on Myanmar genocide case
The United Nations' top court ruled Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time in the court's 80-year history that it has held a state responsible for the crime.
Judges of the International Court of Justice voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown was carried out with intent to destroy the long-persecuted Muslim minority.
Myanmar's military-backed government on Friday dismissed the court's ruling as "unfair," according to The Associated Press. Khine Khine Soe, a spokeswoman for President Min Aung Hlaing, was quoted saying that Myanmar would make its position known after reviewing the court's decision.
Brought by Gambia under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the ruling will have repercussions far beyond Myanmar, according to a legal expert.
But for Ma Roga Bibi, a Rohingya who fled Maungdaw township in northern Rakhine state, the impact was immediate.
"I feel wonderful and grateful," said the 18-year-old, who lives in the world's largest refugee settlement in Bangladesh. "It was an emotional, historic day."
Genocidal campaign
For several weeks in August and September 2017, the Myanmar military attacked and burned to the ground hundreds of Rohingya villages. Soldiers committed rapes and massacred women, men as well as children.
The court estimated that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. It cited estimates that up to 2,109 Rohingya children younger than 5 died, and found the violence was systematic, including the burning of all or parts of 392 villages.
Ma Roga Bibi, then age 9, was one of about 700,000 people to flee to Bangladesh, joining earlier refugee waves. The camps sprawl across a narrow coastal strip a few miles from Cox's Bazar, a busy beach town near Myanmar. Rohingya are denied citizenship on both sides of the border.
"Recognition alone is not enough," she said. "We need justice, accountability, and the opportunity to return home with dignity."
She wants to be a doctor, adding, "in our Rohingya community, there is no girl doctor."
Khin Khin Myint, 18, a refugee leader in activist group Rohingya Youth Voice from Buthidaung Township, also in Camp 16, said Rohingya women and girls have experienced "unimaginable suffering."
"We want the world to listen to survivors, recognize their courage, and include women in decisions about our future," she said. "We expect the international community to move beyond a statement of sympathy."
Rejected defense
Myanmar had argued its military was conducting counterinsurgency operations against an armed group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The court said the military failed to distinguish between civilians and alleged insurgents, and that the scale and nature of the violence could not be explained by counterterrorism.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," said ICJ president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa.
Antonia Mulvey, executive director of Legal Action Worldwide, a human rights group based in Geneva, said the court found evidence from the U.N. and rights organizations credible, and that counterterrorism operations were not a defense to Myanmar's argument.
She said the ruling will affect future genocide cases, including South Africa's case against Israel, on questions such as genocidal intent and state responsibility.
"Although every case must ultimately be decided on its own evidence," she said.
The judgment is binding on Myanmar and on all states that have ratified the Genocide Convention, she explained. All countries should review trade agreements, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and financial and economic ties with the junta, she said, while supporting accountability and reparations for the Rohingya. But the court, which hears disputes between states, can't enforce its decisions.
A group long denied recognition
In Myanmar, Rohingya are widely regarded as interlopers from Bangladesh, despite generations of roots in Myanmar.
Iwasawa, however, identified the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group, saying their language and art set them apart, and that they self-identify as such. He said they have been discriminated against by Myanmar "for decades" and qualify as a protected group.
The United States had previously reached a similar conclusion. In 2022, the Biden administration formally determined that Myanmar's military had committed genocide and crimes against humanity against the Rohingya during its 2016 and 2017 operations.
But tensions have mounted between the Trump administration and international justice bodies. In a statement to NPR on Thursday, the State Department expressed support for Rohingya refugees but raised doubts about the International Court of Justice. "The proper interpretation of the Genocide Convention is of paramount importance, as is preventing politicization of the ICJ. We are studying the decision to fully assess its implications," the State Department said.
In October, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz wrote online, "The ICJ must not be allowed to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide" so it can later be weaponized against U.S. and allied soldiers.
Yet international human rights organizations and the United Nations applauded the court's judgment.
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres called it "a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and said it reaffirms that "impunity for such horrific acts must not stand."
The judgment does not order Myanmar to grant citizenship, saying such the issue fell outside the scope of the measures being considered to prevent future atrocities.
However, Myanmar must take steps to investigate people suspected of involvement in the crimes and prosecute them if warranted, said the court. It also found Myanmar must provide restitution and compensation, with the amount to be set in future proceedings.
The order to enable displaced Rohingya to return runs into a hard reality: The territory is now controlled by ethnic Rakhine armed group the Arakan Army.
Rakhine state has been ravaged by conflict between the military and the group, which now controls most of it.
Su Mon, a senior analyst at the independent conflict monitor Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, said the Rohingya in Myanmar and in the camps are "threatened by multiple armed groups," including Rohingya armed groups, the Arakan Army and the military.
Nearly all are stateless, she said, with few viable ways to earn a living or get food. Many are "on the verge of acute famine" because of aid shortfalls in the camps and a junta blockade in Rakhine.
"Unless the broader conflict dynamics in Rakhine state improve or credible guarantees of safety are secured from all armed actors, the prospects for displaced Rohingya to return to their homes remain bleak," she added.
She urged the military to halt airstrikes, drone attacks and the use of advanced weaponry in northern Rakhine, lift its blockade and give humanitarian groups full access, including in Arakan Army-controlled areas.
Lorcán Lovett reported from Thailand. Michele Kelemen contributed reporting from Washington, D.C.

Nepal PM Balen Shah to visit India on November 22–23
According to the Foreign Secretary, a 34-member government delegation led by PM Shah will depart from Kathmandu for New Delhi to undertake the engagement.
Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah will embark on a State visit to India from November 22 to 23 at the invitation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Nepal's Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai announced on Friday.

Frida Kahlo painting pulled from New York auction at Mexico’s request
The painting, ’Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,’ or ’Congress of the Peoples for Peace,’ had been scheduled for auction on Tuesday

A painting by Frida Kahlo has been withdrawn from an auction in New York at the request of Mexican authorities.
The painting, “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz,” or “Congress of the Peoples for Peace,” which depicts a white dove perched on a fruit-bearing tree alongside a smiling sun, the moon, and two slices of watermelon, had been scheduled for auction by Christie’s on Tuesday.
The auction house confirmed it had withdrawn the painting from this week's auction after Mexican authorities requested the sale be held until questions about the painting's provenance could be clarified, citing a declaration that recognizes Frida Kahlo’s work as an artistic monument of Mexico.
“In collaboration with the seller, we decided to withdraw the lot at this time for further research,” a Christie’s spokesperson said Thursday.
“We look forward to selling this work at a later date."
The same painting was auctioned in 2020 by Sotheby’s without any objections.
In Mexico, Kahlo’s works are considered artistic monuments and are protected under the country's federal law on monuments and archaeological, artistic, and historical sites.
Mexican authorities said they were working with the Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Museums Trust, administered by the Bank of Mexico.
Kahlo painted “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz” in October 1952 and donated it to the World Peace Council's peace congress, held in Vienna that year.
Her health was seriously deteriorating at the time, and she sent the painting to the congress through her husband, the painter Diego Rivera.
She died in Mexico City two years after creating it.
The trip to Vienna was recorded in the memoirs of Emma Hurtado, Rivera’s last wife, and has also been mentioned by historians such as Raquel Tibol.
The painting had left Mexico more than three decades before the 1984 decree declared Kahlo’s work an artistic monument. The decree prohibits the permanent export of her works that were in Mexico when it was published.
Last year, Kahlo’s 1940 self-portrait “El sueño (La cama)," or The Dream (The Bed), sold for $54.7 million.
The price set an auction record for a work by a female artist.

A long-buried ancient library in Rome opens to the public after restoration
The ancient Ulpia Library in Rome has been restored and is reopening to the public this week
ROME -- The famed Alexandria Library in Egypt may have been lost, but another of the ancient world's repositories for texts has been restored in Rome and is reopening to the public this week.
The ruins of the Ulpia library are l ocated in Emperor Trajan’s Forum, just next to the iconic column that celebrates his victorious campaigns against the Dacians and the Roman conquest of what is modern-day Romania. It remained inaccessible for almost a century.
“After the Alexandria Library of Egypt, after the Library of Pergamon in Asia Minor, this one in the Trajan’s Forum was certainly one of the most important, given both the number of ‘volumina,’ as books were called in ancient times, and the quantity of documents," Claudio Parisi Presicce, an archaeologist and Rome's superintendent for cultural heritage, said in an interview with The Associated Press.
The place was in a state of ruin when discovered in 1932 during clearing works by Benito Mussolini's government for the road that became the famous Via dei Fori Imperiali. Later, it was covered in concrete and used as a storage room for some of the countless pieces from Trajan's Forum, the last and greatest of the imperial fora, built in 112 AD.
But the niches in its walls were evidently spots to set cabinets for scrolls, signaling that this was one of the two, two-story buildings comprising the Ulpia library referenced in ancient texts, Presicce said.
Archaeologists from Rome's superintendency for cultural heritage identify it as the Ulpia library's western building, which ancient texts indicate stored Greek-language scrolls.
The new permanent exhibition offers visitors an idea of the space as it used to be, featuring the remains of some of the library’s rich marble decorations — white for the walls, and different colors for its floor and columns. Immersive videomapping is also projected on its walls, showing the history of the library and its discovery. Instead of scroll-filled cabinets, spread throughout the space today are broken Corinthian columns and pieces of sculptures.
The library was a fundamental part of the Forum, and a place that for centuries attracted citizens from all over Rome with its vast collection of edicts and documents.
“The libraries were used by both common citizens, those who could afford a certain cultural level and a better education than those from the lower classes, but also by magistrates who needed access to older documents, or needed to check the norms that regulated the life of the community,” he said.
Restoration started in 2025, and lasted about a year. The 1.75-million-euro cost ($1.92 million) came from the European Union’s pandemic recovery funds — just one of many restoration projects Rome is carrying out across the city with EU money.
It will initially be opened to visitors only on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Visits are scheduled every 40 minutes, 20 people at a time.
The library's eastern building remains buried beneath an 18th-century church, on the other side of Trajan's Forum, and stored Latin-language scrolls. There are no plans for its excavation.
___
AP videojournalist Giulia Arbarello contributed to this report.

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.
Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

- The claim that the Trump Administration's implementation of Project 2025, The Heritage Foundation's blueprint for federal government, caused the Nov. 16 bank outages and undefined impacts on the U.S. power grid is unproven.
- Snopes did not find evidence in Project 2025 of an explicit plan to alter consumer banking access. While Project 2025 does discuss the topic of banking, it does not suggest this particular act.
- Online claims did not say what effects the implementation of Project 2025 would allegedly have on the power grid, so it was not possible to discuss this aspect of the claim.
- Though we found the banking element of this claim was unproven, the claim about Project 2025's alleged impact on the power grid was too vague to rate. Therefore, we leave the claim overall unrated.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces. We contacted The Heritage Foundation to ask whether it sought to cause the events of Nov. 16 through the implementation of any of its policies. We also asked the White House whether implementing Project 2025 caused the events of Nov. 16. We await replies to our queries.
Across four days in November, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights in the U.S. on Nov. 13 and customers at several major U.S. banks experienced difficulties accessing, sending or receiving money on Nov. 16.
Following these events, a claim (archived) circulated online that the Trump administration's implementation of Project 2025, a 1,000-page document that laid out the conservative nonprofit group The Heritage Foundation's vision for the U.S federal government, had caused the events on Nov. 13 and 16 and would bring about undefined effects on the power grid.
For example, one Facebook user posted a video with on-screen text that read:
The bank outages make sense after the FAA grounding if you are aware of project 2025. Banks were next in line on the agenda. They're doing a speed run of Project 2025 because of the Blue Tsunami. Time just got very, very short for MAGA. Power grid's next, for anyone wondering
An identical text that appeared to blame the Trump administration's implementation of Project 2025 for the events of Nov. 13 and 16 and a future, unspecified event related to the power grid also circulated on X (archived). Snopes readers wrote in, asking about the claim.
Snopes previously researched whether Projected 2025 called for "dismantling" or "destroying" the Federal Aviation Administration, finding that while the document did propose restructuring the agency and moving toward a privatized air traffic system, the truth of the claim depended on how it was worded.
We did not find evidence in Project 2025 of an explicit plan to remove consumer banking access. While Project 2025 does discuss the topic of banking, it does not suggest this particular act as a way to implement its suggestions on the topic. Online claims did not say what effects the implementation of Project 2025 would allegedly have on the power grid, so it was not possible to discuss this aspect of the claim.
Project 2025 discusses topics in the context of the governmental departments they fall under. The document discusses policy suggestions regarding the U.S. power grid in the "Department of Energy" chapter (Page 363), and suggestions related to banking in a chapter titled "The Economy" (Page 657).
Though we found the banking element of this claim was unproven, the claim about Project 2025's alleged impact on the power grid was too vague to rate. Therefore, we leave the claim overall unrated.
We contacted The Heritage Foundation to ask whether it sought to cause the events of Nov. 16 through the implementation of any of its policies. We also asked the White House whether implementing Project 2025 caused the events of Nov. 16. We await replies to our queries.
What Project 2025 actually says
Power grid
In the chapter titled "Department of Energy," Project 2025 author Bernard L. McNamee acknowledged that there were "significant cyber, physical, and reliability threats to the electric grid" (Page 373) and that offices within the Department of Energy should focus on identifying and mitigating those threats.
The chapter further advised a future conservative administration to "stop the war on oil and natural gas" which it claimed had "thrust the United States into a new energy crisis" (Page 363).
Snopes outlined how the Trump administration had followed Project 2025's vision for an increased U.S. reliance on fossil fuels in December 2025.
The social media claim did not say how Project 2025's implementation would affect the power grid. Therefore, it was unclear whether the claim was true.
Bank outage
The Associated Press reported on Nov. 16 that customers at some major U.S. banks had experienced difficulties accessing their accounts or sending money. A spokesperson for JPMorgan Chase reportedly told the AP that a "temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system" that affected its customers and any other customers trying to send or receive money from JPMorgan Chase accounts caused the problems some customers faced.
The bank had not said what caused the "temporary issue" by the time of this writing.
Project 2025 does not mention anything about slowing down transactions for JPMorgan Chase or customers making transactions with the bank. It was unclear which of Project 2025's many proposals related to the economy and banking social media users claimed caused the JPMorgan Chase issues in mid-November.
For further reading, Snopes has previously reported extensively on Project 2025 and how the Trump administration has implemented its policy suggestions.

One of the biggest open problems in all of mathematics may have just been cracked by a mathematician using AI.
Levent Alpöge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, said on Friday that he solved the Riemann Hypothesis, which involves prime numbers, using Claude.
"I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe," Alpöge said in a post on his website. "Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Though Alpöge's solution has yet to be formally verified, leading scholars in the field told Business Insider on Friday that should it stand, this would be the biggest breakthrough in math yet.
"If it holds up, it's an extremely big deal," said Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell. "This is the Moby Dick of Mathematics, the great white whale."
Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech, called the claim a "HUGE deal."
"This is not a small potato," he said. "RH was the biggest problem in math."
Strogatz said Alpöge's solution has been verified by a computer-based system, but added that it sometimes makes mistakes.
"So it's fair to say that the claimed proof has not yet been independently verified," he said.
The Riemann Hypothesis was first proposed 167 years ago by a German mathematician named Bernhard Riemann. It proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers.
The task of proving the hypothesis is a Millennium Prize Problem, meaning that solving it earns a mathematician a $1 million prize. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category.
Alpöge's solution is, by his own admission, incredibly long and complicated. The solution's written proof comprises more than 250,000 pages, Alpöge said.
Terence Tao, a leading scholar based at UCLA, said in a post on his website Friday that "digesting" the proposed solution "will take some time."
Alpöge, who joined Anthropic in 2024, said he actually solved the problem on Sunday, but decided to hold off on announcing it after speaking with CEO Dario Amodei and consulting with other mathematicians.
Anthropic, the company behind Claude, went public on the stock market on Thursday. As of Friday afternoon, the price of Anthropic shares has steadily declined.
Alpöge said he didn't want to release "slop" to the public, adding that he still doesn't fully understand the math involved.
Still, he said that as other mathematicians attempt to grapple with the results, Alpöge said he plans to be there every step of the way to help them.
"I intend to do my best to understand and impart understanding of this argument," he said.

For years, a rumor has asserted that drinking Hawaiian pink salt mixed with lemon in water helps people lose weight.
Several posts on Facebook shared a recipe for the drink, claiming it supported weight loss (archived):
One user on TikTok demonstrated in a July 2025 video how she prepared the concoction, to which she also added vinegar and pepper (archived). But this claim dates back years. In 2022 a TikTok influencer who said he helped women older than 40 lose weight posted a video explaining the alleged science behind the claim (archived):
The claim is false, however, and the explanations internet users shared to support it were based on mistaken beliefs rather than science.
Snopes reached out to Allison Childress, a clinical dietitian and an associate professor of practice in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at Texas Tech University, asking for clarifications on this claim.
Childress said the trick is ineffective for weight loss. Rather, it could result in weight gain. "This will not do anything significant to benefit weight loss," she wrote in an email. "In fact too much sodium can lead to water retention which may actually lead to weight gain (however this would be fluid gain, not fat gain)."
Asked if there was any possibility, even remote, that it could at least support efforts to lose weight, she said that "in theory," it could increase hydration, leading to a sensation of fullness that may help a person eat less. "But this is a far reach," she added.
Childress did expound on the nutritional benefits of pink salt, saying that it contained more electrolytes than regular table salt. "However, most people do not need additional sodium," she warned. "In fact, Americans consume more than 50% more than the recommended amount of sodium already."
Asked if there were dangers to consuming too much pink salt, Childress said that the consequences of increased sodium in the diet could be dire, especially for people with certain health issues, "people who have heart, kidney and/or blood pressure issues as increased sodium intake can exacerbate these conditions."
Further, she warned against replacing table salt, which is enriched with iodine, with other types of salt. "There is little to no iodine in pink salt", she said. "Table salt is typically fortified with iodine which helps prevent deficiencies. While iodine deficiencies are relatively rare in the United States (most likely due to our consumption of iodized salt), we have seen a rise recently due to people consuming more pink salt, sea salt, kosher salt etc. instead of table salt." Iodine deficiencies can result in thyroid problems, including an enlarged thyroid (goiter) or hypothyroidism — an underactive thyroid.
Finally, when asked if there were better ways to lose weight, Childress listed the following:
- High-protein meals and snacks, which help create a sensation of fullness for longer.
- Good hydration, as dehydration "can mimic hunger signals and can derail weight loss efforts."
- Exercise, especially "resistance training," she said. "Strength training two to three times per week can preserve lean body mass during weight loss."
- Good sleep. "Poor sleep increases ghrelin, our hunger hormone, which can lead to cravings, specifically for high-calorie foods. Good sleep hygiene can aid in hormone regulation, lead to healthier food choices, improved metabolism and provide more energy for physical activity."
Other tips Childress mentioned included avoiding highly processed foods to favor whole foods, which are more nutritious with a lower caloric density, and monitoring food intake with "a food log or app" to "increase awareness and accountability."
In other words, no single trick can result in weight loss the way healthy lifestyle and habits can.

- The claim that the guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier follow strict rules, such as taking exactly 21 steps in their march, never swearing and never drinking alcohol on or off duty, is a mixture of truth and falsehoods.
- The rumor stems from a post previously fact-checked by Snopes that has made the rounds on social media since at least 2004. It gained steam in November after a group of visitors led by U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth was chastised by one of the tomb guards for not maintaining "an atmosphere of silence and respect."
- Snopes found that while the guards at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier do follow a strict regimen in the course of their duties, the rules aren't quite as stringent as the claim suggests.
On Nov. 11, footage captured a U.S. Army sentinel guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Virginia reprimanding Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and his entourage after one of them talked and laughed on the steps of the monument. Soon after the video spread, Snopes readers searched our site for information about the rules that govern the tomb guards.
First, some background on the monument. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is located in Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. In 1921, the military first laid to rest a soldier of unknown identity there with an inscription reading "Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God." The tomb is intended to honor unidentified war dead and includes the remains of three soldiers of unknown identities who died in World War I, World War II and the Korean War.
Beginning in 1984, the tomb also held the remains of a soldier killed in the Vietnam War. In 1998, after DNA testing confirmed his identity, his remains were disinterred and returned to his family.
A variation of an old Facebook post spread online in 2026, claiming to detail a set of complex rules governing the tomb's guards. Snopes readers also sent us a list of rumors about them. The post stated:
(Facebook user "Whispers of Life/Incredible Stuff")
Snopes covered variations of these questions back in 2004 and concluded the post contained a mixture of true and false information. Below, we look closely at each question and break down the rules for being a guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier:
How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?  
He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.
- True. The guard takes 21-step walks past the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier because 21 is a number of special significance. Snopes previously discussed the origins of the 21-gun salute, which dates back to cannon weaponry salutes in the 14th century.
How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?  
He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.
- Mixture. The guard doesn't do an about-face, and the wait is actually 42 seconds. Instead, the guard marches 21 steps across the black mat, past the unknown soldiers of World War I, World War II and Korea and the crypt of the unknown soldier of the Vietnam War. The guard turns 90 degrees (not about-face) to face east for 21 seconds. The guard then turns 90 degrees again and faces north for 21 seconds. After a moment, the guard paces 21 steps north, turns and repeats the process. At each turn, the guard places the rifle on the shoulder nearest to visitors to signify that he or she stands between the tomb and any threat.
Why are his gloves damp?  
They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.
- True. The Society of the Honor Guard (a nonprofit organization focused on preserving the tomb's history) FAQ confirms this is correct.
Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?  
He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.
- True. The guard shifts the rifle before each 21-step walk to ensure that it is always carried on the outside shoulder, the one away from the tomb, to signify that the guard stands between the tomb and any threat.
How often are the guards changed?  
Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.
- Mixture. As Snopes previously reported, from 1926 through 1937, the tomb was guarded only during the day. Since 1937, it has been guarded 24 hours a day, every day of the year. According to the Arlington National Cemetery, the guard is changed every hour on the hour from Oct. 1 through March 31, and every half-hour from April 1 through Sept. 30. When the cemetery is closed at nighttime, the guard is changed every two hours.
What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?  
Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".
- Mixture. The Arlington National Cemetery website states: "Each soldier must be in superb physical condition, possess an unblemished military record and be between 5 feet, 10 inches and 6 feet, 4 inches tall for men or 5 feet, 8 inches and 6 feet, 2 inches tall for women, with a proportionate weight and build." The rules do not specify waist size.
They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.
- Mixture. As we reported previously, the average tour of duty for a guard is shorter than the two-year period claimed here. The Society of the Honor Guard states: "The average tour at the Tomb is about 18 months. However, there is NO set time for service there. Sentinels live either in a barracks on Ft. Myer (the Army post located adjacent to the cemetery) or off base if they like. They do have a living quarters under the steps of the amphitheater where they stay during their 24 hour shifts. If they are of legal age, they may drink except while on duty."
They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb. After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn. If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.
- Mixture. The "wreath pin" is the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Identification Badge or "Tomb Badge" and it is rarely awarded to guards. According to the Arlington National Cemetery website: "Tomb Guards, members of the 3d U.S. Infantry Regiment (The Old Guard), earn the Tomb Badge for passing five testing phases and demonstrating high proficiency in Army and Tomb Guard knowledge. Tomb Guards who earn the badge are called Sentinels." There is no rule against swearing, but the identification badge can be taken away, even after the recipient has left the service. The Society of the Honor Guard says the badge is permanently awarded after a sentinel has served nine months as a sentinel at the tomb. Around 600 have been awarded since the late 1950s, about 10 badges per year. The Society notes that "while the TGIB can be revoked, the offense must be such that it discredits the Tomb of the Unknowns. Revocation is at the 3rd Infantry Regimental Commander's discretion and can occur while active duty or even when the Sentinel is a civilian."
Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.
- Mixture. According to the Society of the Honor Guard: "The shoes are standard issue military dress shoes" and "have a steel tip on the toe and a 'horseshoe' steel plate on the heel."
Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror. For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television. Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.
- Mixture. Tomb guards are allowed to talk to people and watch television. There are no rules prohibiting this on their off-duty hours. Any soldier wishing to become a sentinel undergoes rigorous training, including several hours a day of marching, rifle drill and uniform preparation, and every tomb sentinel is expected to be completely versed in the history of the tomb and of Arlington National Cemetery. According to the Arlington National Cemetery website, while still on-duty but not guarding the tomb, "the Tomb Guards spend their duty time in quarters below the Memorial Display Room of the Memorial Amphitheater, where they study cemetery history, clean their weapons and help the rest of their relief prepare for the changing of the guard." The Society of the Honor Guard also notes, "It takes the average Sentinel 8 hours to prep their uniform for the next work day." Tomb guards have even remained on duty in extreme weather situations. In 2003 during Hurricane Isabel, soldiers guarding the Tomb refused to go off-duty and seek shelter.
In sum, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier has a long and storied history and the soldiers tasked with guarding it follow a strict regimen. However, the rules in their daily lives are not as stringent as claimed in some social media posts.
Snopes archives contributed to this report.

Following a terrorist attack on November 11 at a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint in Jammu and Kashmir’s Kulgam district, a video went viral on social media with the claim that retired Indian Army officer and journalist Pravin Sawhney described Indian military and counter-terrorism drives in the valley as “false flag operations”.
Social media users claimed that Sawhney said that operations against the Kulgam attack, the Balakot airstrikes, and Operation Sindoor were orchestrated for political gains.
X user @RedDeFactoIND (Red Vanguard) shared the viral clip, which shows an interview conducted by The Wire. (Archive)

Indian journalists and influencers are now openly questioning the government’s narrative.
The voices from within are getting louder.
#CRPFSoldiers #CRPFCampAttack #kulgamattack #Kulgam #KulgamTerrorAttack
— Red Vanguard (@RedDeFactoIND) November 12, 2026
In the viral clip, the interviewer can first be heard saying (translated from Hindi): “Sushant, I want to know from you…the theme of your latest essay is the politicisation of army…During the false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, the way the Bharatiya Janata Party used the military for political gains. My second question is that today while there is a war-like situation in the world…is testing the Pralay missile is an indication of a new false flag operation?”
“On one side China is occupying [Indian land], on the other there are CJP protests…Rahul Gandhi…,” the interviewer goes on to say before his voice is abruptly cut off.
The interviewee then seems to respond with, “Two things are very clear. One, for false flag operations like Balakot and Pahalgam, Operation Sindoor was launched but the Indian army failed. Second, my answers are within your questions.”
Several other users on X and Facebook also circulated the same video with identical claims. Among them were X handles @KaurUdhoke3 and @HinduReformer, along with multiple public Facebook pages focusing on South Asian geopolitics. [Archives: 1, 2]
Fact Check
A closer look at the viral video reveals noticeable lip-sync discrepancies and an unnatural, monotonous cadence in the voices of both men in the interview, which are salient features of AI-generated audio manipulation.
Further, columnist and strategic affairs expert Sushant Singh has been misidentified in the viral video as Pravin Sawhney. In the viral video itself, the interviewer refers to the interviewee as Sushant, and not Pravin. Below is an image of Sawhney, who does not appear in the viral clip.
On November 13, Singh himself took to X to debunk the clip, clarifying that the video was AI-generated, and highlighting that users had also misidentified him.
This is AI generated video of an old interview, which completely fabricates my conversation with @ashubh. This Pakistan-made AI video clip not only gets my identity wrong but creates what was never said.
The original full interview of March 2025 is here: https://t.co/Y6teNLJDfg
— Sushant Singh (@SushantSin) November 13, 2026
In his post, Singh also attached a link to the original YouTube interview from which the visuals were taken. Alt News examined the original video uploaded on The Wire’s official YouTube channel in March 2025.
Comparing the viral clip with the March 2025 interview confirms that the visual frames, including Singh’s attire, the background setting, and lighting, are identical. However, the audio track in the viral clip has been changed using AI.
In the original interview, Singh makes no mention of Kulgam, Pulwama, Balakot, or any ‘false flag operations’. Instead, he is heard discussing civil-military relations and institutional oversight.
To sum up, a manipulated video of journalist and strategic affairs analyst Sushant Singh is circulating on social media with users misidentifying him as journalist and FORCE editor Pravin Sawhney. The claim that the speaker in the video termed India’s counter-terrorism measures in Kulgam and Pulwama ‘false flag operations’ is false as well.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has approached the Maharashtra government and Mumbai Police, seeking urgent security measures for Bollywood personalities following alleged threats from gangsters. The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”
A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.
Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.
The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.
On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.
On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.
The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.
The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.
Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.
Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.
“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.
Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.
“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.
The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.
Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.
“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”
The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.
Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.
After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.
The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.
ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.
Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.
“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.
“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”
There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.
Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.
The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.
Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.
In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.
Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.
“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.
“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.
Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.
Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.
On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.
“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”
After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.
The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

Special Police Officers (SPOs) Rashpal Kumar (45) and Babi Chand (57), posted with the Special Operations Group in Kishtwar, Jammu and Kashmir, went missing on 10 November while heading to an Army operational base. Their bullet-riddled bodies were recovered near a nullah on 12 November, with their service weapons missing. On 14 November, their bodies were brought to their native village, Kiyar, in a dumper without coffins, reportedly without any senior police officer accompanying them. Locals alleged that no stretcher was provided and that they had to arrange one from the Army. The manner in which the bodies were transported triggered outrage and grief among residents, with BJP MLA Shagun Parihar reportedly confronting police officials over the treatment of the slain personnel. Their last rites were subsequently performed with full honours (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this outrage, a video purportedly showing CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar is being shared on social media with the claim that he said the bodies of the SPOs martyred in Kishtwar were transported in a dumper because there was no other option, as all vehicles in the area were occupied, and that the families should be grateful for receiving the bodies of the slain personnel. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar saying the bodies of the martyred SPOs were transported in a dumper due to a lack of vehicles and that their families should be grateful for receiving them.
Fact: The video is digitally manipulated. The original video shows CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar expressing grief over the death of the two SPOs, paying tribute to them, assuring support to their families, and promising efforts to ensure justice. He does not make any remarks about the bodies being transported in a dumper due to a lack of vehicles or the families being grateful for receiving them. Analysis using AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya, indicated that the viral audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, confirming that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to falsely attribute these remarks to him. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify whether CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar made any such statement, we searched Google using relevant keywords. However, we found no credible news reports or official statements corroborating the viral claim.
We noticed the viral video carries an ANI watermark. A keyword search led us to an ANI post on X (archived), dated 16 November 2026, featuring the same footage of CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar, wearing the same attire and speaking against an identical background.
In the original video, Khirwar speaks about the recovery of the mortal remains of the two missing SPOs in Kishtwar. He expresses grief over the loss of personnel, pays respect to the fallen, assures support to their families, and states that efforts will be made to ensure justice for them. The original footage contains no remarks about transporting the bodies in a dumper or about the families being grateful to receive them.
We analysed the viral video using multiple AI voice detection tools, including Hive and Hiya. The analysis indicated that the audio was likely AI-generated or manipulated, suggesting that fabricated audio was added to the original footage to make it appear as though CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar was making the remarks about the transportation of the bodies of the SPOs martyred in Kishtwar in a dumper due to the lack of available vehicles, and that their families should be grateful for receiving the bodies.
To sum up, this viral video of CRPF SDG Sandeep Khirwar making remarks about the SPOs’ bodies being transported in a dumper is digitally manipulated.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is poised to be a hit for Lionsgate.
"Sunrise on the Reaping" is the second prequel Suzanne Collins wrote in her "Hunger Games" series, following Haymitch Abernathy's experience in the 50th Hunger Games. It was an instant bestseller when it was published in March 2025, selling over 1.5 million copies in its first week alone. The film adaptation is following a similar trajectory, already raking in $21 million from preview screenings alone, Variety reported.
It's not a surprise, given how much there is to love about "Sunrise on the Reaping." The novel dives deep into Haymitch's time in the arena, but it's also full of revelations about the "Hunger Games" universe.
Many of those revelations center on the Covey family, who were introduced in Collins' first "Hunger Games" prequel. Most importantly, it reveals that Katniss Everdeen has Covey ancestry, tying her to other girls who defied the Capitol before she was even born.
Spoilers ahead for the "Hunger Games" series.
The Covey first appears in 'The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes'
Collins released her first "Hunger Games" prequel, "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," in May 2020.
Set 64 years before "The Hunger Games," the book follows a young Coriolanus Snow long before he is president. As a student, he mentors the Victor of the 10th Hunger Games: the female tribute from District 12, Lucy Gray Baird.
After she is reaped for the Games and taken to the Capitol, Lucy Gray tells a reporter that she is a member of the Covey family who isn't originally from District 12.
"My people are Covey. Musicians by trade. We just took a wrong turn one day and were obliged to stay," Lucy Gray said. She explained they were from "no district in particular" and used to "move from place to place" playing music before Peacekeepers forced them to stay in District 12 after the first rebellion.
When the book opens, there are six living members of the Covey family living in District 12: Billy Taupe Clade, Clerk Carmine Clade, Tam Amber, Maude Ivory Baird, Barb Azure Baird, and Lucy Gray Baird.
Billy Taupe and Clerk Carmine are brothers, and Maude Ivory, Barb Azure, and Lucy Gray are cousins. Tam Amber is not related to the rest of the Covey by blood, but the group treats each other as a found family.
By the end of the book, only four Covey members are left in District 12. A local kills Billy Taupe after Coriolanus shoots his friend, while Lucy Gray's status is more of a mystery. Coriolanus may have killed her, or she could have fled from him and disappeared into the woods, never to be heard from again in Panem.
The Covey has blended into District 12 in 'Sunrise on the Reaping'
When Collins brings readers back to District 12 in "Sunrise on the Reaping," the Covey has assimilated into the district in the years since the events of "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes."
Tam Amber and Clerk Carmine are still living in the district and are raising their niece, Lenore Dove Baird, together. Lenore Dove is Haymitch's girlfriend, and Haymitch says in the text that her mother died giving birth to her.
Any of the three Covey girls could be Lenore Dove's mother, but based on the text, it's most likely Maude Ivory. At the end of "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch finds graves for both Lucy Gray and Maude Ivory near Lenore Dove's resting place. Lucy Gray's is described as a "mossy slab of stone," while Maude Ivory's is "a creamy white stone," making Maude Ivory's seem slightly newer.
The timeline also makes Maude Ivory the stronger candidate. Lenore Dove is around 16 in "Sunrise on the Reaping," meaning she was born about 24 years after Lucy Gray's Hunger Games. Lucy Gray, who competed in the Games at 16, would have been around 40 when Lenore Dove was born, while Maude Ivory, who was only 8 or 9 during the 10th Hunger Games, would have been in her early 30s.
Katniss is a Covey descendant
In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch says he met Lenore Dove through his friend Burdock Everdeen, Katniss' father.
"She wasn't one of Burdock's Everdeen cousins, but I knew he had some distant ones on his ma's side," Haymitch says of Burdock's ancestry.
Given Maude Ivory's and Lucy Gray's fates, it seems likely Burdock and Katniss were descendants of Barb Azure Baird and distant relatives of the other Covey girls.
Collins laid the groundwork for the similarity between Katniss and the Covey girls throughout "The Hunger Games."
She has a rebellious spirit like her ancestors, and both Katniss and her father are described as having beautiful singing voices throughout the series. Haymitch reinforces singing as a trait Burdock inherited from the Covey in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He says Burdock has a "remarkable voice." A few pages later, he says Lenore Dove loves music: "Like all the Covey, music in her blood."
Later, at Haymitch's mother and brother's funeral, Burdock sings "The Old Therebefore," a song Lucy Gray sings when she thinks she is about to die in the Games. Music, specifically Covey music, is in Burdock's blood, too.
The Covey also inadvertently gives Katniss her mockingjay pin
The mockingjay token Katniss wears in her first Hunger Games becomes an important symbol throughout Collins' series.
The bird represents that the Capitol cannot control everything, as it results from the mating of Capitol jabberjays and naturally born mockingbirds. Katniss embodies that spirit when she leads the rebellion against President Coriolanus Snow and his government, using the mockingjay symbol to help inspire others to act.
Katniss' friend, Madge Undersee, gave her the pin to wear after she volunteered as a tribute for District 12. In "Catching Fire," Madge tells Katniss the pin originally belonged to her aunt, Maysilee Donner, who competed alongside Haymitch for District 12 in the 50th Hunger Games.
In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Haymitch reveals that Tam Amber originally forged the pin. Maysilee never wore it, saying that mockingjays were "ugly old things," to Lenore Dove's anger.
Haymitch explains the mythology surrounding mockingjays to Maysilee while they're in the arena, giving her a new perspective on them. She says she will give the pin another try if she survives the Games, but Maysilee never gets the chance. However, a Covey girl does, bringing the moment full circle.

Indian fugitive involved in exploitation of 14 women deported from UAE: CBI
CBI said the accused allegedly lured the victim with a false promise of marriage, and also subjected her to physical, mental and financial exploitation.
A man wanted by Maharashtra Police in cases of alleged sexual exploitation of women was deported from the UAE on Friday in an operation coordinated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), officials said.
The fugitive, Mohd Mazin, had an Interpol Red Notice against him. He was wanted in connection with a case in which he allegedly lured the victim with a false promise of marriage, established physical relations with her and subjected her to physical, mental and financial exploitation, including dishonestly receiving ₹18 lakh from her, CBI spokesperson Beena Yadav said in a statement.
"The chargesheet has already been filed before the competent court. Investigation further revealed that he had similarly exploited 13 other women on the pretext of marriage, obtained money from them and recorded videos of intimate acts. The accused subsequently absconded abroad," Yadav said.
Deep Dive
The CBI got a Red Notice published against Mazin through Interpol on the request of Maharashtra Police.
"The subject was geo-located and arrested by the UAE authorities. Following due legal process, the UAE authorities granted deportation of the subject to India. The escort team of Maharashtra Police visited the UAE, where the subject was handed over to them. The escort team from India, along with the subject, arrived at the Cochin International Airport on Friday," the spokesperson said.
The agency has successfully secured return of 74 fugitives during 2026 so far using Interpol channels.

A Bengaluru-based inventor has claimed to develop a technology that can transform ordinary chemical elements into precious metals such as gold and silver. Rajah Vijay Kumar has secured an Indian patent for a process called Gravitoradiophysical Nuclear Transmutation (GNT), which he says can change one element into another using specially generated frequencies. The invention has attracted attention because it claims to achieve something that has fascinated scientists and alchemists for centuries: producing gold from another metal. The process uses a specially designed reactor called the 'Boom Tube' and is claimed to work without conventional nuclear fission or fusion. According to reports by The Economic Times and The Times of India, laboratory tests on mercury samples processed using the technology detected traces of gold, silver and other elements. However, the findings do not yet establish that mercury was successfully converted into gold. Independent scientific testing is still needed to verify the claim. Rajah Vijay Kumar is the director and chief scientific officer of the Scalene Energy Research Institute, part of the Organization de Scalene Foundation. His invention, GNT, is based on the idea that specially generated frequencies can be used to separate elements from chemical compounds and then attempt to transform one element into another. The patent application was filed in November 2017, and the patent was granted in 2025. The apparatus described in the patent includes a frequency generator, heating system, vacuum pump, pressure gauges and a reactor known as the Boom Tube. According to the inventor, the GNT technology uses a two-stage process. Stage 1: Breaking down the chemical compound The first step involves using specially generated frequencies to break the chemical bonds in a compound and separate the element from the material it is part of. Kumar has explained that different elements respond to different frequencies. Stage 2: Attempting to transform the element Once the element is separated, another element-specific frequency is applied inside the Boom Tube reactor. This stage is intended to bring about a change in the element itself. The process is claimed to use electromagnetic frequencies and controlled conditions inside the reactor rather than conventional nuclear reactors. The patent-related experiments reportedly involved mercuric sulphate mixed with distilled water. Some of the mixture was kept untreated for comparison, while the remaining samples were processed using the GNT technology. Laboratory analysis reportedly found gold at concentrations of 1.91 milligrams per litre in one sample and 2.3 milligrams per litre in another. The second sample also showed silver at 11 milligrams per litre. The tests also recorded a reduction in mercury content from 33.45 grams to 8.67 grams after treatment. The samples were examined using a technique called Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy (ICP-AES), which identifies and measures the elements present in a material. However, there is an important scientific question that remains unanswered. Detecting gold in a sample does not automatically prove that mercury has been converted into gold. ICP-AES can identify the presence of an element, but it cannot establish how that element was produced or whether it was already present as an impurity. For the claim to be scientifically established, independent laboratories would need to repeat the experiments under controlled conditions and examine the atomic and nuclear properties of the resulting material. In principle, yes. But it requires changing the structure of an atom's nucleus. Gold has 79 protons, while mercury has 80. Therefore, converting mercury into gold requires a nuclear reaction that changes the number of protons in the nucleus. Ordinary chemical reactions cannot achieve this because they only change how atoms interact with one another, not their nuclear structure. This is why Kumar's claim is attracting scientific interest. If the GNT process can demonstrate the proposed transformation through independent and repeatable experiments, it could become an important development in material science. For now, however, the patent and reported laboratory findings should not be treated as proof that the technology can commercially produce gold or silver. Its working mechanism, reliability and potential for large-scale use still need to be established. A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.
District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.
"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.
Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.
The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.
Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.
Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.
"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."
The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.
"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.
NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.
On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.
That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.
Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.
And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.
She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.
"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.
Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.
The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

The reproductive-autonomy jurisprudence as evolved by the Supreme Court under Article 21 of the Constitution is rich yet narrow, focusing primarily on one side of the problem. In Suchita Srivastava v. Chandigarh Administration (2009), the Court held that reproductive choices may be exercised to procreate as well as to abstain from procreating. In X v. Principal Secretary, Health and Family Welfare Department (2022), the Supreme Court extended the right to abortion to unmarried women as an exercise of ‘decisional autonomy’.
These, and nearly all other landmark cases are concerned only with an existing pregnancy. The freedom to pursue parenthood through medical treatment, however, has surfaced only at the margins. The Delhi High Court, in 2023, allowed parole of a life convict to attempt IVF, by recognising a “right to parenthood,” but only as a claim against a barrier the State itself had erected. No court has yet asked whether the State may leave a citizen’s access to infertility care entirely to their own purse. Can a right available to the fertile but structurally withheld from the infertile be called a universal right?
