William and Kate meet PM Modi as they wrap up India tour
- Published
The Prince and Princess of Wales have met India's prime minister as they ended their three-day visit to the country.
Narendra Modi thanked Prince William for bringing his Earthshot prize to the country during the couple's first international tour since 2022.
It comes a day after the royal couple gave out £1m prizes to winners of the environmental award, which was founded by the prince and remains one of his biggest personal projects.
Catherine also visited a maternity hospital, where she comforted a grieving mother who lost a baby after giving birth to premature twin girls.
On Wednesday, William and Catherine travelled from Mumbai to capital New Delhi for the final leg of their trip.
During a meeting at Modi's private residence, a Kensington Palace spokesperson said the royals and Modi discussed the "strength and importance of the UK–India bilateral relationship, reflecting on the deep and enduring ties between the two countries and the opportunities to strengthen their partnership in the years ahead".
The prince and princess also spoke "warmly" of their time in the country, thanking the prime minister and the people for their welcome, and saying how much they enjoyed returning to India, a decade after their last visit.
Modi called it a "pleasure" to meet them, and said he looks forward to "further strengthening" the UK–India partnership for the "shared prosperity of the people of our nations and the wider world".
When Prince William announced earlier this year that The Earthshot Prize ceremony was going to be held in India for the first time, he highlighted India's leadership in climate innovation, its biodiversity and its massive youth population as the key reasons for choosing the country.
The royal spokesperson said that the meeting with Modi touched on the success of the ceremony in Mumbai, and India's "growing leadership in environmental innovation".
The event, founded by Prince William in 2020, was hosted this year by Karan Johar, presenter of The Traitors India and one of the country's most well-known filmmakers.
The couple last met the Indian prime minister on their official visit to India in 2016.
Ahead of their meeting with Modi on Wednesday, William met with film stars during a visit to a film production company, while Catherine visited a maternity hospital, where she met grieving mother Jyoti Karande.
Karande, whose other child remains in intensive care, is receiving treatment in the post-partum ward at Nowrosjee Wadia Maternity Hospital.
Catherine told the 29-year-old: "Stay strong. Well done. You've clearly been very, very brave."
William and Catherine's first official overseas trip in four years was short, but allowed them to combine personal projects - like Earthshot - with diplomacy.
As the future king and queen, they are viewed as a valuable diplomatic asset by the UK government.
And with Catherine recovering well and back on international duties following her cancer treatment, visits of a similar kind can be expected to fill their calendar.

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:
The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.
CTIA said the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”
The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”
The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Manipur’s Chandel district administration on Friday (November 20, 2026) issued an advisory, urging people to report suspected manufacturing, storage, sale or distribution of adulterated liquor.
The public advisory followed the death of 11 people due to consumption of spurious liquor in the district’s Chakpikarong Sub-Division. The deaths have been reported since Tuesday (November 17, 2026).
According to a statement from the Chief Minister’s Office, 180 others are undergoing treatment at two private hospitals in Imphal. Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited these hospitals on Friday and took stock of the treatment being provided to the patients.
Advising the general public to exercise utmost caution, the district administration said the cause of the deaths was yet to be “medically and scientifically established”. It asked people to refrain from consuming locally brewed liquor or alcoholic beverages of doubtful origin, particularly from suspected sources in the affected areas.
“Any person experiencing vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, dizziness, blurred vision, breathing difficulty or other unusual symptoms following alcohol consumption should immediately seek medical attention at the nearest facility,” the advisory read.
It also advised people who may have consumed liquor from the same suspected source to seek medical evaluation even if they are not experiencing symptoms.
“The public is requested to report suspected manufacturing, storage, sale or distribution of adulterated liquor to the nearest police station or the concerned authorities,” the advisory further read, requesting village authorities, civil society organisations, women’s organisations and youth clubs to assist in spreading awareness.
The Manipur government partially lifted 30 years of alcohol prohibition in December 2023, although extremist groups in the State continue to target liquor businesses. Years of prohibition led to certain areas turning into local liquor dens, selling alcoholic beverages of suspect quality.
Spurious liquor has claimed lives in other northeastern States where prohibition is enforced. For instance, 23 people were killed in Nagaland’s Mokokchung and Tuensang districts about two months ago.

West in ‘big trouble’, don’t expect massive climate aid: Steven Koonin at HT Leadership Summit
The 74-year-old Edward Teller Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution argued that it is time to rethink how the world responds to climate change.
Global emissions are soaring, and the finance promised to developing countries from the developed world has not arrived, physicist Steven Koonin said, as he questioned the achievements of the ongoing 31st Conference of the Parties (COP) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change in Türkiye.
The 74-year-old Edward Teller Fellow at Stanford University’s Hoover Institution also argued that it is time to rethink how the world responds to climate change. He made the remarks during a conversation with NDTV consulting editor Gargi Rawat at the Hindustan Times Leadership Summit on November 14.
Asked about his views on the climate negotiations at COP31 that is scheduled to conclude on Friday, Koonin said: “This is the 31st Conference of the Parties that started about a week ago in Turkey. What have they accomplished? Global emissions continue to go up. They are soaring. The promises of financial help from the developed world to the developing world have not materialised. I think it’s time to think about doing the response in a different way than what we have done.”
Deep Dive
He also said he doesn’t expect large-scale aid from the West, given the financial strain caused by ongoing global conflicts.

“The Western nations – I know the US best, but I also know Europe – are in big trouble. And to think that there’s going to be massive amounts of aid coming from the West, given the financial problems that we have – overextension on social security, trade issues, many of the things that we’ve been discussing — I don’t think that’s going to happen,” he said.
As the moderator said, “so, this is a mirage that we’re chasing…”, Koonin said: “I think so. The history of the COPs has shown that.”
During the 2024 climate conference, rich countries agreed to triple climate funding for developing countries to $300 billion per year by 2035, up from the previous goal of $100 billion annually. It also decided to secure the efforts of all actors to work together to scale up finance for developing countries, from public and private sources, to $1.3 trillion per year by 2035.
According to Reuters, the rich countries met their 2020 target two years later. Since then, climate action has slipped down the political agenda for Western governments as US President Donald Trump withdrew international funding, while wars in Ukraine and the Middle East added to inflationary pressures and the need to spend on security.
The latest negotiating draft at COP31 has kept the call to triple adaptation finance by 2035 but leaves out key details around setting a starting point, milestones and a system for tracking progress to next year’s summit in Ethiopia, Bloomberg reported. The negotiations are continuing, meaning the omitted target and other provisions may yet return before a final agreement is adopted.
Fiji climate minister Lynda Tabuya alleged rich nations have closed ranks against putting a dollar figure on adaptation finance at COP31. He described a harder and more coordinated pushback than at previous summits. “It used to be fragmented. Now, it seems to be more of a collective ambition to oppose it,” he said.
Decarbonisation in India
Koonin, during the summit, also spoke on decarbonisation in India, saying the country should get the energy it needs in the most convenient way that it can and must only worry about cutting carbon when “it gets rich enough”.
“Look, India needs energy. If you look at countries that develop, they need more and more energy as they develop, until they get to a certain point, which is far away for India. For every dollar of GDP you increase, you need about 5 megajoules of energy per year. And India should be getting that energy in the most convenient way that it can,” he said.
“Once it (India) gets rich enough, I would think then it can start to worry about decarbonisation. But the energy needs are immediate. They are soluble, whereas the climate threat is distant, vague and uncertain. So I think the pragmatic thing to do is to get that energy. Look, only 15% of Indian households have air conditioning. You should fix that,” he added.

The final mission in GTA 6 Chapter 1 is titled “Discharge Time“. It starts with Lucia heading to Vice City Hospital to discharge Jason, but finds attackers waiting for them. It’s a long mission with a massive shootout, so here’s the full walkthrough with tips and tricks and more.
Note: Unlike GTA games in the past, GTA 6 missions do not have Gold Medal objectives.
Here is a step-by-step quick overview of the mission:
- Where to find the Discharge Time mission
- Go to Vice City Hospital’s second floor and find Jason in Room 203.
- Shoot the attackers with Jason and defend Lucia.
- Defend Jason from the attackers inside the hospital as Lucia.
- Use the shotgun to move away from the door where the attackers are shooting.
- Crawl to the gun before Lucia arrives with the ambulance.
- Defend the ambulance by shooting the masked gang members and corrupt cops.
| Info | Details | 
|---|---|
| Mission Number | GTA 6 Mission 25 | 
| Story Chapter | GTA 6 Chapter 1 | 
| Mission Type | Mandatory (required for 100% completion) | 
| Mission Giver | Begins automatically | 
| Protagonist | Jason (primary) Lucia (secondary) | 
| Location | Vice City, Vice-Dale County in Leonida | 
| Unlocked items | Safehouse: Starlet Motel |

Where to Find the Discharge Time Mission
“Discharge Time” begins automatically right after the “Home Sweet Home” mission in GTA 6, so you don’t need to find it.
Once Lucia exits Andy’s car with her jacket and meets with Cal Hampton, the mission will begin inside Vice City Hospital.
Go to the second floor and find Jason
- Once the mission begins, head to the second floor of the Vice City Hospital.
- Turn left and head straight up the stairs to the second floor.
- Take a right to walk into the ICU rooms corridor.
- Enter Room 203 on your left to find Jason on a hospital bed.
Shoot the attackers to defend Lucia
- After Lucia puts Jason in a wheelchair, use the pistol to shoot the incoming attackers.
- There’s one attacker behind every door, so use the Focus ability in GTA 6 to shoot precisely.
- Press L3+R3/LS+RS to activate the Combat Focus mode.
- Inside the elevator, shoot the two corrupt cops until the door closes.
- Exit the elevator and shoot the attackers down the hallway.
- When Lucia drags Jason, shoot the gunmen to the left.
- Use the SMG to defend Lucia one last time.
Defend Jason
- Once Lucia takes the SMG from Jason, use it to clear the room full of attackers.
- Follow the pink marker to stay close to Jason.
- After the room is cleared, the gameplay switches back to Jason.
- Shoot the incoming attackers to progress.
Use the Shotgun to Move and Crawl to the Gun
- Lucia then leaves to find a ride for them to escape.
- Meanwhile, Jason takes down a corrupt cop and gets a shotgun.
- Use the shotgun on the incoming attackers to move away from the door.
- After Jason gets knocked to the floor due to a nearby gas canister explosion, crawl towards the gun.
Defend the ambulance
- Lucia then enters the scene with an ambulance and escapes with Jason.
- Next, with Jason, shoot the corrupt cops on their tail and defend the ambulance.
- Use L3+R3/LS+RS to activate the Focus ability and shoot more accurately.
- Keep shooting until an oncoming train clears all the police cars.

Can a US-backed mineral highway bring peace and prosperity to DR Congo?
- Published
As trains carrying thousands of tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo roar through her community, 20-year-old Manuela Julia is not thinking about critical minerals or billion-dollar investments.
She is thinking about getting around more easily.
The railway runs through Catumbela, near the Angolan city of Lobito, on the Atlantic coast.
For Julia, it has made travelling cheaper and more convenient.
"Before, I had to use a taxi, which is much more expensive. Now it is cheaper and easier to travel," she says.
But the railway has ambitions far bigger than improving local transport.
It is part of the Lobito Corridor, a US-backed effort to secure access to Africa's critical minerals and promote regional economic cooperation, which Washington hopes will help bring peace to conflict-torn eastern DR Congo.
Under agreements brokered by US President Donald Trump, DR Congo and neighbouring Rwanda have committed to greater economic cooperation, including more transparent mineral supply chains and regional infrastructure development.
The wider plan envisages linking these initiatives to the railway, which transports minerals from Central Africa to Western markets via Angola, rather than east to China as most do currently.
The hope is that formalising the mineral trade and encouraging investment could help curb illicit markets that have helped finance armed groups and fuel instability.
But can a railway built to move minerals to global markets also deliver peace and prosperity?
The Lobito Corridor links DR Congo's mineral-rich south to Angola's Atlantic coast through the Benguela Railway and the Port of Lobito.
Its importance has grown as demand for copper and cobalt rises, driven partly by the global transition to cleaner energy, as both are critical ingredients for all kinds of electrical components.
"The timing matters," says Johannesburg-based political risk analyst Wellington Muzengeza
"Electrification and the energy transition have increased the strategic importance of copper, cobalt and reliable mineral supply chains."
DR Congo is the world's largest producer of cobalt and one of its biggest copper producers, along with neighbouring Zambia. The US sees the corridor as a means to diversify mineral supplies and reduce reliance on China, which dominates much of the world's processing capacity.
A US-DR Congo strategic partnership identifies the route from the Congolese town of Sakania to Lobito as a priority for mineral exports, while the economic framework agreed by DR Congo and Rwanda envisages connecting regional infrastructure and trade initiatives to the corridor.
The project has attracted over $750m (£570m), including funding backed by the US International Development Finance Corporation and the Development Bank of Southern Africa to upgrade railway tracks, signalling systems and trains.
The railway, built in 1902 under Portuguese colonial rule, was originally designed to transport goods and minerals from Central Africa to the Atlantic coast. After years of disruption during Angola's civil war, it was rebuilt and fully reopened in 2015.
The US first got involved in the project under former President Joe Biden but backing has continued under Trump.
At Lobito's mineral terminal, the renewed ambitions are already visible.
When the BBC visited, a train carrying about 12,000 tonnes of copper cathodes from DR Congo had arrived. Workers moved the refined copper sheets into a warehouse before they were loaded on to ships bound for international markets, mostly the US.
The cargo is handled by Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), which has a 30-year concession to operate freight services along the corridor and manage the mineral terminal.
Chief operating officer Nicholas Gregoir says freight volumes have more than doubled since the company took over in January 2024.
LAR expects to transport about 200,000 tonnes of copper through the corridor in 2026.
For mining companies, the railway offers a shorter route to international markets.
"The Lobito Corridor is the shortest route for both Zambia and the DRC," to the Atlantic, says Kátila Vanessa Monteiro da Silva Neto, executive director of the Lobito Port Authority.
Zambia, Africa's second-largest copper producer, also plans to connect its Copperbelt to Lobito through a proposed 830km (515 mile)-railway.
But a more efficient route to market does not automatically translate into economic transformation.
"Joining a corridor is not the same as industrialising," Muzengeza says. "The test is not simply whether Zambia gains another route to the sea. It is whether that route helps build a stronger economy."
Some Angolans believe the railway's greatest value could lie in what it offers businesses and communities beyond mining.
"I call it a corridor of development," says businessman Adérito Areias.
The railway passes through some of Angola's most productive agricultural regions.
Better transport links could help farmers reach larger markets and reduce losses.
"If there isn't an artery carrying products from the interior to where there is demand, those products simply rot where they are produced," Areias says.
But the challenge is turning that ambition into reality.
The Port of Lobito handled about 1.8 million tonnes of cargo in 2025, of which around 158,000 tonnes was minerals. Its mineral terminal can handle up to 3.6 million tonnes annually.
"The port already has the capacity," says Neto. "What we need now is sufficient railway capacity and rolling stock."
For residents along the route, the benefits have been immediate.
State-owned railway operator Caminho de Ferro de Benguela (CFB), which runs passenger services, carried a record 1.6 million passengers in 2025.
LAR says it directly employs nearly 1,000 people, 98% of them Angolan.
"This job allows me to support my family," says Domingos Canhama, a father of four and a forklift operator at CFB.
"I can put food on the table, maintain a home and help support my father," he says.
Muzengeza argues that the bigger opportunity is developing local businesses in engineering, maintenance, warehousing and agricultural processing.
"Businesses in Angola need access to the railway, not just proximity to it. That means feeder roads, electricity, storage and predictable services," he says.
But can minerals and their movement along the railways line help deliver peace to eastern DR Congo, where the battle for control of mineral resources has fuelled decades of conflict?
Most recently, this has seen the M23 rebel group seize control of many mineral-rich areas.
The Congolese government says neighbouring Rwanda is backing the M23 in order to gain access to DR Congo's mineral wealth. Despite overwhelming evidence, Rwanda denies backing the M23.
The Trump-backed agreements between DR Congo and Rwanda seek to promote transparent mineral supply chains, cross-border investment and regional infrastructure, with the aim of ensuring mineral wealth does not finance armed groups.
"The US wants reliable access to minerals essential to defence, advanced technology and energy systems, while reducing dependence on supply chains in which China has substantial influence," says Muzengeza, the political risk analyst
"Lobito is therefore more than a railway but an infrastructure that can reshape trade routes and commercial power."
At a meeting in Paris in November, DR Congo urged the US to turn its strategic partnership into tangible investments, arguing that success should be measured by completed projects rather than signed agreements.
"We want the partnership to support local mineral processing, electricity access for households and businesses and peace in the east," said DR Congo's Economy Minister Daniel Mukoko Samba.
Even if more minerals move through formal channels, better infrastructure alone would not resolve the political and security tensions driving the conflict.
There is also the question of who captures the wealth. Much of the copper and cobalt transported from DR Congo through Lobito is destined for processing and manufacturing outside Africa.
While Angola can earn transit fees and create logistics jobs, much of the higher-value activity takes place elsewhere.
"When you export raw materials, you are also exporting jobs and knowledge," Angola's Foreign Affairs Minister Téte António tells the BBC.
Areias shares that concern.
"We should not export lithium but export batteries," he says, arguing that the corridor should help develop local processing and manufacturing rather than simply accelerate raw material exports.
Back in Catumbela, such debates can feel distant from everyday life.
For Julia, the railway already means cheaper journeys and easier movement.
But its ultimate success will depend on whether it can deliver more than faster mineral exports.
Whether it can also help secure lasting peace in eastern DR Congo, where the minerals are mined, remains the bigger test.

By any measure, it is one of the most extraordinary political stories of our age: a shy Italian girl locks eyes with the scion of an Indian political family, falls instantly and steadfastly in love, “transplanting herself” as a result, suffers soul-shattering tragedies, then takes the reins of power in the world’s largest democracy. It is a life that spans the extremes of privilege and distress, and half a century of seismic national history.
No wonder publishers have been keen to secure the memoirs of the famously guarded Sonia Gandhi, soon to turn 80. Yet when the chance came, the deal with the country’s biggest publisher, Penguin Random House India, fell through at the last minute over what it termed “an impasse over a particular issue” in the text, with HarperCollins stepping into the breach. For those unfamiliar with the sensitive political context, the Nehru-Gandhi family has been in charge of India for about half the eight decades since independence – and the principal opposition to Narendra Modi’s prickly BJP regime for the past 12 years.
As it turns out, Belonging does not read as incendiary. It errs, rather, towards discretion and legacy-building. It is also, at its best, a heartbreaking story of love and loss.
Gandhi’s voice is measured and generally frill-free. Flourishes do accompany the meet-cute at a Greek restaurant in Cambridge in the mid-1960s that sets off the story. “That January Sunday, which was to change my life,” she writes, “the sky [was] a beautiful azure dotted with puffy white clouds as in a Tiepolo fresco.” The introduction to fellow student Rajiv Gandhi was “a bolt of lightning”.
And, as in a film, there is parental resistance. Sonia’s father, a businessman who worked in construction in a small Italian town, is a second world war veteran, nicknamed Maino the Lion. A 1998 New Yorker profile by Patrick French, briefly a collaborator on Belonging, had him down as “an unrepentant fascist” until his death. Well, was he? We don’t get to find out. Wherever expedient, Gandhi maintains her strategic silence.
Stefano Maino, at any rate, is “padre padrone” – literally, “father master”. When he hears about his middle daughter’s love interest, he brings “his fist down on his writing table” with a shout of “Basta!” And yet, he buys her a ticket to India the moment she turns 21.
On the boy’s side is the person who would come to be described as the world’s most powerful woman, Indira Gandhi, the daughter of India’s first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Barely has Sonia landed in Delhi than Indira decides the pair must wed (the news reaches the Mainos via radio; Signor Maino stays away). Indira then manages Sonia’s first pregnancy, directs the name-giving ceremony – you get the picture. Gandhi refers to her, factually, as “my mother-in-law”, but, subverting the stereotype, she becomes a devoted daughter. Walking us through her induction into elite Indian family life, she draws an affectionate portrait of this formidable 20th-century figure.
But family and party allegiance are a distorting lens through which to view history. Charged events, such as Indira’s crushing of a huge railway strike, acquire a benign gloss. The 21 tumultuous months of the 1975 Emergency – which saw members of the opposition arrested, civil liberties curtailed, the press censored, while a despotic nepo-baby (Sanjay, Indira’s younger son) ran amok – are rendered with a brisk calm. Tenderness is reserved for the repercussions on the family in its subsequent period out of power.
Sanjay’s death at 33, just after Indira’s return to power in 1980, leaves the matriarch broken. “In her eyes [Rajiv] was the only one who could come to her rescue.” Gandhi does not interrogate the hereditary approach to democratic politics, but she does recount, affectingly, the fight to protect herself and Rajiv – a commercial pilot with no greater ambitions – and their two children from the inferno.
In the book’s strongest scene, she waits disoriented in a crowded hospital in 1984, “shivering under my dressing gown”, having ferried her mother-in-law’s bullet-ridden body there. Indira was slain by her Sikh bodyguards in revenge for ordering the army into the Golden Temple, Sikhism’s holiest site. As Rajiv embraces her with the words “they want me to be sworn in as prime minister”, Gandhi feels “a rage welling up deep inside me”. “They will kill you too!” she says. “They will kill me anyway,” he replies. The “they” is unspecified, and gives these pages an air of foretold tragedy.
Rajiv’s eventful term plays out under this death cloud. It starts with a pogrom against Sikhs, spearheaded by Congress leaders. Gandhi goes some length to eulogise her husband’s tenure: in reality, it was a troubled and contradictory record. Rajiv was 40, severely underqualified, and grieving. Miscalculations abounded, among them clumsy religious manoeuvring that played into the Hindu-nationalist BJP’s hands, and a military entanglement in Sri Lanka designed to end the civil war with Tamil separatists.
And that death cloud never blows way. The children are withdrawn from school; Gandhi, perpetually anxious, finds her hands trembling in public; Rajiv is once shot at. When he loses the election his successor vindictively withdraws his special security cover. Their son Rahul (the current leader of the opposition) predicts the worst. At a rally in Tamil Nadu in 1991, a Tamil Tiger operative makes to place a garland around Rajiv, then 46, with explosives strapped around her body.
The graphic photograph of the aftermath of that scene is seared into Indian memory. Thanks to the vigilance of her children, Gandhi has never seen it. “I had become the child to be protected, they the parents,” she writes, in a wrenching section. Years later, when she collapses in Japan, a nurse is startled to find her grown children lying on either side of her on the small hospital bed.
Gandhi’s first reaction on hearing the news about Rajiv? “I wanted to die.” Gradually though, she picks up the smithereens of her life. As the remaining Gandhi elder, she picks up the pieces of the splintering Congress party, too.There are few parallels to a life as singular as this. A century ago, Congress had its first foreign-born female president, the British theosophist Annie Besant; farther afield, Janet Jagan, the American-born Jewish wife of Cheddi Jagan herself became president of Guyana – but both women were political activists to begin with. Gandhi, in her words, “had no right – except for the fact that I carried the family name”.
The exhortations to Gandhi to take over the party reveal plenty about Congress culture, and they are eventually successful: the spectator becomes the player. We watch her bone up on her Hindi, lead campaigns, stitch up alliances (including with a party sympathetic to the Tamil Tigers), and combat the BJP, which brands her, among other things, a “Monica Lewinsky” who would establish a “Rome Raj”. In 2004, she leads an alliance of parties to victory.
To her children’s horror, Gandhi is badgered into nearly accepting the post of prime minister. Instead she handpicks a candidate, Manmohan Singh, while keeping charge of the party (eventually leading it for a staggering 22 years) and chairing the ruling coalition as well as an advisory council that keeps a hand on policy levers.
“It had been my choice to become Indian,” she reflects after the long night of the soul that leads her to decline the premiership – a source of fascinated speculation over the years. “I made it out of love for a man, but that love came to encompass his family and his country. And it was this love for India that had demanded the most from me.”
Belonging comes into its own when unpacking those demands, and showing the transition from grief to its successor emotion, resilience.

Omnichannel fast fashion brand Style Union’s parent Nexon Omniverse Ltd has raised ₹485 Cr (nearly $51.8 Mn) in its Series E funding round co-led by Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners. In a statement, the platform said that the round comprised both primary and secondary components. Style Union plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its offline store network across key metros in West and North India. "This is a defining moment for Nexon Omniverse and for Style Union… With their backing, we will take Style Union beyond its southern base into West and North India and into millions of new households across the country." said Nexon Omniverse whole-time director Rajesh Seth. Founded in 2022 by former operations head of Future Retail Rakesh Biyani and his wife Ekta Biyani, Style Union sells apparels for men, women and kids through its own website as well as offline stores. With its core footprint in South India, the brand operates 200 physical stores across Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, among other cities. The platform claims to have closed FY26 with over ₹1,150 Cr in revenue. It competes with the likes of Tata-owned Zudio, V-Mart and Vishal Mega Mart. The funding comes as a growing number of Indian D2C fashion and lifestyle brands are expanding beyond online channels and building omnichannel businesses. Startups are increasingly using physical stores to improve brand discovery and customer experience while continuing to leverage ecommerce for scale. On the back of this, the space continues to attract healthy investor interest. In September this year, D2C fashion and accessories brand Theater bagged ₹75 Cr in its Series A round led by investment firm Niveshaay. Earlier this year in March, omnichannel streetwear brand Bonkers Corner also raised $15 Mn to fuel its offline expansion plans. Prior to this in January, D2C lifestyle brand Salty also raised ₹30 Cr to expand its product portfolio and set up a flagship store. At the heart of all this is the homegrown fashion ecommerce space, which is projected to become a $112 Bn opportunity by 2030.

UnitedHealth Group has sued the federal government over its lowered Medicare Advantage star ratings for next year, further plunging the program’s ratings system into disarray.
UnitedHealth marks at least the 15th Medicare Advantage plan to file a lawsuit against the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for how the agency calculated 2027 star ratings. UnitedHealth is also the largest Medicare Advantage insurer, covering more than 9 million people. Medicare’s annual enrollment period ends Dec. 7.
The government rates Medicare Advantage plans on a scale from one to five stars, based on health screens, customer satisfaction, and other measures that get mixed into a complicated formula. Those with at least four stars earn bonus money. The insurers argue in their lawsuits that the government’s measurement is inconsistent and is inappropriately dropping their scores below the bonus thresholds.

Glenn Phillips scored his second Test hundred on Day 2 of the first Test between India and New Zealand in Wellington on Friday.
Phillips, who resumed from his overnight score of 94*, reached his landmark off 193 balls, with a push through covers on the up off Prasidh Krishna’s bowling.
Phillips in the process also became the first batter to score a T20I hundred, an ODI hundred, and a Test hundred against India in a calendar year.
His rich vein of form began with a prolific series in the T20I leg of the tour where he scored 341 runs in five matches to record the most runs in a bilateral series by a player.
Across those five games, the 29-year-old scored a century and three fifties.
Phillips, who came into bat at number seven when New Zealand was reeling at 70/5, has pulled his team out of trouble with his hundred.
His partnership with Henry Nicholls, who scored his 12th Test century on Day 1, put New Zealand on course for a 350-plus first innings total.
Phillips, like Nicholls, relied primarily on meeting the ball late and using his backfoot to score runs. Phillips scored the majority of his runs through the off-side, especially targeting the backward square region.
Phillips punished the Indian bowlers the most on the full length, and also regularly found the gaps on the good and back-of-a length.
Phillips was eventually dismissed for 118 off 216 balls by Akash Deep, bringing an end to a sensational knock by the Kiwi all-rounder

After reports that the 2027 summit of NATO heads of state in Albania was canceled, a rumor spread that the organization had canceled all upcoming summits to prevent U.S. President Donald Trump from sharing intelligence with Russia President Vladimir Putin.
Putin opposes NATO, which he sees as a direct threat to Russia's security and influence. In a 2022 speech, he said the expansion of NATO was the reason for his invasion of Ukraine.
Several social media posts claimed the reason for the summits' alleged cancelation was Trump's lack of integrity. One X post said "NATO has canceled all upcoming summits until Trump leaves office, amid concerns that sensitive information shared during these meetings could be passed along to Vladimir Putin" (archived):
Meanwhile, Snopes readers searched the website and emailed, seeking clarity on the rumor.
It is true that NATO reportedly said it would skip its 2027 leadership summit, which was initially scheduled to take place in Albania, according to a Nov. 15 article by The Associated Press.
The article cited tensions among NATO member nations regarding the U.S.-Israel war on Iran, Russia's ongoing war on Ukraine and disagreements about defense spending. NATO members agreed to spend at least 3.5% of their gross domestic product on defense by 2035; as of 2025, only seven of the 32 countries reached or surpassed that level, a NATO report showed.
It is also true that an Oct. 21 report by The Atlantic said tensions at the North American Aerospace Defense Command — NORAD, a U.S.-Canadian military organization designed to cooperate on air and maritime defense — were boiling over. The story said Canada was having difficulty staffing its NORAD posts due to its personnel's distrust of the U.S. NORAD's headquarters are located in Colorado Springs, Colorado.
However, it appeared people spreading the rumor had conflated parts of these two different stories, though it's worth noting that neither report cited leaks to Putin.
Snopes found no evidence that concerns Trump would share NATO intelligence with Putin were the reason for canceling the 2027 summit. In addition, it was unclear whether a NATO leadership summit in 2028 — the last year of Trump's second term — would also be canceled.
For these reasons, we've left the claim unrated.
In response to our inquiry about the rumor, a White House spokesperson told Snopes via email that it was "obviously fake."
We also reached out to NATO, NORAD and the office of Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama seeking more details and await responses.
NATO summits do not happen every year
It is worth noting that NATO leadership summits have not taken place every year since the organization's foundation in 1949. The organization has skipped several years. Meanwhile, some years saw more than one summit, for example in February 2022, in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine, followed by another in Brussels a month later and a third in Madrid in June 2022.
Meanwhile, ministerial meetings happen more frequently. In December 2026, foreign affairs ministers of the member countries (including the U.S. secretary of state) are scheduled to gather in Brussels, Belgium, where NATO is headquartered. Defense ministers also met in June 2026.
Further, such summits can be elaborate and expensive affairs due to security concerns, the AP cited NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte as saying.
Meanwhile the article in The Atlantic suggested the distrust among Canadian military staff regarding NORAD was the symptom of a larger breakdown in military cooperation between Canada and the U.S. Among several affronts to the U.S.' northern neighbor, the story cited Trump's threats to annex Canada and the tariffs he imposed on Canadian products.
For further reading, Snopes has covered several rumors about NATO, including the claim that one of its officials said Europe would take every U.S. base if Trump annexed Greenland.

బైకర్ ప్రమాదవశాత్తు కింద పడినప్పుడు తలకి గాయం కాకుండా ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్లతో కూడిన హెల్మెట్లను చైనా తయారుచేసిందంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో విస్తృతంగా ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఈ వీడియోని ప్రముఖ మీడియా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కూడా షేర్ చేశాయి. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: చైనా తయారుచేసిన ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్లతో కూడిన హెల్మెట్ను చూపుతున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఇది AI టెక్నాలజీతో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. వాస్తవానికి కొన్ని సంస్థలు ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్ హెల్మెట్లపై ప్రయోగాలు చేస్తున్నప్పటికీ అవి వీడియోలో చూపించినంత భారీ పరిమాణంలో లేవు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోని పరిశీలించగా, ఇందులో బైకర్ కింద పడుతున్న దృశ్యాన్ని రికార్డ్ చేస్తున్న ఫోన్లో కొంతసేపటి వరకు బైక్, బైకర్ కనిపించరు. ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్లు తెరుచుకున్నాక బైకర్ అకస్మాత్తుగా అదృశ్యమవ్వడం చూడవచ్చు. అంతేకాకుండా, బైక్ అదుపుతప్పి బైకర్ రోడ్డుపై పడే విధానం కూడా చాలా అసహజంగా ఉంటుంది. సాధారణంగా AIతో రూపొందించిన వీడియోలలోనే ఇలాంటి లోపాలు కనిపిస్తాయి.
ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోను AI కంటెంట్ డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఇది AI టెక్నాలజీతో రూపొందించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో అని స్పష్టమైంది.
అనంతరం, ఈ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇది మొదట “Zero Gravity Gang” అనే ఫేస్బుక్ పేజీలో అప్లోడ్ (ఆర్కైవ్) అయినట్లు గుర్తించాం. ఈ పేజీలో వాహనాలకు సంబంధించిన వివిధ ప్రయోగాలను చూపే AI వీడియోలను తరచుగా అప్లోడ్ చేస్తుంటారని స్పష్టమైంది.
వాస్తవానికి, హెల్మెట్లకు ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్లను అమర్చే టెక్నాలజీని కొన్ని కంపెనీలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రయోగాత్మకంగా అభివృద్ధి చేస్తున్నప్పటికీ, అవి వైరల్ వీడియోలో చూపుతున్నంత భారీ సైజులో లేవు. కేవలం హెల్మెట్ లేదా తలను రక్షించేంత పరిమాణంలో మాత్రమే ఆ ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్ హెల్మెట్లు ఉంటున్నాయి.
చివరిగా, ఎయిర్బ్యాగ్లతో కూడిన హెల్మెట్లను చైనా తయారుచేసిందంటూ AI వీడియోని షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.
But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.
"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.
Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.
What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.
"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."
Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths
According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.
Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.
"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.
Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.
Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.
The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.
Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.
White House on Biden role in declines
NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.
"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.
Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."
According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.
"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.
But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.
"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."
Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.
Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.
The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.
"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

The US Food and Drug Administration said on Thursday it had established a new internal safety body within its biologics center, formalizing independent oversight of approved products such as vaccines, gene therapies and blood products once they reach the market.
The CBER Safety Council will report directly to the director of the FDA’s Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research, structurally separating post-market safety reviews from the offices responsible for approving those products, the agency said.
Here are some details:
The council supersedes CBER’s existing Safety Working Group, bringing together senior scientific and regulatory officials to review safety signals, conduct benefit-risk assessments and recommend regulatory actions as warranted.
The new structure formalizes an independent post-market review process at a time when regulators face mounting pressure to closely monitor newer biologic products, including gene and cell therapies, after approval, when they are used across far broader patient populations.
Its mandate will cover emerging safety concerns, potential labeling changes, risk-management measures and safety-related post-market studies, as well as advising on potential market withdrawals.
The FDA said the council is intended to improve accountability and transparency as biologic products grow increasingly complex, particularly in cell and gene therapy, a sector that has seen rapid regulatory expansion in recent years.
The council will coordinate with external bodies including the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the National Institutes of Health, drawing on surveillance systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) and the FDA Sentinel program.
The council takes effect on November 19; the agency said additional details on its structure and membership will be released later.

A 29-year-old woman from Manuguru, who was rushed to hospital after suddenly losing movement in her right arm and leg, regained significant mobility within hours after doctors at two government hospitals coordinated to administer emergency stroke treatment within the critical window.
Rajani’s ordeal began on an ordinary morning when she suddenly developed slurred speech and complete weakness on her right side. Recognising the signs of an acute stroke, doctors acted swiftly to prevent permanent brain damage.
She was first taken to Area Hospital, Manuguru, where Sai Kumar, a General Medicine specialist, identified the symptoms and arranged an urgent referral to Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, nearly 60 km away, for emergency treatment.
Recognising the narrow window for intervention, M. Ramakrishna, medical superintendent of Area Hospital, Manuguru, coordinated directly with Tejaswi Gadde, physician at Area Hospital, Bhadrachalam, to facilitate her transfer.
At Bhadrachalam, doctors immediately conducted a CT scan to rule out bleeding in the brain before administering clot-dissolving medication. With Rajani still within the recommended 4.5-hour treatment window, doctors administered intravenous Tenecteplase at 2 p.m., around 3.5 hours after the symptoms began, said G. Ravi Babu, District Coordinator of Hospital Services (DCHS), Bhadradri Kothagudem.
The response to treatment was encouraging. Before the intervention, Rajani had no detectable movement in her right arm or leg, with her muscle power recorded at 0/5. Following thrombolysis, her muscle strength improved, and she regained the ability to move the affected limbs against resistance, though full strength is yet to return.
She remains under close neurological observation. The case also highlights the availability of advanced emergency treatment in government hospitals serving remote and tribal areas. The thrombolytic medication, which costs around ₹45,000 in the market, was administered to Rajani free of cost.
Dr. Ravi Babu appreciated the doctors, nurses and supporting staff at both hospitals for their prompt decisions and coordination. “Such interventions demonstrate how teamwork between government healthcare institutions can help deliver advanced, life-saving treatment even in geographically remote areas,” he said.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

- GTA 6 features Merlin's Palace Casino in Vice-Dale County, Vice City.
- The casino is located slightly northwest of Lowballer Customs but is currently closed.
- Players cannot enter the casino, although it could become accessible in a future update.
Casinos have been part of the Grand Theft Auto series for years, with GTA Online even featuring the popular Diamond Casino & Resort. With Vice City returning in GTA 6, many players are wondering whether GTA 6 has casinos and whether you can spend your hard-earned money there.
The good news is that GTA 6 does have a casino, but there’s a catch.
Where Is the Casino Located in GTA 6?
Merlin’s Palace Casino is located in Vice-Dale County, in the Balsero neighborhood of Vice City. You can find it slightly northwest of Lowballer Customs on the GTA 6 map.
Unlike the Diamond Casino & Resort in GTA 5, which remained under construction for years before opening in GTA Online in 2019, Merlin’s Palace Casino is already fully constructed. Players can visit the location while exploring Vice City in GTA 6 and see the casino’s exterior.
However, the building is currently undergoing refurbishment, with a sign outside reading that it is temporarily closed.
While the casino is a recognizable landmark in the city, it doesn’t offer any addictive, money-risking activities for players.
Can You Enter the Casino in GTA 6?
No, you cannot enter Merlin’s Palace Casino or participate in any wager-like activities in GTA 6.
The building remains inaccessible throughout the single-player GTA 6 story missions, meaning you cannot play blackjack, roulette, or slot machines.
Developer Rockstar Games has also explained why casinos were left out of the game. Speaking to Kotaku, Rockstar’s VP of Design, Stephen Donkin, revealed that it didn’t fit Jason and Lucia’s story, particularly because the devs wanted to maintain a careful balance in the game’s economy.
However, Donkin also mentioned that the GTA 6 map was designed with the long term in mind, leaving certain locations available for potential future gameplay or story content.
This means Merlin’s Palace Casino could eventually open through a future update or an online multiplayer mode, similar to what happened with GTA Online. For now, though, Rockstar has not confirmed any plans to make the casino accessible in GTA 6.

World Toilet Day is a funny idea with a serious goal: A world awash in toilets
Twenty-five years ago, Jack Sim was flush with excitement. (Please pardon the pun.)
The Singapore entrepreneur was looking for a meaningful project and came upon this thought from the prime minister: "He said we should measure our graciousness according to the cleanliness of our public toilets," Sim recalls.
Thus was born World Toilet Day. The goal was more than cleanliness. It was access, too — billions of people do not have a safe and sanitary toilet to use.
Enshrined as an official U.N. day in 2013, World Toilet Day aims to get people talking and thinking about a topic that maybe is a taboo in polite conversation.
Let's eschew the euphemisms
World Toilet Day is all about peeing, pooping and addressing menstrual hygiene in a clean and safe manner — followed by the "conveyance" of excreta to a sanitary disposal system, notes Kate Olive Medlicott, the sanitation and waste team leader within the WASH team at the World Health Organization. Human diseases are shed in sewage, so a top-notch sanitation system is critical, says Medlicott. Cholera is linked to sewage. Polio is, too.
This year's World Toilet Day theme is "Sanitation and Gender Equality: Safe Toilets, Equal Futures." Even though everyone suffers when they can't find a toilet, the menstrual cycle creates additional complications. If schools or offices lack a safe and sanitary place to attend to period needs and to dispose of period products, girls and women may opt to stay home.
There is another gender issue. Sofia Calltorp, the U.N. Women global head of humanitarian action, says: "When women and girls do not have access to safe toilets," they leave their home and look for a public toilet or a secluded space to do their business, often venturing into unsafe areas. "There is a huge impact in terms of being exposed to harassment or violence," Calltorp says. She points to refugee camps as a place where this issue often arises, with unlit toilets that aren't differentiated by gender.
Now you might well ask: Has World Toilet Day made a difference?
The toilet titans we interviewed say yes, it has, just by talking about toilets in the public arena. The U.N. has stated that access to safe sanitation is a human right. And in just about every country, progress has been made in improving access to sanitary facilities. Since 2015, 1.2 billion people have become part of the world of safely managed sanitation systems.
What are the next steps? Kellogg Schwab, who specializes in water and wastewater contaminants of public health concern at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, stresses that governments should be a force for change but that it shouldn't be top down. It should also be … oh, forgive me again … bottom up. Schwab suggests giving money to communities to figure out what solutions they can come up with to improve the toilet and sanitation situation. There will be flops. But there will be successes that can be scaled up.
So maybe one day — Medlicott of WHO thinks in 50 years or so —- Earthlings will look back and say, How curious that in a world of wealth there were not enough safe and secure toilets.
A toast to toilets
Let's end by reflecting on the present day.
"World Toilet Day is my favorite day of the year," says Medlicott. "People find it fun and funny but it's really important to celebrate and act on something we take for granted."
If you're among the population where toilets are plentiful, she suggests pausing to think of a moment — it's happened to all of us — when you needed a bathroom and couldn't find one. Maybe that incident has turned into a funny story you share with friends. Now imagine if it were to happen every day.
I am deeply thankful that all I need to do is walk down the office hallway to find a clean and private loo.

The Department of Health and Family Welfare on Thursday launched the Karnataka State Action Plan for Containment of Antimicrobial Resistance (KSAPCAR) during a State-level workshop on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Bengaluru.
The action plan was formally unveiled by Rajini M, Director, Health and Family Welfare Services, to focus on strengthening antimicrobial stewardship, surveillance, infection prevention and control, and One Health collaboration to address the growing threat of AMR, said a release.
The workshop brought together Deputy Directors of Health and Family Welfare Services, District Surveillance Officers, District Epidemiologists, District Microbiologists, medical college faculty, programme officers, and public health professionals from across the State.
In her inaugural address, Dr. Rajini highlighted AMR as a major public health challenge and emphasised the need for rational antimicrobial use, stronger laboratory and surveillance systems, robust infection prevention practices, and coordinated action across human, animal, and environmental health sectors.
“The launch of KSAPCAR marks a significant step toward a coordinated, evidence-based response to antimicrobial resistance and is expected to accelerate implementation of AMR containment measures across Karnataka, helping preserve the effectiveness of life-saving antimicrobials for future generations,” the release added.

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.
This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.
“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”
In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.
“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.
Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.
The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)
More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, currently facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.
And Andrew Tate himself denounced the game in a Thursday email blast to his newsletter subscribers. “The establishment does not understand the male spirit,” he wrote from prison in Miami, where he and his brother Tristan Tate are fighting extradition to the UK on charges of rape, human trafficking, and assault. “No man wants to be a slave who breaks his back and gets nothing back.” Promoting a link to classes for building “AI systems,” he exhorted his readers: “Put down the game controller.”
If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.)
Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.
It’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.
What’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

Germany seems to be serious about a TikTok Europe takeover
The company has called the idea “nonsense.”
The Donald Trump-backed plan that resulted in a US-led takeover of TikTok's American business has apparently inspired some leaders in the European Union. This week Germany and Austria proposed a similar move for the app's European operation, and now the German government says that it has lined up investors willing to fork over as much as €25 billion (about $27.4 billion USD) to finance such an arrangement, Politico reports.
"It's a pan-European initiative and we think that they are able to invest around about 25 billion euros in that kind of business," Berlin culture minister Wolfram Weimer told the outlet. "And TikTok Europe should be open to sell 75% to 80% of the shares." Investors from five countries have expressed interest in such a deal, according to Weimer.
If you're thinking, "wait, I didn't know TikTok Europe was for sale," that's because... it isn't. At least not in any official sense. And unsurprisingly, it doesn't seem like ByteDance is at all interested in this arrangement, which a spokesperson has described as "nonsense." Of course, TikTok's US business wasn't officially for sale either. But we all know how that ended.
Whether a similar EU-led takeover of TikTok would actually gain any traction is unclear. The app isn't facing a ban in the region. And, as Bloomberg, pointed out earlier this week, Germany and Austria likely can't strongarm the company into a sale without the backing of the whole European Commission.
EU officials have raised similar concerns as their US counterparts about TikTok's influence and its ties to China. Last year, the EU fined the company more than $600 million for breaking EU privacy laws by funneling some EU user data to China. More recently, regulators have accused the company of breaking its Digital Services Act (DSA) with its "For You" algorithm. The EU Commission has told the company to change the design of its algorithm or it risks another massive fine.

South Korea on Friday reported its first case of cholera in 10 years, with health authorities urging people to take precautionary measures, use only safe water and wash their food properly.
The Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency said health workers confirmed cholera from test samples of a person who had visited a hospital emergency room in the southeastern port city of Changwon earlier this month, showing symptoms of vomiting and diarrhea.
The agency said the unidentified person, who recovered and was discharged on Tuesday, had not travelled overseas in the past two months. It said health workers were trying to trace the source of infection and the people the person had been in contact with.
It was the country's first case of cholera since 2016, when authorities identified three cases suspected to be caused by contaminated seafood. At least 162 people got sick in a larger outbreak in 2001.
The agency issued guidance urging people to stick to safe water and cooked food and to wash and peel fruits and vegetables. It also urged medical facilities to promptly test and report suspected cases.
