Uber Kids will let parents book trips for their children aged 10 to 12 years old
It's a limited pilot program available in just three locations for now.
Uber is giving parents and guardians the option to get their kids a special ride they can track and monitor, at least in a few specific locations. The ride-hailing company has started testing a new service called Uber Kids meant for children aged 10 to 12 years old. According to TechCrunch, it rolled out quietly in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee and Madison, Wisconsin over the past weeks.
The company already has Uber for Teens, but that program lets teenagers aged 13 to 17 make bookings from their own accounts, as long as they're part of a Family profile with a parent or guardian. For Uber Kids, only parents and guardians can order a ride for their children, and they must be present at pickup. Like on rides taken by teens, they'll also be able to access live video feed from inside the car to check in on their child in real time. Guardians themselves can come on the trip, along with additional minors, as long as they have their own parents' or guardians' permission. However, multi-stop rides aren't allowed on Uber Kids, and all trips booked under the program must be to a single destination.
Uber isn't sending Kids ride requests to all drivers on its network. The company is only inviting highly rated drivers to participate in the program, and those interested will have to complete a short course to be able to get in. They will also be required to enable audio and video recordings on their app, as well as to switch on camera and microphone access so that guardians can watch their kids on the ride. Uber says drivers will be notified once Live Video starts and that only the kids' guardians and safety agents will be able to access the realt-time feed.
Since Kids rides come with all these requirements, Uber will pay drivers $7 more compared to a standard UberX trip. Drivers will also get an additional $20 for the first Kids trip they complete. As TechCrunch notes, though, this is just a limited pilot program, and it's not clear if the company has plans to expand it to more locations in the future.

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang repeatedly humiliated and threatened employees during his tenure at the chipmaker, using violent language and public put-downs as part of his management style, a New York Times report said on Friday. The report, citing current and former employees, detailed incidents spanning nearly two decades, including threats to physically harm subordinates and insults directed at them during company meetings.
Huang had spoken about his approach to management during a fireside chat two years ago. “I’d rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,” he said.
The accounts offer details of the management culture at Nvidia, which Huang transformed from a graphics-chip business into a major player in the artificial intelligence industry over 33 years.
Public humiliation and threats at workplace
According to the report, Huang regularly reprimanded managers in front of their teams. In one instance, he went around a room and told managers he would kill them, a person familiar with the incident told the New York Times.
When he reached an employee in their 70s, Huang reportedly said the person was very old and that everyone was hoping they would drop dead.
Huang allegedly told one employee that their mother should have "aborted" them and threatened another that he would rip off their head and “pee on your brain”. 
In another incident, he reportedly told a subordinate he would rip both their arms off and beat them to death with them.
In a separate incident, Huang allegedly threw a water bottle at an executive during a fit of anger. He also reportedly told Jay Puri, Nvidia's then-executive vice-president of worldwide field operations: “I hope you get the flu and I hope it gets worse,” and “I hope you die and put us all out of our misery.”
Complaints over management style date back to 2005
The report traced complaints about Huang's behaviour to at least the mid-2000s. Michael Winston, a former senior vice-president of human resources, threatened legal action against Nvidia in 2005 after alleging he was fired for objecting to Huang's conduct.
During a two-day off-site meeting attended by around 50 employees, Huang allegedly made violent threats. “You have to do this, or I will rip your f–king heart out and stomp on it,” he reportedly said.
Winston wrote in notes at the time that Huang “thinks he can get away with anything” and that employees were “terrorized” and asking him to intervene.
Winston said he confronted Huang and warned him that his behaviour had “crossed the line” and could expose the company to lawsuits. Huang allegedly described the treatment as a “rite of passage” for employees and added: “It has good entertainment value,” according to the report.
Winston was fired that November. Huang reportedly told him he was “not a good fit” and threatened to ensure he would never work again if he sued the company.
Winston later filed a formal complaint with California's Department of Fair Employment and Housing and drafted a lawsuit. He reached a confidential settlement with Nvidia for $1 million before the lawsuit was filed. Winston died earlier this year.
Employees divided over Huang's leadership
Six current and former employees told the New York Times that Huang's management style had created a workplace culture they compared to Stockholm syndrome, in which hostages develop an emotional bond with their abusers.
As Nvidia grew and its employees became wealthy, Huang reportedly told groups of subordinates that money alone was no longer enough to motivate them and that he needed to humiliate them.
The report also said some executives adopted similar behaviour. Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, who works in marketing at Nvidia and effectively served as his de facto chief of staff, reportedly used terms such as “dead-face” for employees who remained expressionless after being reprimanded in meetings. 
She also allegedly called employees “goldfish” if they could not remember something, according to the Wall Street Journal.
Despite the accounts of his management style, Huang retained support among many employees. More than 200,000 people have signed an online petition calling for his reinstatement as CEO.
Nvidia's board has not supported the idea. Interim CEO Colette Kress, who was herself reportedly belittled by Huang during a company meeting, urged employees to “move forward” during the first all-hands meeting held without him, according to sources cited in the report.

The off-and-on switch for U.S. aid leads to a cliffhanger for Zambia and Zimbabwe
This is a story that starts with a remarkable success story. However, the ending has become a cliff hanger — with potentially grave consequences.
The success is clearcut and remarkable: Both Zambia and Zimbabwe are beating back devastating HIV/AIDS epidemics. These neighboring countries in southern Africa are on the cusp of controlling the virus.
Between 2000 and 2025, new infections dropped by 76% in Zambia and 80% in Zimbabwe. In both countries, more than 95% of infected individuals are identified and 95% of them are on treatment, according to data from the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS.
This progress is thanks, in large part, to billions of dollars in U.S. aid over the past two decades.
However, President Trump's new global health strategy is scrambling the landscape. After dismantling without warning the U.S. Agency for International Development in 2025, the administration is now hammering out government-to-government aid agreements as a new framework for how aid is provided.
That process leaves these two countries on very different paths and heading toward uncharted territory.
Just last month Zambian and U.S. officials signed an agreement — albeit for far less annual U.S. health aid than the country received in the past. Zimbabwe, in contrast, lost all U.S. health aid this fall after negotiations collapsed. To get an on-the-ground assessment of what has happened and what the future may hold, NPR interviewed a health worker in each country with experience in the HIV/AIDS world.
Zambia's aid agreement
When the aid agreement was announced on ZNBC — Zambia National Broadcasting Corporation on October 8 — it was branded as "a new chapter" in which the U.S. aid dollars flow primarily through the government and aims to build up the national health system.
The negotiations behind the aid agreement were secretive and became contentious, explains Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV/AIDS advocacy organization Health GAP "There was a massive scandal because activists were able to show that the agreement was planning to condition access to [U.S. global health] funding on access to [Zambia's] copper and rare earth minerals," Russell told NPR. Her organization helped expose this situation. Ultimately, the discussion about mineral rights was decoupled from the health agreement.
"I felt a bit relieved," says the Zambian health worker. But, with the aid agreement finally signed, she says, "the work now begins."
The health worker asked NPR not to use her name because she helped make public that mineral rights were in play and fears government retribution. She worries the Zambian government is ill equipped to face down the obstacles of the HIV/AIDS epidemic.
For example, homosexuality is illegal in Zambia. "Because [people are] scared of being arrested when they go to the public health facility, they would rather just stay home and face the consequences of their illness," she says, adding that such a decision not only leaves them without treatment it also lets the virus spread further via unprotected sexual relations, drug activity and other routes.
Under the previous system, huge amounts of U.S. aid went through international and local non-governmental groups who have staff specially trained to reach those vulnerable populations. This new agreement sidelines those groups and instead aims to build up the government's health systems rather than a parallel system, according to the U.S. strategy.
The Zambian health worker is also concerned the country could trumpet success in addressing HIV/AIDS but that thorough outreach and treatment records won't be kept and the right infrastructure may not be in place. For instance, she says, the government may say: " 'We've employed 5,000 community health workers!' "
But, she asks: "What is the quality? What capacity do they have? Who will they be serving? Which district? "
This health worker says many in the medical field have not received answers about what the future health systems will look like.
"It feels like a big mess, honestly. It's scary," she says, "It feels like doing it right is not the priority, but people's lives are at risk."
The Zambian Ministry of Health did not respond to requests for comment. But in the press conference announcing the agreement, Health minister Roma Chilengi said the department plans to recruit up to 40,000 health care workers, including 15,000 front line workers such as doctors, nurses, midwives, scientists, pharmacists, as well as community health workers.
However apprehensive this health worker is, she says that what's happening in Zambia is still better than the situation in neighboring Zimbabwe.
Zimbabwe's agreement collapses
In February, negotiations over the future of health aid between U.S. and Zimbabwean officials fell apart.
There was plenty of fingerpointing. Zimbabwean officials said the proposed agreement was lopsided. For example, Zimbabwe would have been obligated to provide data and biological samples of pathogens for research but would not have been guaranteed access to any treatments that result from that information. The U.S. Embassy in Zimbabwe said in a press release that the breakdown was regrettable. Whatever the reason, the result was clear. The country went from receiving well over $100 million in U.S. health aid each year to having none.
The health worker in Zimbabwe is baffled by this: "The U.S. put [in] 20 years of support — 20 years of support! — that's a huge investment which I think you cannot just throw away?" But he says that's what he's seeing.
This health worker also asked NPR not to use his name because he fears government retribution for speaking out. Without aid, he says, in his community, people's HIV medications are dwindling. "Within a period of six months or so, you will start to see a very huge impact," he predicts.
But he's concerned the world may never know the real impact. The U.S has had the best data collection and monitoring system for tracking and understanding the HIV epidemic and the response. Going forward the data coming out of Zimbabwe will be hard to verify or trust, he says. "We may not even know…if it's true or not."
The Ministry of Health and Child Care in Zimbabwe did not respond to NPR's requests for comment but this past summer, Zimbabwe's health minister, Dr. Douglas Mombeshora, pledged to expand the health workforce and infrastructure.
In a statement to NPR about the status of aid to the two countries, the U.S. State Department did not address the specific concerns of the health workers but said it's committed to working "with partner governments to define and advance shared global health priorities."
A subdued domestic response
As for public reaction in the two countries? It's been muted, the health workers say.
Both say that in their communities people are mad but that a public outcry has been muted because they fear reprisal from their governments. Russell, of Health GAP, echoed this experience saying many people who she works with are afraid to speak publicly: "The problem is retaliation" because they lived under authoritarian regimes.
"People are trying to not lose more than they've already lost," the health worker in Zambia says. "So even the anger is there, the frustrations are there, but you do not see this very publicly."
Similarly, the health worker in Zimbabwe says, "you can be mad, you can be angry, you can be whatever. But if you talk, you know the consequences of what will happen to you."
Public outcry or not, the global health world will be carefully observing how the next stage unfolds for these two countries.
Jennifer Kates, senior vice president and director of global and public health policy at the research organization KFF, says her team is scrutinizing all the information it can get about the agreement and implementation of the aid agreement in Zambia. And Zimbabwe "is an important one to watch," she says. "It's made a lot of progress, heavily relying on the U.S." — and now the future is uncertain.
For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

For a woman who has been a witness to some of the most significant political moments in modern Indian history, Sonia Gandhi likes to insist her life has been far from remarkable. “Oh, I don’t know that I would say it’s an extraordinary story,” she says, shifting uncomfortably.
It’s hard to reconcile this modest characterisation with the course her life has taken over the last 79 years. Born to a working-class family in a small town in northern Italy, today she sits at the heart of Indian political power, having weathered assassinations and personal tragedy to become one of the country’s most influential figures. She held Indira Gandhi’s bloodied body after the then-prime minster, her mother-in-law, was gunned down at their home in Delhi in 1984. She then became India’s first lady when her husband, Rajiv Gandhi, took his mother’s place as prime minister. And when Rajiv, too, was killed, she threw aside her distaste for politics to step up and lead his fragmenting party. In 2004, having taken Congress to electoral victory, she famously turned down the prime minister post. She can still boast of being the longest-serving president of Congress, both when India’s oldest political party was in power and later, when it became the flailing opposition. When Gandhi stepped down in 2017, her son Rahul was appointed her successor.
Gandhi’s entrance into Indian politics began in Cambridge in the 1960s when, at 18, while she was studying at a language school, she fell in love with a bright-eyed boy at a Greek restaurant. At the time, she had no idea that Rajiv was heir to India’s most consequential political dynasty. “It was a coup de foudre,” she says. “After that, nothing else really mattered. He was, first of all, a handsome man. But I think his eyes told of the way he was – of his inner self. He was loving, he was comforting, he was caring. Everything I could have possibly dreamed of.”
Only later would she learn that Rajiv’s grandfather was Jawaharlal Nehru, Indian freedom fighter and the country’s first prime minister, and his mother was Indira Gandhi, who in 1966 became India’s first female prime minister.
Does she still recognise herself in that innocent Italian girl who was swept off her feet and transplanted to an alien land and culture? “Not really,” she says quietly. “Too much has happened, too much has changed.”
We meet at the grand white Delhi bungalow she has lived in for 36 years – a relic of British colonial rule, where peacocks roam the grounds. It was in this house in 1991 that Gandhi heard her husband had been assassinated by Sri Lankan Tamil separatist terrorists. Over the years, as she took on the mantle of Congress leader, her home became the centre of party operations.
The ghosts of Congress leaders past loom large in her study. A painting of Nehru, photographs of Rajiv, a carved stone bust and portraits of Indira line the walls, while a painting of Mahatma Gandhi, the freedom fighter who shaped the ideology of Congress, also hangs prominently. Heavy gilded tomes fill the floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, and a long meeting table dominates the space, but the vibrant rugs, patterned blinds and scattered antiques suggest Gandhi’s own light touch.
In a dark blue sari and maroon blouse, her signature neat grey hair pushed back with a black headband, Gandhi looks every inch the composed Indian political matriarch as she sits on the sofa. The only hint of her heritage is softly accented English and recognisably Italian gesticulation.
She has, she confesses, been very nervous and tense about our meeting. Gandhi has not done an interview in a decade, and throughout her life in the public eye, has tried fiercely to maintain her privacy. She has only agreed to this rare meeting to discuss her forthcoming memoir, a strikingly personal account of her life, and has asked her daughter Priyanka, also a senior Congress leader, to sit in for moral support.
India’s media has often cast her as cold and aloof, yet today she seems warm, open and often a little unsure of herself. She’s anxious about how personal the book is, worried it will be eviscerated by the Indian media, but suggests that after years of “horrible and crazy things written about me”, it will be comforting for people to know “the truth”.
Gandhi has good reason to be nervous of the press. In today’s India, the mainstream media landscape has been crushed into submission by the hardline, rightwing Modi government and is largely devoted to promoting the prime minister’s agenda, while mercilessly attacking the Congress party, in particular the Gandhi family. She does not hold back on criticism of Narendra Modi – accusing him of being an “authoritarian force bent upon changing the very nature of our country” – and of his party, BJP, which she says has “systematically dismantled our democratic institutions”.
The Hindu nationalist vision of India that Modi has enacted over his 12 years in power is directly opposed to the pluralistic, secular India that was championed by successive Congress leaders and which remains enshrined in India’s constitution. It has led to well-documented oppression of the country’s minority groups, in particular its 200 million Muslims.
“More than disappointing, it’s very painful, having known a different India,” Gandhi says. “In parliament, we are not allowed to debate. In the past, there were discussions, there were meetings between the opposition and the government, there was consultation. Now the opposition counts for nothing.”
Since Modi came to power, she has had barely any interaction with him; he tends to avoid eye contact when they’re in a room together – a stark contrast to the past, when opposition leaders would often meet the government and “treat each other with cordiality”.
A “Congress-free India” is one of the openly declared goals of Modi’s BJP, resulting in highly personal attacks on Gandhi and her children, who have found themselves with numerous police cases filed against them. As we talk, Gandhi’s phone lights up with a call from her son Rahul – later, we learn a judge has just cleared him of defamation in one of these many cases, this time for criticising Modi’s home minister back in 2018. “They are very vindictive and vicious. There doesn’t seem to be a heart there,” Gandhi says.
So effective is the BJP’s crackdown on any form of dissent or criticism – what Gandhi describes as an “atmosphere of fear” – that her memoir almost didn’t see the light of day in India. Penguin Random House India were originally meant to release the book domestically, but after she sent them the manuscript she was met with a deafening silence. Gandhi says simply that Penguin were “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and that after she refused to make certain suggested edits, the publisher dropped the book, just a week before it was due to be announced. It will now be published by another imprint. In a statement, the publisher denied dropping the book, adding, “Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish Belonging because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances.”
Gandhi admits she was disappointed, though not altogether surprised, at what she sees as an attempt to censor her book. It is far from an isolated incident. In the days before we meet, Gandhi’s 26-year-old grandson, who is an artist and curator, is forced to take down dozens of his photographs depicting political protests that had been due to go on show in Delhi.
Gandhi had an early insight into the difficulties and loneliness of being a female leader in India’s deeply patriarchal society. When she arrived in India in 1968, she and Rajiv moved in with his mother, who at that time was two years into her first term as prime minister. Her husband, also a politician, had died years before.
They lived all together in another crumbling colonial Delhi bungalow, in relatively close and modest quarters. To outsiders, Indira was often seen as severe, an “iron lady”, and Gandhi admits that, to begin with, she was deeply intimidated by her formidable mother-in-law. Yet while Indira was imposing in public, she could be vulnerable in private, once confiding to Gandhi how terrified she was when she first bcame prime minister.
“In the newspapers she was portrayed as tough or harsh, but at home she was just like any other mother,” Gandhi says – although Indira’s notoriously explosive temper, frequently directed at political colleagues, would erupt through the house on occasion. Gandhi’s memoir recounts one incident where Indira lost her temper during a family dinner and threw her thali plate across the table.
Gandhi’s book documents the hostility Indira grappled with, both from political opponents and rightwing groups, but also from the old guard of her own party. “I saw her work day and night, constantly under pressure, constantly attacked,” Gandhi says. “It did affect her, like it would anyone. And of course, in that position, there is a loneliness. She had many interests and many friends, but it is a lonely kind of life.”
For several years, Gandhi says, her own life was “carefree”. She and Rajiv were madly in love, often embarrassing their children with public displays of affection that were highly unusual in Indian households at the time. “For this man, I was ready to do everything, to lose even my Italian identity,” she says. Rajiv was working as a commercial airline pilot, and as relations warmed with her mother-in-law, Gandhi set about redecorating the austere Delhi bungalow with some Italian flair, and learning how to cook Kashmiri food. After a traumatic miscarriage, she gave birth to two children, who were doted on by Indira. Even her pangs for fresh Italian ingredients, impossible to find in India in those days, eventually ebbed.
But in 1975 Indira would make the most controversial decision of her political life. Amid mounting political unrest, economic hardship and a concerted effort by the opposition to bring down the Congress government, Indira decided to impose a state of emergency on the country, in a bid to instil order. The repercussions were profound: the constitution was suspended, civil liberties and democratic freedoms abandoned, the media silenced and opponents detained en masse without trial. It lasted for almost two years, and is still seen as the darkest period of India’s democracy; it is regularly used to tarnish the Congress party today.
According to Gandhi, the family was split on the decision. Rajiv was against the move, telling his mother to wait for the next election, but her hotheaded younger son Sanjay pushed for it, arguing at one family dinner that the opposition would destroy his mother and telling her, “They must be stopped.” Sanjay’s forceful influence over his mother was a great source of public controversy at the time. Gandhi recalls that it inflamed tensions within the family, too; Rajiv attempted to confront his mother, but she refused to listen. “Keeping Sanjay in check could have prevented much of the damage that followed,” Gandhi writes in her book.
Today, she says it was a mistake for Indira to call the emergency, and that she believes her mother-in-law came to feel the same. “I always feel that Mrs Gandhi was a democrat at heart,” she says. “I know that many would laugh at this, but I believe she was never comfortable in the course of the emergency. I think it was sitting heavy on her.”
In the following years, Indira would lose one election and be returned to power in another. Rajiv would also be persuaded to enter politics after the premature death of Sanjay. But by 1984, darkness came to their door again.
Months of escalating violence had stricken the north Indian state of Punjab. As separatist militants prepared to declare an independent Sikh state, Indira authorised a military operation at one of the holiest sites in Sikhism, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, where the group were hiding out. The operation caused cataclysmic damage, killing Sikh pilgrims as well as militants, and led to desecration of the temple by tanks and heavy weaponry. Gandhi says that when her mother-in-law was shown images of the devastation, tears rolled down her face.
For Sikhs in India, it was a profound and painful attack on their religion, and Indira was inundated with threats. “She told us what to do in case she died – so she knew,” Gandhi says. “She was making preparations for her death. She told Rahul he must be brave and not to cry.” That summer Indira took her grandchildren on a trip to her ancestral home of Kashmir; Gandhi believes this was to “say goodbye”. Indira also defied advice to remove her Sikh bodyguards – something that turned out to be a fateful decision.
Gandhi was at home on 31 October when she heard what sounded like fireworks going off. Sprinting over to Indira’s office next door, she was confronted by her mother-in-law’s bloodied body, riddled with bullets, lying on the ground. Indira’s own Sikh bodyguards had opened fire on her in retribution for the attack on the Golden Temple.
What came next remains seared on Gandhi’s memory. After Indira was put into a car, she held her bleeding body and tried to revive her mother-in-law as they raced to the hospital. “There was blood everywhere and I realised she wasn’t replying to my questions. It seemed as if she had already gone,” she says.
Even after so many years, the story is clearly painful to recount and she speaks hesitantly, her soft voice growing even quieter. “I remember the drive from the house to the hospital was excruciating. There wasn’t much traffic, but it felt so slow. I also knew that because she wasn’t speaking, it must be over.”
Gandhi admits there are still parts of that experience she can’t bring herself to discuss. “I never talk about it. Only if I’m asked, then I struggle to.” Indira would be declared dead at the hospital. Her body was still lying there, cold, when Rajiv broke the news that he had been asked to step in as prime minister. Gandhi had begged him to stay out of politics and describes that conversation as a “knife going into my heart”.
In the aftermath of Indira’s death, she was traumatised and depressed, living “like a ghost”. Rajiv, too, had no time to grieve. Newly announced as prime minister, he immediately had to deal with deadly anti-Sikh riots that erupted after Indira’s death. He would later be accused of not doing enough to stop the bloodbath. “Rajiv never really showed his pain,” Gandhi says. “I remember seeing him in his mother’s study, on one of the chairs where she sat, with tears. But in public he felt he had to hide it.”
Fear took over their lives. The house became a fortress, with uniformed commandos stationed in the children’s bedrooms. Rahul and Priyanka were pulled out of school and no longer allowed to roam freely. She would worry if Rajiv didn’t come back from an engagement on time. He, meanwhile, would always want her by his side. “Fear was a very real thing,” she says. “My thought was always: he will be killed next.” By 1991, her premonition had come true.
A silence settles over the room as Gandhi struggles to recall how she went on living after Rajiv’s death. A Sri Lankan separatist militant had set off a suicide bomb while he was on the election trail, killing him instantly. Throughout our conversation, she still refers to Rajiv as “Papa”, as he is known to their children.
Priyanka, who sits on the sofa with us, interjects gently. She tells me how her mother would sit in the dark all day, listening to Mozart’s Requiem, engulfed by grief. “You were angry at him,” she says, speaking to her mother. “When you used to cry, you used to shout: how has he left me, why did he leave?”
Gandhi sits quietly for a moment. “After my mother-in-law was killed, we thought that, as we were always together, if something happens to one, it will happen to the other one,” she says. They had even written notes on how they wanted their funerals.
Yet when Gandhi’s sister pleaded for her to return to Italy, the thought was unfathomable. “India was my home, my children’s home,” she says. Gandhi last went back to Italy four years ago, when her mother died.
She found out later that, prior to the attack, Indian intelligence had intercepted death threats against Rajiv by the Sri Lankan separatist Tamil Tigers, angered over India’s intervention in the country’s civil war. However, these had been ignored by the newly elected government, who instead took away his top-level security. She still believes the truth of a wider conspiracy behind his death has yet to come out. The most recent commission to investigate it was shut down by the Modi government. “I don’t think we will get the truth now,” she says with a sigh.
Crucially, just as the foundation of her world was shattered, a wind of change was blowing across north India. A claim that a mosque in the city of Ayodhya was built on the ruins of an ancient Hindu temple had been gaining traction among hardline, rightwing Hindu nationalist organisations and political groups. In December 1992, supporters of the movement – including BJP figures – violently tore down the mosque.
Gandhi recalls crying as she witnessed the demolition on television. She says she knew then that they faced “a long battle for the secular nation that Mahatma Gandhi, Nehru and their colleagues had strived to build”. She accepts that failures of her own party in part contributed to the rise of the BJP and its hardline Hindutva politics. “I think we have been too complacent in many ways. There was a laissez-faire kind of an attitude,” she says. In 2024, Modi delivered on the BJP’s longstanding promise and inaugurated a vast Hindu temple in the place where the mosque had once stood.
Throughout her memoir, Gandhi is open about her distrust of politics, describing it as “menacing”, driven by “ambition, greed and hypocrisy”. But with Congress facing an existential threat and looking likely to fracture, Gandhi succumbed to mounting pressure and agreed to become its president in 1998. It was a decision, she says, driven by a sense of duty to her lost husband. Not only did she have to fight against her own ingrained shyness, she also had to take on political opponents in Hindi, her third language.
She insists she never had political ambition. Despite helping the party to win the most votes in the 2004 election, she shocked everyone by refusing to become prime minister. “It was clear in my mind I would never do it,” she says. “It was just not me.” Nonetheless, until she stepped back from the day-to-day of Congress leadership a few years ago, she had little time for herself. She would carry books to political events, history and autobiographies, to read on the way home. Music, both Indian classical and European operas, also became her solace. Having previously studied art restoration, “once in a while, I would slip away to an art exhibition”.
Today she stays out of the messy day-to-day of politics, though is still kept in the loop by her daughter and attends the occasional meeting. She finds joy in her small vegetable patch, but more than anything in spending time with her children and two grandchildren. Theirs has always been a dog-loving family (Priyanka once had seven golden retrievers) and Gandhi is devoted to her two jack russells, Noorie and Lapo, who were gifts from her son.
Nonetheless, the fortress of security that surrounds her home is a stark reminder of the restrictions still imposed on her freedom. Armed police man the barricades on the road outside, and my car is thoroughly inspected by security before I am allowed to drive through a towering metal gate and into her driveway.
While she was once credited with reviving the fortunes of Congress, over the past decade the Gandhi family have overseen its calamitous decline. Their previous government, in power till 2014, was marred by allegations of rampant corruption. (“In almost every single instance, the ministers resigned,” is Gandhi’s defence.) After taking over from his mother, Rahul lost the last three general elections to Modi, and Congress remains in power in only a few states. Meanwhile, the BJP’s Hindutva has become the country’s dominant political ideology. As the family has maintained its control, Congress has been unable to shake off allegations that it is nepotistic and run by political elites.
Why can’t Congress free itself from the Gandhi family’s leadership, I ask? She is dismissive, perhaps a nerve touched. “You would have to ask the party,” she says. Gandhi also skates over the question of nepotism, simply saying, “We all fight elections: we win them, we lose them. All of us have.” But after so many losses, can a Gandhi-led Congress still be a credible alternative to the BJP? While she is adamant they can, many in the country remain unconvinced.
It is true that we are meeting at an interesting moment, for both Modi and the bruised opposition. As gen Z youth erupted on to the streets in protest against the government over the summer – satirically calling themselves the “Cockroaches” after an online joke transformed into a serious political movement – the long-crushed space for dissent has opened up.
In recent weeks, young Indians have once again been taking to the streets against the government, despite being met with draconian state force. The question of whether they can shake the BJP’s grip on power remains to be seen; so far, the Cockroach movement has kept its distance from the opposition alliance. But “what encourages me is young people are coming out and demonstrating,” Gandhi says. “With determination, they’re calling out the government on things that are not right. I feel like this is a real shift.”
Congress, too, has become more energised than it has been for many years. Images of Rahul and Priyanka being manhandled by police as they tried to protest against the government have gone viral in recent weeks. After once pleading with her children to stay out of politics, Gandhi now says, “It’s good that they’re there. Now more than ever before.” The Gandhi family, it seems, are not done just yet.

Goalkeeper involved in fatal collision gets 12-game ban
- Published
FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono has been given a 12-match suspension by the Spanish football federation's disciplinary committee after his challenge which resulted in the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.
Owono, 25, was sent off after colliding with De Miguel during the closing stages of the second-tier match between their two respective sides on 2 November.
De Miguel died the following day, aged 30.
The disciplinary committee said it had to base its decision "on the facts expressly recorded in the referee's report", which stated the player "was sent off for 'violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play'.
"The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge."
The committee added the "nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances" means that "the maximum sanction, a 12-match suspension, is justified".
Separately, the federation has decided the game between the two sides, which was abandoned seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred, will not be replayed.
"This avoids having to resume play from the precise moment at which the tragic incident occurred," it said.
The teams were drawing 2-2 at the time and that result will now stand, with a federation committee saying that was the "most respectful course of action, given the extraordinary and tragic circumstances of this case".
Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on 4 November, in which he said he was experiencing "the most difficult days" of his life and felt "enormous pain" about De Miguel's death.
On Thursday, FC Andorra manager Carles Manso said Equatorial Guinea international Owono is yet to decide whether he will return to football following the incident.
Manso said Owono is currently spending time with his family and is "completely free to make any decision" with regard to a potential return, adding: "What we have to do is support him in every way and be close to him.
"We will give him space so that he feels completely free to make any decision, whether he wants to return, when, or if he does not want to return.
"When he feels it is appropriate and when he feels genuinely ready to take a decision like that [he will do so]."

In mid-November, following a nationwide halt to U.S. flight departures, social media users shared claims about connections between Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy; his son-in-law, U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso, a Wisconsin Republican; and Air Space Intelligence — the company behind a new artificial intelligence-powered system used by the Federal Aviation Administration.
On Nov. 13, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after communications problems affected air traffic control facilities. The incident happened three days after the agency announced the nationwide expansion of an AI-supported traffic management system called SMART, developed by ASI.
Some posts claimed Alfonso had financial ties to ASI or received the FAA contract through Duffy, while others linked the company to the shutdown. For instance, one Facebook post (archived) read:
On Friday, the FAA grounded every plane in America.
The AI air traffic system at the center of it belongs to Air Space Intelligence. In June, Sean Duffy's department gave them an $875 million contract.
Before that, the company's PAC donated to Duffy's son-in-law, 26-year-old Michael Alfonso. He just won Duffy's old seat in Congress.
Americans deserve answers.
Another post (archived) on X stated, "Sean Duffy's son in law owns the AI company responsible for this FAA disaster yall."
Versions of the claim circulated on multiple social media platforms, including Reddit, X, Instagram and Facebook. Snopes readers also asked whether Alfonso or Duffy owned ASI, whether Alfonso received a multimillion-dollar FAA contract and whether campaign donations influenced the deal.
In short, Air Space Intelligence's PAC did contribute to Alfonso's campaign in March, and the company later received an FAA contract worth up to $875.95 million. However, we found no evidence that Alfonso owned ASI or that the donation influenced the contract award. The FAA also denied that the company's SMART system caused the Nov. 13 shutdown, and rather pointed to problems with its older communications network.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract and that the campaign donation broke no laws or ethics rules, adding, "Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check." The FAA said in a statement that "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel." We have also reached out to Air Space Intelligence and will update this report if we receive a response.
Here's what we know about the rumor:
ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign
According to a filing with the Federal Election Commission, Air Space Intelligence's political action committee donated $2,500 to Alfonso's congressional campaign on March 31:
(Federal Election Commission)
Alfonso's campaign also reported the same contribution:
(Federal Election Commission)
Some social media posts and articles, however, mentioned a larger sum of $12,500. That likely stemmed from a Raw Story article, which cited that amount, but later issued a correction.
News outlets reported on Alfonso's campaign donations even before the FAA shutdown. For instance, in March, ProPublica reported that his campaign received money from lobbyists and companies with interests before the Department of Transportation.
Did Alfonso or Duffy have financial ties to ASI?
Some social media posts claimed Alfonso owned Air Space Intelligence. Snopes readers also asked whether he invested in the company or benefited financially from its FAA contract.
However, we found no evidence supporting these claims. Neither Alfonso nor Duffy was listed among ASI's founders or executives. Alfonso's financial disclosure from April also didn't list any investment in ASI, although it only covered the period until October 2025. Similarly, Duffy's 2026 financial disclosure didn't list ASI among his investments.
In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso said, "Family ties don't earn anyone special treatment, and my father-in-law knows better than anyone that I think for myself." His team did not directly answer whether he ever owned shares or had any other financial interest in ASI.
Who received the $875M FAA contract?
Some social media posts claimed that Duffy awarded a multimillion-dollar FAA contract directly to his son-in-law, sometimes describing it as a no-bid contract. For example, one Bluesky user wrote, "In a surprise to no one, Sean Duffy gave a No Bid contract to his son-in-law to install the AI program into the FAA's system."
However, the USAspending.gov database showed the contract was awarded to Air Space Intelligence, not Alfonso:
(www.usaspending.gov)
The contract began on June 23 and could run for 12 years. Its maximum potential value is $875.95 million, but this does not mean ASI has already received all of that amount.
"No laws or House Ethics rules were violated," Alfonso's team told us via email, adding that "By law, PACs can give up to $5,000 per election. Nobody trades an $875 million federal contract for a $2,500 check."
According to federal records, the FAA received 12 offers before awarding the contract to ASI. The records classified the award as competitive, although they did not identify the other bidders or explain how ASI was selected. Bloomberg reported "the startup beat out larger competitors Palantir Technologies Inc. and Thales SA."
The FAA said in a statement that: "each FAA contract goes through a rigorous, competitive process guided by nonpartisan career experts and personnel. The FAA awarded the contract to Air Space Intelligence (ASI) following an innovative challenge with three vendors who demonstrated the highest levels of reliability, operational performance, and efficiency." The agency did not say whether Duffy was personally involved in the decision, or whether there was any potential conflict of interest involving him or Alfonso.
The FAA announced its search for a company to develop the system in September 2025, months before ASI's PAC donated to Alfonso's campaign, and announced ASI as the winner in June. We found no public evidence that the donation influenced the contract award.
Alfonso's team said he had no part in awarding the FAA contract, pointing out that he was a congressional candidate at the time, and not a government official. In a statement to Snopes, Alfonso also said, "I can't be bought," adding that he would consider each bill separately, including any future FAA funding requests, and "vote based on what's best for Wisconsin."
What caused the Nov. 13 FAA shutdown?
The FAA said its new AI system, SMART, did not cause the nationwide flight shutdown on Nov. 13. During a news briefing the next day, Duffy explained it "is a system that's not tied into or connected to the systems that went down yesterday. It's a tool that gives a prompt to one of our flight managers that they can accept or deny, but it's just better information flowing to them," summarizing that "SMART had zero impact on the occurrences yesterday."
Similarly, ASI wrote on X on Nov. 13 that the "current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."
According to a Nov. 15 statement, the issue involved the FAA's older communications network. The agency identified two possible locations connected to the problem: a site in Arkansas, where contractor L3Harris was installing a new router, and another in Texas. L3Harris confirmed in a news release it was cooperating with the FAA's investigation. As of this writing, the exact cause of the shutdown was still under investigation.

Home services marketplace Urban Company has raised ₹2,500 Cr through a qualified institutional placement (QIP), attracting bids worth over ₹15,000 Cr, more than 6X the issue size. The issue opened on November 16 (Monday) and closed yesterday. More than 60 investors submitted bids, with shares allocated to 33 investors. Of these, 13 did not hold Urban Company shares before the issue. Mutual funds accounted for more than 50% of the allocation, including SBI Mutual Fund, ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund, Mirae Asset Mutual Fund, Invesco Mutual Fund, Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund, Kotak Mutual Fund and Nippon India Mutual Fund, among others. Domestic insurers HDFC Life, Bajaj Life Insurance, and Edelweiss Life also participated. Global institutional investors included Goldman Sachs Asset Management, Norges Bank Investment Management, Amundi, Pictet, and Manulife, while Premji Invest was among the domestic investors. Consequently, Urban Company's Fund Raise Committee approved the allotment of 16.02 Cr equity shares at an issue price of ₹156 apiece, marking a 3.1% discount to the floor price of ₹161.03 per share. The company had said earlier that it may offer a discount of up to 5% to the floor price for the QIP. Funding InstaHelp’s Expansion Urban Company outlined the fundraise plan last month to invest across its businesses, strengthen InstaHelp’s market position, and pursue acquisitions. According to its preliminary placement document, the company plans to deploy ₹600 Cr towards expanding InstaHelp’s service professional ecosystem. This includes minimum earnings guarantees, referral payouts, and training and onboarding costs. The allocation comprises ₹150 Cr in FY27, ₹300 Cr in FY28, and ₹150 Cr in FY29. InstaHelp allows households to book service professionals for tasks such as cleaning, mopping, laundry, and basic meal preparation. The company plans to build service professional availability ahead of demand when entering new neighbourhoods. Urban Company has earmarked another ₹540 Cr for marketing, ₹200 Cr for technology development and cloud infrastructure, ₹85 Cr for lease rentals for offices and training centres, and ₹50 Cr for research and development for Native products. A portion of the proceeds will also fund potential acquisitions and general corporate purposes. Native, Urban Company’s home products business, currently sells water purifiers and smart locks. Yesterday, the company’s board approved adding residential air conditioners to the portfolio, following in-principle approval to explore the category last month. The fundraise follows a widening of Urban Company’s consolidated net loss to ₹182.5 Cr in Q2 FY27, more than tripling from ₹59.3 Cr a year earlier. Operating revenue rose 41.4% to ₹537.3 Cr from ₹380 Cr, while total expenses increased 61.5% to ₹745.7 Cr. The fresh capital will support further expansion while Urban Company builds demand and service professional availability. Management has set FY31 as InstaHelp’s breakeven target, indicating a prolonged investment period for the business. Shares of Urban Company were trading 3.81% lower at ₹169.05 on the BSE at 09:50 IST.

Moving beyond test preparation, listed edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW) has now said that it is establishing a “greenfield digital” university. In an investor presentation, the edtech platform said that the digital university has already been notified by the Punjab government. The digital university plans to offer 16 undergraduate, postgraduate, diploma and certificate courses including BCA, BBA, B.Com, BA, M.Com, MCA, MBA, among others. The edtech major also claimed that the nearly 15,000 sq ft campus will be self-financed and will operate on an asset-light model. Admissions are slated to begin in July 2027. The listed company has opted for a digital delivery model that pairs online degrees with competitive exam preparation (such as B.Com-CA and BA-UPSC combinations). “After Class 12, many learners take a degree elsewhere. PWDU (PW digital university) keeps them with PW, from exam prep to a degree to a career,” read the presentation. PW has received authorisation from the state government under the “Punjab Private Digital Open Universities Policy”. The digital university will have a 3 acre physical campus, but it will serve only as the headquarters for administrative purposes. No regular classes will be held on campus. The announcement came on the same day as the company’s maiden Investor Day in Mumbai. At the event, the company outlined an ambitious target of ₹9,000 Cr to ₹10,000 Cr in revenue by fiscal year 2029-30 (FY30). This implies a 2.5X jump from the ₹3,900 Cr top line that the company reported in FY26 The company expects this growth surge to come on the back of its online business, which it projects will contribute around “two-thirds” of its total revenue by FY30. At its maiden Investor Day in Mumbai, the edtech giant said that it expects its revenue to rise at an compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 25% between FY27 and FY30. It is also targeting an EBITDA margin of over 20% by FY30. “Our FY30 ambition is about profit growing faster than revenue. We will stay disciplined with capital and report our progress every year,” said PhysicsWallah chief financial officer (CFO) Amit Sachdeva. Over the next three to five years, PW plans to focus on premiumisation to drive higher average revenue per user (ARPU), leverage AI to drive efficiencies, scale vernacular courses and tap into the pre-foundation (Class 6 to Class 8) and upskilling markets. The bullish outlook comes as PW reported a consolidated net profit of ₹143.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 106% from ₹69.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also rose 18.2% to ₹1,242.3 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹1,051.3 Cr in Q2 FY26.

The story so far: After 26 years of holding on to its measles elimination status, the United States lost this distinction. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organisation (PAHO) revoked the United States’ measles elimination status. This was after over 5400 cases of measles were reported in the U.S. in 2026.
This is the highest annual total since 1989-91, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention(CDC). As per data put out by the Unicef, 96% of cases are in unvaccinated people or those with unknown vaccination status. Children under five account for 18% of cases and those aged 5-19 for 40%.

Microplastics in the Yamuna in Delhi are accompanied by a complex mixture of organic chemicals, including pharmaceutical residues, pesticides and industrial effluents, with many of these substances classified as human-health and environmental hazards, according to a new study by University of Delhi researchers.
The study, published in the 'Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances' in September 2026, examines microplastic pollution and associated chemical profiles at eight locations along a 48.8-km stretch of the river in Delhi -- from its entry at Palla to its exit at Asgarpur Jagir -- highlighting how pollution patterns vary across agricultural, residential, industrial, recreational and forested areas.
Researchers recovered 2,289 microplastic particles from the samples, with an average abundance of 3.18 particles per litre. The analysis identified 321 distinct chemical compounds across the samples, of which 50 were detected in extracts of recovered microplastic fractions at four or more locations.
Of these 50 compounds, 36 corresponded to structures with Global Harmonized System (GHS) hazard classifications, covering categories such as carcinogenicity, reproductive toxicity, acute toxicity and aquatic hazards.
Seven compounds were detected across all eight sampling locations, including 2-naphthylamine, lidocaine and monobutyl phthalate, the study found.
The researchers also identified pharmaceutical compounds such as atomoxetine, domperidone and telmisartan, along with agrochemical-related substances, including diuron and thiamethoxam.
Radhey Shyam Sharma, head of the Department of Environmental Studies at University of Delhi and one of the co-authors of the study, said the findings highlight the need to look beyond microplastic particles and examine the complex chemical mixtures present in river ecosystems.
"The microplastics problem, along with this cocktail of organic and inorganic substances, needs to be looked at through the lens of mixture toxicity. The land-use pattern has also been explored in the study," Sharma said.
He stressed the importance of nature-based solutions, including strengthening vegetation along riverbanks and protecting natural river ecosystems, to minimise pollution-related risks.
"Vegetation ecosystems can help prevent pollution from entering the river. Natural ecosystems and riverbanks need to be strengthened to minimise these risks. The focus should be on nature-based solutions," he said.
The study found significant variations in microplastic abundance across the eight locations. The highest concentration was recorded at the recreational-hydraulic site near the barrage, followed by a floodplain area where multiple drains converge.
The lowest abundance was recorded at the agricultural entry point at Palla and a forested stretch of the river.
The researchers noted that the Delhi stretch of the Yamuna receives inputs from 22 tributary drains carrying partially treated or untreated sewage, agricultural runoff and industrial effluents, contributing to the diverse pollution profile.
Polyethylene and polypropylene were the predominant polymers identified, accounting for 44.1 per cent and 27.3 per cent, respectively, of the spectrally identified particles.
The researchers cautioned that the detection of hazardous compounds does not, by itself, establish actual exposure or ecological risk. The chemical findings were based on screening-level identification and require further confirmation through quantitative analysis.
They also pointed out that microplastic abundance alone cannot capture the chemical complexity of river pollution, underlining the need for spatially detailed monitoring of both particles and associated chemical substances.

As U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., announced his bid to serve as the next speaker of the House following Democrats' sweeping congressional victories in the 2026 midterm elections, social media users were quick to claim he received money from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a pro-Israel lobbying group.
Posts on X, Instagram and Facebook accused Jeffries of working for Israel's interests as a major recipient of AIPAC funding. Snopes readers also searched the site and emailed us seeking the truth about the matter.
A petition circulated online, garnering more than 930,000 signatures as of this writing, asking Democrats to select someone else as speaker. "Picking our own speaker who does not represent Israel first, is where we start," one of the top comments on the petition read.
The claim was true — Jeffries has received money from AIPAC. He has an extensive history with the lobbying group, and they have publicly expressed mutual support.
We looked at the official Federal Election Commission record (archived) of Jeffries' campaign funding, and found AIPAC had given many thousands of dollars to Jeffries over the years.
OpenSecrets, a nonprofit aimed at tracking money in U.S. politics, estimated Jeffries had received approximately $1.74 million through 2024 from pro-Israel donors generally, putting him slightly ahead of Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. TrackAIPAC, an organization focused specifically on AIPAC and other pro-Israel lobbyists, connected $1.5 million in such donations to Jeffries.
AIPAC identified Jeffries by name in a congratulatory post on Nov. 4, writing on X (archived) that "AIPAC members are determined to expand their political activism in the cycles ahead."
Jeffries has a long history of support for Israel, telling a crowd in 2014: "Israel today, Israel tomorrow, Israel forever." He told the American Jewish Committee in June 2023 that he'd been to Israel six times, more than any other country he'd visited. "I'm from New York City, where we consider Jerusalem to be the sixth borough," he reportedly said.
The Times of Israel reported on Nov. 6: "While some in that younger generation have pushed for a tougher US stance on Israel, Jeffries does not belong to that camp and is likely to toe the line set by his predecessor Pelosi, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and US President Joe Biden, who have long made a point of boasting their pro-Israel bona fides."
As U.S. voters, particularly younger constituents, signal increasing opposition to U.S. support for Israel amid its war in Gaza — which the U.N. declared a genocide — it remains unclear how this will shape Jeffries' stance on Israel.

Neeraj Chauhan is a senior journalist with Hindustan Times and an investigative reporter specialising in national security, terrorism, organised crime, narcotics, corruption, financial crime and complex investigations. With over 21 years of experience across Hindustan Times, The Times of India, The Indian Express and The Pioneer, he has built deep expertise in India’s internal security and law-enforcement landscape. Neeraj has extensively covered India’s principal investigative, intelligence and security agencies, including the NIA, CBI, ED, IB, R&AW, MHA and other central security forces. His work has included deeply reported investigations into terrorism, terror financing, cross-border crime, narcotics trafficking, cybercrime, financial fraud and political and corporate corruption. He has reported on some of the most significant terror attacks and security developments in India over the past two decades, including the Delhi serial blasts, the 26/11 Mumbai attacks, the 2019 Pulwama terror attack and the recent Pahalgam attack. His reporting has also chronicled the rise and decline of the Indian Mujahideen, the activities and subsequent crackdown on the Popular Front of India (PFI), Islamist extremist networks, the conflict in Jammu and Kashmir, insurgencies in the Northeast and Maoist violence. Some of Neeraj’s major breaking stories are in Aryan Khan drug case, Sushant Singh Rajput suicide, interception of a 3,000-kg Afghan heroin consignment worth about ₹21,000 crore at Mundra port, Sri Lanka easter bombings, Aarushi-Hemraj murders in Noida, 2G scam, coal block allocation scam, AgustWestland VVIP chopper deal and major bank frauds and extradition cases involving Mehul Choksi, Nirav Modi and Vijay Mallya. His reporting is marked by an ability to cultivate sources, analyse confidential and complex documents, and follow investigations over several years—from the initial breakthrough to chargesheets, trials and international legal proceedings. He specialises in making complicated security and investigative developments accessible while examining their wider implications for governance and public policy. A Chevening South Asia Journalism Programme Fellow at the University of Westminster, Neeraj also spent time at the Financial Times as part of the fellowship. He was also a Robert Bosch Media Ambassadors India-Germany Fellow, studying at the University of Tübingen and working with Der Tagesspiegel in Berlin. He has previously taught investigative journalism and crime reporting as a guest faculty member at the Times School of Journalism. Over more than two decades, Neeraj has established himself as an authoritative voice on India’s national security and investigative landscape, with his reporting closely followed by officials, investigators, lawyers, policymakers and readers seeking insight into some of the country’s most complex and consequential developments.
NIA seeks UAE documents, permission to question individuals in Flydubai hijacking attempt probe
NIA chief Rakesh Aggarwal said the agency had sought documents and permission to question individuals in the UAE over the September 30 incident.
The National Investigation Agency (NIA) has sent a mutual legal assistance (MLA) request to the UAE seeking documents and permission to interrogate “certain” individuals there in connection with the September 30 hijacking attempt involving Flydubai flight FZ-1073, in which Indian pilot Smit Machchhar was attacked by his co-pilot, NIA director general Rakesh Aggarwal said on Friday.
“We have already sent a MLA request to the UAE asking for copies of certain documents and also permission to examine some persons. We are waiting for a response,” Aggarwal told reporters at a media briefing in Delhi at the end of the two-day counter-terrorism conference of the NIA.
“As far as the objective of the investigation is concerned, there are issues related to pilots (including the attacker, identified as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami), like footprints of his friend circle, etc., which we are looking at,” Aggarwal said.
He further added that the agency would move ahead with the probe as soon as it received the documents from the UAE.
On September 30, Smit Machchhar was attacked with the cockpit’s crash axe by his co-pilot, Omani national Hamam al-Hammami, who, according to UAE investigators, attempted to seize control of the Tel Aviv-bound plane. Despite suffering deep cuts to his head and hands, Machchhar unlocked the cockpit door of flight FZ-1073, which had taken off from Dubai, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker. A reserve crew member on board then flew the Boeing 737 MAX 8, with 174 people on board, to an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, attorney general of the UAE, said in a statement in October that al-Hammami was radicalised while studying in Australia. The attacker, al-Shamsi said, drew inspiration from the 9/11 terrorist attacks of 2001. After hijacking the plane, his target was the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv.
Leaders from across the world, including Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have praised Machchhar for averting a “9/11-like tragedy”. Israel had announced that it would honour Machchhar with the Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism for his “sheer bravery and sound professionalism” in averting a catastrophe.

Union minister for road transport and highways Nitin Gadkari has urged states to adopt the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, citing their potential to expand livelihood opportunities amid crackdowns on bike taxi operations across several states. The remarks came during the 'RIDE – Moving India Forward' event in New Delhi, organised in collaboration with Uber, Ola, Rapido, Bharat Taxi, Zomato, Swiggy and Porter. Gadkari said aggregator platforms have already generated 4 Cr jobs following the introduction of the government's policy framework, despite its adoption by only two states. "If the whole country accepts this, then 10 Cr jobs will be created. And the food and other delivery apps working in this are different. So, if 10 Cr and 8-10 Cr are there, then 18 Cr jobs will be created here," the minister said. He added that these platforms could generate employment without requiring government capital expenditure. “Not everyone can get a government job. Not even so many governments have jobs," Gadkari said. The minister said he has written to state governments, urging them to adopt the framework and enable app-based mobility services to create livelihoods, particularly for people from socially, economically and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds. He also highlighted the expansion of app-based services beyond passenger transport into food and goods delivery, creating opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship. He cited e-rickshaws and e-carts as examples of technology transforming traditional occupations and reducing physical hardship. Gadkari further emphasised the need to strengthen last-mile connectivity in rural areas, arguing that better access to transport services could help people travel to schools and cities, while enabling farmers to take their produce to urban markets. "Children will be able to go to school. They will start coming to the city. If they can bring their milk, fruits, flowers, vegetables to the city, then the economy can change," he said. On regulation, he said the ministry’s objective is to support the sector’s growth while protecting drivers and passengers, and called on companies to share suggestions to improve the framework. “The aim of the ministry is not to control anyone. All of us should come together, think together and work together,” he said. State-Level Bike Taxi Crackdowns Gadkari's push for wider adoption of the aggregator framework comes amid regulatory uncertainty and enforcement action against bike taxi operators across several states. In Kolhapur, the RTO seized 10 two-wheelers allegedly operating as Rapido bike taxis and said no bike-taxi app had been granted permission to operate in the district. In Odisha, the Crime Branch directed Uber and Rapido to discontinue their bike taxi services, terming them unauthorised over the alleged commercial use of private, non-transport two-wheelers. Meanwhile, Karnataka's bike taxi dispute remains before the Supreme Court, with the state challenging a January 2026 High Court ruling that allowed operations to resume. In August, the state’s transport department inspected 220 two-wheelers in Bengaluru, booked 71 and seized 70. In May, Maharashtra’s transport minister Pratap Sarnaik urged the state's cybercrime department to shut down bike taxi services operated by Ola, Uber and Rapido and file FIRs against their management. What The Guidelines Cover Issued on July 1, 2025, under Section 93 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the guidelines provide a framework for states to license and regulate aggregators. They prescribe five-year licences, a ₹5 Lakh grant fee and security deposits of ₹10-50 Lakh, depending on fleet size. Surge pricing is capped at twice the base fare, while drivers using their own vehicles must receive at least 80% of the applicable fare. Aggregators must provide ₹5 Lakh health insurance and at least ₹10 Lakh term insurance for drivers. Requirements also cover training, tracking, panic buttons, round-the-clock support and grievance redressal. Drivers can work across platforms. Clause 23 lets states permit private motorcycles to carry passengers through aggregators under Section 67(3), subject to driver checks, licensing, insurance and training. States may levy daily, weekly or fortnightly fees. This is optional, rather than nationwide permission for private bike taxis. Other aggregator vehicles require applicable permits, including contract carriage permits for cars carrying paying passengers. Subsequent amendments allow apps to offer voluntary tipping only after a trip, with the entire amount credited to the driver. They also require an option to choose a driver of the same gender, wherever available, including female drivers for women passengers.

On the intervening night of November 8 and 9, over 250 PM2.5 data points from Delhi were missing on the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) website, according to an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).
Scientist and air quality analyst Manoj Kumar tweeted the statistics in the early hours of November 9. According to him, out of the 59 monitoring stations, as seen on the official website of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
Missing hourly PM2.5 data raises concerns over Delhi’s air quality assessment.
Since midnight on 8 November until 5 am on 9 November, 227 hourly PM2.5 observations were missing across 59 CPCB monitoring stations in Delhi. Only 14 stations reported complete data, while the remaining 45 had at least one missing hourly observation.
A key concern is that many missing readings occurred when concentrations approached the monitoring instruments’ upper measurement limit of 1,000 µg/m³. These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification.
Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
There is also an unusual pattern at some stations. IGNOU Maidan Garhi, Cantonment Area, Siri Fort and Tikri Kalan recorded PM2.5 concentrations below 30 µg/m³ (Cleanest) during parts of this episode. Given the pollution levels elsewhere, these readings warrant verification for possible instrument or data-quality issues before being used in final averages or AQI calculations.
Reliable air-quality assessment during pollution episodes requires both complete data and transparent treatment of readings that exceed instrument measurement limits.
— Dr. Manoj Kumar (@manoj_kumar_nr) November 9, 2026
Air Quality Index, or AQI, turns air quality data for eight pollutants into one number and one name, providing an easy-to-understand picture of air quality. According to the All India AQI Dashboard, the pollutants are PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, Pb, and NH3. (Lead is not monitored at every station.)
Delhi’s average AQI on the night of Diwali was as follows, according to the CPCB.
However, between 1 am and 3 am on the Diwali night, over 30 monitoring stations were not showing any PM2.5 data. Over the course of the night, more stations failed.
A day after, as the mystery of missing data caused an outrage, the hourly air quality readings missing from the CPCB website became available on the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) website, which showed that the PM2.5 concentration went up to a staggering 3500 micrograms per cubic metre and beyond, which is around 60 times its standard value.
Below is the reading from Mundka station:
Below is the reading from JNU station:
Why does the Missing Data Matter?
India’s air quality figures come from monitoring stations run by state pollution control boards and committees, such as DPCC in Delhi. Stations send their readings to CPCB every 15 minutes. CPCB calculates each station’s AQI by finding a sub-index for every pollutant and taking the highest one. It then publishes the results on its portal, the SAMEER app and its daily bulletin.
A sub-index is the AQI score for a single pollutant on its own. Each pollutant is measured in different units and has a different “safe” range. For example, PM2.5 is in micrograms per cubic metre, and CO is in milligrams per cubic metre. So CPCB converts each pollutant’s reading to the same 0-500 scale, and that converted number is its sub-index.
If the PM2.5 has a sub-index of 75, SO2 has 63, and NO2 has 38, the station’s overall AQI is the highest of these, so here it is 75, driven by PM2.5. One bad pollutant is enough to push the AQI into a worse category, even if the others are fine.
If one looks carefully at the above screenshot from 12 midnight on November 9 from the Anand Vihar monitoring station, one would see that the 24-hour average of the PM2.5 pollutant is the 24-hour average AQI for that particular monitoring station. One would also note that the highest average sub-index determines the AQI.
Now, if PM2.5, which gives a measure of fine particulate matter in the air and is also highest during Diwali due to the bursting of firecrackers, goes missing, the average AQI reading underestimates the pollution in the air to a great extent. According to a Hindustan Times report, if one considers the released readings, Delhi’s AQI for 24 hours until 9 am on November 9 was 384 on a 500 scale against the 370 figure published by CPCB.
Why did the Data Go Missing?
According to Kumar’s post on X (shared when the missing data had not been released), Mundka recorded the highest number of missing hourly observations (10), followed by Dwarka Sector 8, IIT Delhi, Nehru Nagar, Pusa IITM and Uttam Nagar, with eight missing hours each.
Interestingly, the highest reading also came from Mundka at 3,744 µg/m³ at 2 am on November 9. JNU was at 3,023 at 4 am the same night and NSUT’s West Campus at 3,008 at 5 am. Eleven of DPCC’s stations went past 2,000 micrograms per cubic metre.
The CPCB released an official statement on November 10 addressing the data gaps, saying that particulate analysers like PM2.5 were calibrated for 0-1,000 µg/m³. Under the automated validation, hourly readings beyond that range are treated as “outside range” and left out of the computation. CPCB conceded this “may appear as a data gap” during extreme episodes like Diwali firecracker bursting. Those hours don’t count towards the 24-hour average for that station. It also stated that the methodology for processing data beyond the system’s design range is “under review”, with internal deliberations underway.
On November 11, Kumar posted on X, if the 255 missing PM2.5 data points were replaced with 1,000 µg/m³, the upper measurement limit cited by CPCB, the average showed a 49% increase, from 269 to 400 µg/m³.
Alt News spoke to Kumar, who also told us that while the DPCC continued to record data above 1000 micrograms per cubic metre, it was the CPCB, the body ultimately entrusted with calculating and releasing AQI findings, that did not register it. “DPCC had measured and displayed PM 2.5 concentration above 1000 on that day. But it was not reflected on the CPCB website.”
Explaining the process and the gaps, Kumar said, “Let’s say that the instrument’s operating range is between 0 and 1000. But if it is going above 1000, there will be some uncertainty, but uncertainty can be estimated.”
Even in his November 9 post, Kumar made the point that the readings had gone missing as the concentration readings approached 1000. “These observations should not simply be treated as missing when calculating hourly or daily averages or deriving AQI. Doing so could underestimate pollution levels. For a conservative assessment, such readings should be flagged as potentially exceeding the measurement range, with 1,000 µg/m³ considered as a lower-bound value rather than treating them as zero or excluding them without qualification,” he wrote.
Furthermore, to calculate AQI, one would need to have at least 16 hours in a day, if not all 24 hours of data. So missing out on important data points during peak pollution periods underrepresents the AQI value.
It’s also worth noting that aur quality monitoring is not cheap: A 2018 Hindustan Times report put the cost of a conventional station at up to Rs 5 crore.

The monthly medicines bill for the mother of one of us comes to approximately ₹2,900. This month, a chance visit to the Jan Aushadhi outlet near home came as a pleasant surprise. The bill for the same monthly list of medicines was ₹663, a near 23 per cent of the usual spend. It provokes a question: how does a bill fall by more than three-fourths?
The bill is not a fluke. It is the visible end of a long chain of efforts by the Government of India to make medicines affordable for the common people. The Jan Aushadhi scheme, launched in 2008 and revamped in 2015, has put low-cost medicines within the reach of people across the country. It banks on a manufacturing base that has made India the largest supplier of generic medicines in the world. What remains to be done is increasing health expenditure as a percentage of the GDP to ensure meaningful outreach.
