Vijay Deverakonda recently shared a series of pictures from his vacation to Japan on Instagram, offering a glimpse of sweet family moments. He and Rashmika were in the ‘Land of the Rising Sun’ on Diwali, and Vijay even shared a picture saying, “When you find a way to do GOMA (Homam) in Japan on Happy DIWALI.”
Cherishing the days spent in Japan, the Ranabaali actor shared another set of pictures, writing, “Celebrating Life with my favourite people. A few memories doing life right with those that are my life, Japan Nov 2026.”
View this post on Instagram
Visa and passport rules for Indians who want to visit Japan
Japan is getting ready to embrace winter, and before that happens, you might be planning to see the vibrant colours during this fall, or the Koyo (Koh-yoh) season. But wait before you start packing your bags. Why?
Because Japan does not have a visa on Arrival for Indian nationals. Read on to learn the application rules and process for getting a visa before you set off.
As per Vishesh Gakhar, Director, Visa Mitar Immigration Consultants, “You can apply for Japan’s visa either using Japan’s eVisa official website or through an accredited agency such as VFS. The application route depends upon the country of residence, not nationality.”
DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to.
Confused? Let’s understand this.
“Indian nationals residing in India are bound to go through VFS Global, while those living abroad, in countries like the UK, the US, Canada, and Australia, can use
Japan’s official eVisa portal. This eVisa is only for tourism purposes, with a permitted stay of up to 90 days. In case of any other visa category, application procedures and relevance changes apply,” Gakhar says.
View this post on Instagram
He also explains the steps to apply for a Visa:
- Identify the correct Visa Type
- Complete and sign the Japan Visa Application Form
- Prepare Supporting Documents such as passport, photographs, travel itinerary, and flight schedule
- Submit the application and documents at the designated VFS centre; no prior Appointment is required.
- Pay the applicable fees
- Track Application
“In terms of passport validity, Japan does not explicitly state that you need a minimum of 6 months’ validity on your passport when you’re applying for a visa, but it must stay valid during your intended stay,” he adds.
Documents required to apply:
This is what Gakhar mentions:
- A valid passport; submit old passports as well (if any)
- Photocopy of the bio page of the Current Passport
- One passport-size photograph taken within the last 6 months
- Cover letter, if any explanation is needed
- Show flights/cruise schedule
- Travel Itinerary
- Latest ITR and bank statements for the last 6 months
However, he mentions that, in case of a dependent, consent from the parents/spouse, along with the latest Income Tax Return of the parents/spouse (6 months’ bank statements if the ITR is not available), is required. In addition, proof of relationship is required if the applicant is accompanied by any dependent (i.e., passport copy, Marriage Certificate, Birth Certificate), and the embassy may request an interview or additional documents based on your circumstances.
“Effective 19 October 2026, all visa applications for Mumbai, Pune, Ahmedabad, and Goa must be submitted by prior appointment, in accordance with instructions from the Consulate General of Japan in Mumbai. Walk-in submissions will not be accepted,” Gakhar adds.
Visa fees effective July 1, 2026:
On the fee structure, Gakhar says fees for single and multiple entry for Indian nationals are INR 500, while for other nationals they are: single visa at INR 8,650; multiple or Double visa: INR 17,350.

WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit launched last year to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda in Washington, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.
The group started 2025, its first year in operation, with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.
“To have lost over $1 million is pretty notable to me,” said Brian Mittendorf, a professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit accounting.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Two decades ago, a Vespa accident put me in a coma. By the time I came home from acute rehab, I had lost 25 pounds, most of it muscle, and my left side did not work as it should. After months of hospital sponge baths, soaking in a warm bath until my fingers wrinkled was blissful — and then it was time to get out.
I couldn’t. At 40, I did not have the upper body strength to lift myself from the tub; I had to shout for my wife to help. The humiliation was clarifying. I needed a way back, and what I found was exercise.
It began gently, with an Ashtanga yoga instructor who came to the house a few times a week. At first even the warrior pose was a struggle, but week after week, the two sides of my body relearned how to work together, and before long, I could get out of the bathtub on my own.
Later, I traded downhill skiing for skate skiing, the technique biathletes use. With my lingering balance problems, I fell a dozen times or more in every lesson. But once I got the hang of it, the sport was exhilarating and punishing: thighs burning, heart rate high for an hour or more on the trails. One day I told my instructor, Jack Bellorado, a rugged former wilderness guide, that I’d had a great ski and only fallen three times. He looked at me and said, “You must not have been pushing yourself hard enough.”
Nearly everyone caring for me after the accident had been trying, sensibly, to keep me safe. Jack expected something hard of me. I needed both, and medical care for the millions of Americans who suffer challenging concussion symptoms months after their injury is still much better at the first than the second.
For years, the standard advice after a concussion was to rest in a dark room until symptoms passed. Newer research is moving away from that recommendation. In a 2019 randomized trial led by John Leddy at the University at Buffalo, 103 adolescents with sport-related concussions were divided into two groups. One was prescribed aerobic exercise and recovered in a median of 13 days, compared with 17 for those in the other group, who only stretched. In a small 2024 trial, people who had lived with moderate to severe brain injuries for six months or more walked farther and faster after a block of high-intensity training than after conventional rehabilitation. This small but important study needs to be replicated in larger trials and include people with concussions.
Medicine has learned of unhealthy overprotectiveness before. In the early 1950s, heart attack patients were kept flat in bed for weeks, because exertion was thought dangerous. Cardiologists Samuel Levine and Bernard Lown questioned whether prolonged bed rest was helping patients or harming them, and, over strong opposition, got them sitting up in armchairs. Their 1952 paper in JAMA helped start a long shift. Today, supervised exercise is a standard, reimbursed part of recovery after a heart attack. And cardiac care was not alone: over the past few decades, surgeons have moved from keeping patients flat for days to walking them within hours.
Brain injury has been slower to make this turn, in part because Hippocratic caution can turn into overprotection. To many medical professionals, it may seem risky to prescribe exercise. For patients, the injured organ is the one you think with, so trying to do as little as possible can seem wise. Exertion can briefly worsen headache, dizziness, and fog, which can feel like movement is doing harm. There is a grain of truth in the caution: The brain does much of its repair during sleep, so sleeping has a central place in recovery. But adequate sleep and daytime stillness are not the same thing, and the lesson from most other fields is that movement and rest are partners, not rivals.
Exercise may help the injured brain in three ways. The first is better sleep. Sleep problems are among the most common and stubborn complaints after brain injury, and exercise is associated with improved sleep. The second is that exercise alleviates depression, another common complication of TBI. The third is more speculative. Working muscles release lactate, far more of it during hard effort, and lactate can cross into the brain, where studies, mostly in animals, suggest it may help trigger production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, often called fertilizer for the brain. If sleep is when the brain does most of its repair work, a day’s exertion might help twice over: a better night’s rest, and more for the brain to work with during sleep. However likely, that remains unproven but worth testing.
Today I work with the TBI Post-Acute Care Clinic Collaborative. In conversations with clinicians, I repeatedly hear that exercise is rarely encouraged in brain-injury care and even less often formally prescribed. Patients may leave appointments with medications, referrals, and advice to stay active, but without an exercise prescription.
The evidence has limits. Results from adolescent athletes with concussion may not hold for adults with more severe injuries like mine, and such studies are scarce. Some people’s symptoms worsen with exertion. That is why care must be individualized, so patients don’t have to guess. Patients who want to use exercise to improve their recovery should have help determining what they can safely do: an assessment, a written plan with an intensity set for them, a path for progressing it, follow-up to adjust it, and supervision when they need it. Doctors can put this evidence into practice now, and insurers should cover clinically appropriate programs, as they do for cardiac or stroke rehabilitation.
In 1972, a pastor named Robert Perske wrote about tension in appropriate risk-taking. Perske, who led an association for people with intellectual disabilities in Omaha, Neb., was convinced that well-meaning overprotection was smothering the people it was meant to help. Decades before the rise of helicopter parenting, he wrote that “there can be such a thing as human dignity in risk” and “there can be a dehumanizing indignity in safety!” What people needed, he argued, was a “fair and prudent share of risk.”
Perske’s point was not that risk is good for its own sake. It was that a life arranged entirely around safety becomes a smaller life. I got out of that bathtub, and eventually onto those skinny skis, because people took care of me and pushed me. More patients recovering from brain injury should leave their appointments with an exercise prescription, with guardrails suited to their condition. The effort is theirs to make. The plan, and the support in following it, are ours to give.
Scott W. Hamilton is founder of the Brain Care Catalyst Foundation.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has triggered a debate among Indian business leaders on the country’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies. Despite rising AI investments in India, the gap in capital, research capabilities and technical talent highlights the challenges facing homegrown AI companies. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, over 4X the year-ago period, but building a global AI giant will require deeper pools of capital, sustained R&D and stronger technical talent. Anthropic’s stock market debut has offered a glimpse of the extraordinary investor appetite for AI. The Claude parent priced its shares at $83 for the IPO, above its price range of $70-78. The IPO, which values the company at around $1.5 Tn, was oversubscribed by over 10X. The listing is a landmark moment for the AI industry and gave public market investors an opportunity to back one of the companies at the centre of the AI race. For scale, Anthropic’s $1.5 Tn IPO valuation is equivalent to nearly 37% of India’s projected nominal GDP of $4.06 Tn for FY27, as per the IMF’s October estimates. However, the significance of this IPO extends beyond Wall Street. In India, it has sparked a debate about the country's ability to build globally competitive AI companies. The conversation gained momentum after veteran banker and Kotak Mahindra Bank founder Uday Kotak compared Anthropic’s valuation with the combined market capitalisation of India's top 10 companies. In a post on X, he questioned whether Indian businesses were undervalued or whether the country needed to catch up with the new tech economy. “Anthropic, an AI company known for Claude, listed at a valuation of $1.5 Tn. It did not exist until about 5 years ago. This is more than the combined market cap of the top 10 Indian companies. Are we undervalued, or do we need to catch up in the new world? Or both?” Kotak wrote. The debate that unfolded after this comparison saw Adani Group CFO Jugeshinder Robbie Singh label the Anthropic IPO as a “textbook category error in asset pricing”. In a post on X titled “Cross-Regime Category Error: Why Legacy Bankers Can’t Price Synthetic GDP”, Singh argued that India's largest companies and frontier AI businesses operate in fundamentally different economic regimes. “India’s blue chips are neither undervalued nor ‘behind’ — they are yield vehicles monetising the physical human economy,” he wrote, arguing that frontier AI companies are being valued for their potential to create “synthetic GDP” through autonomous AI agents and digital workforces. Ex-Infosys CFO Mohandas Pai questioned the premise of comparing the two. “Every disruption creates new companies with huge valuations. It is the nature of markets. Comparing is silly,” he wrote. Pai argued that the more pertinent question the IPO raises for India is what exactly is needed for an Indian company to recreate an Anthropic-like scale. This reflects a broader question prevalent in the Indian startup ecosystem: whether the country can move beyond valuing existing businesses to fostering innovation and funding deeptech companies that may take years to build. The question gains more significance as funding for Indian AI startups gathers pace despite lagging significantly behind global levels. More Money Flows, But The Gap Remains AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in Q3 2026, with startups in the segment raising a record $438 Mn, up 265% YoY, across 35 deals. This took the sector’s total funding in the first nine months of 2026 to more than $1.1 Bn. The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, while the deal count fell 13%. However, the increase in AI funding has also brought valuations under scrutiny. Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half expect a correction within the next 18 months. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said rising AI valuations are part of a global trend, particularly in the US. He added that vertical AI applications offer a clearer path to building defensible businesses through distribution. “Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said. Vertical AI applications across BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting them to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. The findings suggested that investors were increasingly prioritising commercially viable AI applications over capital-intensive foundational technology. Whether the funding momentum continues will depend on sustainable revenue, defensible businesses and valuations that can withstand a potential correction. What Will It Take To Build India's Next AI Giant? Capital alone, however, will not be enough. Building deeptech companies capable of locking horns with giants like Anthropic also requires research talent, technical expertise and the infrastructure to train and run increasingly sophisticated models. An analysis by General Catalyst's Utkarsh Bajpai of companies valued at over $5 Bn highlighted the role of technical talent in value creation. Researchers lead 16% of these companies but account for 31% of their combined $170 Bn valuation. Nearly 80% of the founders have technical backgrounds. For Indian startups, this means moving beyond products that merely package existing foundation models. As access to these models becomes easier, differentiation will increasingly hinge on proprietary technology, domain expertise and solutions to specific problems. “Gone are the days when you could just build wrappers on top of foundational models. You have to build vertically focused products that solve real problems with an AI-first approach,” Mehta said. The opportunity extends beyond large language models to AI applications, enterprise software, robotics and other deeptech segments. But building globally competitive businesses in these areas requires patient capital and sustained investment in research, talent and infrastructure, often years before commercial returns materialise. India's challenge, therefore, is to move from participating in the AI market to building technology that competes globally. Rising funding signals investor interest, but translating it into durable businesses will require stronger research capabilities, technical talent and a willingness to back ambitious ideas for the long term. A crude bomb was allegedly hurled by ABVP activists at a bookstall set up by the Students’ Federation of India (SFI) in College Street, Kolkata’s principal hub of bookshops and publishing houses, late on November 18.
Titled Sangrami Boipotro (Literature of Struggle), the stall was set up by the Calcutta University unit of the SFI to commemorate the November Revolution. ABVP activists allegedly attempted to vandalise the stall, accusing the Left student outfit of selling ‘anti-national’ books, resulting in day-long tension in the ‘boi para’.
The confrontation began around 11 am on Wednesday and continued late into the evening. Tensions escalated when ABVP activists allegedly hurled a firecracker, locally known as a ‘chocolate bomb’, into the SFI stall as activists, including women, were packing up the books before closing for the day. Video footage shows the firecracker exploding in a small burst of flames and smoke filling up the area.
The incident took place in the presence of a large contingent of Kolkata Police personnel. SFI activists alleged that the police attempted to shield the ABVP activists. The Right-wing student organisation, on the other hand, claimed SFI activists had assaulted its members and vandalised its bookstall.
Reacting to the allegations and counter allegations of violence, BJP state president Samik Bhattacharya said, “These are matters related to student politics. They are young. Political movements were never entirely peaceful here. These things happen.” He also said ABVP was not related to the BJP.
The SFI’s Version of Events
According to SFI activists and videos circulated on social media, the confrontation began around 11 am. The bookstall was scheduled to open at that time, with senior Left leader Biman Bose slated to inaugurate it.
However, as SFI activists were setting up the stall, a group of ABVP activists gathered outside the main gate of Calcutta University, which opens onto College Street, and attempted to prevent them.
To contain the situation, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel formed a human barricade between the two groups. Videos show ABVP activists repeatedly raising slogans and displaying aggression. However, the police did not remove them from the spot.
Around 1 pm, tensions appeared to ease somewhat, with ABVP workers setting up a makeshift bookstall a few metres away from the SFI stall. The two stalls were positioned on either side of the university’s main gate, with the ABVP stall to its left and the SFI stall to its right. Police personnel placed metal barricades in front of the SFI stall to prevent a direct confrontation between the groups.
Around 2 pm, Left leaders Biman Bose and Sujan Chakraborty visited the stall.
However, as Bose was leaving, ABVP workers were heard raising slogans such as “Biman Bose Go Back” and “Slap Biman Bose across the face with shoes”.
The ABVP protest blocked a section of College Street. Its activists allegedly charged towards the SFI stall several times in the presence of police personnel. They also threw water and eggs at the stall, staining a National Flag at the venue and several books, the Left outfit alleged.
Around 7 pm, the situation escalated with the ABVP gathering allegedly hurling bricks, wooden sticks and water bottles towards the SFI enclosure, while police personnel continued to maintain a barricade between the two groups.
Videos also show plastic chairs being hurled form either side.
Around this time, SFI activists were packing up the stall for the day when a ‘chocolate bomb’ was seen flying towards it from the direction of the ABVP gathering.
The firecracker exploded inside the SFI enclosure, producing a flash and filling the area with smoke. The explosion further escalated tensions, with SFI activists seen rushing towards the ABVP gathering. Police personnel struggled to pull them back and prevent a direct confrontation.
Following the incident, the SFI decided to lodge an FIR at the nearby Jorasanko police station. Activists also organised a protest march from College Street to the police station.
According to SFI activists, police initially resisted registering a written complaint but eventually agreed following their sustained pressure.
SFI activists further alleged that after they had left for the police station, ABVP workers vandalised the stall site, damaging tables, benches and chairs.
The SFI is scheduled to reopen the bookstall at the same location on Thursday. It will remain open until November 20.
Trouble Erupted on November 17 as well
According to SFI sources, the organisation has been setting up the bookstall at the same location for the past four years. This year, too, its members informed the Joint Commissioner of Kolkata Police about the stall and its schedule through an email. They also paid the requisite fee to the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) for setting up the stall. However, on Monday, the police informed them that they would not be allowed to erect any permanent structure at the site.
On Tuesday morning, a contingent of Kolkata Police personnel arrived in front of Calcutta University and attempted to prevent SFI activists from setting up the bookstall.
Around 12:30 pm, SFI activists blockaded College Street and began selling books while sitting on the road.
This led to a scuffle with the police, following which 41 SFI activists, including the organisation’s West Bengal state secretary, Debanjan Dey, were detained and taken to Lalbazar, the headquarters of Kolkata Police.
In response, the SFI organised a mobilisation outside Lalbazar, demanding the release of those detained. Around 6 pm, all 41 activists were released.
According to SFI activists, the joint commissioner of police held lengthy discussions with them, following which it was agreed that they could set up the stall without erecting any permanent structure. They were also asked to ensure that the stall did not obstruct traffic on College Street.
The SFI activists attempted to set up the stall on Wednesday in accordance with these conditions. However, their efforts were disrupted by ABVP activists, who objected to the organisation’s programme.
The ABVP’s Response
ABVP further alleged that SFI activists had destroyed books on Swami Vivekananda, claiming that its own bookstall had been set up to encourage reading among students. It accused the SFI of sabotaging an initiative intended to promote education.
The Facebook page of ABVP Paschimbanga also shared a clipping from Bengali news channel TV9 Bangla, which purportedly showed Arunava Dutta, an ABVP national executive council member, being assaulted by SFI activists.
In a separate post, ABVP shared a video showing a stone being hurled from near the Left book stall.
In a separate Facebook post, ABVP Paschimbanga condemned what it described as attacks on its activists at Calcutta University, Calcutta Medical College and Presidency University. “The throwing of bombs inside university campuses and the targeted attacks on ABVP activists by SFI and Left organisations are deeply alarming and condemnable,” the organisation said.
In the video, ABVP national secretary Shravan B Raj said, “The SFI and Left extremist groups are unleashing violence on ABVP karyakartas.”
Vandalism at Calcutta Medical College
In another incident on the same day, intern doctors at Calcutta Medical College, located adjacent to Calcutta University and barely a 100-metre from the site of the book-stall clash, alleged that ABVP-backed miscreants entered the college campus and assaulted them.
The incident came amid a protest by students and junior doctors against show-cause notices issued to eight interns who had spoken out against alleged mismanagement at government hospitals following the stampede at a Durga Puja pandal which claimed 19 lives.
According to a Facebook post by the West Bengal Junior Doctors’ Front, the college principal and other senior officials had initially agreed to withdraw the notices after acknowledging a shortage of medicines. However, following a phone call from a “higher authority”, the principal reportedly refused to issue a written order confirming their withdrawal. This prompted students to stage a sit-in protest.
The post alleged that around 70–80 outsiders subsequently entered the campus, vandalised property and assaulted interns and medical students, leaving several injured. It further alleged that the principal left the campus under heavy police protection while the attackers continued their rampage in the presence of police personnel.

కాంగ్రెస్ నాయకురాలు సోనియా గాంధీ రాసిన ఆత్మకథ ‘బిలాంగింగ్: ఎ జర్నీ ఆఫ్ లవ్’ 10 నవంబర్ 2026న విడుదలైంది. ఇటలీలో ఆమె బాల్యం నుండి 1965లో కేంబ్రిడ్జ్లో రాజీవ్ గాంధీని కలవడం, ఆ తర్వాత భారతదేశానికి వచ్చి ఇక్కడి సంస్కృతికి అలవాటు పడటం వంటి అనేక విషయాలను ఈ పుస్తకం వివరిస్తుంది. మొదటి వారంలోనే ఈ పుస్తకం 2 లక్షల కాపీలకు పైగా అమ్ముడయ్యాయని పబ్లిషర్ హార్పర్ కాలిన్స్ సంస్థ పేర్కొంది.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో, ఈ పుస్తకాలను కాంగ్రెస్ కార్యకర్తలు కిలోల చొప్పున ముంబైలోని ఫోర్ట్ మార్కెట్లో దుకాణదారులకు అమ్మారని, అయితే వీటిని కొనడానికి ఎవరూ ముందుకు రావడం లేదని, అందువలన వీటిని స్క్రా ప్లో(తుక్కు) అమ్ముతున్నట్లు ఒక దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్నట్లుగా ఉన్న వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ఒకటి సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. దీంట్లో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సోనియా గాంధీ ఆత్మకథను ఎవరూ కొనని కారణంగా ఈ పుస్తకాలను ముంబైలో తుక్కాగా అమ్ముతున్నామంటూ దుకాణదారుడు చెప్తున్న వీడియో.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ ప్రచారంలో ఎలాంటి నిజం లేదు. ఇది ఆర్టిఫిషియల్ ఇంటెలిజెన్స్(AI) టెక్నాలజీతో సృష్టించిన ఫేక్ వీడియో. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పు.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోను పరిశీలించగా ఇందులో పుస్తకం పైన ఉన్న అక్షరాలు అసహజంగా ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అలాగే, దుకాణదారుడి చేతి వేళ్లు కూడా ఒకదానితో ఒకటి కలిసిపోయినట్లుగా ఉన్నాయి. ఇంకా పాదచారుల కదలికలు కూడా అస్పష్టంగా ఉన్నట్లు చూడవచ్చు. సాధారణంగా AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియోలలో ఇటువంటి పొరపాట్లు కనిపిస్తాయి.
దీని ఆధారంగా, ఈ వీడియోను AI డిటెక్షన్ టూల్స్తో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరీక్షించగా, ఇది AI తో రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించబడింది.
అలాగే, ఈ వీడియోను ఫేస్బుక్లో అప్లోడ్ చేసిన పోస్ట్ (ఆర్కైవ్) కింద “AI Content” అనే లేబుల్ ఉండటాన్ని చూడవచ్చు. దీన్ని బట్టి, వైరల్ వీడియో నిజమైన ఘటన కాదని, ఇది AI ద్వారా రూపొందించిన వీడియో అని నిర్ధారించవచ్చు.
చివరిగా, సోనియా గాంధీ పుస్తకాలను తుక్కుగా అమ్ముతున్నారంటూ షేర్ అవుతున్న ఈ వీడియో AIతో సృష్టించబడింది.

A mathematician working at artificial intelligence company Anthropic has claimed to have proved the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis, one of the most famous unsolved problems in mathematics, with the help of the company’s AI model Claude, reported Scientific American.
Levent Alpöge said he had discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis while working with Claude, and that the method also extended to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a much broader mathematical conjecture.
“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a statement posted on his personal website on Friday.
The claim has not yet been independently verified by the mathematical community. Alpöge has made the purported proof available as code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalise mathematical arguments and check their logical correctness.
Scientific American described the Riemann Hypothesis as one of the most famous open problems in mathematics. Technology publication OfficeChai also reported that the proof had been released in 14 parts and that independent verification was still pending.
Alpöge said the formalisation of the argument was complete but acknowledged that the proof was extremely long and that he had not yet produced a readable mathematical paper explaining it.
What is the Riemann Hypothesis?
First proposed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers, numbers that can be divided only by themselves and one.
Although prime numbers appear to occur irregularly along the number line, mathematicians have established patterns governing their distribution. The Riemann Hypothesis proposes a deeper relationship between these patterns and the zeros of a mathematical function known as the Riemann zeta function.
It also states that all the non-trivial zeros of the function have a real part of exactly one-half.
Proving the hypothesis would provide a much more precise understanding of how prime numbers are distributed. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems identified by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers a $1 million prize for a correct solution.
The institute’s website continued to list the Riemann Hypothesis as unsolved on Friday.
How did Claude help with the purported proof?
In his statement, Alpöge described the work as a collaboration in which he guided the research while Claude supplied several crucial mathematical ideas.
He said the breakthrough came from combining two different approaches in number theory. One of the central ideas involved adapting a technique known as Stepanov’s method, previously used to address an analogous version of the Riemann Hypothesis in the mathematical setting of function fields.
The challenge was to find a way to reproduce the role of multiplicity in ordinary number theory, where the conventional technique could not be directly applied.
Alpöge said Claude suggested using a sequence of mathematical operations known as theta lifts to address this difficulty. He described the AI model as having substantially outpaced him towards the end of the work.
“Tens of such occurred,” he wrote, describing the number of occasions when Claude came up with unexpected mathematical steps.
He also acknowledged that parts of the argument were beyond his own technical expertise and that the proof would need to be simplified and explained in a form that other mathematicians could understand.
The purported proof has been formalised in Lean, a proof assistant that allows mathematical arguments to be checked step by step by a computer.
A year of rapid progress in AI-assisted mathematics
The announcement comes after a series of developments involving Alpöge and Claude that have attracted attention in the mathematical community.
In August, Anthropic reported that an unreleased research version of Claude had improved a longstanding lower bound on the proportion of zeros of the Riemann zeta function lying on the critical line from 41.6% to 67.2%. That was progress on a related question, not a solution to the Riemann Hypothesis.
In September, Scientific American reported on Alpöge’s AI-assisted work on the 1947 Hopf problem concerning the existence of a complex structure on a six-dimensional sphere. The publication reported that mathematicians had begun reconstructing and examining the argument.

About 20 Youth Congress workers were kept under preventive arrest for staging a protest at Meta’s office in Hyderabad’s Madhapur on Friday.
The protest was held with the Youth Congress workers alleging that Meta had withheld their social media pages. They also alleged that many of their posts were removed by the platform.
They were released after three hours.
Speaking to The Indian Express, State Youth Congress president Shiv Charan said they went to the office for a peaceful protest but were not allowed into the building. “META is in with the RSS and the BJP and have turned hostile towards the Congress’ content on social media. So we went to their office to give a representation. They did not let us in and the police arrested us,” Charan said.
Sources said while the workers had managed to enter the premises, they did not make it to the main building of the company.
When The Indian Express reached out to Madhapur police, officials said that the workers had not entered the main premises of Meta and hence no case was registered. “The incident of breaking a flowerpot happened outside the office,” a police official said.
The police said that no complaint was lodged by Meta officials.
Posting a video of the party workers storming the premises, the Indian Youth Congress (IYC) wrote in its Instagram post: “#BREAKING: IYC workers stormed into BJP ka BETA -META’s Hyderabad office! Enough of blocking opposition accounts and silencing independent voices! @meta must follow India’s Constitution, NOT the BJP’s orders. Remove restrictions from all accounts within 7 days, or we will shut down your offices everywhere! Stop the censorship. The countdown begins!.”
What the video showed
The video showed several workers running on the premises of the Meta office, placards in hand and raising slogans. One worker could be seen picking up a flowerpot and smashing it to the ground even as two police personnel rush in in an attempt to control him.
In another video, the functionaries could be seen swaggering down what looked like a cafeteria and raising slogans while the staff looked on in apparent bewilderment.
In one shot, a man could be seen jutting his head out of a police vehicle, and raising slogans. The workers were also seen sitting on stairs, clapping and chanting slogans even as, in another shot, a few police personnel tried to restrain a functionary.
In a post later in the day, claiming that IYC president and incharge’s Instagram accounts were restored within 15 minutes of its “action”, the Youth Congress wrote: “When Youth Congress raises questions, BJP gets uncomfortable. When its voices grow louder, Meta faces questions over selective takedowns. And when IYC takes to the streets, the accounts are suddenly restored. IYC IS NOT GOING TO BE SILENCED.”
They claimed to have held similar protests in Mumbai and Gurugram.

Six months after an Ebola outbreak was declared in Congo, the disease remains out of control and efforts to contain it are faltering.
More than 11,000 cases have been recorded, and nearly half of those infected have died, according to Government data. It is the deadliest of Congo's 17 outbreaks and is on track to surpass the death toll from the West African outbreak that killed 11,000 people between 2014 and 2016.
Basic containment measures, including contact tracing and isolation, remain inadequate, raising doubts about authorities' ability to halt the outbreak. Experts say there is little chance of bringing it under control within the next year.
By the time the outbreak was announced in mid-May, 43 deaths had already been recorded, suggesting the virus had circulated undetected for an extended period. It has since spread to eight of the country's 26 provinces, moving at a pace aid groups have likened to wildfire.
New hotspots continue to emerge, stretching an already strained health care system.
Questions over funding and management
Community transmission remains high. According to the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, 80% of new cases are being detected outside health surveillance, meaning most infections have not been tracked by authorities.
One-third of deaths occur at home or elsewhere in the community, where burials and other procedures are often conducted without specialist supervision, increasing the risk of transmission.
Health workers have repeatedly gone on strike over pay that is months overdue, sometimes leaving patients with confirmed infections without treatment.
Aid groups have also questioned how the response is being managed. Last month, the Africa CDC raised concerns about more than $700 million in Ebola aid that remains unaccounted for.
“A troubling disconnect between the considerable resources mobilised for the response and what is actually reaching patients, frontline workers, and communities continues,” said the humanitarian organisation Doctors Without Borders, known by its French acronym MSF.
Children face high death rates
Children are particularly vulnerable to Ebola, especially those with preexisting conditions such as malnutrition, experts say.
Most children affected by the disease have not received specialised care, contributing to high death rates.
According to UNICEF, children accounted for 35% of deaths recorded through November 4. Children under 5 accounted for 21% of all deaths, and nearly 72% of infected children in that age group have died.
Conflict and attacks hamper response
Health workers face difficult conditions as Ebola prevention and containment measures clash with social and cultural practices.
Since the outbreak began, health workers have been attacked, some fatally, adding to the dangers of working in an already volatile region. Health facilities have also come under attack.
The outbreak has been concentrated in eastern Congo, particularly Ituri and North Kivu, where communities face both the epidemic and armed conflict.
Fighting between Government forces and hundreds of rebel groups, including the Rwanda-backed M23, had already helped create one of the world's most severe humanitarian crises. The Allied Democratic Forces, an Islamic State-affiliated rebel group, also attacks civilians.
The virus's rapid spread has raised fears of wider transmission across Africa. Nigeria, Kenya and Uganda have confirmed cases, making this the most geographically widespread Ebola outbreak on record.

Toward the end of the second episode of "Melania: The Series," director Brett Ratner told first lady Melania Trump that one of his takeaways from filming her is the "beautiful relationship" that she shares with President Donald Trump.
"Well, people, they don't see that because we are not so public outside," Melania Trump said in the two-part docuseries, which premiered on Amazon Prime Video on Friday. "We are not that way. It's not my style. You know, that's private."
In "Melania: The Series" — for which Amazon paid $40 million for the licensing rights, alongside the "Melania" documentary released in January — the notoriously private first lady opens up about her nearly 22-year marriage to Donald Trump, including their public disagreements.
Donald Trump and Melania Trump married in January 2005 at Bethesda-by-the-Sea Episcopal Church in Palm Beach, Florida. Their reception was held at Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate.
Marc Beckman, senior advisor to Melania Trump and an executive producer of both the film and docuseries, told Business Insider that the series "goes deeper into her relationships with her husband, her son, and her father, so at a certain level, it's more personal."
The Office of the First Lady declined to comment. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
PDA and public scrutiny
The president and first lady's public displays of affection — or apparent lack thereof — have made headlines in the past.
In her 2024 memoir, also titled "Melania," the first lady recalled a widely reported incident where she appeared to swat her husband's hand away on a 2017 trip to Israel, characterizing it as "a mere misunderstanding" caused by protocol when greeting foreign leaders.
In the docuseries, the first lady said that she doesn't dwell on the public scrutiny.
"I don't need to answer to anybody," she said. "I don't need to explain anything to anybody. Whatever anybody thinks about me, let them think. I know who I am and that's all that matters."
'I let him be who he is'
When asked about being married to Donald Trump for over 20 years, Melania Trump cited their support for each other despite their differences of opinion.
"I think you need to let them be who they are, and you cannot change the person," she said in the docuseries aboard a presidential jet. "Sometimes, of course, you disagree with them, and that's normal. That's healthy for the relationship. That's nothing wrong. I let him be who he is, and he supports me and lets me be who I am."
Melania Trump has occasionally publicly broken with her husband and the Republican Party on political issues. In her 2024 "Melania" memoir, she expressed support for abortion rights, writing that "A woman's fundamental right of individual liberty, to her own life, grants her the authority to terminate her pregnancy if she wishes."
In the docuseries, Donald Trump said that he and his wife "don't have very many arguments," but that when she spoke about her stance on abortion, "people respected her views."
Another issue the couple will continue to disagree on: Donald Trump's dance moves.
"She feels very strongly that everything should be very presidential," Donald Trump said. "And when we were doing rallies, if, on occasion, I'd break into a dance, I'm not sure she loved it so much. But the people loved it."
"Well, sometimes the situations were like, 'I don't think it's a good day to dance,'" Melania Trump said.

This exchange, following the FAA nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, truly occurred Nov. 16 outside the White House. While some posts paraphrased the question and answer, Trump responded to the question about ensuring safe air travel, in part, "Well, they fly a little bit slower, but very safe."
In mid-November, a rumor spread that U.S. President Donald Trump answered a reporter's question about ensuring safe air travel by saying, "Well, they'll just have to fly a little slower."
The claim, purporting that Trump said he believed pilots would fly slower for safety reasons, circulated after the Federal Aviation Administration experienced an outage of the air traffic control system on Nov. 13 and ordered a nationwide ground stop — the longest such stoppage of air travel since the Sept. 11 attacks. The Trump administration said the outage was caused by the upgrading of new technology overloading older parts.
For example, some people shared the purported quote on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), TikTok (archived) and X (archived).
(@liquidmagik via TikTok)
In sum, Trump truly said these words (though some posts paraphrased the exchange). Therefore, we've rated this quote as correctly attributed to him.
A search located the quote in a transcript on the Roll Call website. The exchange, between Trump and ABC News journalist Rachel Scott, occurred Nov. 16 outside the White House (emphasis ours):
SCOTT: Can you assure Americans that it's safe to fly, given that nationwide ground stop?
TRUMP: Very safe.
SCOTT: How can you assure them that this won't happen again?
TRUMP: Very safe, well they fly a little bit slower, but very safe. But we want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress.
SCOTT: Why didn't Republicans pass that when they had the majority for the last two years?
TRUMP: People have been trying, well we've been trying to get the money for two years to fix it, and [former Democratic Transportation Secretary Pete] Buttigieg ruined the system. He totally ruined it. The Democrats really, it's very old, but what they did really set back the system a long way.
SCOTT: But Republicans had the majority [inaudible].
[Trump walks away, waves arm at Scott.]
Scott's question appears at the 11:59 mark in an official White House video featuring the same media gaggle:

The Union Health Ministry has proposed an amendment to the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, to include ‘antimicrobials’ in the definition of ‘New Drug’ under Rule 2(1)(w)(v).
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global public health concern and the proposed amendment has been initiated in view of concerns regarding the grant of manufacturing licences for antimicrobial products without adequate regulatory scrutiny, including the requirement for studies such as bioavailability and bioequivalence and stability studies.
The proposed amendment seeks to bring antimicrobials within the regulatory framework applicable to new drugs under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019. Accordingly, manufacturers would be required to obtain permission from the Central Licensing Authority before applying for a manufacturing licence from the concerned State Licensing Authority. This is expected to strengthen central regulatory oversight and help ensure the quality, safety and efficacy of antimicrobial products.
Meanwhile, the Ministry has also proposed amendments to the Drugs Rules, 1945, to introduce a separate application form (Form 19-BC) and licence form (Form 20-BC) for the sale of bulk drugs (active or inactive bulk substances), distinct from the existing licensing provisions for formulations.
At present, a common licence covers the wholesale sale of both formulations and bulk drugs. The proposed amendment seeks to establish a dedicated licensing framework for bulk drugs, enabling more focused regulatory oversight of their wholesale sale and greater accountability in the pharmaceutical supply chain.
The proposal was agreed upon by the Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) in its 67th meeting held on November 17, 2025, and by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 93rd meeting held on February 16, 2026.
Under the proposed framework, the licence will capture the categories of bulk drugs handled by wholesalers, including drugs covered under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985. The sale of bulk drugs will be carried out under the personal supervision of a competent person, thereby strengthening accountability in their distribution and handling.
“Upon implementation, the proposed amendment will: give better control over the sale of bulk drugs by way of wholesale, strengthen enforcement control in relation to antimicrobial resistance and the movement of NDPS drugs and require wholesalers of bulk drugs to obtain a separate license for sale.” Stakeholders and members of the public are invited to submit their objections and suggestions.

'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
- Published
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.
When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.
