Social media posts about this announcement failed to make a distinction between calendar year 2026 and fiscal year 2026. The Department of Veterans Affairs announced in November that nearly 49,000 homeless veterans have been permanently housed in fiscal year 2026, which runs from Oct. 1, 2025, to Sept. 30, 2026.
Social media users are spreading a rumor that under U.S. President Donald Trump, the Department of Veterans Affairs has provided permanent housing to nearly 49,000 veterans experiencing homelessness "in 2026 so far."
Posts on Facebook and Instagram claimed the data came "directly from the Department of Veterans Affairs."
"These are not temporary shelters or short-term beds. They are permanent housing placements for veterans who were living on the streets," said one popular post.
(Facebook page David J Harris Jr.)
This claim is mostly true, although it gets the timeline slightly wrong. The Department of Veterans Affairs announced in a Nov. 12 news release (archived) that the agency "permanently housed 48,968 homeless Veterans across the country in fiscal year 2026 – an average of more than 4,000 Veterans housed per month."
The federal government's fiscal year 2026 ran from Oct. 1, 2025, to Sept. 30, 2026. Since posts claimed the VA provided housing to nearly 49,000 veterans in 2026 "so far," it appears the claims misunderstood the VA's announcement to mean the calendar year of 2026, not the fiscal year.
Posts online also implied that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration's efforts represented an outpouring of support for housing veterans. One post even claimed that Trump "took money meant to house illegal aliens and used it for our veterans."
It is true that the VA's data indicates that the second Trump administration has housed a few thousand more veterans per fiscal year than former President Joe Biden. However, the Trump administration has a mixed record of following through with its promises to support the VA's decades-long efforts to end homelessness. It is also worth noting that housing veterans experiencing homelessness is a bipartisan policy issue.
Since fiscal year 2019, the VA has housed at least 38,000 veterans a year. The Trump administration's high rates of housing veterans followed a year-over-year increase under Biden, per the VA's own data from its November news release, which Snopes visualized in the line graph below:
Contextualizing the numbers
Veteran homelessness has steadily dropped for decades — and Congress has steadily increased spending in support of the VA's goals to end veteran homelessness, appropriating approximately $3.2 billion in fiscal year 2025. In fact, both Biden and Trump's first administration put out news releases touting record lows in veteran homelessness under their respective presidencies.
The Department of Housing and Urban Development uses a "Point-in-Time" count — a count of the number of people without a home on a single night — to estimate the number of veterans without stable housing. According to the most recent HUD data available, 32,495 veterans experienced homelessness on a single night in January 2025. That's the lowest number of veterans counted since HUD first began recording Point-in-Time data for homeless veterans in 2009, per the VA, and a 56.1% decline since 2010.
According to the VA, the Point-in-Time data compared to the VA's housing data from 2024 and 2025 indicates "a significant increase in the number of Veterans needing homelessness assistance that VA and its partners were able to just keep ahead of."
Federal officials have consistently stated that a primary reason for the VA's success in housing veterans is a voucher program between the VA and HUD known as HUD-VASH, or the HUD–Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing program, which combines housing vouchers with VA case management and support services. HUD-VASH began as a collaboration between the two departments in the 1990s; Congress has appropriated funds for the program since fiscal year 2008.
In fact, as of 2026, Congress has funded 20,900 more HUD-VASH vouchers than are being used, according to three Democratic senators who want to loosen eligibility requirements.
The VA also attributes its success to community grants for programs that support housing. The second Trump administration awarded more than $2 billion in grants to organizations dedicated to reducing veteran homelessness.
"Under President Trump, VA is working harder than ever to get homeless veterans off the streets and back on the path to self-sufficiency," VA Secretary Doug Collins said in the VA's November news release.
That news release notes that Trump's VA established a $29 million fund to provide assistance to homeless veterans in the HUD-VASH program. It also touts supposed efforts to create a center for homeless veterans on the West Los Angeles VA Medical Center campus, although NPR reported in May that Trump's budget gave no money toward the center. The LA Times reported in September that the project, financed through VA funds and California state tax credits, would create only 24 units of housing for $1.25 million per apartment.
Furthermore, Trump has come under fire among veterans and their advocates for institutionalizing homeless veterans, making various budget cuts impacting VA programs and ending a home loan program (that was eventually replaced by a new program to help veterans avoid foreclosure).

In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement’s midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA’s own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group’s priority was ever winning elections in the first place.
The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.
The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA’s clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.
According to Stat’s findings, of the $10.5 million the MAHA PAC spent on the midterms, less than a tenth—roughly $1 million—went to messaging on political candidates, which are expenses called “independent expenditures.”
Andrew Mayersohn, a committees researcher at OpenSecrets, called the spending “pretty unusual,” explaining that “Major super PACs spend most of their money on independent expenditures.”
MAHA perks
In some cases, the scant political spending was dwarfed by spending on luxuries. For instance, in a key House race in Northern California, MAHA supported Kevin Kiley over his political rival, pediatrician Richard Pan. Despite calling the race “the most direct ideological confrontation” between MAHA and its opposition “anywhere on the 2026 ballot,” the PAC only spent $49,900 to back Kiley. That’s a little less than the $50,100 it spent at Mastro’s Steakhouse, an upscale restaurant that offers $110 porterhouse steaks in Washington, DC. Further, it’s less than a third of the $155,900 the PAC spent at Ned’s Club, a luxury club near the White House that has become a popular gathering spot among Trump officials.

The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organization officials said Monday, November 16, 2026.
WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.
The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.
"Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine," said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO. "Unlike COVID-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people's lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should," said Nyemazi.
In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.
A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly nine countries in 10 had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around four in 10.
But only 42 countries -- less than one in five -- said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.
"Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets," she added.
Poor access to diagnostics
One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36% of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO -- well short of the 80% target set for 2030.
"Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work," said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.
The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals. The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.
There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.
Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added.

Keralam: Ex-Indian athlete Padmini Thomas quits BJP, likely to return to Congress
Thomas, a recipient of the Arjuna award and who won medals for the country at the 1982 Asian Games, said she plans to return to the Congress
Former Indian athlete Padmini Thomas announced on Friday that she was quitting the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) due to ‘non-fulfilment of promises’ made to her.
She is the second prominent BJP leader to quit the party in less than 24 hours after Padmaja Venugopal in the state.
Thomas, a recipient of the Arjuna award and who won medals for the country at the 1982 Asian Games, said she plans to return to the Congress.
“As an athlete and former president of the Kerala State Sports Council, I wanted to contribute to the sports sector. But there weren’t many opportunities given to me. I was promised a ticket in the Assembly elections, but I was denied. I wasn’t interested in contesting the municipal corporation elections (in Thiruvananthapuram), but had no choice but to fight. I complained a few times, but there was no resolution,” Thomas told media persons.

A video showing two women pleading with folded hands to stop the demolition of their house as a bulldozer demolishes tin-roofed houses is going viral on social media (here, here, and here), with the claim that it shows minority homes being demolished in Tripura and Assam. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows minority homes being demolished by a bulldozer in Tripura and Assam.
Fact: The video shows an anti-encroachment drive in the Kalshi area of Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh, on 20 May 2026, during which authorities demolished illegal constructions. The demolition reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured. The video is unrelated to Tripura or Assam. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to multiple Bangladeshi media reports (here, here, and here) featuring the same visuals. According to these reports, the video is from the Kalshi area of Mirpur in Dhaka, Bangladesh, where the administration conducted an anti-encroachment drive to remove illegal constructions on 20 May 2026. The demolition drive reportedly triggered clashes between authorities and residents, leaving several people injured.
To sum up, a video of an anti-encroachment drive in Dhaka is falsely shared, linking it to India.

Former Brazilian President 
Jair Bolsonaro
 was taken to hospital on Friday after suffering "severe abdominal pain".
My father has just been taken to the hospital again after experiencing severe abdominal pain. It was obvious that this moment would come, with an active man kept imprisoned, without having stolen a single cent from public coffers, under the pretext of a “coup plot,” and having undergone more than 9 surgeries after being stabbed by a former PSOL activist, an arm of the PT, and with his health deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility and the psychological torture he suffers daily," said his son Carlos Bolsonaro in a post on X
"The goal is still to kill Jair Bolsonaro. One way or another. And the worst part: the only son Moraes allows to visit him, twice a week for just two hours, is me.. I have no words or feelings to describe this man!" he added.
Initially saying that he couldn't be by his father's side, Carlos, later said that, "Since there are no family members at the hospital, I was asked to stay with him until further notice, and the request was approved. On my way there, and I’ll keep everyone updated! See you!"
Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, is the second son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and a politician who has served as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro. A prominent supporter of his father's political movement, he has been involved in shaping the Bolsonaro family's social media strategy and political messaging. Carlos has also been investigated in the alleged illegal surveillance operation involving Brazil's intelligence agency ABIN. He is the brother of Flavio Bolsonaro, who contested the 2026 presidential election against Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
Meanwhile, the 71-year-old has a history of hospitalisations and surgeries following a stabbing in the abdomen during a campaign event in 2018. 
He has since undergone several procedures related to complications from the attack.
Bolsonaro, who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2022, was sentenced to 27 years in prison last year for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. He is currently serving his sentence under house arrest on medical grounds.
The hospitalisation comes weeks after another setback for the Bolsonaro family in Brazil's presidential election. Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son, Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, lost the October 25 runoff to incumbent Lula, who secured a fourth presidential term.
Flavio subsequently left Brazil with his family and arrived in the United States after travelling through Argentina and Ecuador. He had refused to concede defeat and questioned the election result. His departure drew criticism from Lula, while the Trump administration allowed the family to enter the US.

Two days after Diwali was celebrated across India, on November 10, Tuesday, the nation woke up to grim newspaper headlines and reports highlighting the sharp deterioration of air quality across major cities. According to reports, 93 Indian cities appeared among the world’s 100 most polluted locations, several parts of Delhi reportedly witnessed a staggering Air Quality Index (AQI) of 3,000+, and six cities recorded an AQI above 1,000 at 9 pm on Diwali night.
Newspaper reports suggested that despite bans and restrictions, the bursting of firecrackers remained untethered across states, resulting in not only a severe surge in air pollution, but major fire accidents, noise pollution, and several people, stray animals and birds suffering burn injuries.
The front page of the Delhi edition of The Times of India on Tuesday led with a report headlined ‘Delhi pollution on Diwali rockets to worst in 5 yrs’.
“Delhi saw its most polluted Diwali day in five years, with AQI touching 376 at 4pm Nov 8, the worst since 2021. The city, however, narrowly escaped its worst post-Diwali pollution day in five years, with Monday’s AQI touching 370 at 11am before improving to 344 by 4pm, better than 2025’s post-Diwali air quality,” the report read, while highlighting that “several monitoring stations failed to report crucial AQI data”.
The front page also carried reports on the death of 10-year-old Rishi Garg in Delhi’s Narela after suffering a deep injury on his chest while bursting a firecracker; the hourly PM2.5 concentration at Jahangirpuri surging to 4,985 µg/m³ on Diwali night, which is 83 times the daily national ambient air quality standard; and X “locking” the account of TOI photojournalist Anindya Chattopadhyay after he posted visuals of smog in Delhi, citing violation of its rules.
The Mumbai edition of the paper on Tuesday reported “a record number of firecracker accidents” across the city on Diwali, with the headline ‘390 fires caused by crackers across Mum region on Diwali’. The report highlighted that the local train services on the Western line were disrupted due to a fire damaging signalling cables between Virar and Nalasopara. It noted that over 60 people suffered burns across Mumbai Metropolitan Region and over 30 stray animals and birds sustained burn injuries due to crackers, among various other major accidents and mishaps across MMR.
Similarly, the Kolkata edition led with a story on firecracker-related noise complaints. With the headline, ‘This Diwali, city seeks max number of noise complaints’, the report highlighted the widespread bursting of banned high-decibel firecrackers across the city, well beyond the permissible hours, making Sunday night one of the noisiest in recent years. Kolkata’s air quality deteriorated sharply over the same period, with readings lying between the “very poor” and “severe” categories from Sunday night to the intervening morning, and PM2.5 rising from 74 to 409 in Ballygunge and 115 to 444 in Salt Lake within a span of 2 hours, the report highlighted.
The front page Delhi edition of The Indian Express on Tuesday carried the lead story on pollution with the headline ‘Delhi wakes up to toxic post-Diwali air, 8 stations in ‘severe’ zone’. It reported that the capital had recorded its “worst” Diwali-day air quality in the last five years. Pollution levels rose sharply after sunset and remained elevated into the following morning, with PM2.5 concentrations touching nearly 5,000 µg/m³ at some monitoring stations. India’s 24-hour national ambient air quality standards prescribe a safe limit of 60 µg/m³ for PM2.5 and 100 µg/m³ for PM10.
The lead story of the Hindustan Times carried the headline, ‘Delhi pollution monitors went dark as AQI surged on Diwali’. According to the report, 43 of Delhi’s 59 air quality monitoring stations went “blank” on Diwali night just as PM2.5 readings surged towards 1,000 µg/m³. The data gaps reportedly affected the calculation of the capital’s daily AQI, raising questions about the reliability of pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours.
The front page also featured reports on Punjab recording nearly 200 stubble burning incidents on November 9, Monday; the sale of firecrackers continuing in Delhi despite a Supreme Court ban; and the rampant bursting of firecrackers leading to an increase in ambient noise levels across most monitoring stations in Delhi.
The Telegraph featured a collage showing the contrast of visibility of Delhi’s India Gate before and after Diwali, with photographs taken on October 30 and November 9 respectively. With the lead headline reading ‘Diwali cocktail of cacophony’, the front page reports covered the aftermath in both Delhi and Kolkata, highlighting data gaps in Delhi’s pollution monitoring during peak pollution hours and administrative inaction in Kolkata.
“Slackness in the seizure of banned fireworks. Stalls selling crackers at almost every neighbourhood. Lackadaisical police response to noise complaints. Political endorsement at the highest level in the name of religion. Several factors made this Diwali the most deafening in years, according to environmentalists, former pollution control board members, Opposition politicians and ordinary Calcuttans,” the report read.
The Telegraph reported that this Diwali celebration was Delhi’s most polluted Diwali in five years. It noted that, over 18 hours, from 10 pm on Sunday to 4 am on Monday, 59 air quality stations in the national capital should have recorded 1062 hourly readings; however, around 24% are missing from the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data.
On Kolkata’s exceeding noise pollution levels, the report stated that “even a minister and an MLA from the BJP complained of the “unbearable” noise…However, asked about the rampant violation of noise pollution norms, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari politicised the issue, saying it was the “communists” and those unnerved by the “stupendous rise of Sanatan” that were complaining.”

The Hindu on Tuesday carried a standalone image of thick smog enveloping Rashtrapati Bhavan on Monday morning with the caption ‘Pollution unlimited’. On Page 6, it further reported that air pollution levels in Delhi had spiked to 200 times the World Health Organization’s recommended limits during Diwali.
Hospitals Report Burn Patients; Doctors Raise Concerns
“I am honestly surprised that we are still alive. I do not think this kind of air is suitable for human survival,” Dr Vijay Hadda, professor, department of pulmonary medicine and sleep disorders at AIIMS, told ANI on Monday.
He said that the green crackers reduced emissions by only 30 per cent, but as far as the particulate matter was concerned, 70 per cent of the emissions remained the same as conventional firecrackers. He raised concerns over people breathing this ‘poisonous’ smoke and said, “You should understand that you are simply inhaling poison and exhaling it.”

The general public forgets, and even policies remain somewhat in a grey area, making it difficult to understand how they should be interpreted. Overall, the situation is not good at all. In the aftermath of Diwali, doctors in Delhi began reporting an alarming number of juvenile patients, including newborns, arriving with breathing difficulties, even as hospitals are witnessing a significant rise in respiratory illnesses. According to reports, 397 patients with Diwali-related injuries were treated at four major hospitals in Delhi. The cases included burns, firecracker injuries and eye trauma.
AIIMS reported 42 burn injury cases by 11 am on November 9. Of these, 37 were caused by firecrackers. Eleven patients sustained major injuries, while 31 had minor injuries. Eight were admitted, including one in critical condition. Moreover, 18 of the 42 patients were under 18, including six below the age of 10. An eight-year-old child at AIIMS was in critical condition after sustaining burns over 45 per cent of their body surface area. Safdarjung Hospital recorded 135 burn injury cases. Of these, 129 were attributed to firecrackers and six to traditional diyas. Seven patients sustained major burns requiring hospital admission. The hospital also treated 35 children with firecracker-related injuries in its outpatient department.
Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital treated 41 patients with burn injuries from 9 am on Saturday. 18 of these injuries were reportedly caused by firecrackers, with two patients requiring admission. Eight patients were hospitalised overall, while approximately 10–12 of those treated were children. Guru Tegh Bahadur Hospital reported 172 patients with firecracker burns and other Diwali-related injuries within 24 hours. Among them were 25 children and 56 women. Thirty-four patients also suffered eye injuries.
The toll was not limited to burn injuries. The Dr Rajendra Prasad Centre for Ophthalmic Sciences at AIIMS received nearly 110 patients with eye injuries on Sunday and during the early hours of Monday, most of them with firecracker-related ocular injuries. 18 patients suffered corneal perforations or lacerations and underwent surgical intervention.
In Pali, Rajasthan, sparks from firecrackers being burst on a road reportedly reached a firecracker shop near Swarn Mandir in Falna town, gutting three shops and killing two people. One person sustained burn injuries and three others were initially reported missing.

Google's latest home page redesign makes Gemini even more prominent
A new collapsible sidebar in AI mode shows your most recent searches.
Google is doubling down on Gemini AI in its desktop search, despite protestations from users and employees alike. The latest feature is a collapsible sidebar in AI mode that shows your most recent searches, in case you want to jump back to a previous query. "In testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress and continuing to explore the web," wrote VP of search Robby Stein on X.
The new sidebar is only available in Google Search's AI mode. Clicking anywhere on the left of the AI search window opens up the sidebar, showing all recent searches, both AI and organic. Then, selecting any of the sidebar descriptions opens up an AI mode search window on the subject. You can close the AI search sidebar at any time by clicking on the "close sidebar" icon at the top right.
New on the Google desktop homepage globally: we're rolling out a collapsible sidebar to easily find & jump back into your recent AI searches.
People are coming to Search with more questions that aren't just one and done – and in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for... pic.twitter.com/mKHz295tzK
— Robby Stein (@rmstein) November 19, 2026
If you're like me and never use Google's dedicated AI Search mode, you won't see the new sidebar. Still, it's bound to ruffle some feathers among users and publishers who think there's already too much Gemini in Google Search. (As an, er, sidebar, I'd add that the feature would be nice to have in regular Search, as a list of recent queries would save me from having a zillion tabs open.)
Google seems to value its AI search development more than actual money, given that its market cap recently dropped by $500 billion after it admitted that AI search isn't earning as much as organic search. However, the company is likely focused on maintaining its AI search lead over rivals like ChatGPT and Claude. And, as CEO Sundar Pichai put it in the company's last earnings call, Google's commitment to AI is "long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise."

A Sprawling Empire: Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which is then used by robots for training. Overall, its data collection operations span more than 20 countries across Latin America and Asia. Recordings inside homes and factories could capture personal information, which has made consent and storage safeguards critical. 7-week-old elephant calf Raja, born with fractured leg, air-lifted to Vantara for treatment
The airlift, being facilitated by Vantara founder Anant Ambani, will be the third such operation in India, according to a release.
A seven-week-old elephant calf suffering from a fractured thigh bone and multiple health complications, is being airlifted from Assam to Vantara in Gujarat's Jamnagar for specialised treatment.
The airlift, being facilitated by Vantara founder Anant Ambani, will be the third such operation in India, according to a release issued by the wildlife care facility on Friday.
The elephant calf, named Raja, was born last month in Gogamukh, Assam, and sustained a fracture in his right hind leg shortly after birth. Since then, the calf has been receiving treatment at his owner's residence in Assam's Pohumara.
Also Read | Vantara brings the world's wildlife community to Jamnagar for EARAZA Annual Conference 2026
However, Vantara said that his deteriorating condition has now necessitated specialised hospital care.
The airlift journey from Assam's Guwahati to Jamnagar is expected to take around four hours. Transporting the calf by road would have involved travel of over 2,500 km, and could have posed additional risks to his already fragile health condition.
How did Raja suffer a fracture?
According to Vantara, Raja's 11-year-old mother was young and inexperienced while giving birth. Following the delivery, she became frightened and anxious, and kicked the newborn calf, causing a complete fracture of his right femur, the large bone in the thigh.
Owing to the injury, Raja has been unable to stand or put any weight on his right hind leg. The elephant calf also did not receive his mother's colostrum or milk, which provides newborns with essential nutrition and immunity. Vantara's Rapid Response Team reached Raja on October 8, nearly a week after his birth, after the elephant calf's caretakers sought assistance. X-rays of the injured leg revealed a complete overriding fracture. On October 10, Raja was oved to his owner's residence, where the Vantara team continued his treatment and monitoring.
Also Read | Vet shares what should be immediate first aid steps for injured stray animal
Health complications
Raja's condition deteriorated owing to other health problems, including diarrhoea. Lab tests detected a Klebsiella pneumoniae bacterial infection. He also experienced recurring episodes of low blood sugar.
Blood tests also showed elevated liver markers, and prolonged periods of lying down resulted in pressure sores on his head. He was additionally diagnosed with umnilical hernia and generalised weakness.
The calf now requires advanced diagnostics and specialised orthopaedic treatment, with structured nutrition and a rehabilitation programme, which can be provided only at a well-equipped hospital, the Vantara facility said.
On reaching Jamnagar, Raja will be admited to Vantara's elephant hospital for a comprehensive diagnostic assessment, pain management and medication, mobility therapy and rehabilitation.

Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chipmaker TSMC down about 6%.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by over 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Anthropic’s shares jumped 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Anthropic’s floation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
- Published
Donald Trump went into his trilateral meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping with little on the agenda and no clear asks – and he left with little in return.
In the end, the visuals of the meeting – the "optics", as political wags like to say – may be the only lasting impression from the summit, billed by some as a historic "Yalta 2.0" meeting of great powers.
The pomp and the ceremony, in the end, may be what the US president wanted most. Trump, bruised by his Republican Party's drubbing in midterm congressional elections earlier this month, clearly relished the global spotlight during his three-day trip to Asia and the historic nature of the first-ever US-Russia-China trilateral meeting.
In an interview on Wednesday with Fox News, Trump noted his prominent seat at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) dinner on Tuesday and his reception upon arriving in China - "the fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people" – as evidence that the trip already was a success.
That might appear to be a low bar, but it's one that could satisfy the American president.
So far, however, the US has been remarkably silent following the three-party meeting.
While China was quick to release a joint communique detailing the discussions and Putin expounded during an hour-long post-meeting press conference, Trump has made minimal public comments, instead promising a news conference at the White House on Friday.
On his trip to China earlier this year and following his meeting with Xi at the APEC summit in South Korea last October, Trump spoke with the press early in his flight back to Washington.
For the moment, the White House is letting the joint communique, released Thursday after the three met, do the talking. But the document is mostly a vague endorsement of efforts to ensure "strategic stability and international security".
That, along with the visuals of three powerful men sitting in the same room to amicably discuss global issues, might offer some reassurance no catastrophic conflicts are on the horizon. But pledges of further "dialogue" and an acknowledgement that nuclear war "must never be fought" provide minimal substance beyond the rhetoric.
"In general, it's good for the leaders of the major global players to come together in various formats, even if the results appear to be modest at best," David Firestein, head of the Bush Foundation for US-China Relations, told the BBC.
A line about boosting "the production and supply of refined petroleum products" seems directed at Putin, given that nation's role as a major source of fossil fuels on the international market. And it was hard to miss the condemnation of the International Criminal Court – a recent target of American ire.
If there's one thing the leaders of the three major world powers can agree on, it's that multilateral global organisations that attempt to enforce international law shouldn't have the teeth to back up those efforts.
While in China, Trump called Putin his "friend", and praised his "outstanding personal relationship" with Xi after sharing a handshake and hug with the Chinese leader.
But once Trump returns to Washington, he is likely to face a political environment where views of his Asia trip range from measured concern to outright criticism.
"I am concerned by how we are characterising our relationships with geopolitical adversaries. Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are not our friends," Republican Senator John Curtis of Utah said in a statement to the BBC on Thursday.
"Diplomacy is important, but it should never come at the expense of clarity about who our adversaries are."
Illinois Republican Congressman Darin LaHood, who was re-elected with Trump's endorsement earlier this month, says the US should have discussions with both allies and adversaries abroad. But he adds that Putin is a "dictator" and "an international criminal".
"I worry a little bit about the images of giving him a platform on a world stage as somehow equal to the United States," he tells BBC News.
"We have to remember what Putin has done in Ukraine," LaHood says. "He invaded a sovereign, independent, democratically-elected country, and continues to engage in aggression there."
Democrats, for their part, did not mince words.
"American security cannot be traded away for photo opportunities or personal aggrandisement," nine senators on the foreign relations committee wrote in a letter to the White House.
Trump is hardly the first American president to seek an international diplomatic breakthrough as a salve following domestic political setbacks. Democrats Bill Clinton and Barack Obama took overseas trips as presidents shortly after their party's own midterm electoral defeats.
In those cases, any boosts to their standing proved short-lived. And while Trump may have gotten the images he wanted from his Asian summit, the lack of substantive progress accompanying them likely means this trip also will be quickly forgotten.
Brandon Drenon contributed to this report.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): The issue of land in Laharpur and four neighbouring villages dominated the fifth day of hearings on objections to the draft Bhopal Master Plan-2047 on Friday. Farmers and residents demanded that their private land be excluded from the proposed submergence zone, arguing that it had neither been acquired nor compensated for.
MP Alok Sharma strongly backed the residents of Laharpur, Bag Mugalia, Bag Sewania, Pipariya Pende Khan and Barkheda Pathani, demanding that non-acquired private land be removed from the submergence zone.
Sharma said it was unjustified to keep private land under the submergence classification when neither acquisition had taken place nor compensation had been paid to landowners. He asserted that injustice to Bhopal residents would not be tolerated.
A total of 1,209 objectors were called for Friday's hearing, of whom 630 appeared to present their cases. Residents from Khanugaon, Samardha, Satgarhi, Narela Sankal, Pipaliya Jahir Peer and Mindora were among those who attended.
Irrigation requirement has reduced significantly
MP Sharma said Laharpur had undergone a major transformation, with residential colonies developing in its surrounding areas. Consequently, the need for irrigation in the area had become negligible.
He further pointed out that most of the approximately 61 acres of land affected by the dam were government-owned. Therefore, the remaining private land that had not been acquired should be excluded from the submergence zone.
Objection to commercial complex on 24-metre road
Meanwhile, objector Ajay Patidar raised strong objections to the proposed commercial mixed-use complex along a 24-metre-wide road in Misrod.
Citing the area's dense population, increasing traffic pressure and public safety concerns, he suggested shifting major commercial activities to roads proposed to be 45 or 60 metres wide instead of allowing them along the narrower 24-metre road.
Official statement
Joint director of Town and Country Planning (T&CP) Neeraj Anand Likhar said hearings would remain suspended on Saturday and Sunday due to holidays. The next hearing will be held on Monday, when around 1,000 objectors have been called to present their objections and suggestions.
